title: Authoring
description: Sketches are edited in two places, and both present the same side panel and the same gestures.
outline: A component by reference is read-only in the level
body:
Sketches are edited in two places, and both present the same side panel and the same gestures. The **asset editor** opens when you open a **Cluster Sketch** asset. The **in-level mode**, listed in the Modes dropdown as **PCGEx | Cluster Sketch**, makes the sketch components on selected actors editable where they sit. Every mutation goes through the model's own API as one undo transaction, so selection, undo and the gesture set behave identically in both hosts. ## Two hosts, one panel _Open an asset, or enter the mode and select actors; when several sketches are live, the panel header's picker chooses which one the gestures address._ The panel is the same in both hosts. Its pinned header holds the sketch picker, a **Work on** toggle between the Geometry and Sites layers, and **Select All**, **Clear** and **Snap**. Under it, an icon rail down the left edge switches between the pages, and only the page beside the rail scrolls: | Page | Holds | | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Selection** | What is selected, the data record it reads its values from, and the constraints it can host | | **Settings** | The sketch's own properties, the snap provider among them, and the schema of each layer | | **Cleanup** | The validation readout and the cleanup actions | | **Editor** | Per-user authoring preferences, mirrored in Editor Preferences under **PCGEx \| Cluster Sketch Authoring** | A **PCGEx Cluster Sketch** component holds its content one of two ways, and the details panel resolves them in a fixed order: an **inline** payload on the component itself wins outright, then the instance's own `Sketch Asset`, then the class's `Default Sketch Asset`. > Figure: STILL | id: sketch-component-in-level | SHOWS: A Cluster Sketch component reads as a first-class level object, drawing its own vertices and edges the way a spline component draws its curve | FRAME: Level viewport, an actor selected carrying a PCGEx Cluster Sketch component, its sketch drawn as a dozen vertex markers joined by edges. Details panel visible on the right with the Cluster Sketch category expanded, showing the Sketch Asset row empty and the Inline Payload row populated | CALLOUTS: the drawn vertices, the drawn edges, the Cluster Sketch category in the details panel | SOURCE: a scratch level with one actor carrying an inline sketch | NOTE: pick a sketch with at least one junction so it does not read as a path > A sketch component in a level, drawing what it holds. In the in-level mode the panel is the view of an inline sketch. Until the selection holds one, a **landing** covers the whole panel and offers what that selection needs: | Selection | Landing shows | | --- | --- | | No actor | "Select an actor to start sketching." | | Actors with no sketch set up | The actor's label, then **Create Inline Sketch**, **Create Fork From Asset...** and **Attach Existing Asset...** | | A component following an asset | The actor's label, "Following" and the asset's name, then **Fork This Sketch** and **Change Asset...** | **Create Inline Sketch** starts an empty sketch. **Create Fork From Asset...** picks a **Cluster Sketch** asset, or makes one on the spot with **New Cluster Sketch...**, and seeds the inline sketch from it; the asset itself is never edited. **Attach Existing Asset...** points the component at an asset and follows it, read-only, and **Change Asset...** repeats that pick later. **Fork This Sketch** is the same fork, seeded from the asset the component already follows. Every action runs on each selected actor at once, as one undo step, and the sketch it makes becomes the panel's active one. An inline sketch anywhere in the selection shows the panel instead, on that sketch. On each actor the action sets up the sketch component already there, whether it came from a Blueprint's component tree or from **Add Component** in the Details panel, and an actor with no sketch component gets one. The exception is a component added by an **Add Component** node in a construction script: nothing set on it survives the next construction-script run, so the landing never targets it. Such an actor is skipped, the landing says so in a warning line, and the fix is to add the component in the Components panel instead. > **Warning.** > **A component by reference is read-only in the level** > > A component pointing at an asset draws it and can be inspected, but the authoring gestures are refused, because the content is not the component's to change. Selected on its own it gets the landing, with the fork and the asset change one click away. Picked from the header's picker beside an inline sketch, it gets the panel, whose Selection page says: "Read-only: follows the Cluster Sketch asset \. Select this actor on its own to fork it or change the asset." The component's own Details panel carries the same moves as three buttons, available with or without the mode: | Button | Does | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Create Inline Sketch** | Mints the payload, seeded from the asset in force, so the visible sketch is what you start editing. Refuses if a payload already exists. | | **Save To Asset** | Saves the payload as a new **Cluster Sketch** asset through the standard save dialog and references it, either externalizing a sketch authored in the level or forking the referenced one. | | **Delete Inline Sketch** | Drops the payload and follows the asset again. Transacted; undo restores it. | In the in-level mode the same move is one click away from the viewport. While the mode is active, a **Create** pill sits at the bottom of the hovered level viewport, greyed until an actor is selected. Its menu offers two routes, each one undo step across every selected actor, and the sketch it makes becomes the panel's active one: | Menu item | Does | | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Inline Sketch** | On each selected actor, forks a sketch component that still follows an asset into an editable inline sketch, or adds a new sketch component when there is none to fork. | | **Inline Sketch From Asset** | Pick a **Cluster Sketch** asset, or make one on the spot with **New Cluster Sketch...**, and the inline sketch is seeded from it. The asset itself is never edited. | Colours are the one per-sketch expression: `Override Colors` on the component swaps the vertex and edge colours for that instance. Meshes, materials and sizes stay project-wide, in Editor Preferences under **PCGEx | Cluster Sketch**, so every sketch shares one geometry vocabulary. The same settings carry `Asset Editor Immediate Mode`, under **General**: on, the asset editor draws with screen-space points and lines instead of the configured meshes. Components in a level are unaffected: an idle one always draws as meshes, and one being edited always draws as points and lines. ## The gesture set _Click selects, Ctrl adds, Shift connects, Alt deletes, and empty space belongs to the camera._
GestureDoes
Click an elementSelect it. Shift+click toggles, for additive selection.
Ctrl+click empty spaceAdd a vertex. On the Sites layer, a site instead.
Drag a vertexMove it. Dropping onto another vertex merges the two, inside the same undo step.
Drag an edgeMove both endpoints together, anchored at the grab point.
Shift+drag from a vertexConnect: release on a vertex to link them, release on empty space to extrude a new connected vertex. The far vertex becomes the selection, so the gesture chains into a walk.
Alt+click an elementDelete it: a vertex goes with its edges, and orphaned tool-inserted vertices go with them.
TabCycle the placement guide, while a placement gesture is live.
Space, heldSurface snap: the gesture lands on the level geometry under the cursor. In-level mode only.
DeleteDelete the selection.
EscapeLeast destructive first: release a held guide, else cancel the drag, else clear the selection.
A plain click or drag on empty space is deliberately not captured, so camera navigation stays stock. Holding **Ctrl** previews where the vertex would land, guide included, and holding **Alt** highlights the hovered element and everything its removal would cascade to. Two placements resolve themselves: adding a vertex on an occupied spot reuses the existing vertex rather than twinning it, and a vertex landing on an edge splits that edge at the vertex. ## Snapping _A snap provider describes a lattice; bound vertices are lattice nodes, and one rule keeps coordinates and locations coherent._ A sketch can be authored free-form or against a **snap provider**. **Uniform Grid** ships built in, with a cell size, origin, rotation, and a toggle per axis: drop one axis for a planar grid, two for a linear one. The provider lives on the sketch's own details, on the panel's **Settings** page, and `Show Basis` on the component draws the lattice axes at the origin as a live cue that the snap model is on. That makes every vertex one of two kinds. A **free** vertex is authoritative in its own transform. A **lattice-bound** vertex _is_ a lattice node, and its location is derived from its coordinate. The rule that keeps those coherent runs in one direction: editing the coordinate re-derives the location, and any other edit re-snaps the coordinate from the location first, so a hand-dragged vertex can never end up dangling off-lattice. Move or rescale the grid and every bound vertex follows. The **Snap** toggle in the panel header decides whether gestures snap to the lattice; bound vertices stay snapped regardless. Bound vertices draw in their own colour, so the two kinds are legible at a glance. ## Placement guides _Guides are inferred direction rails; the cursor captures one by running near it, and Tab overrides the inference._ > Figure: STILL | id: sketch-lattice-and-guides | SHOWS: Placement is guided rather than freehand: the lattice and the inferred direction guides are both visible while a vertex is being placed | FRAME: Level viewport mid-gesture in the sketch editor mode, a uniform grid snap provider active so the lattice is visible, one vertex being placed with the inferred placement guides drawn from the anchor and the candidate guides shown alongside | CALLOUTS: the lattice, the active guide, the alternative guide candidates | SOURCE: a scratch level, uniform grid provider at default cell size | NOTE: the gesture must be mid-drag so the guides are on screen > Placement infers a direction and offers the alternatives, rather than leaving the vertex to land anywhere. Guides come from several sources, each with its own toggle: the lattice axes, walks along the lattice's other declared step directions (diagonals, hex steps), the complement axis a rank-deficient lattice does not span (the deliberate lift-it-off-the-plane move, withheld whenever the result would be snapped), and the lines of the anchor's own edges. With no snap provider on the sketch, its own X, Y and Z axes stand in for the lattice axes, so a free-form drag still has rails to leave the work plane. Dragging an edge adds two of its own: along the edge, to slide it, and across it, to offset it sideways. Capture is sticky in both directions: a guide holds the cursor a little wider than it caught it, a rival must beat it by a margin, and nothing captures until the cursor has travelled clear of the anchor. The candidate rails draw faint and brighten as the cursor swings toward one. **Tab** cycles through the candidates by hand, past the last one returns to inference, and **Escape** releases the guide entirely. Snapping runs after guides, untouched: a guide steers where the cursor resolves to, never whether the result lands on the lattice. All of it is configurable per user, on the panel's **Editor** page and mirrored in Editor Preferences under **PCGEx | Cluster Sketch Authoring**: inference on or off, the capture radius, candidate previews, and each guide source individually, the free-form axes under `Guide Freeform Axes`. Each source draws in its own colour, set in the style settings under **Guides**. ## Surface snapping _Hold Space and the gesture lands on the level geometry under the cursor; the surface is the rail, and the guides stand down._ In the in-level mode, holding **Space** during any gesture (adding, moving a vertex, an edge or a site, connecting, extruding) traces a line from the cursor into the level and places the result where it hits. A disc drawn in the surface plane, with its normal, marks the hit, and the placement guides stand down while it holds. The asset editor has no geometry to hit, so the key does nothing there. A surface hit is the hand's intent, so it outranks the lattice: a free vertex lands on the surface itself, never on the lattice node nearest it, and a vertex added on a surface is free. A lattice-bound vertex still binds, to the lattice node nearest the surface point. The settings sit on the panel's **Editor** page under **Surface Snapping**: | Setting | Does | | ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Place On Surface` | Off by default. On, every gesture places on the surface whenever the trace hits something, and holding **Space** asks for the work plane instead. | | `Surface Trace Channel` | The collision channel the trace runs against. | | `Surface Trace Complex` | Trace per-triangle collision, so the vertex lands on the visible face and never on a hull. | | `Surface Ignore Host Actor` | Never hit the actor carrying the sketch, whose own meshes would otherwise catch every trace. | | `Surface Snap Offset` | How far along the hit normal the point is lifted off the surface. | | `Surface Snap Align To Normal` | Also turn the moved vertex or site so its Z follows the hit normal. Off keeps the authored rotation. | | `Surface Trace Distance` | How far the trace reaches from the camera. | Space is only the sketch's while a gesture is previewing. With nothing live it keeps its editor meaning and cycles the transform gizmo's mode. ## The transform gizmo _Off by default; on, the editor's translate gizmo moves the selection under the same rules as a drag._ `Use Transform Gizmo`, on the panel's **Editor** page under **Gizmo**, puts the editor's transform gizmo at the centroid of the selected vertices or sites, in the in-level mode only. Translating it moves the selection as a mouse drag would: bound vertices re-snap, constraints solve, the whole move is one undo step, and a gizmo grabbed and released in place records nothing. Translate is all it does; rotate and scale are not supported in this version. > **Warning.** > It is off by default for a reason: the gizmo claims the Ctrl and Shift chords for its own gestures and starves the sketch's. Turn it on when you want gizmo moves, and expect the modifier gestures to give way while it is up. ## Crossings stay crossings _An intersection without a vertex is an offer, never an imposition._ Two edges that meet where there is no vertex are left alone. The editor shows the intersection as a ghost you can click to materialize, which inserts the vertex and splits both edges. Until you do, nothing is cut. That is deliberate: an X-brace with no joint at the middle is legitimate geometry, and a tool that welded it automatically would make that undrawable. Splitting is offered, never imposed. An edge passing _through_ a vertex is a different case, and that one does get fixed. A cluster cannot represent it, so after a gesture the editor splits such edges at the vertices they contain. Collinear vertices A, B and C can carry A-B and B-C, but never A-C. ## Cleanups and validation _The named cleanups on the panel's Cleanup page, next to a live count of what they would fix._ The **Cleanup** page carries a validation readout, counting per issue class: invalid edges, self-loops, duplicates, isolated vertices, collocated vertices, data-layer issues, and constraint issues. Above it sit the cleanup buttons, each one transaction, on an inline payload as on an asset: | Button | Fixes | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Merge Collocated** | Vertices sharing a location, which a cluster cannot carry. | | **Remove Invalid Edges** | Self-loops, duplicates, and edges whose endpoint no longer exists. | | **Split Overlapping Edges** | Edges passing through vertices, and crossings, in one pass. | | **Purge Unused Data Records** | Records no element references any more. | **Clean Up** runs every one of them in one undo step. The same issues that these fix are what the print warns about, so a warning at execute time names the button that resolves it. What each issue does to the printed cluster is covered in [Printing](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/printing).

title: Constraints
description: A constraint is an authored relationship between sketch elements that the editor keeps true while you edit: hold this vertex on that line, keep this edge at that length.
body:
A **constraint** is an authored relationship between sketch elements that the editor keeps true while you edit: hold this vertex on that line, keep this edge at that length. The solver runs during gestures and bakes its result straight into the element positions, so nothing downstream knows constraints exist: a print reads positions, and only positions.

## Attaching one

*The Selection page offers the types that fit what is selected.*

**Add Constraint** sits on the panel's **Selection** page, and it only offers types the current selection can host: **Along** attaches to exactly one selected vertex with no edges selected, **Length** to exactly one selected edge. Each attached constraint gets its own details body on the page, naming a selected element, with a live residual readout: "off by N" while the geometry disagrees with the rule, or a warning when the constraint names an element that no longer exists.

Constraints can be disabled without being removed: a disabled constraint is skipped by the solver and the validation alike, but keeps its subjects, so toggling one back on restores the rule intact.

Constraints are an ordered list, and the order is the priority: when two disagree, the later one projects later and wins.

## Along

*One vertex held on the segment between two anchors.*

**Along** keeps its subject vertex on the segment between two anchor vertices, either at a fraction of the segment's length (the default, at 0.5) or at a fixed distance from one end, with `From B` choosing which end. The anchors are read, never moved.

The segment is a phantom: it needs no materialized edge between the anchors, and is drawn as one while the subject is selected. Attaching the constraint infers the anchors from the chain the vertex sits on, which is why it asks for a single vertex and nothing else.

Dragging the subject along its segment re-parameterises the constraint rather than fighting it, so sliding a constrained vertex to a better spot is a normal move, not a struggle against the solver.


> Figure: A chain of four ringed vertices. The two outer ones are labelled anchor A and anchor B, and a dashed blue phantom segment runs straight between them. The subject vertex, ringed in orange, sits on that phantom at a bracketed fraction of 0.35 from anchor A. The real edges are solid and grey: the one from anchor A to the subject lies under the phantom and is dimmed, the next two bend away through a fourth vertex before reaching anchor B. A faint ghost of the subject sits further along the phantom with a thin arrow from the subject to it, showing a drag sliding it along the span and never off it. A note says there is no edge between the anchors.
> The rule lives on the phantom segment; the drawn edges are free to disagree with it.


## Length

*One edge held at a fixed length.*

**Length** keeps its subject edge at a fixed length. When both endpoints are free to move, they move symmetrically; when one is held (by a gesture, or by another rule), the other moves alone. A vertex a gesture is actively holding is never moved by the solver, whatever the constraints say.

## Extending

*A new constraint type is a new struct; the model does not change.*

The constraint set is an extension point: a project adds its own type by deriving the constraint struct in C++, declaring how many subjects it takes and how to project them, and the picker, the solver and the validation pick it up from reflection. Nothing in the sketch format changes, and types may live in any module.

title: Data Layer
description: A sketch carries authored metadata in four tiers, built on the property system described in Collection Properties.
body:
A sketch carries authored metadata in four tiers, built on the property system described in [Collection Properties](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties). One tier annotates the sketch as a whole; the other three annotate its vertices, edges and sites.

## Four tiers

_One sketch-wide tier and three element layers, each printing somewhere different._

| Tier                  | Prints to                                                                          |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Sketch Properties** | The `@Data` domain of the printed Vtx, mirrored onto the Edges and the site points |
| **Vertex Layer**      | Attributes on the printed Vtx points                                               |
| **Edge Layer**        | Attributes on the printed Edge points                                              |
| **Site Layer**        | Attributes on the printed site points                                              |

**Sketch Properties** carries no records: there is exactly one sketch, so its schema entries are the values. The three element layers each pair a **Schema**, declaring what fields exist and their defaults, with a set of **Records**.

## Schemas and records

_Fields are declared once; records supply the values elements share._

A record is a named bundle of overrides on top of the layer's schema defaults. Vertices, edges and sites do not hold values directly: they name a record, and anything the record does not override resolves to the schema default. An element naming no record is entirely schema defaults. A name the schema declares always resolves to a value, so a dropped or missing record degrades to defaults rather than to nothing.


> Figure: STILL | id: sketch-data-layer-panel | SHOWS: The authored data tier as the panel presents it: a schema declaring fields on one side, named records holding override values on the other, and the selected vertices pointing at one of them | FRAME: The sketch authoring panel open on its Settings page, picked from the icon rail, the Vertex Layer expanded showing a schema with three or four declared properties and two or three named records beneath it, one record selected with its override values visible, and a selection of vertices in the viewport that reference it | CALLOUTS: the schema entries, the record list, the override values on the selected record | SOURCE: a sketch authored with a small vertex schema | NOTE: the record labels should read as real authoring names, not Record 1 and Record 2. The shot on file predates the icon rail and shows the old Selection, Sketch, Options tab strip; reshoot
> Fields are declared once in the schema; records supply the values elements share.


Records are addressed by an internal id, and the label is only what the picker shows, so renaming a record is free and breaks nothing.

## Assigning records

_The Selection page assigns one record to whatever is selected, and says who else shares it._

Select elements and the panel's **Selection** page shows the record picker for their layer. Picking **\<None>** stores nothing, so every field resolves to the schema's own value. A "Shared by N" indicator says how many other elements point at the same record, and two buttons manage divergence:

| Button          | Does                                                                                                                    |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Make Unique** | Mints a record seeded from the current one and points the selection at it, leaving every other element on the original. |
| **Break Link**  | Drops the reference; the selection falls back to the schema's own values. The record itself stays until it is purged.   |

A selection spanning vertices and edges at once offers no picker, because one record assignment cannot mean two things. The page also warns when a selected element points at a record that no longer exists.



## Sharing semantics

_Many elements share one record, and every editing gesture preserves that on purpose._

The consequence to plan around is that **many elements can share one record**. Give forty edges the record named `Structural` and editing it once changes all forty. It is also what makes editing lossless: split an edge and every new segment inherits the parent's record, so one record still describes the whole original span.

Merging follows the same logic in reverse. When two vertices merge, the survivor inherits the absorbed vertex's record only if it had none of its own, so a deliberate assignment is never overwritten by a cleanup gesture.

Extrusion has its own pair of preferences, under **PCGEx | Cluster Sketch Authoring**: by default an extruded vertex inherits the source vertex's record, so a drafted chain carries its authored values, while inheriting the source's _edge_ record is off by default, because a junction or a loose end has no unambiguous parent edge.

Records nothing references any more accumulate silently; **Purge Unused Data Records** on the panel's **Cleanup** page clears them.

**Print-time decorators**


Beyond the authored tiers, a sketch holds an ordered list of **decorators**: instanced objects that run during the print and can write attributes onto the vertices, edges and sites as they are produced. They see the print context rather than the model, so they are the place for anything computed rather than authored. They add attributes only, never topology.

The class is an extension point and ships abstract, with no concrete decorators in the box. It exists so a project can add its own without touching the sketch format. Disabled decorators are skipped by the print.

title: Printing
description: How a sketch becomes a live cluster: the nodes, the collection type, property output, and what survives the print.
outline: Sketches inherit the staging pipeline whole
body:
A sketch holds no baked point data at all. There is no stored Vtx or Edges dataset waiting to be loaded: the model is **printed** into a live cluster at execute time, once per consumer, per target. Editing a printed sketch, or anything it references, re-executes the consuming component, so a sketch behaves like any other tracked source.

> Figure: On the left a single panel labelled Cluster Sketch holds a small model of six ringed vertices and seven edges, annotated as a model and no point data. Flow arrows lead right to three target points at different heights, and from each target another arrow leads to a printed cluster: the same six-vertex model, each drawn at its own rotation and its own size, so the three visibly differ. Each printed pair carries its own cluster tag in mono, PCGEx slash Cluster colon 31, 32 and 33, showing them as three independent clusters rather than three references to one.
> The asset holds a model. The clusters come into existence at execute time, one per target.

## From the level

*Get Sketch Data reads components off actors and prints them in world space.*

**Get Sketch Data** discovers actors, either through the standard PCG actor selector or from actor references on an input pin, and prints every sketch component they carry. Output lands in world space at the component's transform, so it matches the level one to one.

The source actor can be written onto the printed Vtx and site points as a `@Data` attribute (on by default, named `ActorReference`), so downstream work knows where each cluster came from. Actors with no sketch component warn rather than fail, and the warning set is shared with the print itself, below.

## From assets

*Staging : Load Sketch prints sketch assets onto staged points, one cluster per target.*

**Staging : Load Sketch** takes target points and prints one cluster per target, inheriting the target's transform through the standard transform details. Each distinct sketch is printed once, then duplicated onto every target referencing it, so a hundred targets sharing one asset cost one print.

`Source` decides where each target's sketch comes from:

| Source | Resolves |
| --- | --- |
| **Collection Map** | From a staged pick, through a Collection Map pin. Requires points staged by a distribution node. |
| **Asset** | From a direct asset reference: a constant, or a per-point path attribute. |

Two forwarding controls carry per-target variation onto otherwise identical duplicates: `Targets Attributes To Cluster Tags` promotes target attributes to tags on the printed clusters, and `Targets Forwarding` writes target attributes onto the printed Vtx. Both also apply to the duplicated site points.

> **Warning.**
> A forwarded attribute whose name equals an authored sketch attribute replaces it on that duplicate, because forwarding recreates the attribute. Same name, same intent is a feature; a name collision by accident is silent.

In Collection Map mode, a pick that resolves to something other than a sketch flows past without an error: mixed hosting is what Omni collections are for, and a mesh pick passing this node is expected. Targets whose pick resolves to nothing at all warn with a count.

## The collection type

*Sketches are first-class staged assets, with their own collection.*

**\[PCGEx] Collection | Cluster Sketch** holds weighted sketch assets, and behaves like every other collection: weights, categories, sub-collections, and the same staging pipeline. A distribution node picks a sketch per point, and **Staging : Load Sketch** prints what was picked.

Rows also arrive by capture. When a PCG Data Asset Collection exports a level or an actor's subtree, every sketch component it meets becomes a point on the export's Sketches pin, backed by a row in a sketch collection the host maintains across all its exports: a component referencing an asset yields a row referencing that asset, and a component holding its sketch inline yields a row holding an export-owned copy. The copy is read-only in the collection; the component stays the place the sketch is edited, and re-exporting refreshes the row. The capture side is described under [Capturing Scenes](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes).

> **Note.**
> **Sketches inherit the staging pipeline whole**
>
> Because the collection type is a first-class one, everything the [Asset Staging](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/asset-staging) section describes applies: weighted picks, category filtering, collection maps, and swapping one collection for another. A library of hand-authored structural pieces distributes exactly like a library of meshes.

## Property output

*Everything authored prints by default; Explicit mode picks and renames.*

Both nodes print the authored data tier as attributes, governed by `Property Output Mode`. **All Found**, the default, outputs every property the sketch carries, attribute names matching property names. **Explicit** switches to a hand-picked list with optional renaming, for when a sketch carries authoring-side data the graph should not see, or when downstream expects different names.

Both nodes also carry a Param output pin labeled `Map`: the **Map sidecar**, holding external resources referenced by the printed properties. A sketch property holding a Collection Entry pick, for instance, needs its Collection Map to travel with the points for downstream staging to resolve it; the sidecar is how it travels. It shares its label with Load Sketch's Collection Map *input*, and the two are unrelated: one feeds picks in, the other carries referenced resources out.

## What survives the print

*The sketch format is more permissive than the cluster it prints, so some things get dropped.*

You can draw things a cluster has no way to represent. Rather than refuse the edit, the sketch keeps it and reports at print time:

| Drawn | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| A vertex with no edges | Dropped. A cluster is at minimum two vertices and the edge joining them |
| Two vertices in the same place | Cannot be carried. The editor merges them on drop; a raw edit gets warned at print |
| An edge from a vertex to itself | Dropped |
| The same pair connected twice | Only the first survives |
| An edge whose endpoint index is out of range | Dropped |
| An edge passing through a vertex | Degenerate for a cluster; warned, with **Split Overlapping Edges** named as the fix |

None of these stop the print. They warn, and the printed cluster is the valid subset of what you drew, which is what to check before concluding that a sketch came through wrong. Each warning names the cleanup on the panel's **Cleanup** page that resolves it (see [Authoring](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/authoring)), and the `Quiet` toggle silences the lot for sketches that are deliberately mid-draft.

Sites are exempt from all of it: they print independently, cluster or no cluster, as [Sites](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/sites) covers.

title: Sites
description: A cluster drawn as walls and corridors implies rooms, and Find Cells is the PCGEx node that extracts them: it takes seed points and outputs the enclosed cells they land in.
body:
A cluster drawn as walls and corridors implies rooms, and [Find Cells](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/node-library/pathfinding/cells/find-cells) is the PCGEx node that extracts them: it takes seed points and outputs the enclosed cells they land in. A **site** is that seed, authored in the sketch itself: a free-placed marker inside a cell, carrying whatever metadata the cell's contents will need downstream. Sites live on their own layer, print as plain points on their own pin, and are never part of the cluster.

## The Sites edit layer

*One toggle in the panel header decides whether the gestures address geometry or sites.*

The panel header carries a **Geometry / Sites** toggle under the label **Work on**, and it is the sole switch: there is no keyboard shortcut, deliberately. On the Geometry layer, sites stay visible but dimmed and never interactive. On the Sites layer, the gesture set narrows to sites:

| Gesture | Does |
| --- | --- |
| **Ctrl+click** empty space | Place a site. Successive placements chain off the selected one. |
| **Drag** a site | Move it. Guides steer, and nothing snaps or merges. |
| **Shift+drag** from a site | Duplicate it, record reference included, and drag the copy. |
| **Alt+click** a site | Delete it. Nothing cascades: sites have no edges and no constraints. |
| **Tab** | Cycle the placement guide, while a gesture is live. |
| **Space**, held | Land the site on the level geometry under the cursor. In-level mode only; see [Authoring](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/authoring). |

The toggle is global across every sketch bound in the level mode, because the layer is a property of your hand, not of any one sketch. Switching it cancels the live gesture and clears the other layer's selection.

Sites are free placement by design. A site is never lattice-bound, because a marker sitting exactly on a lattice node would land degenerately on the very edges and vertices that point-in-cell containment tests against. The placement guides still run, so a site can be lined up precisely; it is the snapping and merging that stay out.


> Figure: STILL | id: sites-layer-and-cells | SHOWS: Sites are placed inside enclosed faces and the editor answers with an inset preview of the cells they claim | FRAME: Level viewport in the sketch editor mode with the Sites edit layer active, a sketch enclosing four or five faces, sites placed in three of them, each claimed cell drawn as an inset outline, one cell holding two sites and drawn in the multi-site colour | CALLOUTS: a site marker, a claimed cell outline, the multi-site cell | SOURCE: a scratch level, a sketch with a handful of enclosed faces | NOTE: leave at least one face without a site so claimed and unclaimed read side by side
> Placing a site claims the face it sits in, and the preview says so immediately.


## Site data

*The Site Layer is a third element layer, with the same schema and records as the other two.*

Sites carry authored metadata exactly the way vertices and edges do: the **Site Layer** pairs a schema with records, sites name a record, and everything unset resolves to the schema default. The Selection page tools work unchanged. See [Data Layer](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/data-layer).

This is where a site earns its place over a plain scattered seed: the attributes authored here arrive on the printed site points, so whatever distinguishes one room from another (a type, a tag, a budget) travels with the seed into the graph.

## The cell preview

*The editor runs the same face enumeration Find Cells does, and outlines what each site would claim.*

While the Sites layer is active, each cell containing a site draws as an inset outline: one colour for cells claimed by exactly one site, another for cells holding several. The enumeration behind the preview is the exact one Find Cells uses.


> **Warning.**
> Cells are resolved by projection, in the preview and in Find Cells alike. Even with the projection method set to **3D Surface**, extraction behaves best on a topology that survives being flattened, and a multilayered sketch, floors stacked above one another, should expect artifacts. The preview also projects on an advisory plane of its own, so the graph node's settings may differ: it informs, it never promises.


Several sites in one cell is legitimate authoring, and the second colour is a flag, never an error. Find Cells keeps one winner per cell, so co-resident sites are how a sketch carries alternative configurations for the same room, disambiguated downstream by their site attributes.


> Figure: Two panels joined by a flow arrow labelled Find Cells. On the left, one enclosed cell of a sketch, six ringed vertices with grey edges and faint stubs leading off to the rest of the sketch, holds two amber site markers, each with a small mono chip reading config A and config B, and the cell carries an inset amber outline. On the right, the same cell at the same position is tinted and outlined green as the single cell output, site A and its chip drawn as before, site B and its chip faded with the word unclaimed beside them.
> The sketch happily holds both options; the graph picks.


## What comes out

*Plain points on the Sites pin, independent of whether the cluster itself printed.*

Both nodes carry a **Sites** output pin. It emits plain point data: no cluster tags, no graph membership, one point per site in authored order. Each point carries the site's full transform, a spatial seed derived from its location, the Site Layer attributes, and the sketch-wide **Sketch Properties** mirrored into its `@Data` domain. Wire it straight into Find Cells' `Seeds` input.

Two contract details are load-bearing. A sketch with no sites emits nothing on the pin, rather than an empty data set. And sites print independently of the cluster: a sketch too broken to print Vtx and Edges still outputs its sites, so a seed workflow keeps working while the geometry is mid-repair.

On **Staging : Load Sketch** the sites are duplicated per target alongside the cluster, inheriting the target's transform, tags and forwarded attributes the same way. On **Get Sketch Data** they arrive in world space with the source actor reference written on, like the Vtx. The node specifics live in [Printing](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/printing).

title: Overview
description: Authoring clusters by hand the way a spline component authors a curve: place vertices, connect them, annotate them, and print the result into a graph.
body:
Every other way to get a cluster is generative: scatter points, run a rule, take what comes out. A **Cluster Sketch** is the opposite. You place the vertices, you draw the connections, and what you drew is what prints. It is to clusters roughly what a spline component is to a curve.

> **Note.**
> **Stable Beta**
>
> Cluster Sketch ships as its own plugin, in beta. **The authoring surface is usable and the data model is settled**, but expect UX to move. See Installation.

## A model, printed on demand

_A sketch holds a model and nothing else; clusters come into existence at execute time._

A sketch lives in the level, on a **PCGEx Cluster Sketch** component holding its content inline or referencing a **Cluster Sketch** asset, or standalone as that asset. Either way it holds no baked point data: the model is printed into a live Vtx and Edges pair at execute time, once per consumer, per target, and everything it prints is an ordinary PCGEx cluster.

The sketch format is deliberately more permissive than the cluster it prints. You can leave a vertex unconnected, a crossing uncut, a draft half-drawn; the sketch keeps all of it, and the print warns and emits the valid subset. Drawing never fights you to stay cluster-legal, and [Printing](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/printing) owns exactly what gets dropped and why.

## What a sketch holds

_Geometry, an authored data tier, sites, and the rules that keep them coherent._

**Vertices and edges** are the geometry, authored free-form or against a snap lattice. On top of them sit three things: a **data layer** of schemas and records annotating every element, **sites** marking cells for extraction, and **constraints** the editor maintains while you work.

| Page                                       | Covers                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Authoring](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/authoring)     | The two hosts, the gestures, snapping, guides and surfaces, the gizmo, crossings, cleanups |
| [Data Layer](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/data-layer)   | Schemas, records, and the sharing semantics that make editing lossless |
| [Sites](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/sites)             | Cell markers, the cell preview, and the Find Cells handoff             |
| [Constraints](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/constraints) | Along, Length, and attaching them                                      |
| [Printing](concept:working-with-cluster-sketch/printing)       | The nodes, the collection type, property output, what survives         |

Read them in that order the first time: each page leans on the ones above it.

## Related

* [Clusters](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- the model a sketch prints into
* [Building and Refining](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) -- the generative routes to a cluster
* [Collection Properties](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties) -- the property system the data layers are built on
* [Asset Staging](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/working-with-pcgex/asset-staging) -- the distribution machinery the collection type plugs into

title: Additional Systems
description: The systems outside the main path and cluster track: what each one is for, and which are worth learning before you need them.
outline: Systems you meet inside other nodes
Modules you go to on purpose
body:
Five systems sit outside the core workflow. Two of them turn up inside nodes you are already using, and three are modules you go to deliberately when the work calls for them.

## Systems you meet inside other nodes

*Sub-node families that many unrelated nodes depend on.*

| System | What it does |
|---|---|
| [Blending & Sampling](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/blending-and-sampling) | Sampling queries the world and writes what it finds onto existing points. Blending decides how values combine wherever a node has more than one source for an attribute |
| [Matching](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/matching) | Rules deciding which candidate dataset each source is meant to work with, so a whole set resolves in one pass instead of a loop |
| [Pickers](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/pickers) | Sub-nodes naming indices into a collection, independent of how many entries it has |

**Sampling is the one to learn early.** It is how data moves between datasets that were never connected, how attributes are recovered after a stage that dropped them, and how points learn anything about the world around them. Most graphs of any size use it repeatedly.

Blending is harder to avoid than to find: any node combining several sources into one value is blending, whether or not you configured it. Its defaults are where surprises come from.

## Modules you go to on purpose

*Self-contained, and worth knowing exist.*

| System | What it does |
|---|---|
| [Shapes](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/shapes) | Parametric point primitives generated per seed: circles, polygons, grids, spheres |
| [Tensors](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/tensors) | Directional fields built from points, splines or noise, read by extrusion, orientation, connection and pathfinding |
| [Topology](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/topology) | Triangulating clusters, paths and point clouds into dynamic mesh surfaces |

These three are also the ones that chain well. Shapes give structured seed positions, tensors steer how those points connect or extrude, and topology turns the result into geometry.

## Related

* [What's different](concept:working-with-pcgex/what-pcgex-adds) -- the sub-node pattern all of these follow
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- the largest transverse system, with its own section
* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- traversal and heuristics, also its own section

title: Blending & Sampling
description: Points meet constantly, and whenever they do, something decides what their values become.
outline: The quaternion case changes shape at three sources
A blend op's own Weight is ignored by most consumers
body:
Points meet constantly, and whenever they do, something decides what their values become. That decision is blending.

## What blending decides

*Any operation that collapses several values into one has to answer for every attribute.*

Two overlapping points fuse into one. A path is smoothed, and each point takes on some of its neighbours. Two paths cross, and the crossing point has to come from somewhere. A segment is subdivided, and the points invented in between need values. A flood fill spreads outward through a cluster. A sampler finds three targets in range and has to return one answer.

Every one of those is the same question: several values, one slot, what goes in it. Blending answers it whether or not you configure anything.

Most of that happens inside a single dataset. A smooth blends a point against its own neighbours, **Uber Blend** blends a point's attributes against each other, **Path : Attribute Rolling** accumulates along a path, **Cluster : Flood Fill** and **Cluster : Diffuse** carry values across topology. Reaching into a second dataset, which is what sampling does, is one case among many rather than the typical one.

## Three ways to control it

*Which one you get is the node's choice, not yours.*

### Blend ops, for targeted control

A **BlendOp** sub-node names one attribute, one blend mode, and where the result lands. Operand A and an optional Operand B feed the mode; with B disabled, A serves as both sides. The result writes back over A by default, or to B, or to a new attribute, or to a transient one that exists only for the duration of the pass.

Several ops on a **Blend Ops** pin run in sequence, ordered by `Priority` ascending. That order is what makes chaining work: an op can read the transient output of an earlier one through `#Previous`, or `#N` for a specific index, and referencing forward is a hard error rather than a silent misread.

**Uber Blend** and **Path : Blend** require a Blend Ops pin. **Sampler : Vtx Blend**, the sub-node that does the blending inside **Cluster : Sample Neighbors**, is built on the same pin.

### The monolithic block, for everything at once

An inline settings block on the node: a `Blending Filter` of All, Include or Exclude, a `Default Blending` mode for everything the filter admits, per-property overrides, and a name-keyed map of per-attribute overrides.

That covers more than attributes. The nine point properties are in scope too: Density, Bounds Min and Max, Color, Position, Rotation, Scale, Steepness, and `Seed`.

The whole fuse and union family is monolithic-only: **Fuse Points**, **Cluster : Fuse**, **Path : To Clusters**, **Cluster : Simplify**, **Path : Fuse Collinear**, **Path : Resample**, **Points to Bounds** and their kin. Four nodes let you pick between the two through a `Blending Interface` setting: **Sample : Nearest Point**, **Sample : Nearest Bounds**, **Path : Smooth** and **Cluster : Edge Properties**. Where an op and a monolithic setting both claim one attribute, the op wins.

### Sub-points blending, for invented points

Nodes that invent points between existing ones need a different question answered: not how to merge sources, but how to fill in a point that has no values of its own. **Path : Subdivide**, **Path : Insert**, **Path : Hatch**, **Path × Path Crossings**, **Path × Bounds Intersection** and the navmesh pathfinding nodes all carry this as a dropdown rather than a pin.

Four choices, each carrying its own blending block underneath: **Interpolate** lerps between the surrounding points, **Inherit First** and **Inherit Last** copy from one end of the span, and **No Blending** leaves the new points with whatever they were initialised to.

## What the defaults actually do

*Monolithic blending averages everything it is given, and "average" means different things to different types.*

Left alone, the inline block admits every attribute at `Average`, and since the property overrides all start off, positions, rotations, colours and seeds average with them.

Nodes differ in how much they protect you from that, and the panel looks the same either way. **Fuse Points**, **Path : Fuse Collinear**, **Points to Bounds** and **Path × Path Crossings** ship with Position pinned to `None`, so merged points keep a real location. **Cluster : Fuse**, **Path : To Clusters**, **Cluster : Simplify**, **Path : Smooth** and **Cluster : Edge Properties** do not, and average it.


> **Danger.**
> **Monolithic Average reaches the Seed**
>
> `Seed` is a blendable point property, and the default covers it. Fused points end up with the integer mean of their sources' seeds, which is deterministic, meaningless, and prone to collisions that quietly break every downstream node that randomises from it. **Path : Resample** ships an `Ensure Unique Seeds` counter-measure for exactly this; most nodes do not. Set Seed's override explicitly wherever points merge.


Then there is what `Average` means once a type is involved. For floats and vectors it is the arithmetic mean you expect. Elsewhere:

| Type | What Average does |
|---|---|
| `bool` | A logical OR. One `true` among a hundred sources produces `true` |
| `int32` | Truncating integer division, so an averaged index or id lands on a plausible wrong value |
| `FName`, `FString` | The first non-empty value wins; nothing is combined |
| `FRotator` | A component-wise mean in Euler space, with no wrap handling near the poles |
| `FQuat`, `FTransform` | A true slerp for exactly two sources. Three or more silently falls back to a component-wise Euler mean |


> **Warning.**
> **The quaternion case changes shape at three sources**
>
> The three-source fallback drifts near +/-180 degrees, and nothing in the panel distinguishes the two cases, so a fuse that looked right on sparse data can misbehave where points cluster.


Project settings carry a per-type default for each of fifteen types, which overrides a node's own `Default Blending` when set. Out of the box only the text and soft-path types are set, all to `Copy`, which is why strings and asset paths survive a blend intact while everything else averages. Those settings carry no tooltips in the editor, and they reach some blenders and not others: a project-wide rule changes **Path : Smooth** and **BlendOp : Blend All** while leaving the whole fuse and union family untouched.

Attributes whose names carry the PCGEx prefix are forced to `Copy` regardless of any of this, which is what keeps internal identity values from being averaged into nonsense.

## Weights

*Average counts how many sources contributed. Weight counts how much.*

A consumer scores each contributing source before blending. The `Weight Mode` decides how: by distance, by an attribute on the target, or by both multiplied, shown as `Att x Dist`. A `Weight Over Distance` curve then remaps that score, so falloff is authored rather than linear. The path and spline samplers add `Inside Weighting`, which decides how a shape the point sits inside is weighed against one it is only near.

The two modes that use those scores differ in the finish. `Average` accumulates and divides by the number of sources, ignoring the weights entirely. `Weight` divides by the total weight instead, so near sources dominate, and it leaves the sum un-normalised when the weights add up to less than one. `Weight (Always Normalize)` is the unconditional version.


> **Warning.**
> **A blend op's own Weight is ignored by most consumers**
>
> On samplers and fusers the consumer supplies the weight and the op's `Weight` value is never read; only its curve applies, remapping what the consumer passed. The op's own weight is used on **Uber Blend**, **Path : Attribute Rolling**, **Cluster : Flood Fill** and **Cluster : Diffuse**, which have no distance to derive one from. Setting it anywhere else changes nothing.


## Sampling, the most obvious consumer

*The word is narrower in PCGEx than in vanilla PCG.*

Vanilla samplers generate points: a surface sampler turns a mesh into a scatter. PCGEx samplers do the opposite kind of work. They take the points you already have, ask a question about the world around each one, and write the answer back as attributes. The output is your input, annotated.

Source points ask, targets answer, attributes carry the result. **Sample : Nearest Point** asks other point sets, **Sample : Nearest Spline** asks splines, **Sample : Nearest Surface** and **Sample : Line Trace** ask world collision, **Sample : Texture** asks a texture at a UV, **Cluster : Sample Neighbors** asks a Vtx's own neighbours. **Sample : Stamp Points** turns the question round: each target carries its own range and stamps the source points inside it, so the reach belongs to the target instead of the point. Where a query returns several targets at once, everything above decides what the point actually receives.


> **Note.**
> **One node breaks the rule**
>
> **Sample : Sockets** reads static mesh paths and outputs the sockets as new points, without forwarding its input at all. It is the only sampler that does, which is why the book files it under staging.


This is what makes sampling the recovery tool. When a workflow has converted points to a cluster and back, or fused them, or rebuilt them from scratch, the values lost along the way are still sitting on the original dataset. A nearest-point sample against that original brings them across.


> Figure: A row of five target points across the top, and below them a row of six source points, each carrying an empty attribute slot. A thin arrow runs from every source point up to whichever target is nearest it. Below that, the same six source points are drawn again at exactly the same horizontal positions and the same spacing, unchanged in count and in place, except that each slot now holds a value written in green.
> The point set going out is the point set coming in, carrying one more attribute.


**Discard By Overlap** and **Self Pruning** sit here too, and only ever remove: the first drops whole datasets that overlap others, the second drops points that overlap inside one.

## Related

* [What's different](concept:working-with-pcgex/what-pcgex-adds) -- blend ops are sub-nodes, and follow that pattern
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- deciding which points a sampler acts on
* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- where sampling recovers attributes lost in conversion
* **Blending** and **Sampling** -- every node, with its settings

title: Matching
description: When a node has many things on one pin and many candidates on another, something has to decide which goes with which.
body:
When a node has many things on one pin and many candidates on another, something has to decide which goes with which. Doing that by hand means a loop: iterate the sources, isolate one, isolate its target, run the operation, gather the results. Match rules exist so you do not have to.

## Matching replaces the loop

*State the pairing rule once, and one node handles the whole set in a single execution.*

Give a node twenty source datasets and twenty targets, and matching is what lets it work out the twenty correct pairings internally and process them all in one pass. The alternative is a loop that runs the node twenty times over single-element slices, which costs more, reads worse, and has to be rebuilt whenever the counts change.

That is the design intent behind the whole family. Anywhere you would reach for iteration to apply the same operation across pairs or groups, a match rule usually removes the need.


> Figure: Two panels. In the first, labelled Without matching, a column of four source dataset panels on the left and four target dataset panels on the right are joined by sixteen thin lines, every source reaching every target, forming a dense unreadable mesh. In the second, labelled With a match rule, the same eight panels are joined by only four green lines, each source reaching exactly one target, and each pair carries the same shared tag written in mono inside both of its panels to show what the rule matched on. The twelve rejected combinations are not drawn.
> The pairing a loop would have enumerated, resolved inside one node instead.


## A rule compares two datasets

*Given this dataset and a pile of candidates, which one is it meant to work with.*

A match rule is handed one dataset and one candidate, and returns whether they go together. Both sides are whole datasets, so the rule reads their tags and their `@Data` attributes rather than anything per-point. Feed a sampler twenty targets and matching is what decides which single one it reads against, instead of all twenty.

A few nodes run the same rules once per element instead, so every point picks its own target rather than inheriting the dataset's. **Copy to Points**, **Copy Clusters to Points** and **Copy to Paths** work that way, and it is the exception rather than the model: everywhere else, matching pairs data with data.

| Rule | Pairs on |
|---|---|
| **Match : Attributes** | An attribute value on each side, compared numerically or as strings |
| **Match : Tags × Attributes** | A tag on one side against an attribute value on the other |
| **Match : Shared Tag** | Tags in common: a named one, any shared, or all shared |
| **Match : Overlap** | Bounds intersection, with configurable expansion |
| **Match : By Index** | Position, with clamp, wrap and yoyo for mismatched counts |
| **Match : Random** | A seeded threshold, so the randomness is deterministic |
| **Match : Copy Tags** | Nothing. It rides along and copies tags from the matched target when the other rules succeed |

## Required and optional

*Every rule carries a strictness, and the default is the permissive one.*

Rules stack on one pin, and each has a **Strictness**:

- **Required** means a failure sinks the whole match, whatever else passed.
- **Optional**, the default, means a failure is survivable as long as something else matched.

That default is the thing to know. Adding a single rule and expecting it to gate the pairing gets you a rule that can be ignored, so a rule expressing a hard constraint has to say so. Each rule also has **Invert**, which turns a match into a rejection and is how you express "anything except these".


> Figure: Two panels sharing one setup drawn identically at the top of each: one source dataset panel and one candidate dataset panel, with two rules listed below them, the first outlined green because it passes and the second faded and struck through because it fails. In the first panel, labelled Both optional, a flow arrow from the pair leads to a green matched result, because one rule passing was enough. In the second, labelled Second rule required, the failing rule is tagged required in orange and the same arrow leads to a rejected result, faded and struck through.
> Identical rules and identical verdicts. Only the strictness of the failing rule differs.


Above the individual rules, the consuming node's matching mode decides how their verdicts combine: **All** requires every test to pass, **Any** accepts a single pass, and **Disabled** skips matching so every combination goes ahead. Two more controls sit alongside it: one caps how many targets a source may match, and one routes unmatched data to a separate output rather than dropping it.


> **Note.**
> **Unmatched data goes quiet**
>
> Data that matches nothing is usually silent, which makes a mis-specified rule look like a working one that found nothing. Where a node offers to split unmatched data onto its own pin, wiring it up is the cheapest way to see whether the rules did what you meant.


## Related

* [What's different](concept:working-with-pcgex/what-pcgex-adds) -- the sub-node pattern both families follow
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- per-element verdicts, where matching works dataset to dataset
* **Data Matching** -- every match rule, with its settings
* [Pickers](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/pickers) -- the other small selection family, choosing indices rather than pairs

title: Pickers
description: A picker answers one question: which indices.
outline: The Pickers pin on Cluster : Pick Closest takes targets
body:
A picker answers one question: which indices. It is the smallest sub-node family in the plugin, and it exists because "the third one", "the last one" and "the middle one" are things you need to say about a collection whose size you do not control.

## A picker names indices

*Author the selection once, and it resolves against whatever collection it is handed.*

Pickers arrive on a **Pickers** pin like any other sub-node family, and several stack to build a compound selection. What they produce is a set of indices, resolved at execution against the collection the consuming node is working on. Nothing about a picker refers to a specific dataset, which is what lets the same picker be reused across nodes and across collections of different sizes.

| Picker | Selects |
|---|---|
| **Picker : Constant** | One index |
| **Picker : Range** | A contiguous span, auto-swapped if given backwards |
| **Picker : Indices from Set** | Several discrete indices, read from attributes |
| **Picker : Ranges from Set** | Several ranges read from `FVector2D` attributes, merged where they overlap |

The two `from Set` variants are the ones that make pickers data-driven: the indices come from attributes rather than from the node, so a selection can be computed upstream and handed over.

## Three behaviours they all share

*The settings that decide what an index means.*

**Negative indices count from the end.** `-1` is the last element, `-2` the one before it. That alone covers a large share of what pickers get used for.

**Treat as Normalized** reads the value as a `0-1` position across the collection instead of as an index, with a rounding mode deciding where a fractional result lands. This is the setting that earns the system its keep: a pick at `0.5` is the middle whether the collection holds four entries or four hundred.


> Figure: Two rows of cells representing collections, drawn one above the other and left-aligned to the same total width. The upper row, labelled 4 entries, is divided into four wide cells numbered 0 to 3. The lower row, labelled 40 entries, is divided into forty narrow cells with only 0, 20 and 39 numbered. A single green vertical marker labelled 0.5 runs down through both rows at the halfway point, meeting cell 2 in the upper row and cell 20 in the lower, both of which are outlined and tinted green to show what the same normalized pick resolved to.
> One normalized pick, two collection sizes. The index changes so the position does not.


**Safety** decides what an out-of-range index does, and the four answers are genuinely different tools:

| Mode | Out-of-range index | Past the end of three entries |
|---|---|---|
| **Ignore** | Skipped, leaving a smaller selection | `0, 1, 2` then nothing |
| **Tile** | Taken modulo the size, so it comes round again | `0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2` |
| **Clamp** | Pinned to the nearest end | `0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2` |
| **Yoyo** | Mirrored at the boundaries, reversing each time | `0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1` |

**Tile** is how a short list of picks covers a long collection by repeating. **Yoyo** does the same without the seam a tile creates, since it reverses instead of jumping back to zero.

## Who takes pickers

*A handful of nodes, and one filter.*

| Node | Uses them to |
|---|---|
| **Cherry Pick Points** | Keep the picked points. **Invert** discards them instead, and the remainder can be routed to a Discarded pin rather than dropped |
| **Promote Attributes** | Choose which entries supply the values being promoted to tags or the data domain, with **Picker (First)** and **Picker (Last)** narrowing that to a single one |
| **Uber Filter** and **Uber Filter (Data)** | Restrict which points the filter stack tests, instead of testing all of them |

The pin is required on the first two, which have nothing to do without it. On the Uber Filters it is optional, and leaving it empty tests everything.

**Filter : Picker** is the one that widens the reach. It turns "is this index picked" into an ordinary filter verdict, so every node that accepts filters can be driven by index selection without knowing pickers exist.


> **Warning.**
> **The Pickers pin on Cluster : Pick Closest takes targets**
>
> **Cluster : Pick Closest** shows a pin labelled **Pickers**, and it accepts points rather than picker sub-nodes. Those points are proximity targets: the node selects clusters by distance to them, and nothing about it is index-based. The shared label is an internal naming collision, so read that pin as "targets" and do not wire a picker into it.


## Related

* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- where **Filter : Picker** puts index selection
* [Matching](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/matching) -- the other pairing family, working dataset to dataset
* [What's different](concept:working-with-pcgex/what-pcgex-adds) -- the sub-node pattern pickers follow
* **Pickers** -- every picker, with its settings

title: Shapes
description: Every builder offers two resolution modes, and this is the choice that matters most:
outline: One shape per seed, cut to the seed
φ Sphere is the fast one by a wide margin
body:
**Create Shapes** produces clean parametric arrangements from seed points: rings, grids, polygons, spheres. What makes them worth having is not the primitives themselves but that their resolution follows their input, so a shape can be any size and still come out with the point density you asked for.

## Fixed count, or fixed spacing

*The resolution mode decides which property survives a change of scale.*

Every builder offers two resolution modes, and this is the choice that matters most:

- **Fixed** produces the same number of points however large the shape is, so a big shape has its points spread further apart.
- **Distance** targets a spacing instead, so a big shape gets more points and the interval between them holds steady.

Distance is what makes the system useful. Seeds in real graphs vary in scale, and points generated from them are usually going to be scattered assets, connected into a cluster or read as a path. Every one of those cares about spacing and none of them cares about count, so a resolution that adapts to the input is the difference between a primitive you can use downstream and one you have to resample first.


> Figure: Two panels, each containing the same three circles at clearly different sizes, small, medium and large, generated from three seeds drawn at their centres. In the first panel, labelled Fixed, every circle carries the same twelve points, so the points on the small circle sit tightly together and those on the large one are spread far apart. In the second, labelled Distance, the gap between neighbouring points is identical on all three circles, so the small circle carries six points, the medium twelve and the large twenty-four.
> Same three seeds. Fixed holds the count steady, Distance holds the spacing steady.


Builder parameters can also be driven from attributes on the seed, so one builder can produce genuinely different geometry per seed rather than the same shape at varying scales.

## One shape per seed, cut to the seed

*The seed's transform decides where the shape goes, how it is oriented, and how big it is.*

**Create Shapes** takes seed points and one or more **shape builder** sub-nodes, and every seed becomes the origin of its own shape. The seed's position places it, its rotation orients it, and its scale sizes it.

This is generation rather than duplication. A large seed does not receive a stretched copy of a small seed's output: its shape is built at that size from the start, which is what lets the resolution rules above apply per shape.

Output can be grouped three ways: **Per Dataset** merges everything into one collection, **Per Seed** gives each seed its own, and **Per Shape** groups by which builder made it. Points can carry a `ShapeId` naming their builder, and shapes falling under a minimum point count can be dropped rather than emitted as fragments.

## The four builders

| Builder | Produces |
|---|---|
| **Shape : Circle** | A ring or arc, with configurable start and end angle |
| **Shape : Polygon** | A regular polygon, optionally with skeleton spokes from the centre |
| **Shape : 3D Grid** | A three-dimensional lattice with per-axis resolution |
| **Shape : φ Sphere** | Points on a sphere by Fibonacci lattice |

**Shape : Polygon**'s skeleton is the one with extra reach. Spokes run from the centre to the vertices, the edge midpoints, or both, and the points come out tagged with whether they sit on the hull, their angle from the centre, which edge they belong to and how far along it they are. That is a radial structure with its own addressing scheme, ready to drive a cluster or select a subset.


> **Note.**
> **φ Sphere is the fast one by a wide margin**
>
> The Fibonacci lattice places points by golden-ratio spiral rather than by latitude and longitude. It is deterministic, hits an exact point count, and avoids the bunching at the poles that UV sphere sampling produces. It is also between a thousand and two thousand times faster than the conventional sphere-sampling algorithms, which puts sphere distributions well inside the budget of graphs that could not previously afford them.
>
> [Fibonacci Lattices](https://observablehq.com/@meetamit/fibonacci-lattices) is an excellent interactive explanation of the principle, and worth a look if the spacing is not obvious from the output.


## Related

* [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) -- a closed shape read as a path
* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- shapes as structured input for connection
* **Shapes** -- every builder, with its settings

title: Tensors
description: A tensor gives direction to empty space.
body:
A tensor gives direction to empty space. Where a normal attribute says something about a point, a tensor says something about everywhere, so any operation can ask "which way, here" and get an answer at a position nothing occupies. Wind, current, magnetic pull and grain are all the same shape of problem.

## Effectors, tensors, and the field

*Points emit influence, a tensor turns that into direction, and the tensors on a pin composite into one field.*

Three levels stack, and keeping them apart is most of understanding the system.

**Effectors** are points. Each one is a source of influence with its own position and bounds, and they arrive on a required **Effectors** pin as an ordinary point dataset. Their bounds decide reach, always as a sphere whose radius is the length of the scaled extents. The panel offers no choice about that despite an unused Box/Sphere enum surviving in the source.

**A tensor** is a sub-node that reads those effectors and decides what kind of direction they produce. The same twelve points become a pull toward each of them under **Tensor : Pole**, a directional current under **Tensor : Flow**, or a set of vortices under **Tensor : Spin**. Each tensor carries a **Tensor Weight** and a falloff curve controlling how influence decays with distance. Where several of its own effectors reach the same place they are always averaged by weight: the panel shows a **Weighted / Closest / Strongest** picker beside them, but nothing reads it, so all four settings behave as Weighted.

**The field** is every tensor on the consumer's pin composited together. Stack a broad flow with a few local poles and a noise and you get something with structure at more than one scale, which is the reason to have a field rather than a direction.


> Figure: Three full-width bands stacked one above the other, each showing the same five effector points at identical positions, drawn as ringed markers with a faint circle around each showing its influence radius. Across each band a loose grid of short headless strokes, each with a dot at its tail, shows the direction the field gives at that location, and marks fall only where an effector reaches, so the bare ground between them is where the field has nothing to say. In the first, labelled Tensor Pole, every stroke points radially away from the effectors around it, which is what the default guide gives. In the second, labelled Tensor Flow, the strokes run broadly left to right, bending between effectors as the blend shifts from one heading to the next. In the third, labelled Tensor Spin, the strokes circle each effector, forming visible vortices.
> The same seven effectors. The tensor decides what kind of direction they mean.



> Figure: Two full-width bands stacked one above the other, over the same five effectors and the same influence circles as the three tensors shown separately above, so each band can be compared with them position for position. Both bands show one field composited from all three of those tensors at once, drawn with the same headless strokes. In the first, labelled Equal weights, Pole, Flow and Spin each carry a weight of 1 and the result carries something of all three: a broad left to right drift, radial spread near the effectors and a curl between them. In the second, labelled Flow weighted up, the same three tensors are mixed with Flow at a weight of 3 against 1 each, and the strokes straighten out toward the flow direction, with the radial and circling structure surviving only close to the effectors.
> The same three tensors both times. Only the weights differ.


## What drives a tensor

*Points, curves, geometry, or nothing at all.*

| Driven by | Tensors |
|---|---|
| **Effector points** | **Pole**, **Flow**, **Spin**, **Inertia**, **Null**, **Noise (Bounded)** |
| **A path or spline** | **Path Flow**, **Path Pole**, **Spline Flow**, **Spline Pole** |
| **Surface geometry** | **Surface**, which samples nearby surfaces and adds every connected source together |
| **Nothing** | **Constant**, **Inertia (Constant)**, **Noise**, which fill the whole field with no source geometry |

The flow and pole distinction repeats across the families and is worth reading once: a **Flow** tensor points *along* its source, following a direction or a tangent, while a **Pole** tensor points *at* it, pulling in or pushing away. Everything else is what the source happens to be.

**Tensor : Null** is the eraser. It contributes no direction of its own and cancels other influence where its effectors reach, which is how a field gets dead zones.


> **Note.**
> **Constant is the safety net**
>
> Sampling a field can fail, in the sense that a position no tensor reaches has no direction to give. **Tensor : Constant** covers the whole field with a fallback, so adding one at a low weight turns a field with gaps into one that always answers. Reach for it when an extrusion stops early for no obvious reason.


## Sampling the field

*How the consumer reads it, and what it may do to the answer afterwards.*

Consumers read the field through a **sampler**, which trades accuracy against cost. The default takes one sample at the position. **Six Points** averages six cardinal offsets, which smooths a noisy field. **RK4** takes four weighted samples per step for consistent accuracy along a curve, and **Adaptive RK** varies its step size, working finer where the field bends and coarser where it does not.

Once sampled, **mutations** reshape the answer before it is used:

| Mutation | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Invert** | Mirrors the sampled direction |
| **Bidirectional** | Compares the sample against an axis of the point's own transform and flips it when they disagree, so a field can drive symmetric behaviour without fighting itself |
| **Scale** | Multiplies direction and magnitude per axis |

Scale is the one to remember, because a scale of `1,1,0` flattens a field to the ground plane. A three-dimensional field driving something that should stay level is a common enough situation that this is the standard fix.

## Who reads a field

*Two nodes consume it directly, and three systems take it as an optional influence.*
