| Node | What it does with the field |
|---|---|
| **Tensors : Extrude** | Steps seed points along the field, generating paths. Handles intersections, child extrusions, closed loops and stop filters |
| **Tensors Transform** | Moves and rotates existing points in place, over a configurable number of iterations |

Beyond those, a field turns up as a steering influence inside systems that already had their own logic:

* **Probe : Tensor** biases which connections **Cluster : Connect Points** creates, so a cluster can be grown with the grain of a field
* **Heuristics : Tensor** makes pathfinding prefer edges that agree with the field
* **Filter : Tensor Dot** turns alignment with the field into a filter verdict

That list is the actual argument for the system. A field authored once can orient assets, shape connectivity, steer routes and select points, and none of those consumers needs to know how it was built.

## Related

* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- where **Filter : Tensor Dot** fits
* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- routes that follow a field
* [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) -- what **Tensors : Extrude** produces
* **Tensors** -- every tensor, sampler and setting

title: Topology
description: Clusters and paths describe structure without being geometry.
outline: Quick helpers, and where to go instead
Surfacing needs a cluster that survives being flattened
body:
Clusters and paths describe structure without being geometry. Topology nodes close that gap, triangulating structure into dynamic mesh surfaces that render and collide.


> **Warning.**
> **Quick helpers, and where to go instead**
>
> PCGEx is not a geometry scripting toolkit. These nodes cover the common case of getting a surface out of structure you already have, quickly, and they stop there.
>
> For real dynamic mesh work, [PCGUtils](https://github.com/mharris382/PCGUtils) provides a proper set of dynamic mesh tools for PCG and is the better place to go.


## Four ways to a surface

*What you already have decides which node you reach for.*

| Node | Takes | Approach |
|---|---|---|
| **Topology : Cluster Surface** | A cluster | Finds the closed cells in the edges and triangulates each one |
| **Topology : Path Surface** | Closed paths | Reads each path as a polygon boundary and triangulates it |
| **Topology : Point Surface** | Loose points | Delaunay triangulation straight from the positions, no connections needed |
| **Clipper2 : Triangulate** | Closed paths | Constrained Delaunay, with fill rules resolving overlaps and holes |

**Topology : Cluster Surface** does the most work. It walks the edges to identify closed cells, projects them, filters them through the same constraint block cell extraction uses, then triangulates what survives. Constraints on area, perimeter, point count, compactness and convexity are how you keep the faces you meant and drop the slivers.

**Clipper2 : Triangulate** is the one for paths that overlap or nest. Its fill rules, **even-odd**, **non-zero**, **positive** and **negative**, decide which enclosed regions are solid and which are holes, so a shape with cutouts comes out correct instead of filled in.


> Figure: Three panels showing one progression at identical coordinates throughout. The first, labelled Cluster, holds twelve ringed vertices joined by edges that enclose five interior regions. The second, labelled Cells, keeps the same edges and vertices but tints each of the five enclosed regions in a different strength of one muted blue, showing them identified as separate faces. The third, labelled Surface, replaces the tints with triangulation: each region is subdivided into triangles by thin interior lines, and the vertex rings are gone because the output is mesh rather than points.
> Edges enclose regions, regions become faces, faces become triangles.



> **Warning.**
> **Surfacing needs a cluster that survives being flattened**
>
> **Topology : Cluster Surface** projects before it triangulates. A cluster lying roughly in a plane surfaces cleanly, and a tilted or gently curved one works with the projection aimed along its dominant axis.
>
> A volumetric cluster does not. **Cluster : Delaunay 3D** and **Cluster : Voronoi 3D** produce topology whose faces overlap from every viewing direction, so flattening collapses unrelated geometry onto itself and you get nothing useful rather than an error. **Topology : Point Surface** is the node for genuinely three-dimensional input, and [Cells & Hulls](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/cells-and-hulls) covers the same limit where it first appears.


## Volumes and colliders

*The same footprint, turned into something gameplay can query.*

**Clipper2 : Volume** takes a closed path footprint and extrudes it upward into a solid, which is a different output from everything above: not a surface to look at, but a shape to test against.

It handles concave footprints by decomposing them into convex pieces and writing each one as a vertical prism into the actor's convex collision. There is no BSP involved, so the result works in the editor and in a cooked build alike. Two output modes decide what you get:

| Mode | Output |
|---|---|
| **Volume** | An `AVolume` subclass of your choosing, so a footprint becomes a trigger volume, a post-process volume, or any custom gameplay volume. Comes back as `UPCGVolumeData` |
| **Primitive** | A simple static-mesh collider with convex simple collision, for contexts where an actual volume actor is unsuitable. Comes back as `UPCGPrimitiveData` |

A **Base Mode** decides where each piece's floor sits: **Flat** puts every piece on one shared floor at the footprint's lowest point, while **Min**, **Max** and **Average** derive each piece's floor from the points it contains. Collision is configurable on both paths, defaulting to the `Trigger` profile in Volume mode.

This is the quiet workhorse of the section. Any procedural region you can express as a closed path, a plaza, a district, a danger zone, becomes something gameplay can query without hand-placing a single volume.

## What the surface nodes share

*Different inputs, one output stage.*

Whichever surfacing route you take, the back half is common: normals are computed and can be flipped, edges can be welded, UVs are generated through a choice of projection methods, and a material and default vertex colour are applied. Those settings sit in the same block on every node, so swapping between cluster-based and path-based generation is not a reconfiguration.

What comes out is PCG dynamic mesh data, which **Spawn Dynamic Mesh** turns into PCG-managed `DynamicMeshComponent` actors. They are cleaned up when the graph regenerates, like anything else PCG manages.

## Related

* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- where a surfaceable cluster comes from
* [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) -- closed paths as boundaries and footprints
* [Cells & Hulls](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/cells-and-hulls) -- the cell model Cluster Surface uses
* **Topology** -- every node, with its settings

title: Asset Staging
description: Collections, selectors, and the pick that travels as one attribute until something at the end of the graph spawns it.
body:
Asset staging is how PCGEx puts assets on points: collections describe what can be picked, selectors decide which entry each point gets, and the pick travels with the point until the end of the graph turns it into a mesh, an actor, a level instance or more PCG data. This section explains the system end to end; the per-node reference lives in **Staging**. **Staging separates deciding from spawning.** The decision is recorded as plain data on the point, so everything between the decision and the scene, fitting, filtering, swapping, reading values back, works on points like any other PCG operation.
*** ## Why a collection _What the asset does that an array of soft references cannot._ The natural alternative is a hand-rolled data asset: an array of mesh references and weights, read by a loop. A collection starts in the same place, weighted rows of assets, and then covers the ground that data asset would have to grow toward, one feature request at a time: * **Rebuilds bake the expensive part ahead of time.** Each entry carries staging data: the asset path, its bounds, its socket transforms, baked when the collection is rebuilt. Picking, bounds-fitting and filtering all run against those baked values, so distributing thousands of picks never loads a single asset. * **A pick is one attribute.** A staged point carries its entire resolved identity, the collection, the exact entry, the material variant, in a single int64, with a small Collection Map dataset alongside to resolve it. No paths on points, no per-point structs. * **The ecosystem already understands it.** Re-fitting, variant swapping, routing by entry type, reading entry data back onto points, extracting sockets: each is an existing node consuming the same staged points, and none of them re-decides anything. * **Entries carry data you define.** Collections declare typed custom properties, reusable across assets through schemas, overridable per category and per entry, and resolvable onto points in one node. * **Collections can be captured, not only authored.** An Actor Collection entry records how a placed actor differs from its class defaults and re-applies that at spawn. A Level Collection reads its entries out of a level. A PCGDataAsset Collection exports a whole level into spawnable PCG data. Scenes you already built become libraries. * **The editor is part of the system.** Collections open in a purpose-built editor: a thumbnail grid grouped by category, drag-drop from the Content Browser and between open collections, batch weight and sort tools, create-from-selection, and staging that rebuilds itself when a referenced asset changes. A hand-rolled data asset gets the default details panel. * **Iteration is live.** Editing a collection propagates into graphs already generated this session, so tuning weights or swapping an asset shows up in the level without a regenerate-and-wait loop. ### Pick now, spawn later _The two-phase model that shapes a staging graph._ Staging decides and records the pick; spawning happens later, in vanilla mesh spawners driven by **PCGEx Mesh Selector Staged**, or in the dedicated **Staging :** spawn nodes for actors, levels and PCG data. The deciding node is **Staging : Distribute**: points in, points out, with a pick recorded on each and a Collection Map emitted beside them. Everything spawn-shaped, blocking loads, component creation, actor spawning, sits at the end of the graph where it belongs, and the middle of the graph stays pure data. > Figure: Flow diagram: two collection panels feed a Staging : Distribute node with a Selector sub-node attached. Distribute emits staged points carrying an int64 pick plus a small Map dataset, drawn together in one card. That card flows as one payload through the consumer stages Fitting, Swap, Type Filter and Load Properties, crosses a threshold line marked first load, and only then reaches the spawn routes Mesh Spawner, Spawn Actors, Spawn Level and Load PCGData. > The decision happens once, on the left. Everything after it consumes the same two datasets. ### What a staged point carries _One attribute on the point, one small dataset beside it._ A staged point has a single int64 attribute, `PCGEx/CollectionEntry`, packing which collection, which entry and which material variant the pick resolved to. The **Collection Map**, a small attribute set emitted on the **Map** pin, lists the collections involved so any downstream node can resolve the hash back to the exact entry, including entries reached through nested sub-collections. Points stay light, and the pick stays resolvable without loading anything. > **Note.** > **Staging : Distribute** can instead write plain attributes, the asset path and optional per-slot material paths, for consumers outside the staging ecosystem. That is the `Point Attributes` output mode: vanilla-readable, at the cost of the resolvable identity. The default, `Collection Map`, keeps it. *** ### In this section _The pages, in reading order._
PageAnswers
[Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collections)The asset model: the collection types, entries, weights, categories, sub-collections, and the staging data baked into them.
[Authoring Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/authoring-collections)The collection editor: grid view, categories, batch tools, and rebuilding staging.
[Selecting Entries](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/selecting-entries)How a point gets an entry: Distribute, seeds, categories, the selectors and the modifiers.
[The Collection Map](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/the-collection-map)The pick hash and the Map, the two output modes, and the downstream contract they create.
[Fitting](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/fitting)Scale-to-fit, justification, and variations, at distribution time or as a standalone pass.
[Staging & Spawning](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/staging-spawning)Turning picks into scene content, routed by entry type, and sockets as attachment points.
[Capturing Scenes](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes)Building collections from placed actors and levels: property deltas, level harvesting, PCG data export.
[Collection Properties](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties)Typed custom data on entries, schemas, category overrides, and reading it all back onto points.
[Staging Pipelines](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/staging-pipelines)Automating collection authoring: Blueprint hooks on every staging rebuild.
[Collections & Grammar](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collections-and-grammar)Entries as grammar modules: symbols and sizes, and feeding vanilla PCG subdivision from collections.
[Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming)Variant Collections and rewriting picks after the fact: biomes and themes without re-distributing.

title: Authoring Collections
description: Creating collections and working in the collection editor: the grid, categories, batch tools, and rebuilding staging.
body:
Collections have their own editor, and most collection work never touches a details panel: entries are tiles in a grid, weights are edited in place, and assets arrive by drag and drop.

## Creating a collection

_From a menu, or from the assets you already selected._

Two routes:

* **From the Content Browser's new-asset menu**, under the PCGEx category. This gives an empty collection of the chosen type.
* **From a selection.** Right-click selected source assets and choose **Asset Actions ▸ PCGEx ▸ Create or Update Asset Collection(s) from selection**: matching collection types are created next to the selection with one entry per asset. Run the same action with a collection _in_ the selection and the source assets are appended to it instead.

The same menu offers **Merge Collection(s) into Omni Collection**, which creates or picks an Omni Collection and appends a copy of every entry from the selected collections, keeping the sources untouched.

> Figure: STILL | id: authoring-create-menu | SHOWS: Where collection creation lives in the Content Browser context menu | FRAME: Content Browser with several static meshes selected, right-click menu open at Asset Actions, PCGEx submenu expanded showing Create or Update Asset Collection(s) from selection and Merge Collection(s) into Omni Collection | CALLOUTS: The PCGEx section header, then the create-from-selection entry | SOURCE: Any project with a few meshes; example project content preferred | NOTE: Both menu entries must be readable, crop tight to the menu
> Selection in, collection out. The reverse direction, adding to an existing collection, is the same menu entry.

## The Grid View

_Entries are tiles, grouped by category, edited in place._

Opening a collection lands on the **Grid View** tab: category groups on the left, each a wrap of thumbnail tiles, and a details pane on the right editing whichever entry is selected. Weight and the sub-collection flag sit directly on each tile, along with the entry's category and its asset picker; everything else lives in the right-hand pane.

Tiles wear their state: an index badge, and small markers for variations (`V`), sockets (`S`), tags (`T`) and enabled property overrides (`P`), so a scan of the grid shows which entries carry extra data. Double-clicking a tile opens the referenced asset's own editor.

> Figure: STILL | id: authoring-grid-view | SHOWS: The collection editor layout as a whole: category groups of tiles on the left, single-entry details on the right | FRAME: A Mesh Collection with two named categories plus an Uncategorized group, one tile selected, its details visible in the right pane, toolbar visible at top | CALLOUTS: A category header with its entry count, the weight spinner on a tile, the V and S badges on a tile that has them, the selected tile and its details pane | SOURCE: An example-project mesh collection with categories authored | NOTE: Pick a collection where at least one tile shows badges so the callouts have something to point at
> Weight, category and the payload are on the tile; the pane carries the rest.

Editing is direct throughout:

* **Drag assets in** from the Content Browser: onto a category group to land in that category, anywhere else to land uncategorized.
* **Drag tiles** between categories, reorder them inside one, or drag them into another open collection editor; hold Alt to copy instead of move. Incompatible entries are skipped with a toast, never silently converted.
* **Select** with click, Ctrl and Shift; **Ctrl+D** duplicates, **Delete** deletes.
* **Categories** are created inline: the tile's category dropdown ends in a `+ New...` row.

On an Omni Collection the add flow first asks which entry type, and each tile shows the picker matching its own row's type; the grid otherwise behaves identically.

## Batch tools

_Weights, sorting, and per-type maintenance, one menu each._

The grid's header toolbar carries the batch operations:

| Tool               | Does                                                                                                          |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Add entries        | Appends the current Content Browser selection.                                                                |
| Weight tools       | `Normalize to 100`, reset, set-to-index, add, multiply, randomize: quick reshaping of the whole distribution. |
| Sort tools         | Sort entries by ascending or descending weight.                                                               |
| Cleanup Categories | Removes category-override rows whose category no longer matches any entry.                                    |

Mesh and skinned mesh collections add collision tools (disable collision across every referenced asset's descriptors) and descriptor tools (switch all entries between per-entry and collection-inherited descriptors). Actor collections add **Add Selected Actors**, which captures the actors selected in the viewport, a by-name actor search, and cleanup actions for entries whose source actor or level has gone missing. Those capture flows are the subject of [Capturing Scenes](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes).

A footer row of property filters (`Variations`, `Fitting`, `Tags`, `Materials`, and so on) toggles whole property groups in and out of the details pane, which keeps the pane short when a pass only cares about one aspect. The filter state is shared across collection editors and remembered.

## Rebuilding staging

_Three scopes of rebuild, and the automation that usually makes them unnecessary._

The toolbar's **Rebuild** bakes staging data for this collection: entry paths, bounds, sockets ([Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collections) covers what that data is). Beside it sit a recursive variant, which also rebuilds every sub-collection, and a project-wide variant that sweeps every collection asset in the project.

Manual rebuilds are the fallback. By default the editor re-stages an entry when its referenced asset is saved, and re-stages stale entries when a collection is opened, detecting staleness by content rather than file dates. Both behaviors are toggles under **Editor Preferences ▸ Plugins ▸ PCGEx | Collections**.

> **Warning.**
> Staging data is what selectors and fitting read at pick time. A collection whose staging is stale picks and fits against yesterday's bounds, so if size-aware selection or fitting looks wrong after asset edits made outside the editor, rebuild before debugging the graph.

Rebuilds only dirty the asset when something actually changed, so the project-wide sweep is safe to run on a clean checkout without producing a wall of modified files.

title: Capturing Scenes
description: Building collections from things you placed: actor property deltas, level harvesting, and exporting levels or actor subtrees to PCG data.
body:
Collections can be authored row by row, and they can also be captured: from actors you configured in a viewport, from levels you dressed by hand. The capture routes are where a collection stops being a list you maintain and becomes a recording of work you already did.

## Actors that remember their settings

_An entry can carry the difference between your actor and its class._

An Actor Collection entry references a class, and classes spawn with defaults. The capture flow closes that gap: point an entry at a placed actor (`Delta Source Actor`, filled from the viewport selection with the row's pick button, or through the editor's **Add Selected Actors**), and the entry records a **property delta**, the serialized difference between that actor and its class defaults. At spawn time the delta is re-applied, so the spawned actor ends up exactly as the captured one was configured: tweaked light intensities, component settings, assigned assets, all of it, without a subclass or a preset asset per variation.

Re-running the capture against the same source updates the delta in place, so the placed actor stays the editable original and the entry stays a recording. The reference is a path into the actor's level, so the capture works with that level closed: the rebuild loads it on demand, except a World Partition level, which cannot be read closed. A source that cannot be reached leaves the previous delta in place with a warning, and the editor's cleanup actions handle the decay cases, deltas whose source actor or level has since disappeared.

**When a component needs more than the delta: fixups**

A delta restores property values, and for most components that is the whole job. Some components hold state that has to be _reconstructed_ after their properties land rather than merely assigned, and those get a **fixup**: a post-apply step run per component type. The plugin registers built-in fixups for the engine components that need one; a custom component whose spawned state comes up wrong despite a correct delta is the sign it needs its own, implemented and registered in C++ from `PCGExComponentFixups.h`.

> Figure: STILL | id: capturing-actor-delta | SHOWS: An actor entry bound to a placed actor through its delta source reference | FRAME: An Actor Collection open in the collection editor, one entry selected, the details pane scrolled to the Delta Source Actor row showing a placed actor filled in, the source actor visible in the viewport behind the editor window | CALLOUTS: The Delta Source Actor row, the pick-from-viewport button and the go-to button beside it | SOURCE: A level with one configured actor, captured into a small actor collection | NOTE: The viewport actor and the entry must plausibly be the same object in the shot. Reshoot wanted: the produced still shows the grid view and never reached the delta row
> The entry references the class and remembers this actor's differences.

## Harvesting a level

_A Level Collection's staging pass reads the level so you do not retype it._

Level Collection entries reference level assets, and rebuilding staging walks each one: actors in the level are gathered, filtered, and folded into the entry's staging data, bounds accumulated across everything that counts, socket-provider actors turned into baked sockets. The default content filter keeps infrastructure out -- hidden actors, editor-only actors, loose brushes, navigation data and their kind. That rejection is part of the default filter itself, so a custom filter takes over the whole decision; only the `StaticIgnore` actor tag and socket-provider stripping are enforced unconditionally.

Two `Blueprintable` objects decide the details, assigned on the collection (or project-wide in settings): a **content filter** choosing which actors count, tag and class based out of the box, and a **bounds evaluator** deciding what each actor contributes to the bounds, with sensible defaults that ignore editor-only and lighting components. Both are extension points: a project with its own notion of "what matters in a level" writes one Blueprint, not a new pipeline.

## Level to PCG data

_The deepest capture: a level, or an actor's subtree, exported into spawnable PCG data._

A **Collection | PCGDataAsset** entry can point at a PCG data asset directly, at a **level**, or at a placed **actor**. In level mode, rebuilding staging exports the level into a generated PCG data asset: meshes become staged points, actors become an embedded **Collection | Actor** complete with the property deltas above, and nested level instances become staged points of their own. Other modules can teach the export a kind of their own through **Level Export Handlers**, which is how a cluster sketch component comes out on its own pin with its own collection. Mesh and nested-level references, and any handler's shared kind, pool into collections the host collection maintains across all its entries, and once the export lands the collection stamps the result with its Collection Map. Spawning it back is **Staging : Load PCGData** plus the ordinary routes of [Staging & Spawning](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/staging-spawning).

Actor mode exports the actor's attached subtree the same way, as if it were a level of its own. The actor itself stays out, and every point comes out relative to its transform, so the arrangement carries no trace of where it stood. It shares the delta capture's rule for reaching the actor: its level loads on demand unless it is World Partition, and an unreachable actor keeps the previous export.

Any actor can be that root, and the plugin ships one made for the job, **Assembly Root**: an inert marker with no mesh and no collision, an editor billboard to grab it by, and nothing to export of its own. Placing one is how you declare "this subtree is an arrangement" in the level itself, and the tooling reads that declaration: the exporter treats a marker it meets inside another export as a grouping pivot, never as an entry, and Valency's cages recognise the same interface. It also marks the seam for going further in C++, where an actor implementing the interface can bound the descent or supply its own frame.

Dress a level by hand, or build an arrangement under one actor, list it as one entry, and a single pick now places the whole arrangement, with every actor configured as authored.

> **Note.**
> Generated data lives embedded in the collection by default. For teams and version control, `External Storage` on the collection moves the generated assets into a content folder of your choosing, with names that stay stable across rebuilds so re-exports are edits, never churn.

## Keeping capture cheap at runtime

_Capture work is editor work; runtime only ever resolves._

Every capture route above runs in the editor, at staging-rebuild time. What ships is baked: deltas, bounds, sockets, exported data. The one runtime cost worth managing is asset loading at spawn, and **Resources** exists for exactly that: preload a collection's assets ahead of generation, release them when a graph is done, so spawn-time loads never hitch a running game.

title: Collection Properties
description: Entries carry whatever data you declare on them: costs, gameplay tags, curve profiles, footprint hints, anything typed.
body:
Entries carry whatever data you declare on them: costs, gameplay tags, curve profiles, footprint hints, anything typed. Properties are the extension surface of the collection system, and the reason a collection can model your project's vocabulary.

## Declaring properties

_On the collection, locally or through shared schemas._



A collection declares its properties in one of two places: locally, as named typed slots on the asset, or by importing **Property Schema** assets, reusable declarations shared across collections. Imports resolve recursively and dedupe by name, locals first, so a collection can adopt a studio-wide schema and still add its own fields.

Declared properties are shapes with defaults. Values come from the override tiers below.

Properties are read on both sides of the pick. Downstream, they flow onto points (below); upstream, several selectors run on them: **Selector : Range-Based** reads its per-entry ranges from properties, **Selector : Curve-Remapped Weight** evaluates curve properties, **Selector : Closest Match** compares point attributes against property values, and **Selector Modifier : Quota** takes its caps and minimums from them. Declaring a property can be how a collection _selects_, not only what it carries.

## Three tiers, one resolution

_Entry beats category, category beats collection, and mismatches fall through._

A property resolves per entry, walking three tiers and taking the first usable value:

1. The **entry's own override**, if enabled.
2. The **category's overrides**, if the entry's category has a row.
3. The **collection's declared default**.


> Figure: Three columns, one per entry, each stacking the three tiers of one Cost property: entry override over category row over collection default. For Crate the enabled entry override wins, marked with a green outline, and the tiers below are faded because they are never consulted. For Barrel the entry override is disabled with an empty checkbox, a small arrow passes the question down, and the category row wins. For Lamp the entry override is disabled and the category tier has no row, drawn as an empty dashed slot, so the question falls through both to the collection default. A skipped slot always hands the question down, never a blank value.
> Same property, three entries, three answers, one rule.


> The fall-through is safety-shaped: a disabled slot, a wrong-typed slot, or an absent row never blanks the value, it passes the question down. Overriding one field for one category can never break the ninety entries that were happy with the default.

Category overrides are edited from the grid: each category group header carries a gear opening that category's override row. The cleanup tool removes rows whose category no longer matches any entry, and deliberately keeps rows with nothing enabled yet, because an empty row is what in-progress authoring looks like.

## Harvested from actors

_Actor entries can bring their properties with them._

Actors carrying a PCGEx property collection component contribute their declared properties during capture: rebuilding an Actor Collection's staging scans the source actors, merges their schemas into the collection, and fills per-entry overrides from each actor's values. Combined with the delta capture of [Capturing Scenes](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes), a placed actor hands the collection both how it should spawn and what data it should carry.

## Reading values back

_One node writes any of it onto points._

**Staging : Load Properties** resolves staged points against their entries and writes the requested values as point attributes. Resolution runs once per unique entry and fans out, so cost follows the size of the collection, never the point count.

Three groups of outputs, each opt-in:

* **Your properties**, mapped name to attribute. Sampleable types go further: a float-curve property can be _evaluated_ at a per-point time and written as the sampled value, so one authored curve becomes a per-point gradient, and the same curve can be sampled at several times into several attributes.
* **Entry data**: weight, category, tags, bounds, asset path, and the entry's type.
* **Grammar data**, for graphs feeding grammar-driven subdivision.


> **Note.**
> Two of the entry-data outputs sound alike and answer different questions: `CollectionType` is the type of the _hosting collection_, so every row of an Omni Collection reports Omni, while `EntryType` is the resolved entry's own type, the value **Staging : Type Filter** routes by.


## In Blueprint

_The same properties, from the authoring side._

Staging pipelines ([Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collections)) and editor utilities read and write the same property system through a Blueprint library, get and set by name on entries, categories and collections, so batch authoring, validation passes, and generated collections all speak properties too. The node library's **Collection Staging Pipeline** pages cover the callable surface.

title: Collections
description: The collection asset model: seven types, one entry anatomy, sub-collections, and the staging data baked into every row.
body:
A collection is a data asset holding weighted entries, and every collection type shares one anatomy: what differs per type is the asset an entry points at, and what gets baked into it. Learn the anatomy once and all seven types read the same way. ### The type roster _Dedicated types, one generic host, and one mutator._
IconTypeAn entry holds
**Collection | Mesh**A static mesh, optional material variants, and its component descriptors.
Skinned Mesh CollectionA skinned mesh, same shape as the mesh entry.
**Collection | Actor**An actor class, optionally with a captured property delta from a placed actor.
**Collection | Level**A level asset, spawnable as a streaming instance.
**Collection | PCGDataAsset**A PCG data asset, or a level exported into one.
**Collection | Omni**Any of the above, plus Generic entries holding any asset nothing spawns. One list mixing entry types freely.
**Collection | Variant**Overrides for entries of other collections, for end-of-pipeline swapping. Covered in Swapping & Theming.
The dedicated types came first, each holding one kind of asset. The **Omni Collection** came later and hosts entries of every registered type in one list, which makes it the usual starting point: begin mixed, and nothing is lost if the list turns out to hold only meshes. A dedicated collection can always be converted into an Omni one ([Authoring Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/authoring-collections) covers the merge action); the conversion has no reverse. **What picking Omni changes, and what it costs** On the PCG side: nothing. A staged pick is type-blind, the runtime cache resolves entries the same way whatever asset hosts them, and every downstream node dispatches on the resolved entry's type, never on the collection's. There is no performance tier between the two. The differences are authoring-side. Omni rows are type-wrapped, so adding an entry first asks which type. Collection-wide settings that a dedicated type carries as plain properties (a Mesh Collection's global descriptors, say) appear on an Omni Collection as explicit per-type settings blocks, one per entry type present. And the conversion is one-way. The **Variant Collection** sits on a parallel track. It holds no library of its own and exists only in terms of other collections, overriding their entries; a mutator over collections. It gets its own page, [Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming). ## Anatomy of an entry _Weight, category, tags, payload, and a slot of baked data._ Every entry, whatever its type, carries: | Field | Does | | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Weight` | Relative likelihood, integer, minimum 0. Every pick treats it as `Weight + 1`, a weight of 0 means disabled. | | `Category` | An optional name grouping entries. Selectors can route by it, and property overrides can target it. | | `Tags` | Names carried by the entry, forwarded onto spawned content or read back as attributes when a consuming node asks for them. | | `Is Sub Collection` | Flips the entry from an asset to a reference to another collection. | | Fitting overrides | Per-entry `Variations`, `Scale to Fit` and `Justification`, each switchable between the entry's own values, the collection's globals, or off. [Fitting](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/fitting) owns what they mean. | | Property overrides | Per-entry values for the collection's declared properties. [Collection Properties](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties) owns the system. | | Staging data | The baked slot: asset path, bounds, sockets. Below. | Mesh entries add **material variants**: weighted material overrides on one slot (`Single Slot`) or across several (`Multi Slots`). The variant is picked alongside the entry and packed into the same pick hash, which is what lets a later pass re-roll materials without touching the entry picks; [Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming) covers that move. ### Sub-collections _Nesting is free, and the weight semantics are per-level._ Any entry can reference another collection, of any type: a Mesh Collection can nest an Omni Collection, and mixed trees are ordinary. When a pick lands on a sub-collection entry, selection descends into the child and picks again, and the recorded pick names the final entry, so downstream nodes never see the nesting. The parent entry's weight governs how often the _subtree_ is entered. Odds inside the child are the child's own, re-rolled at each level: > Figure: A parent collection panel with three weighted entries: Crate weight 2, Barrel weight 1, and Props weight 1, a sub-collection entry. Beside each entry its first-roll share: 2/4, 1/4 and 1/4. A tapered reference arc, heavy at the parent end, links the Props entry to a child collection panel holding Lamp weight 3 and Bench weight 1. Beside each child leaf its share is a product of two fractions, 1/4 times 3/4 for Lamp and 1/4 times 1/4 for Bench, with the 1/4 inherited from the parent roll dimmed. > A leaf's share is the product of the rolls above it, one per level. However the top-level pick is decided, descent into a sub-collection is a plain weighted roll on the child's own weights; [Selecting Entries](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/selecting-entries) returns to what that means once smarter picking is in play. A sub-collection entry's staging bounds are an aggregate of its children, and the collection chooses how: `Union AABB` by default, or mean, weighted-mean, or max extents. Circular references are detected and refused rather than recursed into. **Staging : Distribute** can also stop before the descent entirely with `Flatten Sub Collections`, treating nested collections as assets in their own right. ## Staging data _The baked slot every entry carries, and the reason picking is cheap._ Rebuilding staging walks the entries and bakes three things into each: the resolved **asset path**, the asset's **bounds**, and its **sockets**. From then on, everything before the spawn stage runs against those baked values: selectors that consider size read the baked bounds, fitting solves against them, socket extraction reads the baked transforms. The assets themselves stay unloaded until something actually spawns them. * **Bounds** come from the asset: a mesh's bounding box, or, for actors and levels, whatever the collection's bounds evaluator reports, which is a Blueprintable choice ([Capturing Scenes](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes)). Each entry can additionally carry a **bounds modifier**, offsetting, scaling or padding the baked box before anything downstream reads it. * **Sockets** are of two kinds. _Managed_ sockets are extracted on every rebuild, from a static mesh's own sockets or from socket components on an actor, and are wiped and re-extracted each time. Sockets you add to the entry by hand sit beside them and survive rebuilds. When staging happens, and what keeps it fresh, is editor workflow: [Authoring Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/authoring-collections) covers the rebuild actions and the staleness handling.

title: Collections & Grammar
description: Entries as grammar modules: symbols and sizes on collections, and reading them out for vanilla PCG subdivision.
body:
Vanilla PCG's subdivision nodes build structures out of module descriptions: a symbol, a size, a scalable flag. Collections can carry exactly that on their entries, which makes a collection double as a grammar module library, with everything else on it, weights, properties, staging, still attached.

## Grammar on an entry

_A symbol, sizes per axis, and how sub-collections answer._

An entry's grammar block declares a **Symbol**, the name subdivision grammars refer to it by, a **Size** per enabled axis, either fixed or derived from the entry's staged bounds, a **Scalable** flag for modules allowed to stretch, and a debug color. The block can be authored per entry or deferred to the collection's global, and the editor's tiles wear it as the axis letters and the colored symbol badge in their corner ([Authoring Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/authoring-collections)).

Sub-collection entries answer grammar questions through their `Grammar Mode`: `Inherit` uses the child collection's own grammar, `Override` answers with the entry's block as if the subtree were one module, and `Flatten` hoists the children up as if they were local entries.

## Reading it out

_One node turns a collection into grammar-ready data._

**Get Collection Data** reads a collection into an attribute set shaped for grammar work: one row per entry, carrying the symbol, the per-axis sizes, the scalable flag, weight, category, bounds, and any custom properties requested. The collection can be picked on the node, resolved per input from soft-path attributes, or resolved from _entry hashes_ against an upstream Collection Map, which is the recursive case below.

The controls that matter:

* **Sub-collection handling** defaults to grammar semantics: each entry's own `Grammar Mode` decides whether the row is the subtree or its children.
* **Skip flags** drop rows that contribute nothing: entries with no symbol (the default skip), entries whose axes miss the requested ones, duplicates.
* **Category filters** include or exclude by category, and excluding a sub-collection container skips its whole subtree.
* **Every row also carries the entry hash**, always, under the same attribute staged points use.

The output is grammar data _and_ staged data at once.

## The loop

_Subdivide with the symbols, spawn with the hashes._

A grammar workflow through collections closes in three moves: **Get Collection Data** emits the module set, a vanilla subdivision node consumes the symbols and sizes to build the structure, and the resulting modules still carry their entry hashes, so the spawn routes of [Staging & Spawning](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/staging-spawning) finish the job with the node's Collection Map.

> Figure: Three stages joined by flow arrows. Left, a collection panel whose entries carry symbol letters and sizes: A Pillar 120, B Wall 200, C Crate 160. Middle, a span subdivided into adjacent segments stamped B, A, A, C, A, with widths matching the sizes; one segment carries an int64 chip showing the entry hash riding along. Right, the same span with the letters replaced by the matching silhouettes: wall, pillar, pillar, crate, pillar. The subdivision stage reads only symbols and sizes, the spawn stage reads only hashes.
> The grammar half reads symbols; the spawn half reads hashes; the rows carry both.

The hash source mode makes the loop recursive. A row whose entry is a sub-collection can be fed back into another **Get Collection Data** in its entry-hash mode, expanding one level deeper against the upstream Map: a building grammar picks a facade module, the facade is itself a collection, and its own grammar subdivides the next level down. Hierarchical grammars fall out of collection nesting, with no dedicated asset type carrying the hierarchy.

title: Fitting
description: A point has bounds; an entry has staged bounds.
body:
A point has bounds; an entry has staged bounds. Fitting is how the second gets placed inside the first: a scaling rule, a per-axis alignment, and optional randomization, all solved against the baked bounds so nothing loads.

## Scale to Fit

*How the asset's size relates to the point's.*

Three modes, then a rule per axis:

- **`None`**: the asset keeps its own size, whatever the point's bounds.
- **`Uniform`**: one scale factor on all three axes, chosen by a rule: `Min` scales until the tightest fit axis is met, `Max` until the loosest is, `Average` splits the difference. Proportions are preserved; the difference between rules is which axis wins when the shapes disagree. The exception is `Fill`, which matches every axis of the point's bounds exactly and spends proportions to do it.
- **`Individual`**: a rule per axis, each scaling its own axis independently. Proportions are spent to fill the box.


> Figure: Four panels compare scale-to-fit rules on the same dashed point bounds and the same arch-shaped asset. Fill stretches the asset to match the box exactly on both drawn axes, spending its proportions. Min scales it uniformly until the tightest axis is met, so it sits inside the box with its proportions kept. Max scales it uniformly until the loosest axis is met, so it covers the box and overflows top and bottom. Individual, here X Fill with Y None, stretches only the width to the box and keeps the natural height.
> One asset, one box, four answers. The rule decides which axis wins.


## Justification

*Where the asset sits inside the point, per axis.*

Justification aligns a point on the asset's bounds (`From`) with a point on the point's bounds (`To`), independently per axis: `Min`, `Center`, `Max`, `Pivot`, or a `Custom` value, with `To` defaulting to mirroring `From`. Ground-snapping is the everyday case, asset bottom to bounds bottom on Z, and reads as one axis toggled with `From` and `To` on `Min`.


> Figure: Six one-axis panels, each with the same dashed bounds span and the same shorter asset bar. A filled dot marks the From point on the asset, an open ring marks the To point on the bounds, and in every panel the two coincide where justification moved the asset. Min to Min, Center to Center and Max to Max land the asset inside the span at its start, middle and end. Min to Max parks the asset entirely outside past the bounds end, Max to Min entirely outside before the bounds start, and Pivot to Min puts the asset pivot cross on the bounds start with the asset hanging either side of it.
> Two dropdowns, one rule: the From point moves onto the To point.


Custom values can come from attributes, so justification can vary per point, which is how staggered or attribute-driven alignment is authored without touching transforms downstream.

## Variations

*Per-entry randomization, and one distinction that decides everything about it.*

Variations add random offset, rotation and scale per point, with amplitudes authored on the entry (or the collection's globals). Each of the three channels is independently `Disabled`, applied `Before fitting`, or applied `After fitting`, and the two timings answer different needs:

- **`Before fitting`** varies the asset before scale-to-fit solves, so the fit and justification have the last word. A rotation changes the footprint the fit solves for: under `Min` and `Fill` a randomly rotated crate still ends up inside its cell, shrunk back inside where a per-axis fit cannot hold the rotated shape, while `Max` and `Average` fit the rotated footprint by their own rule and can overhang. A uniform scale is absorbed on every axis the fit sizes. An offset is scaled with the fit, then undone on every justified axis, so it only moves the asset along an axis left unjustified or justified from `Pivot`.
- **`After fitting`** perturbs the final result, so the variation survives untouched but can push the asset out of the fitted bounds: right for scatter that should feel loose.


> Figure: Three rows, Offset, Rotation and Scale, each pairing Before fitting on the left with After fitting on the right, all under the default fit: uniform Min and centred justification. Every panel holds the same dashed point bounds with the point at its centre, and a faint outline marks where the crate lands with no variation. Offset: before fitting the crate lands on that outline, undone by justification; after fitting it sits shifted sideways off the point and overhangs the bounds on one side. Rotation: before fitting the crate is turned and shrunk until its turned footprint fits inside the bounds; after fitting it keeps its fitted size, turned, and its corners cross the bounds above and below. Scale: before fitting the crate lands on the outline again, absorbed by the fit; after fitting it is larger than the outline and overhangs the bounds on every side.
> Same variation, two timings, two results. The timing is the setting that matters.


## Vanilla parity

*Staged defaults fit; a bare spawner does not.*

**Staging : Distribute** ships with fitting on: uniform `Min` scale-to-fit and justification active on all three axes. A vanilla Static Mesh Spawner does none of that, it spawns the mesh at the point's transform as-is, so the same points produce visibly different results through staging than through a bare spawner. The defaults are historical and frozen: productions depend on them, so they will not change.


> **Warning.**
> To reproduce vanilla spawner behavior exactly, turn the fit off explicitly: `Scale to Fit` to `None`, and all three justification axes disabled. Anything less leaves a default rule active, and the result quietly differs from what the same points would have spawned without staging.



> Figure: Three panels share one dashed point-bounds box, one point and one crate. In the Vanilla spawner panel the crate sits at its natural size on the point transform and overhangs the bounds on every side. In the Staging defaults panel the same crate is Min-scaled and justified to sit inside the box. In the third panel, with Scale to Fit None and justification off, the crate is drawn identically to the vanilla panel: the off-switches restore the vanilla outcome exactly.
> Defaults on the left of each comparison are not neutral. The off-switches are.


## Where fitting runs

*At distribution by default, or as its own pass.*

**Staging : Distribute** applies fitting as it stages, with per-entry overrides honored by default, so most graphs never need more. The standalone **Staging : Fitting** exists for the second pass: it resolves bounds either from staged picks through the Map, or straight from a mesh path attribute for points that never went through a collection, and runs the same scale, justification and variation stack.

Two situations call for it:

- **After a swap.** [Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming) rewrites picks without re-fitting, and the original fit was solved against the *source* entry's bounds. If the replacement's footprint differs, a re-fit pass restores the intent.
- **Points fitted against something other than their pick**, or picks made in `Point Attributes` mode, where only the path attribute survives.

Fitting can also record what it did: the computed offset is written to a `FittingOffset` attribute on request, and **Staging : Spline Mesh** reads it to deform segments consistently with the fit.

title: Selecting Entries
description: How each point gets its entry: Staging : Distribute, seeds and determinism, category routing, and the selector family.
body:
Selection is one question asked per point: given this collection, which entry? **Staging : Distribute** asks it, and a **Selector** sub-node answers it.

## The hub

_Distribute asks, a selector answers, the pick gets recorded._

**Staging : Distribute** takes points and collection(s) _(a constant asset, or a per-point path attribute)_, consults the selector wired into its **Selector** pin for every point, and records the winning entry as the pick ([The Collection Map](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/the-collection-map) covers what "recorded" means). Point filters on the node narrow which points participate at all; by default, points that end up with no valid pick are pruned.

A selector is required. A Distribute with an empty **Selector** pin errors on execution, which makes it the most common first-contact failure: wire a **Selector : Classic** in weighted-random mode.

The node ships preconfigured entry points for its two re-distribution uses, **Staging : Redistribute** and **Staging : Randomize Materials**; both are this same node reading an upstream pick instead of making a first one, and [Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming) picks them up.

## Seeds and determinism

_By default, only the point's seed matters._

A pick is deterministic: same points, same collection, same settings, same result. Out of the box the roll folds in nothing but the point's own seed attribute; the selector's `Seed Components` setting can additionally fold in its own local seed, and the node and component seeds, which travel as a pair: enabling either of those two folds both.

> **Warning.**
> Adding or removing an entry, or changing any weight, reshapes the whole weighted table, so every point in the collection's reach re-rolls, never only the points that could have picked the changed entry. Treat the entry list of a shipped collection as layout-affecting, and use [Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming) when the goal is changing _what spawns_ without changing _what was decided_.

Some selectors are deterministic by construction and ignore the seed entirely: **Selector : Interleaved** reads point order, **Selector : Noise Field** reads world position, **Selector : Closest Match** is a pure nearest-value match. For those, re-rolling means changing what they read, never the seed.

## Categories

_Route points to a slice of the collection by name._

Every selector can restrict itself to a category, either a constant or read per point from a name attribute. Three details carry the semantics:

* A **blank category is a real value**: it routes to the uncategorized entries, never to the whole collection.
* A category the collection does not have triggers `Missing Category Behavior`: skip the point, fall back to the whole pool, or fall back to the uncategorized pool.
* Matching is by name, preserving authored casing without being case-sensitive.

## The selectors

_Eight ways to answer "which entry", each one sentence here and a full page in the node library._

| Selector                                                                                                              | Picks by                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Selector : Classic**                             | Weighted random, uniform random, or an index you supply per point. The baseline.                                                                                                                             |
| **Selector : Best Fit**                           | Comparing the point's bounds against every entry's staged bounds, by volume, per-axis size, or aspect ratio, then rolling among the best matches.                                                            |
| **Selector : Closest Match**                 | Matching point attributes against entry property values across one or more axes; pure nearest match, no randomness.                                                                                          |
| **Selector : Density-Weighted**           | Point density, bending the weighted roll toward uniform at low density or sharpened weights at high density.                                                                                                 |
| **Selector : Noise Field**                     | Sampling a wired noise stack at the point's world position and mapping the value across the weight bands: spatially coherent variety.                                                                        |
| **Selector : Range-Based**                     | Entries declaring value ranges on their properties; a point picks among the entries whose ranges contain its values on every axis.                                                                           |
| **Selector : Interleaved**                     | Point order, spreading entries evenly along the sequence: pattern-free variety without long runs.                                                                                                               |
| **Selector : Curve-Remapped Weight** | Each entry's own float-curve property evaluated at a per-point driver, so an entry's likelihood varies along a gradient. A curve at or below zero drops the entry entirely, so curves double as range gates. |

Several of these read the collection's custom properties as their inputs: Closest Match compares against them, Range-Based reads its ranges from them, Curve-Remapped evaluates curves stored in them. [Collection Properties](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties) is where those values come from.

> **Warning.**
> A selector shapes only the first pick. Descent into sub-collections is always weighted-random on the child's own weights, whatever selector made the top-level pick: a **Selector : Best Fit** choosing a sub-collection entry size-matches the subtree's aggregate bounds, and the leaf inside it is then a plain weighted roll.

## Modifiers

_Selectors that wrap selectors._

Three modifiers change how an inner selector's answers play out, and because they are selectors themselves, they nest:

* **Selector Modifier : Anti-Repeat** re-rolls the inner selector while its pick matches recent history, trading determinism for runs without visible repeats: history lives per processing run, and runs split along the machine's core count, so results reproduce on one machine without being portable across machines.
* **Selector Modifier : Cascade** takes several selectors in priority order and returns the first valid pick, which is how "try the range match, fall back to weighted random" is spelled.
* **Selector Modifier : Quota** enforces per-entry caps and minimums read from collection properties: capped entries leave the candidate pool before the inner selector rolls, and minimums are reserved evenly across the points.

> Figure: A Staging : Distribute node wired to a nested selector stack: an outer Quota layer, annotated removes exhausted entries, contains an Anti-Repeat layer, annotated retries recent repeats, which contains a Best Fit core, annotated scores bounds. A tapered reference arc, heavy at the collection end, runs from the stack to a weighted collection panel. The nesting shows one composed decision: the innermost selector picks, each wrapper only constrains or retries it.
> One composed decision per point: the core picks, the wrappers constrain.

> **Note.**
> An unconnected modifier falls back to plain weighted random inside itself, so a **Selector Modifier : Quota** alone is a legitimate node: caps and minimums applied to the default roll.

**The Legacy mode**

_The old inline distribution settings, kept alive for old graphs._

Nodes saved before the selector system carry `Selector Mode = Legacy`, where the old inline Index / Random / Weighted Random settings still apply and the **Selector** pin is ignored. Legacy mode runs a **Selector : Classic** internally and warns on every execution; it is scheduled for removal. Migrating is mechanical: wire a **Selector : Classic** configured the way the inline settings were, and switch the mode to `External`.

title: Staging Pipelines
description: Rebuilding staging is the moment a collection bakes its data, and staging pipelines are how you attach your own logic to it: Blueprintable objects on the collection that run with every rebuild, entry by entry.
body:
Rebuilding staging is the moment a collection bakes its data, and staging pipelines are how you attach your own logic to it: Blueprintable objects on the collection that run with every rebuild, entry by entry. Anything a team would otherwise enforce by hand across a hundred entries, naming-driven tags, derived properties, convention checks, becomes a pipeline that keeps enforcing it.

## What a pipeline is

*An instanced object on the collection, running at rebuild time, in the editor only.*

A pipeline is a Blueprint (or C++) subclass of the collection staging pipeline base, added to a collection's `Staging Pipelines` array. Several compose in array order, later ones seeing what earlier ones changed. Everything about them is editor-side: pipelines run during rebuilds, never during cooking, and ship nothing to runtime; what they leave behind is baked into the collection like any hand-authored value.

The hook surface today centers on entries.

## The hooks

*Three events, one contract.*

| Hook | Fires |
|---|---|
| `On Pre Rebuild` | Once, before the rebuild touches entries. |
| `On Process Entry` | Once per re-staged entry, after its staging data is baked, with the entry index and whether it is a sub-collection. |
| `On Post Rebuild` | Once, after the rebuild completes. |

Inside a hook, context helpers hand back the owning collection and, during `On Process Entry`, the current entry index. The contract is small: mutate entry *values* in `On Process Entry`, never add or remove entries there; sub-collections recursed into do not run their own pipelines; and a rebuild triggered from inside a hook does not re-fire the hooks, so a pipeline that touches staging cannot recurse into itself.

## What a hook can reach

*The property system and the assets themselves.*

Pipelines speak the same property system as everything else. The accessor nodes read and write by name: declared properties at the entry, category or collection tier, and reflected members on one entry or on the collection itself; a switch-on-collection-type node serves pipelines shared across types (**Collection Accessor Nodes**, **Switch on Collection Type**). The **Collection Staging Pipeline** page covers the hooks themselves.

A companion inspection library reads the referenced meshes: triangle and vertex counts, LOD counts, bounds, material slots. Put together, that is the shape of most real pipelines: read something true about the asset, write it somewhere the rest of the system uses. A pipeline that reads each mesh's triangle count and writes it to a cost property has, in one hook, produced the input a **Selector Modifier : Quota** budgets by ([Collection Properties](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties), [Selecting Entries](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/selecting-entries)).

title: Staging & Spawning
description: Turning staged picks into scene content: the spawn route for each entry type, and sockets as attachment points.
outline: Mixed picks need no splitting to work
The Map goes into the spawner's override pin
body:
Staging decides and records the pick; spawning happens later, in vanilla mesh spawners driven by **PCGEx Mesh Selector Staged**, or in the dedicated **Staging :** spawn nodes for actors, levels and PCG data.

## Routing by type

_One staged dataset, one route per entry type._

| Entry type    | Route                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Mesh          | Vanilla **Static Mesh Spawner**, with **Staging Data** as its mesh selector. |
| Skinned mesh  | Vanilla **Skinned Mesh Spawner**, with the **Staging Data (Skinned)** of the same selector -- see the caveat on that page: the engine's skinned spawner does not expose a selector picker yet. |
| Actor         | **Staging : Spawn Actors**                                                                                   |
| Level         | **Staging : Spawn Level**                                                                                     |
| PCG data      | **Staging : Load PCGData**                                                                                   |
| Generic       | Nothing spawns it. The asset path is read back onto the points, for whatever consumes the asset, by **Staging : Load Properties**; see [Collections of Anything](concept:working-with-pcgex/tips-and-tricks/collections-of-anything). |
| Path segments | **Staging : Spline Mesh**, meshes deformed along a path.                                                 |

> **Tip.**
> **Mixed picks need no splitting to work**
>
> Every staging spawn node follows through on the entries matching its own type and ignores the rest, so a mixed staged dataset can be wired to **Staging : Spawn Actors** and **Staging : Spawn Level** in parallel and each takes its share.

Splitting is for being explicit about it: **Staging : Type Filter** routes points by resolved entry type, its `Pin Per Type` mode giving one output pin per type, and its `Entry Shape` mode splitting along a different seam entirely, points whose entry is a resolved leaf versus points whose entry is a sub-collection. 

> The type roster is read from the registry, never hardcoded, so custom collection types registered by other plugins appear as routes on their own.

> Figure: STILL | id: spawning-route-graph | SHOWS: A working spawn stage: one staged dataset split by type and fed to the mesh spawner and the actor spawn node, with the Map visibly reaching everything including the spawner override pin | FRAME: A PCG graph with Staging : Distribute feeding Staging : Type Filter in Pin Per Type mode, its Mesh pin wired to a Static Mesh Spawner and its Actor pin wired to Staging : Spawn Actors, the Map wire reaching Type Filter, Spawn Actors, and the Static Mesh Spawner override pin | CALLOUTS: The Map wired into the Static Mesh Spawner override pin first, then the Type Filter per-type output pins, then the spawner with its mesh selector set to the staged selector | SOURCE: A small demo graph over an Omni Collection with mesh and actor entries | NOTE: The Map-to-override-pin wire is the one thing this shot must make unmissable
> The split happens on resolved entry types, so one collection can feed every route at once.

## Meshes

_The vanilla spawner does the spawning; the selector feeds it picks._

There is no PCGEx mesh spawner, deliberately: instanced-mesh spawning is what the vanilla **Static Mesh Spawner** already does well. **PCGEx Mesh Selector Staged** slots into that node's mesh selector, reads the pick hash and the Map, and hands the spawner its instance lists directly, applying the pick's material variant and the entry's component descriptor on the way.

> **Danger.**
> **The Map goes into the spawner's override pin**
>
> The Static Mesh Spawner has no Map input of its own, so the selector reads it from the node's override pin: wire the Collection Map there. Without it the selector cannot resolve a single pick, and nothing about the node suggests the connection.

> **Note.**
> A _mesh selector_ is a vanilla concept: the swappable brain inside the Static Mesh Spawner. It is unrelated to the **Selector** sub-nodes of [Selecting Entries](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/selecting-entries), which decide picks upstream. The two meet in this one node and nowhere else.

Entries' custom properties can also be packed into per-instance **Custom Primitive Data** through the selector's layout settings, which puts collection-authored values in reach of materials, per instance, with no attribute plumbing.

## Actors

_Spawned in batch, cleaned up by PCG, faithful to their capture._

**Staging : Spawn Actors** resolves actor entries, loads the classes in one batch, and spawns per point. Entries that carry a captured property delta ([Capturing Scenes](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes)) get it re-applied on spawn, so the actor ends up configured exactly as captured. Construction scripts run before the delta lands, against class defaults: a Blueprint that generates content from a component it also captured builds from the class version of that component. Spawned actors are registered as PCG-managed, so regeneration cleans them up like any other generated content, and each point can record a reference to the actor it produced for downstream graphs.

## Levels

_The spawn form follows the context: editor content while authoring, streaming at runtime._

**Staging : Spawn Level** places one level per point. While authoring, the level's actors are duplicated into the current level as ordinary, individually selectable content, or as one Level Instance actor per point with `Spawn As Level Instance`. At runtime, and for components generating at runtime, each point streams the level in instead. Every form is PCG-managed and cleaned up on regeneration.

## PCG data

_Staged points become more PCG data, recursively if you let it._

**Staging : Load PCGData** loads each picked PCG data asset once, then instantiates its contents per point, transformed into the point's frame. Data can route to custom output pins by name, and cluster data inside the assets is re-indexed per instance, so each instance's Vtx and Edges stay paired to their own.

This route is the one that chains. A level exported to PCG data ([Capturing Scenes](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/capturing-scenes)) generates its own per-type collections on the way, and what **Staging : Load PCGData** emits is _staged points again_, with a merged Collection Map covering those embedded collections. Spawning the arrangement is the rest of this page one more time: wire the output and its Map into the mesh spawner and the spawn nodes, and the whole captured scene comes out through the ordinary routes.

## Along paths

_Segments get meshes, deformed._

**Staging : Spline Mesh** walks path segments and builds one spline mesh component per segment, taking its mesh from staged picks or picking live from a mesh collection with its own **Selector** pin. It reads the `FittingOffset` attribute that [Fitting](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/fitting) can write, so segment deformation stays consistent with how the points were fitted.

## Sockets

_Attachment points, as points._

Entries' baked sockets ([Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collections)) become usable through **Staging : Load Sockets**: for every staged point it emits one point per socket on a dedicated **Sockets** output, transformed into the host point's frame, with the socket's name, tag and category available as attributes. Those points are ordinary points, so the attachment workflow is the whole toolkit again, filter them, stage _them_, spawn accessories at them.

> For points that carry a mesh path but never went through a collection, **Sample : Sockets** emits socket points the same way, straight from the mesh, consuming its input rather than forwarding it.

title: Swapping & Theming
description: Reskinning a result after distribution: Variant Collections, pick rewriting, and material re-rolls.
body:
A distributed layout is a set of decisions, and themes should not have to re-make them: the desert village and the snow village are the same picks wearing different assets. Swapping rewrites what a pick _resolves to_ while leaving the pick itself, and its layout, untouched.

## Variant Collections

_A layer of overrides on top of collections that keep working without it._

A Variant Collection declares **sources**, the collections it themes, and overrides for their entries. It stores no library of its own: every row is "when the pick was this source entry, resolve to this instead". Three kinds of authoring:

* **Per-entry swaps**: an explicit replacement for one source entry. The replacement is a full entry, so it can be a different asset, different materials, different fitting, even a different _type_: a mesh swapped for an actor is legal.
* **Asset Swaps**: asset-path rules, "every entry staging this asset swaps to this", one rule covering however many entries reference the asset, with explicit per-entry swaps winning over rules.
* **Pass-through**, the default: entries with no swap resolve as themselves. A variant only has to name what changes.

Nothing is baked: mappings resolve against the live sources each time a consumer runs, with rows bound to source entries by stable entry ids, so a source that gains, loses, or reorders entries keeps resolving and edits land on the next execution with no re-save of the variant. The one thing a variant needs from its source is those ids. They are minted when the source is opened in the editor and persist only once the source is saved, so a source never saved since then resolves nothing, and **Staging : Swap** says so at run time; a single row whose entry was deleted is skipped with its own warning.

## The Swaps editor

_Sources on the left of the arrow, your overrides on the right._

Opening a Variant Collection shows the **Swaps** grid: one group per source collection, one tile per source entry, each tile either dimmed pass-through or carrying its declared swap. Declaring starts from a copy of the source entry, so swapping the asset is a one-field edit with weights and variations carried over, or from a fresh entry of any type.

> Figure: STILL | id: swapping-variant-editor | SHOWS: The Swaps grid with pass-through and swapped tiles side by side, reading as a mapping over a source collection | FRAME: A Variant Collection open on its Swaps tab, one source group expanded showing several dimmed pass-through tiles and at least two declared swaps, one swap selected with its payload in the right pane, the Add Source and Add Asset Swap buttons visible in the toolbar | CALLOUTS: A dimmed pass-through tile, a declared swap tile, the Asset Swaps group holding one path rule | SOURCE: A variant themed over an example-project mesh collection | NOTE: The dimmed versus declared contrast is the point of the shot
> Only the differences are authored; everything dimmed resolves as its source.

## Asset Swaps

_One rule per asset, covering every entry that stages it._

The toolbar's **Add Asset Swap** opens an asset picker with no class filter, meshes, actors, levels, anything a source might stage. Picking an asset authors a rule: every source entry staging that asset swaps to the rule's payload, across all declared sources at once, so a placeholder staged by three sources retargets in one move.

> When more than one rule matches the same asset, the first wins.

**Asset Swaps entries are owned by the Variant Collection**

Rules gather in their own **Asset Swaps** group in the grid. A rule tile shows the asset it matches; once a payload is declared it shows the replacement, with the matched asset as its corner badge like any other swap tile. If a declared source already stages the picked asset, the payload seeds from a copy of that entry automatically, ready for the one-field asset edit. Otherwise the rule starts unset, dimmed like an unswapped entry and covering nothing, until its **+** declares the payload: a fresh entry of a chosen type, or a copy of a source entry staging the asset once one exists.

Entries covered by a rule wear a link marker in their source group, and edits to the rule's payload reach every one of them. To make one covered entry differ, specialize it: the covered tile's **+** declares an explicit per-entry swap, which overrides the rule for that entry alone while the rule keeps covering the rest.

> Rule tiles carry two removals. **×** revokes only the swap payload, so the asset reference stays as an unset rule and covered entries revert to pass-through; the delete button removes the rule entirely.

## Staging : Swap

_The rewrite, applied to staged points._

**Staging : Swap** takes staged points, the Map, and one or more Variant Collections, and rewrites each covered point's pick hash to the variant's override, emitting an updated Map that includes the variant collections. Uncovered points pass through unchanged when the node writes the layer it read; with a distinct output layer set, they land in that layer as a copy of their source pick. Variants stack: several can be supplied, later ones winning where they overlap, and the collection choice can be constant, per-data, or per-point, which is how "theme by region" is spelled: a per-point attribute naming the variant does it.

> **Warning.**
> Swapping does not re-fit. The points' transforms were fitted against the _source_ entries' bounds, and a replacement with a different footprint keeps the old fit. When a theme changes silhouettes rather than surfaces, chase the swap with **Staging : Fitting**; [Fitting](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/fitting) covers the pass.

Because the swap is a hash rewrite on ordinary points, it costs what a redistribution never could: nothing upstream re-runs, layouts stay byte-identical across themes, and the same staged dataset can be swapped differently per platform, per biome, or per run.

Cross-type replacement carries this further than reskinning. A swap can replace an entry with a different type entirely, or with a reference into another collection, which turns the source collection into a **greybox template**: a library of placeholder boxes distributed, fitted and iterated on with no real assets in it, while variants alone decide what actually spawns.

## One level down: materials

_The same move exists inside a single entry._

Mesh entries carry weighted material variants ([Collections](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collections)), and that pick is part of the hash too. Re-rolling it alone is the **Staging : Randomize Materials** preset of **Staging : Distribute**: every point keeps its entry, and only the material variant re-rolls.
