It composes with variant swaps, since a swapped entry's own variants are picked fresh on request.

title: The Collection Map
description: Once a pick is made, it has to travel: through filters, transforms, merges, and whatever else the graph does before spawning.
body:
Once a pick is made, it has to travel: through filters, transforms, merges, and whatever else the graph does before spawning. PCGEx moves it as two pieces, an attribute on the point and a small dataset beside it, and that pair is the contract the whole staging ecosystem is built on. ## The pick hash _One int64 holds the entire decision._ A staged point carries `PCGEx/CollectionEntry`, a single int64 packing three things: which collection the pick resolved in, which entry, and which material variant. Nested picks are already flattened at this stage, so an entry reached three sub-collections deep is named directly, and downstream nodes never re-walk the nesting. Because the pick is an ordinary attribute, staged points survive anything points survive: they can be merged with other staged points, filtered, partitioned, sorted, copied, written to and read from PCG data, and the decision rides along. A point carries **one pick per staging layer**. The attribute name is derived, never chosen: the default layer writes `PCGEx/CollectionEntry`, and a named `Staging Layer`, a setting every staging node carries, appends its name to it (`PCGEx/CollectionEntry/Props`). Property outputs mint layers the same way: a **Collection Entry** property written by a properties node lands as a pick on a layer named after that output, with no `Staging Layer` setting involved. Staging already-staged points on the same layer overwrites the earlier decision; a decision that must coexist with it gets its own layer, and each downstream consumer reads whichever layer it is set to. Most graphs never leave the default layer, and content that layers spatially, an accessory on a prop, a decal on a wall, still spawns from its own points, which is what socket points and copied datasets are for ([Staging & Spawning](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/staging-spawning)). > Points whose pick failed, no valid entry, a missing category, an exhausted quota, are pruned by default; with pruning off they carry a sentinel value instead, and downstream staging nodes skip them. ## The Map _The lookup that makes the hash resolvable, on its own pin._ The hash names a collection, and the **Collection Map** is where names get resolved: a small attribute set emitted on the **Map** pin, one row per collection the picks involve, including every nested sub-collection and any collection a written **Collection Entry** property points at. Downstream nodes take the points on one pin and the Map on the other, and can hand back the exact entry for any point. > Figure: A staged point carrying one attribute chip labeled PCGEx/CollectionEntry, decomposed into its three packed parts: collection, entry and variant. A reference arc runs from the collection part to the highlighted row of a small Map table listing collections by index, and on from that row to a collection panel named Props. Longer reference arcs run from the entry part to the highlighted Lamp entry inside the panel, and from the variant part to one highlighted variant swatch on that entry. The point carries only the chip, the Map carries only the collection list, and the entry stays in the asset. > Resolution is a lookup, so the data never grows with the number of picks. Keeping the lookup out of the points is what keeps staged data light: ten thousand staged points cost ten thousand int64s plus a Map with one row per collection, whatever the entries carry. The Map merges as readily as the points do: when staged branches meet, combine their Maps with the stock PCG **Merge Attributes** node and pass the result downstream, and every pick from either branch keeps resolving. > Figure: STILL | id: collection-map-merge | SHOWS: Maps from two staging branches combined by a stock Merge Attributes node into one Map feeding a downstream staging node | FRAME: A PCG graph with two staging branches, both Map pins wired into a Merge Attributes node, its output wired to the Map pin of a downstream staging node beside the merged points | CALLOUTS: The two Map wires entering Merge Attributes, the merged Map wire leaving it | SOURCE: Example project staging graph | NOTE: Author supplies this still, swap the src and this brief when it lands > The Map is ordinary attribute data, so vanilla merging is all it takes. ## The downstream contract _Every staging consumer takes the same two inputs._ Each node in the roster below takes staged points plus the Map, resolves picks, and does one job. One of them also talks back: **Staging : Load Properties** can emit a Map of its own, covering the collections referenced by any **Collection Entry** properties it writes.
NodeJob
**Staging : Fitting**Re-fit staged points against their entries' bounds.
**Staging : Swap**Rewrite picks to variant overrides.
**Staging : Type Filter**Route points by their resolved entry type, including one-pin-per-type splitting.
**Staging : Load Properties**Write entry data and custom properties onto the points.
**Staging : Load Sockets**Expand entries' sockets into new points.
**Staging : Spawn Actors**Spawn actor entries.
**Staging : Spawn Level**Spawn level entries as streaming instances.
**Staging : Load PCGData**Load PCG data entries into the graph.
**Staging : Spline Mesh**Build spline mesh components along staged path segments.
Resolution work scales with _unique_ picks, not with points: a consumer resolves each distinct hash once and reuses the result, which is why reading a dozen properties onto a hundred thousand points costs a handful of lookups. ## Two output modes _The Map is the default; plain attributes are the escape hatch._ **Staging : Distribute** offers two ways to record the pick: * **`Collection Map`**, the default: the hash plus the Map, everything above applies. * **`Point Attributes`**: the resolved asset path written as a plain soft-path attribute, optionally with per-slot material path attributes beside it. No Map is emitted, and the resolvable identity is gone; what remains is readable by anything that understands a path attribute, including vanilla spawners with no PCGEx involvement. Point Attributes mode is for leaving the ecosystem on purpose. Staying in Collection Map mode costs nothing at spawn time, because the mesh spawn route reads the hash directly ([Staging & Spawning](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/staging-spawning)). ## Re-distribution _A pick can be partially re-decided, because the hash separates its parts._ **Staging : Distribute** can also take already-staged points as its source and re-roll only part of the decision: * **Redistribute Collections** re-picks points whose entry is a sub-collection, descending again while leaving direct picks alone. * **Redistribute Micro Cache** keeps every entry pick and re-rolls only the material variant. Both ship as preconfigured palette entries, **Staging : Redistribute** and **Staging : Randomize Materials**. [Swapping & Theming](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/swapping-and-theming) builds on the same separability.

title: Clusters
description: Point data says where things are.
outline: Vanilla nodes, and what the pairing survives
A cached cluster is checked by point count alone
Pack and Unpack are for storage
body:
Point data says where things are. A cluster adds which of them connect, carried as two point datasets read as one: vertices in the first, connections in the second. Keeping those two halves paired is most of what cluster work involves. ## Two datasets, one structure _Vtx carry positions, Edges carry which Vtx connect._ A cluster is a pair. **Vtx** is a point dataset where each point is a vertex. **Edges** is a point dataset where each point is a connection. Every cluster node takes both, on two pins, and anything that edits one half has to account for the other. A cluster is at minimum two vertices and the edge joining them. There is no cluster of one: a vertex that ends up with no connection is dropped rather than emitted on its own. The pairing is carried in the data itself, not by the wires. Each half is tagged with its role, `PCGEx/Vtx` or `PCGEx/Edges`, and both carry a shared `PCGEx/Cluster` tag whose value is the pair's id. That is what lets a node receiving a tangle of datasets work out which Edges belong to which Vtx. Inside, two attributes do the connecting. Each Vtx carries `PCGEx/VData`, packing its **endpoint id** together with the number of edges it expects. Each Edge carries `PCGEx/EData`, packing the endpoint ids of the two vertices it joins. A node reading a cluster builds a lookup from ids to current row positions, then resolves every edge through it. > Figure: Three tables in a row. On the left a Vtx table with columns row, id and edges, headed PCGEx slash VData, whose ids are deliberately not in row order. In the middle a small lookup table mapping each id to the row it currently sits at. On the right an Edges table with columns row, start and end, headed PCGEx slash EData. Green arrows leave one edge row, reach the two lookup rows for the ids it names, and only then continue into the two Vtx rows those ids resolve to. > An edge names ids, never rows. The lookup turns them into rows, every execution. That indirection is worth understanding, because everything else in this section follows from it. The id travels with the point as an attribute, so a vertex can move to a different row and still be found. What it cannot survive is being deleted, because then the id is not in the lookup at all, and any edge naming it has nowhere to go. ## Degree is the vocabulary _How many edges a vertex has is what nearly every cluster operation is phrased in terms of._ The plugin names three cases and uses them everywhere: a vertex with one edge is a **leaf**, with two is **binary**, and with more than two is **complex**. Refinements talk about stripping leaves, chain operations walk runs of binary vertices, and anything that converts to paths stops at the first complex one. That last one is also the bridge back to [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths). A path point is permanently binary: one predecessor, one successor, no room for a third. Complex is exactly what a path cannot express, and it is the reason to reach for a cluster at all. > Figure: One small cluster of eight vertices joined by nine edges, every vertex drawn identically as a ringed disc. Three of them are called out by name with the count beneath: one with a single edge is labelled leaf, degree 1; one with four edges is labelled complex, degree 4; one with two edges is labelled binary, degree 2. Nothing distinguishes the three except how many lines arrive at them. > Leaf, binary, complex. A path point is always the middle one. ## One Vtx dataset, several clusters _Each Edges dataset is one connected component._ A single Vtx dataset commonly pairs with several Edges datasets, and that is the normal output shape rather than an unusual one. When a generator finishes, it splits its result by connected component and emits one Edges dataset per island, all sharing the one Vtx dataset and the one pair tag. > Figure: On the left a single tall panel labelled Vtx holding fifteen ringed vertices in three spatially separate groups, with no connections drawn between any of them. On the right three separate panels labelled Edges, one level with each group, each holding only that group's connections drawn as lines with a small open square at the middle of every one, and the vertices themselves ghosted because they belong to the other dataset. All four panels carry the same tag, PCGEx slash Cluster colon 4821. > Three clusters, one Vtx dataset, one shared pair tag. Two nodes change that arity when you need it. **Cluster : Partition Vtx** gives each Edges dataset its own Vtx dataset, one to one, and **Cluster : Merge Vtx** collapses several back onto one shared Vtx dataset. Partitioning costs you the saving the shared shape exists for, since each cluster now carries its own copy of the vertices and the work done once per Vtx dataset is done once per cluster instead. Reach for it when something genuinely needs one Vtx dataset per cluster, rather than as a way of separating clusters. ## Vanilla nodes, and what the pairing survives _Cluster data is point data, so everything can touch it. Not everything should._ Vtx and Edges are ordinary point datasets, and PCGEx registers no pin type that would keep vanilla nodes away from them. The interchange runs both directions: cluster data flows into any point pin, and plain point data flows into any cluster pin. Every PCGEx node that outputs a cluster outputs a well-formed one, so nothing in this section applies to staying inside the plugin. It applies to the round trip out and back. Most of what you would reach a vanilla node for has a cluster-aware equivalent that uses the topology instead of ignoring it. **Cluster : Relax** moves vertices around without touching a single connection. **Cluster : Filter Vtx** and **Cluster : Refine** remove vertices and edges while keeping both halves consistent. **Cluster : Vtx Properties**, **Cluster : Edge Properties** and **Cluster : Sample Neighbors** derive attributes from what a vertex is connected to, which is the one thing a vanilla node cannot see. Going outside the family is worth it when nothing in it fits, and the rest of this section is about doing that with your eyes open. What survives depends on what the operation does to the two things the pairing rests on, the ids and the point count.
OperationOutcome
Rotating or scaling VtxSafe
Moving Vtx positionsTopology survives, but see the caching hint below
Reordering or sorting VtxSurvives in principle, since ids travel with the points, but see the caching hint below
Deleting VtxFatal. Edges naming them resolve to nothing, and the cluster fails to rebuild
Deleting Edge pointsThe remaining vertices expect edges that are gone, and the rebuild fails
Duplicating Vtx, or merging two Vtx datasetsSilently wrong. Ids collide, one copy wins the lookup, and the cluster builds anyway
Dropping the tags or the two attributesThe data stops being recognised as cluster data at all
> **Warning.** > **A cached cluster is checked by point count alone** > > Clusters are cached between nodes by default, and the check deciding whether a cached one still matches its data compares point counts. A vanilla operation that preserves the count therefore keeps the old cluster: sort your Vtx and every vertex in the cached cluster now reads the wrong point, move them and the positions refresh while the cached bounds do not, so proximity queries miss. > > It is the one case where the pairing looks intact and is not, which is why **Cluster : Repair** exists. Repair rebuilds the whole cluster from its attributes and is expensive, so it earns its place once, on the way back from a round trip you could not avoid. Staying inside the cluster family costs nothing and needs no repair. **What Cluster : Repair fixes, and what it cannot** Repair rebuilds every edge from scratch. It drops edges whose endpoints no longer resolve, re-splits the result by connected component, renumbers the ids on both halves, prunes vertices left with no edges, removes duplicate connections, and re-stamps the tags with a fresh pair id. It cannot recover a deleted vertex: the connections that named it are gone, and dropping those edges is the repair. It also cannot detect ids that collide inside a single Vtx dataset, because from the inside that damage looks like valid data. Three things to know before reaching for it. It is expensive, since every edge is resolved and the whole structure recompiled. It does delete points, despite its tooltip saying otherwise, since orphaned vertices and unresolvable edges both come out. And it moves every edge point to the midpoint between its endpoints by default, so it is not a pure topology fix. The node was called Sanitize Cluster in earlier versions, and several error messages still say so. ## Working with many clusters _One node, many clusters, each processed on its own._ A cluster node takes everything on its two pins, works out which Edges belong to which Vtx, and processes each resulting cluster independently. Work that depends only on the Vtx dataset, like the id lookup, is done once and shared by every cluster paired with it, which is the practical reason the one-Vtx-many-Edges shape exists. To loop over clusters one at a time, **loop over the Edges**. Each Edges dataset is one cluster, so a loop over that pin is already a loop over clusters. Inside the body, **Find Clusters** in `Vtx from Edges` mode takes the Vtx collection on its input and the loop's single Edges dataset on its search pin, and hands back the matching pair. That costs essentially nothing: Find Clusters matches the tags and forwards the data through rather than copying any of it. The same node earns its keep outside loops. Because it can pull a pair out of a mixed bag, both halves of a cluster can travel through one named reroute together and be separated again wherever they are needed, instead of running two parallel wires the length of a graph. > **Note.** > **Pack and Unpack are for storage** > > **Cluster : Pack** folds a cluster into a single dataset, which is what you want when exporting to a PCG Data Asset and two pins are inconvenient to carry. It is not a way to make looping easier: the Edges pin already gives you one dataset per cluster, and packing adds a fold and an unfold for nothing. **Why "cluster" and not "graph"** Partly because "graph" already means the PCG graph you are standing in. Mostly because the plugin uses it for something else: a **graph** is the transient structure a generator builds up while it works, before any of it is point data, and a **cluster** is the paired datasets that come out and travel on pins. Different lifetimes, different things. The word survives in user-facing names only where it means a specific mathematical object, as in **Cluster : Edge Dual Graph**, or where it names the Blueprint extension point, as in **Cluster : Build Custom Graph**. ## Related * [Building & Refining](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) -- where clusters come from, and how to cut them down * [Cluster Sketch](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/cluster-sketch) -- authoring one by hand instead of generating it, in its own plugin and its own book * [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) -- the structure that cannot branch, and how to convert between the two * [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- Vtx and Edge filters, and why they only work where a cluster exists * **Clusters** -- every cluster node, with its settings

title: Building & Refining
description: Generate connections generously, then take away the ones you did not want.
outline: Coincidence prevention makes probe order matter
body:
Generate connections generously, then take away the ones you did not want.

## Where clusters come from

*Points in, cluster out, with the generator deciding what counts as a connection.*

The generators split by what they consume.

**From a point cloud.** **Cluster : Delaunay 2D** and **Cluster : Delaunay 3D** triangulate, connecting points that share a circumcircle. **Cluster : Voronoi 2D** and **Cluster : Voronoi 3D** build the dual, the cell boundaries around each point. **Cluster : Convex Hull 3D** takes the outer shell. **Cluster : Connect Points** is the open-ended one, driven by probes.

**From something that already has structure.** **Path : To Clusters** turns ordered points into connections, **Mesh to Clusters** and **Dynamic Mesh to Clusters** read geometry, **Clipper2 : Decompose** breaks a footprint into convex cells, and **Get Sketch Data**, from the [Cluster Sketch](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/cluster-sketch) companion plugin, reads clusters authored by hand on actors.

**From an existing cluster.** **Cluster : Cell Diagram** turns cells into vertices, **Cluster : Edge Dual Graph** turns edges into vertices, and **Cluster : Connect Vtx** adds connections to a cluster you already have.


> **Warning.**
> **Voronoi builds its own vertices**
>
> A Delaunay cluster's vertices are your input points, attributes and all. A Voronoi cluster's vertices are the **corners of the cells**, which are new points that never carried your attributes. Your original points come back on the optional **Sites** pin, which is where to look when a Voronoi result seems to have lost everything you wrote onto it.



> Figure: Two panels side by side, separated by a vertical rule, built from one triangulation of the same eight scattered points. On the left the Delaunay result: fifteen edges joining those same eight points, which are drawn as ringed vertices. On the right the Voronoi result: the cell boundary edges, whose vertices sit at the cell corners, nowhere near the input points, which appear faded and are keyed as coming back on the Sites pin.
> Same eight points. Only one of these outputs is made of them.


### Probes, for connecting a cloud

**Cluster : Connect Points** has no opinion of its own about what should connect. It takes **probe** sub-nodes, and each probe answers one question for one point: given the points nearby, which of them should this one connect to.

Around seventeen ship. Some look at one point at a time, wired as `Probe : ` nodes, deciding by proximity, direction, index or an attribute comparison. Others consider the whole dataset at once, wired as `G-Probe : ` nodes, doing things like nearest-neighbour graphs, clustering, spanning structures and flow-following. They mix freely on the same pin.

Several probes on one pin **union** their proposals. Every probe adds connections, none removes another's, and the result is every connection any of them wanted. Two filter pins narrow who participates: one decides which points may start a connection, the other which points may be connected to.


> **Note.**
> **Coincidence prevention makes probe order matter**
>
> By default a point will not accept two connections heading in nearly the same direction. That makes the probes order-sensitive, since a probe earlier on the pin can claim a direction and leave a later one with nowhere to go. Turn it off and the probes become fully independent of each other.


Search radius lives on each probe rather than on the node, so different probes on one pin can reach different distances.

### What every generator does at the end

Three behaviours are common to all of them, and each surprises somebody:

- **Points that got no connection are dropped.** No setting keeps them, and **Remove Small Clusters** only discards more, dropping whole clusters that fall below a Vtx and edge count you set.
- **The result splits by connected component**, one Edges dataset per island.
- **Vtx order changes.** Survivors come out grouped by cluster, all of one component's Vtx together and then the next, keeping their relative order inside each group. Only a result that is a single component keeps the simple compacted order. Generators that make new points are the exception again: those come out in spatial order.

## Refining

*Take a dense cluster and remove connections by rule until it is the one you wanted.*

**Cluster : Refine** does the removing, and what comes out depends on a `Mode` setting that changes the shape of the output entirely. This is the thing to understand first, because it explains why refinement sometimes changes your point count and sometimes does not.

| Mode | What comes out |
|---|---|
| **Clusters** | A rebuilt cluster containing only the surviving edges, with any vertex they orphaned removed. The default |
| **Points** | Two plain point datasets, **Kept Edges** and **Removed Edges**. No cluster at all |
| **Attribute** | The original cluster, unchanged, with a boolean written on each edge |


> Figure: A dense nine-vertex cluster is drawn at the top, labelled source, with three flow arrows fanning down to three panels that draw their results at the source's own size. The first, Clusters, holds a rebuilt sparse cluster: the removed edges are not there at all, and neither is the one vertex they orphaned. The second, Points, holds two labelled groups of loose square edge points, Kept Edges and Removed Edges, with no connections drawn at all. The third, Attribute, holds the original dense cluster intact, its surviving edges green and its removed ones faded and struck through.
> One rule, three outputs. Only the first mode removes anything.


The rules themselves group into a handful of kinds. Some compare **edge length** at each vertex, keeping or removing the longest or shortest. Some compare a **score** and need heuristics wired in to produce one. Some apply **geometric tests** from proximity-graph theory, like Gabriel and beta skeleton, or remove edges that cross. Some are **structural**, extracting a minimum spanning tree, finding the edges whose removal would split the cluster, or stripping leaves once or repeatedly. One traces against **world geometry**. Two are driven by **filters**, which is how a condition you author decides what survives.

**Cluster : Relax** is the sibling that never touches topology. It moves vertices around under Laplacian, force-directed, Verlet or fitting rules, and every connection stays exactly as it was.

## Bridging and cutting

*Two operations that get confused, and do opposite things.*

**Cluster : Connect** takes separate clusters and **inserts** connections between them, joining islands by their closest vertices. **Refine : DFS (Tarjan)**, one of the refinement rules, **finds** the edges whose removal would split a cluster, and by default takes them out.

One builds bridges, the other identifies them. The names do not help, so it is worth holding the distinction deliberately.

**Cluster : Cut** is the third in this family, using paths as cutting geometry against a cluster.

## Related

* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- the model, the pairing, and what breaks it
* [Paths & Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/paths-and-clusters) -- converting in and out, and what each direction costs
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- Vtx and Edge filters, which drive the filter-based refinements
* **Clusters** -- every generator, refinement and relaxation, with its settings

title: Common Cluster Operations
description: A task-oriented index into the cluster nodes. Being rewritten once the cluster nodes themselves are documented.
body:
This page is being rebuilt.

Its job is to answer "I want to do X, which node does it?" across the cluster family. The previous version was written before the cluster nodes were documented from source, and a source pass found node names that do not exist, one entry describing the opposite of what its node does, and a link pointing at an unrelated node. Rather than leave those in place, it is empty until the per-node documentation exists to build a truthful index from.

Until then, [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) covers the model and [Building & Refining](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) covers where clusters come from. The node library under **Clusters** lists every node.

title: Paths & Clusters
description: Ordered points and connected points answer different questions, and a lot of procedural work needs both answers about the same geometry.
outline: Attributes survive the crossing better than structure does
body:
Ordered points and connected points answer different questions, and a lot of procedural work needs both answers about the same geometry. Crossing between the two is routine rather than exceptional, and the crossing nodes are some of the most useful in the plugin.

## Paths into clusters

*One node, and a setting that decides whether junctions appear.*

**Path : To Clusters** reads paths and builds a cluster from them. On its own that is a mechanical conversion: each path's consecutive points become connections, and a closed path contributes its seam.

The setting that matters is the fusing. With it on, which is the default, points that land in the same place weld into one shared vertex. **Every point is a candidate, not just the two at each end of a path**: a path whose last point lands partway along another welds there just as readily as two paths meeting end to end, and a path can even weld to itself. That weld is where junctions come from: two paths that merely crossed on screen now genuinely meet, and the vertex they share has a degree of three or four instead of two. Everything a cluster can express that a path cannot starts here.

What the conversion costs is order. A cluster records which points connect, never which came first, and once points have welded there is nothing saying which path a given point belonged to. Carry that in an attribute before converting if you need it downstream.

## Clusters into paths

*Several extractors, each answering a different question about the structure.*

| Node | What comes out |
|---|---|
| **Cluster : Break to Paths** | Runs of degree-two vertices, each becoming one path. Chains stop wherever a junction appears |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cells** | The closed region enclosing each seed point, as a path around its boundary |
| **Pathfinding : Find All Cells** | Every closed region in the cluster, exhaustively |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cluster Hull** | One path per cluster, tracing its outer boundary |
| The **Pathfinding :** family proper | The route between two points, as a path |

Cells are the one worth dwelling on, because they answer a question that is awkward any other way: *what regions did these connections enclose?* Build a cluster over a scatter of points, and the cells are the faces of the resulting mesh of connections. Each one comes back as a closed path you can offset, inset, subdivide or spawn along.


> Figure: Two panels joined by a flow arrow. On the left a cluster of twelve ringed vertices and fifteen edges, whose connections enclose four regions of different sizes and shapes. On the right the same four regions have become four separate closed paths, each drawn just inside the border it came from, each carrying order chevrons all the way round and a ringed marker at the point it starts from. The original cluster edges are faded behind them.
> The faces the connections enclosed, handed back as paths you can operate on.


Coming back this way costs the junctions. A chain terminates at every vertex with more than two connections, so a cluster with one junction in the middle yields three paths rather than one, and the fact that they met is not recorded in any of them.

## The round trip

*Neither structure is the destination.*

The common shape of cluster work is a loop rather than a line. Scatter points, connect them into a cluster, refine the connections down to the ones you meant, extract cells or chains as paths, operate on those paths with everything the [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) family offers, and feed the result back in as the input to another cluster.

Each crossing is lossy in one direction and generous in the other, which is what makes the loop useful rather than circular. Going to a cluster buys adjacency and everything phrased in terms of degree. Coming back buys order, and with it every operation that needs to know what follows what: offsetting, subdividing, sweeping a mesh along a run.


> **Note.**
> **Attributes survive the crossing better than structure does**
>
> Both directions carry point attributes through. What each drops is the structural claim the other cannot hold, order in one direction and adjacency in the other. When something is lost that you needed, [Blending & Sampling](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/blending-and-sampling) against the pre-conversion data brings it back, since the geometry has not moved.


## Into pathfinding

The cell and hull extractors are named **Pathfinding :** for a reason: finding the boundary of a region is walking the cluster, the same traversal that finding a route between two points needs. Once a cluster exists, the whole [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) family is available on it, and everything it produces is a path.

## Related

* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- the model and the pairing
* [Building & Refining](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) -- where clusters come from, and cutting them down
* [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) -- ordered points, and why they cannot branch
* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- routes, cells and hulls, all of which come out as paths

title: Filters
description: Nearly every node in PCGEx reaches a moment where it has to decide whether to act on the element in front of it.
outline: A point filter on an edge pin reads the edge
A spatial filter on an attribute set reads the world origin
body:
Nearly every node in PCGEx reaches a moment where it has to decide whether to act on the element in front of it. Rather than each node growing its own conditions, one system answers that question everywhere: the condition is its own node, and you wire it in. Around seventy nodes accept one.

## What a filter is

*A filter is a question with a yes or no answer. What happens to the answer is the consumer's business.*

A filter node holds a condition and nothing else. It reads no points, writes no attributes, and produces no data of its own. The node you wire it into is what runs it, once per element, and what decides the consequence: one consumer keeps the elements that pass, another routes passes and failures to separate pins, a third fires an event wherever the answer changes.

The saving is in what you never have to build. **Filter : Distance** measures each point against a set of targets: it indexes the targets, runs the query and compares the result, and none of that touches your data. By hand it means writing a distance attribute, comparing it, then remembering to clean it up.

Most filters carry an `Invert` toggle that flips their verdict.

## The four families

*What a filter can see decides where it is allowed to go.*

Filter nodes are prefixed with their family, and that same word is the label on the node's output pin. The label is the passport.

| Family | Reads | Accepted by |
|---|---|---|
|  **Filter :** | One point: its attributes, its position, or its relationship to reference data you supply | Every filter pin, Vtx and Edge pins included |
|  **Data Filter :** | A whole dataset: its tags, its `@Data` attributes, its entry count, its bounds | Every filter pin |
|  **Vtx Filter :** | A vertex and what it connects to: degree, neighbour direction, edge angle | Only where a cluster exists |
|  **Edge Filter :** | An edge: its length, its direction, or a test run on its two endpoints | Only where a cluster exists |

The asymmetry is the part to hold on to. A point filter works everywhere, because a Vtx and an Edge are both points and the filter is handed the right index. A cluster filter needs topology that plain point data does not carry, so it belongs only where a cluster is in play. The editor will let you make the wrong connection: a Vtx filter drops onto an Edge pin without complaint and is discarded at execution with a warning, which reads as the filter having no effect.

Point filters, much the largest family, fall into three rough kinds. **Comparisons** test a value against a constant, another attribute, or a string. **Arithmetic and geometry** work on the point itself, through dot products, angles, modulo. **Spatial tests** measure against data you feed the filter: distance to targets, containment in bounds, inclusion in a spline. The **Filters** reference has the full roster, grouped the same way.


> **Warning.**
> **A point filter on an edge pin reads the edge**
>
> Wire **Filter : Compare (Numeric)** into an **Edge Filters** pin and it tests the attribute on the edge, not on the vertices at either end. Edges are points too, and a point filter binds to whichever dataset the pin is about. The attribute has to exist there.


## Filtering an attribute set

_Attribute rows are filtered like points, and a spatial filter will quietly agree to it._

Many PCGEx nodes take an attribute set where they take points, and filtering is one of them: **Uber Filter** and **Uber Filter (Cascade)** split or annotate the rows of an attribute set exactly as they would points. For a filter that reads attributes, which is most of them, this is genuinely the same operation and nothing is lost.


> **Danger.**
> **A spatial filter on an attribute set reads the world origin**
>
> An attribute set has no positions, so each row is handed to the filter as a default point: position `0,0,0`, no rotation, unit scale, default bounds. Attribute-reading filters do not care. **Filter : Distance**, the **Inclusion** filters, **Filter : Raycast** and every other filter that reads a position or bounds will happily run and answer for a stack of coincident points at the world origin.
>
> Nothing is logged, and the verdict is usually uniform, which reads as the filter having no effect rather than as a mistake. If a spatial question needs asking about an attribute set, turn its rows into real points first.


## Where they plug in

*The pin label tells you what the condition gates.*

The naming is consistent enough to read cold. A pin called **Filters**, or **Point Filters**, **Vtx Filters**, **Edge Filters**, decides *which elements the node processes*. A pin whose name ends in **Conditions** decides *where something happens*: **Path : Split** takes **Split Conditions**, **Path : Bevel** takes **Bevel Conditions**, **Path : Orient** takes **Flip Conditions**. The first kind narrows a set. The second marks positions inside it.


> Figure: Two filter nodes, Filter : Distance and Filter : Compare (Numeric), feeding a Filter Group set to AND, whose single output fans out to three consumers: the Filters pin of Transform Points, the Filters pin of Uber Filter which outputs Inside and Outside, and the Split Conditions pin of Path : Split.
> One group, three consumers, and three different pin names for the same connection.


A handful of nodes exist to run filters and little else:

| Node | What it does with the verdict |
|---|---|
| **Uber Filter** | Splits points to **Inside** and **Outside**, or in Write mode annotates them in place as a bool, a counter or a bitmask |
| **Uber Filter (Data)** | The same split at dataset level, keeping or dropping whole collections. When every filter it holds can judge a dataset on its own it asks each one once; otherwise it tests the elements and decides on how many passed, by All, Any, or a proportion |
| **Uber Filter (Cascade)** | Several filter pins tried in order, the first one a point satisfies claims it |
| **Cluster : Filter Vtx** | The cluster equivalent, splitting Vtx with an optional edge condition |

## Stacking and grouping

*Several filters on one pin is AND. **Filter Group** is how you get anything else.*

Connect three filters to one pin and all three must pass. Evaluation stops at the first failure, so the rest never run.

Everything beyond AND goes through **Filter Group**: one node, one **Filters** pin, and a `Mode` of `And` or `Or`. Its own `Invert` turns those into NAND and NOR, and the node subtitle reads `AND` or `OR` with `(NOT)` appended when it is inverted. To whatever consumes it a group is a single filter, because it combines its children internally and returns one verdict. That is also what lets groups nest.


> Figure: Four filter nodes feeding two Filter Groups set to AND, both of which feed a third Filter Group set to OR, whose output goes to the Filters pin of Transform Points.
> Two AND groups under an OR group: pass if either pair is satisfied.


Nesting has no depth limit, and groups sit alongside loose filters on the same pin. A group wired next to two individual filters reads as `(X OR Y) AND A AND B`.

One pattern is worth naming because the obvious construction is wrong. To keep everything *outside* several regions, put the region filters in an `Or` group and invert the group. Inverting each filter individually asks for points outside region A and outside B and outside C, which is a different and usually unintended question.


> **Note.**
> **Evaluation order comes from Priority**
>
> Filters are sorted by `Priority` before they run, lowest first. Every filter starts at zero, and the sort is stable, so filters left at the same priority keep the order you wired them in. Raising or lowering one is what moves it: to have a cheap test run before an expensive one, give it a lower priority. A non-zero value shows in the node subtitle as `[N]`.
>
> A group is the exception: its priority is its own value or the highest among its children, whichever is greater. Its `Priority` field is a floor rather than the number used, so a group holding one expensive filter sorts late however low you set it.


A few filters take filter pins of their own, and they all mean one thing: the question is redirected to a different element. **Filter : Check Nearest** runs its sub-filters against the nearest target point rather than the point being tested. **Edge Filter : Endpoints Check** runs them against the edge's two endpoints.

## When a filter fails

*Two policies on every filter node decide what happens, and their defaults differ.*

A filter can fail at its job in two ways, and every filter node carries a policy for each under `Warnings and Errors`. Both offer the same three choices: **Error**, **Pass**, **Fail**.

`Missing Data Policy` covers filters that take a data input of their own, like **Filter : Distance** and its **Targets** pin. When that input arrives empty, Error cancels the node, while Pass and Fail substitute a constant filter of that verdict. It defaults to Fail, so a distance filter with nothing to measure against rejects every point rather than waving them all through.

`Initialization Failure Policy` covers a filter that cannot bind what it needs, a misspelled attribute name being the usual cause. It defaults to Error. Pass drops the filter and stands an always-true one in its place, which changes nothing where filters already AND together. Inside a **Filter Group** that replacement appears only when the failure would otherwise leave the group empty, because a stray true in an `Or` group would pass everything. Fail discards the whole stack and replaces it with always-false, so one filter set to Fail decides the outcome for every filter beside it, and inside a group it flattens that group's verdict while the rest of the stack carries on.


> **Danger.**
> **Error means two different things**
>
> On `Missing Data Policy` it cancels the node. On `Initialization Failure Policy` it logs a warning and carries on with that filter removed from the stack. If the failed filter was the only one on its pin, the stack is now empty, and an empty stack passes every element. The symptom is not that nothing came through, it is that nothing was filtered. Set that policy to **Fail** wherever a silent pass would be worse than an empty result.


An unconnected pin is a different case, and a deliberate one. The node falls back to a default verdict picked to match what the pin is for. A pin that chooses which elements to work on defaults to all of them passing, so no condition means no narrowing. A pin that marks an exception or an event defaults to nothing marked: **Path : Shrink** takes **Stop Conditions** and never stops without them, **Path : Fuse Collinear** takes **Keep Conditions** and preserves nothing, **Cluster : Cut** takes preservation filters that protect nothing. The label and its tooltip tell you which kind you are holding.

## Reuse

*One filter, many consumers, and the expensive part is paid once.*

A filter output is ordinary PCG parameter data, so all the usual plumbing applies: one output feeds as many pins as you like, reroute nodes tidy the wiring, and named reroutes let you keep filter definitions in one corner of a graph and reach them from anywhere in it.

Reuse is not only tidiness. Spatial filters build real structures before they run: **Filter : Distance**, **Filter : Inclusion (Bounds)**, **Filter : Inclusion (Path/Splines)**, **Filter : Check Nearest** and their kin index their target data once, on the filter itself, and every consumer wired to that filter shares the result. Two copies of one filter with identical settings build the same index twice.


> Figure: A graph shown across a subgraph boundary. Outside, Filter : Distance connects to the Filters pin of a subgraph node. Inside, the subgraph Input node exposes a Filters pin which meets an internal Filter : Compare (Numeric) at a Filter Group set to OR, whose output drives Uber Noise.
> The caller supplies a condition on the left, and it meets the subgraph's own filters at a group inside.


Filters cross subgraph boundaries like any other data, which enables the one packaging pattern worth learning. Inside a subgraph, expose a **Filters** input pin and merge it with the subgraph's internal filters through a Filter Group. Callers can then add conditions to a packaged operation without opening it up, and because the group's `Mode` is overridable, whether their conditions extend or narrow yours can itself be a graph parameter.

## Related

* [What's different](concept:working-with-pcgex/what-pcgex-adds) -- the sub-node pattern filters are the largest instance of
* [Building & Refining](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) -- filters deciding which edges survive
* **Filters** -- every filter node, by family

title: Odd Jobs
description: Most of this book covers systems: clusters, paths, filters, staging.
outline: The stock node, with the corners filled in
Deciding whether to run at all
body:
Most of this book covers systems: clusters, paths, filters, staging. Alongside them the plugin ships several dozen nodes that belong to no system at all. They do one narrow thing each, they photograph badly, and in production they are reached for constantly, because the problem that stalls a graph is rarely the interesting one.

This page is a tour rather than a reference. Nothing here is explained in depth; the point is to know these exist, so that the next time a graph needs a specific small thing, you go looking instead of building it out of five stock nodes.

## The stock node, with the corners filled in

_Familiar operations that got the flexibility the original was missing._

Several nodes shadow something vanilla PCG already does. What they add is the case the original does not cover _(or used not to)_, which is usually the case you have.

| Node                                                                                                                                                      | What it adds                                                                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Copy Attributes**                                                                        | Copies between datasets, and promotes a single `@Data` value onto every element as it goes                                                   |
| **Attribute Remap**                                                                        | Remaps one attribute or property, with proper control over the input and output ranges                                                       |
| **Format Attributes**                                                                    | Replaces literal tokens inside `FName` and `FString` attributes using values read from other attributes                                      |
| **Promote Attributes**                                                                        | Turns element values into tags or into `@Data` values                                                                                        |
| **Sort Points** and **Sort Data** | Multi-rule sorting, the second working on the `@Data` domain                                                                                 |
| **Partition by Values**                                                         | Splits points into one output per distinct attribute value, each named after its value                                                       |
| **Merge Points**                                                                                    | Merges collections, optionally grouping them by [Matching](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/matching) rules rather than merging everything |
| **Transform Points**                                                                  | The transform variations from asset collections, with attribute overrides, applied to plain points                                           |

## Making randomness repeatable

_Deriving stable values from the data rather than from an incrementing seed._

Procedural work needs variation that survives a regeneration, and the usual failure is a seed that shifts when something upstream changes. These derive their value from the data itself.

| Node                                                                                                                                          | Produces                                                                                       |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Data Hash**                                                                       | One deterministic value per dataset, from any combination of point count, type and bounds      |
| **Attribute Hash**                                                             | A hash over an attribute or property                                                           |
| **Write GUID** and **Get GUID** | Stable per-point identity, with Get GUID resolving the same value a given index would receive  |
| **Refresh Seed**                                                                  | Rewrites each point's seed from its position, so identical positions give identical randomness |
| **Write Index**                                                                      | The current element/data index as an attribute or tag among other things                       |

**Refresh Seed** deserves the callout. Anything downstream that reads the point seed becomes position-stable, which means moving one point changes that point and nothing else.

## Bounds, axes and projection

_The geometric chores._

| Node                                                                                             | Does                                                                          |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Points to Bounds**            | Collapses a group of points into a single point representing their bounds     |
| **Bounds To Points**          | The reverse, generating points on the surface of the bounds                   |
| **Bounds Axis To Points** | Two points from one axis of the bounds                                        |
| **Find point on Bounds**   | The closest point on the dataset bounds                                       |
| **Move Pivot**                     | Moves a point's pivot relative to its own bounds                              |
| **Normalize**                         | Position within the data bounds, written as a `0-1` vector                    |
| **Flat Projection**           | Flattens positions onto the XY plane                                          |
| **Best Match Axis**           | Rotates toward a direction or a target while keeping the transform orthogonal |

**Best Match Axis** is the archetypal member of this page. It exists because "point this at that, without shearing the transform" is fiddly to get right and comes up constantly.

The same corner of the plugin also holds a few genuinely exotic entries: **Fuse Points**, **Lloyd Relax 2D** and **3D**, and **Bin Packing 3D (Q4RealBPP)**, which implements bin packing with weight limits, category affinities and load bearing from the paper it names.

## Deciding whether to run at all

_Control flow, which vanilla PCG leaves fairly bare._

| Node                                                                                            | Decides                                                                 |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cull on Empty**                                                                               | Deactivates an output pin when every input is empty or missing          |
| **Discard Same**               | Drops whole datasets that match on a chosen set of parameters           |
| **Discard by Point Count**                                                                      | Drops datasets by size                                                  |
| **Spatial Triage**           | Which data is relevant to a given bounds, as a fast box-to-box test     |
| **Uber Branch**               | Routes collections down different pins by filter rules                  |
| **Branch on Data**         | The same, on a single `@Data` attribute                                 |
| **Break**                                                                                       | Tracks a counter and conditions across recursive subgraph calls         |
| **Iterations**                                                                                  | Emits lightweight dummy entries to drive a loop node                    |
| **Dispatch Subgraphs** | Runs a per-entry-resolved subgraph, deduplicated by graph and overrides |
| **Wait for PCG Data**   | Blocks until other PCG components have produced their output            |

**Cull on Empty** and **Break** are the two that quietly prevent a lot of misery, the first because an empty branch that keeps executing produces confusing downstream failures, the second because recursive subgraphs otherwise have no clean way to stop.

## Seeing what the data holds

_Inspection, which is most of debugging a graph._

**Attribute Stats** reports statistics for an attribute, which answers "is this range what I think it is" faster than any amount of staring. **Reduce Data** collapses a `@Data` attribute down. **Draw Attributes** renders attribute values in the viewport, and **Flush Debug** clears persistent debug lines when a previous draw has left the level cluttered.

## Reading from the level

_Getting authored data out of actors and into the graph._

**Get Properties Data** resolves actor and component references and writes the properties they expose as per-row attributes, which is the direct route from hand-placed actors to graph data. **Pack Actor Data** does the same job through a Blueprint you write, for anything the generic path cannot reach. **Destroy Actor** removes actors the executing PCG component previously spawned.

## Go and browse

The node library is organised by what a node does rather than by which module it came from, and these are spread across a few of its sections. They reward a slow scroll:

| Section                                           | Holds                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Metadata**   | Hashes, keys, remapping, formatting, cleanup, blending and bitmasks          |
| **Utilities** | Control flow, discarding, partitioning, sorting, noise, matching and pickers |
| **Spatial** | Bounds, projection, pivots, relaxation and packing                           |

Every node page carries its full settings, so the tour above is only the way in. If a graph is doing something awkward in four nodes, there is a fair chance one of these does it in one.

## Related

* [What's different](concept:working-with-pcgex/what-pcgex-adds) -- the patterns these follow where they use sub-nodes
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- what **Uber Branch** and the discard nodes take
* [Tips & Tricks](concept:working-with-pcgex/tips-and-tricks) -- working alongside vanilla PCG

title: Pathfinding
description: Pathfinding turns connections into routes.
outline: Routes run on the edges you built
A query is a seed, a goal, and a picker
Heuristics are required, and they are the whole cost model
body:
Pathfinding turns connections into routes. A cluster's edges are the navigable network, so a route follows edges that exist and can never cross where none does, and what comes back is a path you can offset, subdivide or spawn along like any other.

## Routes run on the edges you built

_The network is decided before the search, which makes refinement the real control._

A pathfinding node takes a cluster and walks it. Wherever an edge exists a route may follow it, and wherever refinement removed one, no setting will let a route cross. Shaping the network is therefore the first half of every pathfinding problem, and it happens in [Building & Refining](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) rather than here.


> Figure: Two panels side by side over the same twelve ringed vertices at identical coordinates in both, with the same seed marker at bottom left and goal marker at top right. The left panel, labelled All edges, is densely connected and a green route runs almost straight between seed and goal. The right panel, labelled Refined, has had roughly a third of its edges removed, each shown faded and struck through where it used to be, and the green route between the same two markers now takes a long detour around the gap the removals left. Untaken edges are faded in both panels.
> Same query, same heuristics. The only thing that changed is which edges exist.



> **Note.**
> **Heuristics steer, refinement forbids**
>
> A heuristic can make an edge expensive enough that routes avoid it, and an expensive edge is still a legal one: given no cheaper option, the search takes it. When an edge must be impossible rather than unattractive, remove it from the cluster with **Cluster : Refine** before the search runs.


Two nodes read a different network. **Pathfinding : Navmesh** and **Pathfinding : Plot Navmesh** query the engine's navigation mesh, so they need no cluster and take no heuristics. They pose their queries the same way everything else does.

## A query is a seed, a goal, and a picker

_Seeds say where routes start, goals say where they end, and the Goal Picker decides which pairs with which._

**Pathfinding : Edges** takes two required point inputs. **Seeds** are the starting points, **Goals** are the destinations, and both are ordinary point datasets that get matched to their nearest cluster vertex. One query is one seed paired with one goal, and one resolved query becomes one path.

Which goal a seed gets is the **Goal Picker**'s decision, chosen from a dropdown in the node's settings:

| Picker              | Pairing                                                                           |
| ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Default**         | Seed _n_ goes to goal _n_, by index                                               |
| **All**             | Every seed queries every goal, so ten seeds and ten goals produce a hundred paths |
| **Index Attribute** | An attribute on the seed names its goal, or several goals                         |
| **Random**          | A random goal per seed, or a fixed or random number of them                       |

**Pathfinding : Plot Edges** poses the question differently and needs no goals. It takes one ordered set of points and routes through all of them in sequence, joining each consecutive pair through the cluster, and returns the whole run as a single path. Reach for it when the waypoints are known and the connections between them are what you want solved.


> Figure: Three panels over one identical cluster of fourteen ringed vertices, each panel showing a different query resolving into routes. The first, labelled Default, has three seed markers on the left and three goal markers on the right, joined by three separate green routes that each pair one seed with the goal at the same index. The second, labelled All, has two seeds and three goals, and six green routes fan out from the two seeds so that every seed reaches every goal. The third, labelled Plot Edges, has four numbered waypoint markers scattered across the cluster and one single green route threading through all four in numeric order, drawn with order chevrons along its length. In every panel the cluster edges the routes follow are solid and the untaken edges are faded.
> The same network, three ways of asking. Each resolved query becomes one path.


## Heuristics are required, and they are the whole cost model

_The algorithm decides how to search, the heuristics decide what searching costs._

Every route-finding node on a cluster needs heuristics, and wiring nothing in stops it with `Missing valid base heuristics`. There is no built-in default and no implicit shortest-distance: an unguided search has no notion of what a good path is, so PCGEx makes you say.

The commonest answer is a single **Heuristics : Shortest Distance**. From there heuristics stack, each contributing a weighted score, so a route can prefer short edges while also avoiding sharp turns and steep ground. [Heuristics](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/heuristics) covers the providers and how their scores combine.

Which search strategy consumes those scores is a separate choice, made in the node's **Search Algorithm** dropdown, and every one of them uses your heuristics. [Algorithms](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/algorithms) covers what separates them.


> **Note.**
> **Dropdowns here, sub-nodes there**
>
> Heuristics arrive on a pin as sub-nodes, because you compose several. The Goal Picker and Search Algorithm are single choices, so they are instanced dropdowns inside the node instead, configured in place. Each still exposes an optional overrides pin for driving its settings from data.


## What the family produces

_Routes between points, boundaries around regions, and values spread outward from seeds._

Everything below traverses a cluster, and almost everything hands back paths.

### Routes

| Node                                                                                                        | What comes out                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Pathfinding : Edges**                            | One path per resolved seed and goal pair                            |
| **Pathfinding : Plot Edges**             | One path through every plot point in order                          |
| **Pathfinding : Navmesh**           | One path per seed and goal pair, over the engine navmesh            |
| **Pathfinding : Plot Navmesh** | One path through every plot point in order, over the engine navmesh |

### Regions

| Node                                                                                                  | What comes out                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cells**                         | The closed region around each seed, as a path    |
| **Pathfinding : Find All Cells**                 | Every closed region in the cluster               |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cells (Bounded)**         | The same, triaged against a bounds input         |
| **Pathfinding : Find All Cells (Bounded)** | The same, triaged against a bounds input         |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cluster Hull**           | One path per cluster, tracing its outer boundary |

Regions are covered in [Cells & Hulls](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/cells-and-hulls).

### Spreads

| Node                                                                                       | What comes out                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Cluster : Flood Fill**         | Paths tracing the lanes the fill travelled, plus depth and distance per vertex |
| **Cluster : Diffuse**     | Attributes written onto the vertices reached, and no paths                     |
| **Cluster : BFS Depth** | Depth and distance from the nearest seed, per vertex                           |

Spreads are covered in [Growth & Diffusion](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/growth-and-diffusion).

**Counting traffic instead of collecting routes**


**Pathfinding : Edges** has an `Output Mode` with a second setting. In `Visited` mode it emits no paths at all: it forwards the Vtx and Edges through unchanged and writes onto each one how many of the paths it would have produced passed over it.

That turns a batch of queries into a heat map of the network. Vertices and edges everything routes through score high, and the ones nothing touches score zero, which is a direct way to find the load-bearing parts of a structure or to prune the parts no route ever wanted.



## Related

* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- the structure every search runs on
* [Building & Refining](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/building-and-refining) -- shaping the network before searching it
* [Paths & Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/paths-and-clusters) -- crossing between ordered and connected points
* **Pathfinding** -- every node in the family, with its settings

title: Algorithms
description: Every search algorithm in PCGEx runs on your heuristics.
outline: Negative costs come from a negative Weight Factor
Attribute alone gives A\* nothing to aim at
body:
Every search algorithm in PCGEx runs on your heuristics. There are no built-in edge weights underneath them and no algorithm that ignores them, so choosing an algorithm never changes what a route costs. It changes how much of the cluster gets examined on the way to finding one.

## What all four share

*The same cost model, and the same stopping rule.*

Each algorithm asks the heuristics handler for the cost of every edge it considers, and that answer is the whole cost model. Swapping A\* for Dijkstra on an unchanged setup gives you a different search, not a different notion of expense.

All four also carry **Early Exit**, on by default, and it is worth knowing that it changes no result. On A\* and Dijkstra the goal is marked visited on the same dequeue that would have ended the loop, and a visited Vtx is never relaxed again, so the route is identical either way. On Bellman-Ford and Bidirectional the flag is copied into the operation and never read at all. Leave it alone; the setting to reach for when a route looks wrong is the heuristics stack, which is the entire cost model.

## What separates them

*Only one looks ahead toward the goal.*

| Algorithm | How it expands | Looks ahead | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A\*** | Toward the goal, guided by an estimate of what remains | Yes | Default choice for point to point |
| **Dijkstra** | Outward from the seed in order of accumulated cost | No | The pull toward the goal is overriding your weights |
| **Bidirectional** | From both ends at once, until the two frontiers meet | No | Long routes across large clusters |
| **Bellman-Ford** | Relaxes every edge repeatedly, N-1 times over | No | Costs can go negative |

**A\*** is the only one that asks what the remaining cost to the goal is likely to be, and it asks your heuristics for that too. A good estimate lets it ignore most of the cluster. A poor one leaves it exploring broadly, which is Dijkstra with extra bookkeeping.

**Dijkstra** spends more, and in exchange it weighs accumulated cost without any bias toward the destination. When a carefully weighted stack produces routes that look like they are cutting corners toward the goal, this is the switch to try.

**Bidirectional** halves the depth each side has to reach, which is where its speed on large clusters comes from. It runs the backward search with the seed and goal swapped so directional heuristics still read correctly in reverse, and it holds two sets of state, so it trades memory for the saving.

**Bellman-Ford** is the robust one and much the slowest, visiting every edge once per node in the cluster. It detects negative cycles by default, and a query that contains one fails rather than looping.


> Figure: Three panels over one identical cluster of forty-two ringed vertices, each with the same seed marker at bottom left and goal marker at top right, and the same green route between them in all three. What differs is the shading: each panel tints the vertices the search actually examined. The first, labelled A star, tints a narrow corridor of ten vertices hugging the route. The second, labelled Dijkstra, tints every vertex in the cluster, a broad disc spreading outward from the seed in all directions. The third, labelled Bidirectional, tints two discs, one grown from the seed and one from the goal, with a line of small dots marking the frontier where the two expansions touched.
> Same route, same cost model. What changes is how much of the cluster was examined to find it.



> **Note.**
> **Negative costs come from a negative Weight Factor**
>
> A heuristic's own output is clamped at zero, so no provider produces a negative score on its own. The **Weight Factor** multiplies afterwards, and setting it below zero is what puts negative costs into the search. That is the situation Bellman-Ford exists for, and it is worth knowing you created it deliberately.



> **Warning.**
> **Attribute alone gives A\* nothing to aim at**
>
> The lookahead estimate is supplied by the heuristics, and **Heuristics : Attribute** is the one provider with no opinion about where the goal is. An A\* search guided by attribute cost alone therefore has a flat estimate and explores as broadly as Dijkstra would. Add a distance or azimuth heuristic alongside it, or pick Dijkstra and skip the overhead.


## Related

* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- the query model these resolve
* [Heuristics](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/heuristics) -- the scores every algorithm reads
* **Algorithms** -- each algorithm's settings

title: Cells & Hulls
description: A cluster's edges divide space into regions, and those regions are usable geometry.
outline: A cell is a face of the network
Cells need a cluster that survives being flattened
Dead ends make a cell double back
Bounds come out alongside the paths
body:
A cluster's edges divide space into regions, and those regions are usable geometry. Cell extraction hands each one back as a closed path, which is how a network of connections becomes a set of shapes to inset, offset, fill or build on.

## A cell is a face of the network

*The smallest closed loop of edges that encloses an area.*

Draw a cluster over a scatter of points and the connections carve the space between them into faces. Each face is a **cell**: a closed run of edges with nothing crossing its interior. A **hull** is the same idea applied to the whole cluster, tracing its outer boundary rather than an interior region.

Both come back as closed paths, so everything in [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) applies to the result.


> Figure: Two panels over one identical cluster of fourteen ringed vertices and eighteen edges. The left panel, labelled Cells, fills five interior regions in five strengths of the same muted blue, each carrying an order chevron on its own border, showing that the connections carve the interior into separate faces. The right panel, labelled Hull, leaves the interior unfilled and draws a single closed green path around the outermost vertices only, with a ringed marker at the point it starts from, ignoring every interior edge, which are faded.
> The same connections read two ways: every interior face, or the outer boundary alone.


## Seeded, or exhaustive

*Either you point at the regions you want, or you take them all.*

| Node | Input | What comes out |
|---|---|---|
| **Pathfinding : Find Cells** | Seeds | The cell enclosing each seed |
| **Pathfinding : Find All Cells** | Holes, optionally | Every cell in the cluster |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cells (Bounded)** | Seeds and bounds | The same, split by how each cell sits against the bounds |
| **Pathfinding : Find All Cells (Bounded)** | Bounds, and holes optionally | The same, split by how each cell sits against the bounds |
| **Pathfinding : Find Cluster Hull** | Nothing extra | One boundary path per cluster |

Seeded extraction places a point inside the region you want and takes the cell around it, which suits a specific courtyard, plot or room. Exhaustive extraction takes the complete decomposition, which suits treating the whole network as a set of tiles.

**Find All Cells** accepts a **Holes** input, and any cell containing one of those points is dropped. That is the direct way to carve out the regions something else already occupies.

The bounded variants sort their results onto three pairs of pins, **Inside**, **Touching** and **Outside**, according to how the cell sits against a spatial input. Cells that straddle the edge of your working area are usually the ones to discard or treat differently, and this saves testing for that downstream.

## When seeds compete

*Two seeds can land in the same cell, and something has to break the tie.*

Seeded extraction resolves ownership with a **Seed Ownership** setting:

| Method | Winner |
|---|---|
| **Seed Order** | The lowest-indexed seed. The default |
| **Closest** | The seed nearest the cell centroid in 3D |
| **Closest (Projected)** | The same, measured in the projection plane |
| **Best Candidate** | Whichever seed wins under sorting rules you supply |

Seeds also report back. **Find Cells** has **SeedGenSuccess** and **SeedGenFailed** output pins, so a seed that landed outside the cluster or in a region that failed the constraints can be caught rather than silently producing nothing.

**Seed Growth** expands a seed's claim outward: depth 1 takes the immediate neighbouring cells, depth 2 their neighbours, and the depth can be driven per seed from an attribute. With **Merge Adjacent Cells** on, everything one seed claimed dissolves its shared interior edges and comes back as one larger closed path, which turns a scatter of seeds into a set of grown territories.


> Figure: Three panels over one identical cluster whose edges enclose twelve small cells, each panel carrying the same single seed marker inside one central cell. The first, labelled Growth 0, fills only the cell containing the seed. The second, labelled Growth 1, fills that cell and every cell sharing an edge with it, each still drawn as its own closed path. The third, labelled Merge Adjacent, fills the same area but the interior edges between those cells are faded and struck through, and one green closed path with order chevrons runs around the whole merged region.
> One seed, three claims. Merging dissolves the interior edges into a single boundary.


## Constraints decide what counts

*A closed loop of edges is a candidate, and the constraints say whether it survives.*

Every cell node carries the same constraint block, and on all but one of them it filters on what the cell measures: **point count**, **area**, **perimeter**, **bounds size**, **segment length** and **compactness**, each with a minimum and a maximum. **Convex only** and **Concave only** filter on shape.

**Pathfinding : Find Cluster Hull** is the exception, and the block being on its panel is misleading. It reads **Duplicate Leaf points** and nothing else: the hull is built through a separate path that constructs its own unfiltered constraints, so every limit and both shape filters are inert there, and so is **Output Winding**.

One measurement is worth knowing before you set a limit against it: **Bounds size** is the *diagonal* of the cell's 3D bounding box rather than a side, and the limits do not all work in the same space. Perimeter and segment length are measured in 3D, while area and compactness are measured on the projection, so compactness is not computed from the perimeter that **Min perimeter** tests.

Cell finding is a planar operation. Every candidate loop is evaluated in a 2D projection, and the **Projection** setting decides which plane that is.


> **Warning.**
> **Cells need a cluster that survives being flattened**
>
> A cluster lying roughly in a plane projects cleanly, and its faces come back as you would draw them. A tilted or gently curved one works too, with the projection aimed along its dominant axis.
>
> A genuinely volumetric cluster does not. **Cluster : Delaunay 3D** and **Cluster : Voronoi 3D** produce topology whose faces overlap from every viewing direction, so flattening them collapses unrelated geometry onto itself and cell finding yields nothing useful rather than reporting a problem. Their 2D counterparts are what cell extraction is built for.



> **Note.**
> **Dead ends make a cell double back**
>
> An edge leading to a leaf vertex encloses nothing, so a cell containing one traces out along it and straight back. **Keep Cells With Leaves** is on by default and produces exactly that spike in the path. Turning it off discards those cells, and **Duplicate Leaf Points** decides whether the turnaround vertex appears once or twice in the output.


## Bounds come out alongside the paths

*Every cell node also emits an oriented box per cell.*

Next to the paths pin sits a **Cell Bounds** pin, giving one point per cell whose transform and extents are that cell's oriented bounding box. It is the fastest route to placing something in a region without processing its boundary: spawn on the point, scale to its bounds, and the cell shape never has to be read.
