Cells also arrive carrying their own measurements, so area, perimeter and compactness are available as data rather than something to compute from the point positions.

## Related

* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- the family these belong to
* [Paths & Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters/paths-and-clusters) -- why extraction is half of a round trip
* [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) -- what to do with a closed path once you have one
* **Cells** -- every cell node, with its settings

title: Growth & Diffusion
description: Some traversals have nowhere to be.
outline: Named for clusters, grouped with pathfinding
Lanes, and how much they overlap
Fill Controls say when to stop
The legacy Heuristics pin on Flood Fill
body:
Some traversals have nowhere to be. Instead of a goal they have seeds, every connection to spread along, and a rule for when to stop, so what they produce is shaped by where they ran out. Roots, rivers, cracks, blast radii and territory maps all come from this half of the family.

## Filling a cluster from seeds

*Spread outward across every connection at once, and record what the spread reached.*

Three nodes flood a cluster rather than tracing single runs through it. All three take seeds, and they differ in what they hand back and in how much of the machinery below they use.

| Node | Result |
|---|---|
| **Cluster : Flood Fill** | Paths tracing the lanes the fill travelled, plus what it learned on the way |
| **Cluster : Diffuse** | Attributes written onto the vertices reached, with no paths at all |
| **Cluster : BFS Depth** | Depth and distance from the nearest seed, on every reachable vertex |

**Cluster : Flood Fill** is the general-purpose one, and it records as it spreads: diffusion depth, that depth normalised, the order vertices were reached, the distance travelled, and whether a vertex was where a lane ended. A normalised depth is a ready-made gradient running from every seed outward, so these attributes are frequently the whole reason to run the node.

**Cluster : Diffuse** carries seed attributes onto the vertices it reaches, and how values combine where diffusions meet is decided by blend operations on its own pin, covered in [Blending & Sampling](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/blending-and-sampling). Writing metadata rather than paths is what lets overlapping diffusions genuinely overlap, which suits influence maps where several sources contribute to one vertex.

**Cluster : BFS Depth** is the plain one, and plainer than it looks: hop count and distance from the nearest seed, and that is the whole node. It takes no **Fill Controls** pin and no **Heuristics** pin, so nothing on this page about stopping conditions or edge costs applies to it. Its spread is a flat hop-by-hop walk that runs until it runs out of cluster. The one extra pin it can grow is **Trigger Filters**, which appears only when `Trigger Count` is switched on and is then required, since counting triggers is meaningless without a condition saying what one is.


> Figure: One cluster of forty-two ringed vertices spanning the full panel, with two seed markers placed well apart. Every vertex the fill reached is tinted, in four steps from strongest at the seeds to faintest three hops out, and a mono numeral beside one vertex at each step reads its diffusion depth: 0 at a seed, then 1, 2 and 3 outward. A dashed line runs between the two seeds where their spreads meet, along the vertices equidistant from both. The eight vertices further than three hops are left untinted, showing where the fill stopped.
> Depth from the nearest seed, written onto every vertex the spread reached.



> **Note.**
> **Named for clusters, grouped with pathfinding**
>
> These three carry the **Cluster :** prefix because they operate on cluster topology like the rest of that family. They are documented here because they traverse, which is the machinery this section explains. **Cluster : Flood Fill** and **Cluster : Diffuse** also consume heuristics; **Cluster : BFS Depth** does not, and counts hops instead.


## Lanes, and how much they overlap

*A flood reaches everything at once, so turning it into paths means deciding where one path ends.*

**Cluster : Flood Fill**'s `Path Output` decides what comes out of the paths pin:

| Mode | What you get |
|---|---|
| **None** | No paths. The attributes written onto the Vtx are the output |
| **Full** | One path per lane, each running the whole way from its seed to where it stopped. Heavy overlap near the seeds |
| **Partitions** | The same coverage cut into segments that meet end to end, overlapping only at their endpoints |

**Full** is the honest picture of every route the fill found, and near a seed that means dozens of paths lying on top of each other, all sharing their first few points. **Partitions** cuts the same structure at the branch points, so what comes back reads as a branching tree rather than a bundle: one trunk, then separate limbs. Partitions can be split by **Length**, **Score** or **Depth**.

That distinction is what makes flood fill usable as a growth system. A river network, a root system or a crack pattern is a branching structure, and partitioned output is the shape that describes it.

## Fill Controls say when to stop

*Sub-nodes on a pin, each answering whether the fill may take one more step.*

A flood with no limit reaches everything, so **Fill Control** sub-nodes are how a fill acquires a shape. Each one inspects a candidate and can refuse it, and they stack on one pin the way heuristics and filters do. This applies to **Cluster : Flood Fill** and **Cluster : Diffuse** only: **Cluster : BFS Depth** has no such pin and cannot be shaped this way.

| Group | Controls |
|---|---|
| Where it may go | **Edge Filters**, **Vtx Filters**, **Keep Direction** |
| How far it goes | **Count**, **Depth**, **Length**, **Branch Limit** |
| What it costs | **Heuristics Scoring**, **Heuristics Budget**, **Heuristics Threshold** |
| What the data says | **Attribute Threshold**, **Attribute Accumulation**, **Running Average** |

The heuristics group is how the scoring system reaches flood fill. **Heuristics Scoring** computes a cost per candidate, **Heuristics Budget** stops a lane once its accumulated cost exceeds an allowance, and **Heuristics Threshold** stops on a single expensive step. A fill given a budget spreads far across cheap ground and barely at all across expensive ground, which is a spatial falloff expressed entirely in cost.

**Branch Limit** deserves singling out. A flood across a dense cluster branches constantly, and the result reads as a stain rather than as structure. Capping the branching is what turns it back into something with visible lanes.


> Figure: Three panels over one identical dense cluster of thirty-six ringed vertices, each with the same single seed marker at the left edge, showing how far a fill got. The first, labelled No controls, has every vertex in the cluster reached and tinted and every edge traversed, filling the panel evenly. The second, labelled Depth 3, has only the vertices within three hops reached, forming a compact blob around the seed with the rest of the cluster faded. The third, labelled Branch Limit 3, reaches as far across the panel as the first but along only three distinct visible lanes, leaving most of the cluster faded between them.
> The same seed and the same cluster. Fill controls are what give a flood a shape.



> **Warning.**
> **The legacy Heuristics pin on Flood Fill**
>
> **Cluster : Flood Fill** still exposes a direct **Heuristics** pin, kept for graphs built before fill controls existed. Use **Fill Control : Heuristics Scoring** instead: it does the same work and composes with the other controls rather than sitting outside them.


## Related

* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- the goal-directed half of the family
* [Heuristics](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/heuristics) -- the scores the heuristic fill controls consume
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- what the Vtx and Edge fill controls take
* **Pathfinding** -- every node and fill control, with its settings

title: Heuristics
description: A heuristic answers one question about one edge: what does crossing this cost.
outline: Invert is how you ask for the scenic route
Feedback remembers where routes have been
body:
A heuristic answers one question about one edge: what does crossing this cost. Everything a route does follows from the answer, because the search has no other notion of good or bad. Stack several and you describe a preference with real texture: short, but flat, and without hairpins.

## Cheap is what gets chosen

*Every heuristic returns a cost, and the search minimises it.*

A heuristic scores an edge from zero upward, and lower wins. **Heuristics : Shortest Distance** hands a long edge a high score and a short one a low score, so a search minimising cost prefers short edges and the familiar shortest path falls out.

Each score is normalised against the cluster before it leaves the heuristic, so a distance score and a steepness score arrive on the same scale and can be compared. That is what makes stacking work: without it, whichever heuristic happened to measure in larger units would drown the rest.

Every provider shares four settings that reshape its answer without changing what it measures:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Weight Factor** | Scales this heuristic's contribution against the others. Relative values are what matter |
| **Invert** | Flips the score, so the heuristic prefers what it previously avoided |
| **Score Curve** | Remaps the normalised value, turning a linear cost into a threshold, a plateau or a steep penalty |
| **Local Weight Multiplier** | Reads a per-Vtx or per-Edge attribute and multiplies the score by it, so weighting varies across the cluster |


> **Note.**
> **Invert is how you ask for the scenic route**
>
> A shortest-distance heuristic with **Invert** on makes long edges cheap, and the search will happily wander. Combined with a curve, this is the usual way to get a route that meanders within limits instead of taking the obvious line.


## The providers

*Grouped by where the number comes from.*

### From geometry

| Heuristic | Scores |
|---|---|
| **Heuristics : Shortest Distance** | Edge length |
| **Heuristics : Steepness** | Vertical slope of the edge |
| **Heuristics : Azimuth** | Alignment of the edge with the direction to the goal |
| **Heuristics : Turn Penalty** | Angle between this edge and the previous one |
| **Heuristics : Inertia** | Deviation from the direction already being travelled. Expensive |

### From data

| Heuristic | Scores |
|---|---|
| **Heuristics : Attribute** | A Vtx or Edge attribute read as the cost directly |
| **Heuristics : Gradient** | Rate of change of an attribute between the two endpoints |
| **Heuristics : Tensor** | Agreement between the edge and a sampled tensor field |

### From the search itself

| Heuristic | Scores |
|---|---|
| **Heuristics : Least Nodes** | Hop count, which prefers fewer vertices regardless of distance |
| **Heuristics : Feedback** | How much traffic the edge has already carried |

**Heuristics : Attribute** is the general-purpose escape hatch. Anything you can compute and write onto Vtx or Edges becomes a cost, which covers the cases the built-in providers do not: a danger field baked from gameplay data, a material cost, a hand-painted mask.

## Several heuristics, one number

*The consumer decides how the individual scores collapse.*

Wire several heuristics into one pin and each scores every edge independently. How those scores become the single number the search uses is the consuming node's **Heuristic Score Mode**:

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Weighted Average** | Balanced blend, normalised. The default, and the right answer most of the time |
| **Weighted Sum** | Direct contribution with no normalisation, so the scale grows with the number of heuristics |
| **Geometric Mean** | Sensitive to extremes: one low score pulls the result down hard |
| **Harmonic Mean** | Emphasises low scores more strongly still, so cheap dominates |
| **Minimum** | The most permissive. Any single heuristic can make an edge attractive |
| **Maximum** | The most restrictive. Any single heuristic can make an edge unattractive |

Weight Factor works within whichever mode is chosen. Two heuristics at weights 1 and 0.5 mean the second matters half as much, and the absolute numbers are irrelevant.

A stack reads more clearly with numbers on it. Say a route should prefer short runs, avoid steep ground, turn gently, and spread apart from routes already found:

| Heuristic | Weight Factor | What it is doing |
|---|---|---|
| **Shortest Distance** | 1 | the base cost everything else is judged against |
| **Steepness** | 1.5 | half again as important as distance |
| **Turn Penalty** | 0.5 | a nudge, not a rule |
| **Feedback** | 2 | the strongest voice, pushing each route off the last one |

Only the ratios matter, so 2, 3, 1 and 4 would behave identically. What changes the character of the result is the score mode above, not the weights: the same four heuristics under **Maximum** give a route that avoids anything any one of them dislikes, and under **Minimum** a route that is happy as long as something likes it.


> Figure: One cluster of sixteen ringed vertices drawn identically in three panels, each with the same seed marker at bottom left and goal marker at top right, and a different green route between them. The first panel, labelled Shortest Distance, shows a direct route that takes several sharp turns. The second, labelled plus Turn Penalty, shows a slightly longer route that changes direction gently instead. The third, labelled plus Steepness, shows a longer route again that detours around a dashed orange region marked steep, which is drawn faded in the first two panels because those two are not being charged for it. Untaken edges are faded in all three.
> One network, one query. What changes is only what the search was told to value.


## Feedback remembers where routes have been

*A heuristic whose score depends on what previous routes already did.*

**Heuristics : Feedback** raises the cost of vertices and edges that have already been used, so later routes are pushed onto fresh ground. It is what separates a bundle of queries that all collapse onto the single best corridor from a set that spreads out and looks deliberate.

It has two ranges, and which one does anything depends on the node:

- **Global** shares one memory across every query a node resolves, so routes avoid each other and each is influenced by whichever resolved before it.
- **Local**, the default, scopes that memory to a single query. A query made of several legs accumulates across them, so later legs avoid ground the earlier ones took.

Only a plot is made of several legs. **Pathfinding : Plot Edges** resolves one query per plot and one leg per consecutive pair of plot points, which is what local feedback exists for. **Pathfinding : Edges** resolves one seed to one goal, a single leg with nothing to accumulate against, so local feedback does nothing at all there and global is the only setting with an effect.


> Figure: Two panels over one identical cluster of twenty ringed vertices, each with the same four seed markers down the left edge and one shared goal marker at the right. In the left panel, labelled No feedback, the four green routes converge onto one another early and run to the goal sharing most of their length. In the right panel, labelled Global feedback, the same four routes stay apart, each taking a visibly different course across the cluster before arriving at the same goal. Untaken edges are faded in both panels.
> Four queries, one goal. Feedback is what stops them collapsing onto the same corridor.



> **Warning.**
> **Feedback needs a base heuristic**
>
> Feedback scores traffic, and on an untouched cluster there is no traffic, so it has nothing to say about a first route. Wiring it as the only heuristic stops the node with `cannot work with feedback alone`. Pair it with a base heuristic that has an opinion about the geometry.


## Seeing what a stack costs

*Preview it on the cluster, or write it out as an attribute.*

The plugin ships a **PCGEx_DebugHeuristics** subgraph that draws a heuristic stack as a heatmap across the cluster, and **Cluster : Edge Properties** can write the same score onto the edges as an attribute. Either is the quickest way to check that a stack charges roughly what you intended before wiring it to a search.

Both are approximations, and for the same reason. **Inertia**, **Turn Penalty** and **Feedback** score an edge by how a route arrived at it, and outside a running search there is no arrival to read. What those contribute to a real traversal cannot be previewed, so a heatmap that looks even can still produce uneven routes.

## The other consumers

*Anything that needs to score an edge can take heuristics.*

The heuristics pin turns up wherever a cluster node needs a cost per edge rather than a yes or no per edge. **Cluster : Refine** uses it for the score-based refinements, keeping or cutting edges by what they cost. **Cluster : Centrality** and **Cluster : Decomposition** use it to weight traversal. **Cluster : Edge Properties** writes the computed score onto the edges as an attribute.

Flood fill reaches them through its own sub-nodes instead, as **Fill Control : Heuristics Scoring**, **Heuristics Budget** and **Heuristics Threshold**.


> **Note.**
> **Filters decide, heuristics prefer**
>
> Both are sub-node families wired onto a pin, and they answer different kinds of question. A filter returns a verdict, and something is in or out. A heuristic returns a number, and the search weighs it against every other number. Reach for a filter to make a rule absolute, and a heuristic to express a preference.


## Related

* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- the query model heuristics guide
* [Algorithms](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding/algorithms) -- the search strategies, all of which consume these scores
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- the other transverse sub-node system, for conditions rather than costs
* **Heuristics** -- every provider, with its settings

title: Paths
description: A path is a spline with the flexibility taken out.
outline: A path is points in order
Anything that reorders points rewrites the path
What a path carries, and what it works out
Reach for Parallel Transport when a spline mesh twists
When a path is too short
A path that comes back unchanged may have been refused
Where paths end, and clusters begin
body:
A path is a spline with the flexibility taken out. Same idea, points in a sequence describing a run through space, without control handles, without a curve type, without an asset to manage. If you are comfortable with splines you already have the model.

## A path is points in order

_Nothing marks a dataset as a path. The order does._

There is no path data type and no path tag. A **Paths** pin is an ordinary points pin wearing a label, and what makes the points a path is that a path node reads index 0, then 1, then 2, and treats each consecutive pair as connected. The connections are built on the spot, from the arithmetic `i` to `i + 1`, and thrown away when the node finishes.

That is worth taking literally, because clusters went the other way: they register three data types of their own, and a Vtx dataset announces itself as one. Paths announce nothing. The upside is that every vanilla PCG node works on path data without conversion, and so does every PCGEx node that takes points. The cost is on the same coin.


> **Warning.**
> **Anything that reorders points rewrites the path**
>
> The order is not metadata that a node could validate; it is the path itself. A vanilla operation that sorts, merges or re-indexes your points has produced a different path, and nothing anywhere will report a problem, because from PCGEx's side nothing is wrong. It is still point data on a pin called Paths.


One piece of state does travel alongside: `@Data.IsClosed`, an ordinary boolean attribute in the Data domain. Set, the path wraps from its last point back to its first. Absent, the path is open, which is why data arriving from elsewhere behaves as open until you say otherwise. Splines are the exception, answering from their own closure rather than the attribute.


> Figure: Two panels side by side, separated by a vertical rule. Both place the same six points, numbered 0 to 5, at identical positions on a loose ring. On the left the path is open: five segments join point 0 through point 5, with a gap left between point 5 and point 0. On the right the path is closed: the same five segments, plus a sixth drawn in green across that gap from point 5 back to point 0. Order chevrons run along every segment, the closing one included. The left panel is captioned Data dot IsClosed unset, the right one Data dot IsClosed set.
> Six points make five segments open, and six closed. The extra one spans the seam.


## Segments, and the off-by-one

_N points make N minus 1 segments, until the path closes and makes N._

A segment is the span between two consecutive points. It is never data you can see: no segment point set, no segment attributes, nothing on a pin. It exists while a node runs and then it is gone.

The consequence surfaces everywhere, because **anything a segment needs is read from the point where it starts**. A path of five points has four segments, and the fifth point starts none of them. Its attributes are read by nothing.


> Figure: One open path of five points, numbered 0 to 4, running left to right with order chevrons. Above each point sits a different mesh silhouette: a circle on point 0, a square on point 1, a triangle on point 2, a diamond on point 3, a pentagon on point 4. Each of the first four silhouettes reappears, smaller, just inside the segment that follows its point. Point 4 has no segment after it, so its pentagon is drawn faded and is annotated no segment to reach.
> The value sits on the point; the effect lands in the gap after it.


**Path : Spline Mesh (Simple)** is where this is most visible: assign meshes per point along an open path and the last point's mesh never appears, because there is no segment for it to fill. The source calls that point "only used for maths reasons". Close the path and it appears, because now there is a seam segment for it to drive.

**Path : Solidify** takes the logic one step further and changes the point count. It turns each segment into an oriented box, and since an open path's last point begins no segment, `Remove Last Point` is on by default: five points in, four boxes out.

**Which operations think in segments, and which think in points**


The test is what the operation produces one of: one thing per gap, or one thing per position.

**Per gap.** Subdivide, Bevel, Solidify, both Spline Mesh nodes, Path × Path Crossings, Path × Bounds Intersection, Fuse Collinear, Insert, Hatch, Split.

**Per position.** Offset, Smooth, Orient, Slide, Blend, Attribute Rolling, Write Tangents, Shift, Shrink, Reverse Order, and the per-point half of Properties.

**Path : Offset** is the one most often mistaken for a segment operation. It consults the normals of the segments either side to work out which way "outward" is, then reads its offset value at the point and moves that point. Every point moves, including the last one on an open path.



## What a path carries, and what it works out

_Direction, closure, and a set of vectors nothing stores._

Direction is array order and nothing else. There is no direction attribute to read or set, so reversing a path means reversing its points, which is what **Reverse Order** does. Winding is never stored either; the nodes that care recompute it from a flattened projection each time.

Normals and tangents are the same story: derived when a node needs them, never carried between nodes. Both matter more than that makes them sound, because they decide how anything oriented sits along the path.


> Figure: Two panels side by side, separated by a vertical rule. Both hold the same five points in the same wobbling left-to-right line. On the left they are numbered 0 to 4 from the left, the order chevrons point right, and a green offset copy of the path runs above it. On the right the identical points are numbered 4 to 0 from the left, the chevrons point left, and the green offset copy, at the same distance, now runs below the path instead.
> Nothing moved but the numbers. Outward follows the arrow.



> **Note.**
> **Reach for Parallel Transport when a spline mesh twists**
>
> Normals come in several modes, and the up-vector-based ones degenerate where a segment runs close to vertical, which shows up as a sudden roll in whatever you have deformed along the path. **Parallel Transport** carries the frame along the path instead of rebuilding it per segment, so it stays continuous through the vertical case. You will find it on **Path : Solidify** as `Normal` and on **Path : Offset** as `Direction`, which are the only nodes that take a normal mode. It is not a setting on **Path : Orient**, which resolves one fixed world up vector independently at every point and has no continuity mechanism of its own.


**How tangents get their values**


Tangents are opt-in, not automatic: only **Path : Write Tangents**, **Create Spline**, both Spline Mesh nodes and **Copy to Path** ask for them. They come from an instanced choice with five providers, so the endpoints and the interior can follow different rules, and the default treatment of the first and last point is inherited from the base rather than fixed by any one provider.



## The families

_Twenty-eight nodes, six things they do._

| Family                                | What it does                                 | Examples                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Building and converting in**        | Turn something else into ordered points      | **Spline to Path**, **Copy to Path**, **Path : Extrude**, **Path : Hatch**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Changing the point count**          | Add or remove points, keeping the run        | **Path : Subdivide**, **Path : Insert**, **Path : Reduce**, **Path : Fuse Collinear**, **Path : Resample**, **Path : Shrink**, **Path : Bevel** |
| **Changing positions**                | Same points, moved                           | **Path : Offset**, **Path : Smooth**, **Path : Slide**, **Path : Solidify**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Order, splitting, joining**         | Rearrange the sequence, or cut and join runs | **Path : Split**, **Path : Stitch**, **Path : Shift**, **Reverse Order**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Reading and writing along the run** | Derive values from position in the sequence  | **Path : Properties**, **Path : Write Tangents**, **Path : Orient**, **Path : Blend**, **Path : Attribute Rolling**                                                                                                                                     |
| **Crossings and output**              | Where paths meet, and what they become       | **Path × Path Crossings**, **Path × Bounds Intersection**, **Create Spline**, **Path : Spline Mesh (Simple)**                                                                                                                                                                                 |

Every one of them is in the node library under **Paths**, with its settings.

## When a path is too short

_Two points is the floor, and nodes disagree about what to do below it._

A single point describes no run, so path nodes reject anything under two points. What happens to the rejected data is the part to watch: some nodes drop it, some forward it untouched, some duplicate it, and the setting that controls this carries three different names across the family. A node that produced nothing and a node that passed your data straight through are both normal outcomes here.


> **Warning.**
> **A path that comes back unchanged may have been refused**
>
> Because forwarding is one of the fallbacks, a node quietly declining to work on your data looks identical to a node that had nothing to change. Whether you can confirm it from the log depends on which gate refused it. The entry gate, the one that forwards, does raise an aggregated graph warning, so there the log tells you. The **Paths Output Settings** block on **Pathfinding : Edges**, **Pathfinding : Plot Edges** and **Tensors : Extrude** is silent: it disables the output before writing it and logs nothing, so a path culled by its minimum or maximum leaves no trace at all.


## Where paths end, and clusters begin

_A path point has exactly one successor, and that is the whole limitation._

The connection rule is `i` to `i + 1`. One successor, arithmetically, with no room for a second. A path cannot fork, cannot rejoin, cannot carry a junction, and no setting anywhere changes that, because there is no adjacency to configure in the first place.

Clusters are the answer to precisely that. Where a path point is permanently binary, a cluster vertex holds however many links you give it, and the plugin's own vocabulary marks the difference: a vertex with more than two connections is _complex_, and complex is the thing paths cannot express.


> Figure: Two panels side by side, separated by a vertical rule, each headed with the same rule, i goes to i plus 1. On the left, a path: five numbered points, each joined to the next by one segment carrying one order chevron. On the right, the same five points, but point 2 also sprouts two further segments down to two unnumbered points. That whole junction is faded and struck through with a red diagonal cross, so it reads as refused rather than merely unusual.
> One successor per index. There is nowhere to put a second.


Crossing between the two is a pair of nodes. **Path : To Clusters** reads paths and builds a cluster, welding coincident points by default, which is the moment junctions become possible at all. Any point can weld, not only the two at each end of a path, so a path that stops partway along another joins it there. **Cluster : Break to Paths** goes the other way, walking chains of degree-two vertices and stopping wherever a junction appears, writing each chain's closure correctly as it goes.

Neither direction is lossless. Going to a cluster costs you order: the cluster records which points connect, never which came first, and once points have welded, which path a point belonged to is gone unless you carried it in an attribute. Coming back costs you the junctions, since a chain terminates at every vertex with more than two links.


> Figure: Three panels in a row, joined by flow arrows labelled Path colon To Clusters and Cluster colon Break to Paths. The first panel holds two separate numbered paths: a four-point run, and a second four-point run whose last point stops just short of a point partway along the first. In the second panel they have fused into one cluster of ringed Vtx joined by plain edges, with no numbering anywhere; the two coincident points are now a single Vtx ringed in cyan and labelled degree 3. In the third panel three separate chains run out from that same cyan-ringed Vtx, each with its own order chevrons and still no numbering.
> Two paths in, three chains out, and no numbering survives the middle.


## Related

* [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) -- what to reach for when the run has to fork
* [Blending & Sampling](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems/blending-and-sampling) -- how points invented along a path get their values
* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- the **Conditions** pins that mark where a path splits, bevels or flips
* **Paths** -- every path node, with its settings

title: Common Path Operations
description: A task-oriented index into the path nodes. Being rewritten once the path nodes themselves are documented.
body:
This page is being rebuilt.

Its job is to answer "I want to do X, which node does it?" for the path family. The previous version was written before the path nodes were documented from source, and several of its entries described behaviour the nodes do not have. Rather than leave those in place, it is empty until the per-node documentation exists to build a truthful index from.

Until then, [Paths](concept:working-with-pcgex/paths) covers the model and names the families. Every node, with its settings, is in the node library under **Paths**.

title: Collections of Anything
description: The collection system spawns meshes, skinned meshes, actors, levels and PCG data.
outline: The entry is the pick, the path is the payload
An empty Asset slot still picks
An entry without an override writes the collection default
Where an actor collection already does it
body:
The collection system spawns meshes, skinned meshes, actors, levels and PCG data. Everything else is a **Generic** entry: one `Asset` slot that takes any asset, hosted only by an **Omni Collection** (**Collection | Omni**). Nothing spawns it. The asset becomes the entry's staged path, so weights, categories, tags, selectors, sub-collections, swapping and preloading work unchanged, and **Staging : Load Properties** (**Staging : Load Properties**) hands the path to whatever consumes the asset.

## The entry is the pick, the path is the payload

*Add Generic rows to an Omni Collection, distribute as usual, read the asset path back onto the points.*

1. Create an Omni Collection. Add rows with **+ Add** and pick **Generic**, or drop the assets from the Content Browser: any asset no other entry type claims lands as a Generic row. A Blueprint whose parent is not an actor lands there too, with the Blueprint asset itself as the path.
2. Distribute as usual. Weights, categories, tags, selectors and sub-collections read nothing type-specific, so a collection of decal materials behaves like a collection of meshes up to the point where something would spawn.
3. Read the pick back with **Staging : Load Properties**. `Write Asset Path` writes the entry's asset as a soft object path attribute (`AssetPath` by default) on every staged point, and `Write Entry Type` writes `Generic`. Whatever applies the material, plays the sound or spawns the system reads that attribute.

Everything keyed on the staged path treats a Generic entry like any other: **Staging : Swap** and a **Variant Collection** swap it by path, **Preload Resources** loads it, cooking gathers it as a dependency, and the collection editor shows the asset's own thumbnail (**Staging : Swap**, **Collection | Variant**, **Resources**).

In an Omni Collection these rows sit beside real mesh, actor and level rows. **Staging : Type Filter** (**Staging : Type Filter**) routes them on their own `Generic` type, as a toggle in Include and Exclude and as a pin in Pin Per Type. The spawn nodes skip a Generic pick like any type that is not theirs, so a mixed dataset can still be wired straight to **Staging : Spawn Actors**, which warns per skipped pick only when its `Quiet Invalid Entry Warnings` is off.


> **Warning.**
> **An empty Asset slot still picks**
>
> A Generic row with no asset is a valid pick that stages nothing, a weighted "spawn nothing" slot that still carries bounds, unless the collection's `Do Not Ignore Invalid Entries` is on. The same rule governs an empty mesh slot. **Staging : Load Properties** writes an empty path for it, so filter on the attribute downstream when an empty pick must not reach the consumer.


## Bounds

*Generic entries take the collection's Default Staging Bounds; the per-entry bounds modifier tunes them.*

Nothing is loaded to measure a Generic asset. Every rebuild copies the collection's `Default Staging Bounds` into the entry's staged bounds, whether or not the `Asset` slot is filled. The setting sits with the shared collection settings (**Asset Collection**), next to `Subcollection Bounds Mode`, and defaults to a one metre cube centred on the origin. Fitting, spacing, selectors that reason about entry size and the bounds outputs of **Staging : Load Properties** all read the result.

Per-entry footprints come from the entry's `Bounds Staging Modifier`, the same slot every entry type carries: Offset Min/Max, Scale, Pad / Expand or Scale + Offset, applied on top of the default. A decal's projection box or a particle system's rough extent is a modifier on its row, with the default sized for the common case.


> Figure: On the left a collection settings chip labelled Default Staging Bounds, and beneath it a square centred on an origin cross, labelled min -50 max 50. Flow arrows run from it to three Generic entry rows on the right, each naming a different asset with its own glyph: M_DecalRust, NS_Smoke and BP_Lamp. The first row carries no modifier and its staged box is the default square exactly. The second carries a Scale modifier and its box is twice as wide and half as tall, with the default drawn dashed behind it. The third carries a Pad / Expand modifier and its box is the default grown on every side, again over a dashed copy of the default.
> One default box for every Generic row; a modifier on the row is the only thing that reshapes it.


Only Generic entries read the default. An empty Mesh, Actor, Level or PCG data slot still stages an empty box, and an entry whose staging is authored keeps its authored bounds.

## Specialising the picker

*Generic Allowed Class narrows the Asset picker to one class and its subclasses.*

`Generic Allowed Class`, on the same collection settings, restricts what the `Asset` slot of every Generic row offers, in the grid tile, the grid detail pane and the Entries tab alike. A decal collection set to a material class offers materials and nothing else; None offers any asset. It is editor-only and a picker filter only: existing entries are never checked against it, and Content Browser drops are not filtered by it. Changing it updates the open editor's pickers on the spot.

## Fallback: typed collections

*A Mesh Collection can still carry the asset in a Soft Object Path property, with an empty or placeholder mesh slot.*

For a typed **Mesh Collection** (**Collection | Mesh**), or a project that cannot move to Omni, the asset lives in a custom property instead of the entry's asset slot. Declare a **Soft Object Path** property on the collection, locally or through a **Property Schema**; its `Allowed Class` narrows the picker the way `Generic Allowed Class` does. Add one entry per asset, enable the property override on the entry and pick the asset. Read it back with a `Properties Mapping` row on **Staging : Load Properties**, which writes the property as a soft object path attribute. Declaring and overriding are covered in [Collection Properties](concept:working-with-pcgex/asset-staging/collection-properties).


> **Warning.**
> **An entry without an override writes the collection default**
>
> Values resolve entry, then category, then the collection's declared default, and the default of a Soft Object Path property is empty. An entry whose override was never enabled still picks, and writes an empty path. Filter on the attribute downstream, or give the category an override so the fall-through lands on something visible.


The rows are mesh rows throughout: **Staging : Type Filter** routes them as Mesh, so give them a category or a tag when they need routing of their own. The mesh slot is either empty or a placeholder:

| Mesh slot | Pickable | Staged bounds | Grid thumbnail | If the points reach a static mesh spawner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Empty | Yes, unless the collection's `Do Not Ignore Invalid Entries` is on | None | *No Asset* | Nothing spawns, silently |
| Placeholder mesh | Yes | The mesh's bounding box | The mesh | The placeholder spawns |

An empty slot is the lighter choice when nothing downstream needs bounds. The staged bounds of an empty mesh entry stay an empty box: fitting, spacing and the bounds outputs of **Staging : Load Properties** have nothing to work with, and a bounds modifier leaves an empty box untouched. A placeholder mesh sized to the asset's footprint gives those systems something real, and gives the collection editor a thumbnail to tell entries apart by. The price is that the placeholder is a genuine mesh pick: keep those points away from the static mesh spawner, or accept the placeholder as a visible proxy while authoring.

## Where an actor collection already does it

*Anything that is an actor is an Actor Collection entry.*

An **Actor Collection** entry (**Collection | Actor**) references an actor class, and **Staging : Spawn Actors** spawns it (**Staging : Spawn Actors**), so a decal actor, a Niagara actor or a light Blueprint needs no Generic row. The two combine: an actor entry can carry the decal class while a Soft Object Path property on the same entry carries the material to apply, so one actor class serves a whole collection of decals, with weights and categories deciding which material each point gets. When the actor class is fixed downstream and only the material varies, a collection of Generic material entries is the alternative: the points carry the material path from `Write Asset Path`, and whatever spawns the fixed class applies it.

title: Merge before Spawn
description: Vanilla PCG nodes process the input data one after the other -- that's a strong design choice and it's good for your memory; but it also makes processing lots of smaller dataset _very slow_.
body:
Vanilla PCG nodes process the input data one after the other -- that's a strong design choice and it's good for your memory; but it also makes processing lots of smaller dataset _very slow_.

Most of the time, **there is a significant speed gain to be had by merging point data right before you feed them into a static mesh spawner** -- the same applies to debug nodes.


> **Tip.**
> This is even more important if your data is about to generate multiple exclusive ISMC configurations.




### Buy why?

The spawner' partitioning code is actually very efficient, but it has to be setup in a particular way each time a new data object is processed, and when there is a lot of inputs to process, it tanks the performance.

**Merging point is obviously not free, but it's definitely worth looking into if you find your spawners to be sluggish.**

## **Less Spawners is better**


> **Danger.**
> Even if using the exact same configuration, using two different nodes will generate two unique components; **ultimately increasing drawcalls.**


On that same note, it's worth mentioning that less spawners is much better as well, so make sure to consolidate your point data before spawning as well.

ISMC (Instanced Static Mesh Component) are created for each unique combination of the following criterias:

* Static Mesh
* Material
* Descriptor overrides
* **Node**       ← _\*sad trombone\*_

title: What's different
description: Any toolkit that grows past a certain size hits the same fork: one node with fifty settings and a dozen mutually exclusive modes, or a separate node for every combination anyone might want.
outline: The editor accepts wiring the consumer will reject
The only data type PCGEx adds
Identity lives in attributes and tags
body:
Any toolkit that grows past a certain size hits the same fork: one node with fifty settings and a dozen mutually exclusive modes, or a separate node for every combination anyone might want. PCGEx takes a third route. Configuration is its own node, and the node consuming it does the work.

## Sub-nodes configure, consumers execute

_Configuration is a node, so it composes like a node._

A **sub-node** describes how something should be done. A condition to test, a cost to score by, a strategy for picking an asset. It produces no points and edits nothing. The **consumer** is the node with a matching input pin, and it is where the work actually happens: it reads every sub-node on that pin, builds what it needs from them, and runs it against its own data.


> Figure: A PCG graph in which Tensor : Spline Flow connects into Heuristics : Tensor, which connects into Fill Control : Heuristics Budget, which connects to the Fill Controls pin of Cluster : Flood Fill. Two BlendOp nodes connect to the same consumer node's Blend Ops pin.
> A tensor feeds a heuristic, the heuristic feeds a fill control, and Cluster : Flood Fill consumes that alongside two blend ops.


Sub-nodes chain into each other as readily as they feed consumers, because a sub-node with an input pin of its own is an ordinary consumer from that pin's point of view.

> Profiling splits the same way. A sub-node's own execution is negligible, and the cost of the work it describes lands on the consumer that runs it, which is where to look when a graph gets slow.

## Spotting one in the graph

_The title prefix names the family, and the pin carries its icon and colour._

Sub-node titles are prefixed with their family and a colon: **Filter : Compare (Numeric)**, **Heuristics : Shortest Distance**, **Shape : 3D Grid**, **Selector : Classic**. The editor additionally prefixes every PCGEx node title with `PCGEx |` , which is how you tell them apart from vanilla nodes in a crowded palette.

Each family also owns a pin icon and a pin colour, so a Heuristics pin looks like a Heuristics pin on both the sub-node and its consumer. The colours are yours to change, under `Colors and Semantics | Subnodes` in project settings.


> Figure: STILL | id: what-pcgex-adds-subnode-anatomy | SHOWS: The three things that mark a sub-node apart from the node consuming it | FRAME: Two nodes side by side in the graph editor at a zoom where titles and pins are legible, one sub-node wired into the matching input pin of one consumer | CALLOUTS: The family prefix in the sub-node title, the pin icon on its output, the same icon repeated on the consumer input pin | SOURCE: example project, any Filter node feeding an Uber Filter | NOTE: shoot with bUseNativeColorsIfPossible turned off in project settings, otherwise filter pins render the engine colour instead of the PCGEx palette colour the page describes
> The prefix names the family, and the icon repeats on both ends of the wire.


## Stacking several on one pin

_Most sub-node pins take many connections, and each family decides what several of them mean together._

Connect three filters to one **Filters** pin and the consumer gets all three. What happens next belongs to the family, not to the consumer: filters all have to pass, heuristics average into a single score, probes pool the edges they each propose.

**How each family combines**


| Family                                                                                                        | How several combine                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|  Filters                    | Tested in sequence, all must pass, the first failure stops the rest                                                                                       |
|  Filter Group               | Nests a stack of filters under OR, and inverts to NAND or NOR. The only route to anything but AND                                                         |
|  Heuristics             | One of six modes, a weighted average by default                                                                                                           |
|  Probes                      | The union of the edges each one proposes, though they share a coincidence set, so one probe claiming a direction can suppress another's edge there        |
|  Actions                    | Run in sequence, every one of them                                                                                                                        |
|  Blend Ops                 | Run in sequence. A single op supersedes a monolithic one writing the same attribute, and a composite clashing with its own components is refused outright |
|  Fill Controls         | Depends on the capability: accumulated, ANDed, or the smallest wins                                                                                       |
|  Tensors                    | Directions blend by weight, rotations compose by successive slerp                                                                                         |
|  Match Rules             | Under All, every rule must pass. Under Any, every required rule and at least one optional                                                                 |
|  Selectors                | Exactly one, and more is an error. Several combine upstream through **Selector Modifier : Cascade**, which takes the first that yields a pick             |
|  Sort Rules               | A tiebreak cascade: the first rule decides, the next breaks only its ties, and so on down                                                                 |
|  Partition Rules     | Nested subdivision, so every distinct combination of all their values becomes its own partition                                                           |
|  Pickers                    | The union of the indices each one picks                                                                                                                   |
|  Noise                     | Stacked, each compositing onto the result below it through its own blend mode and weight                                                                  |
|  Shapes                      | Every builder constructs its own shape from every seed, and you get all of them                                                                           |
|  Vtx Properties        | Each writes its own attributes. Two aiming at one attribute name overwrite each other in no fixed order                                                   |
|  Neighbor Samplers | Each samples the neighbourhood independently. Where two write the same attribute, the last one wins                                                       |
|  Texture Params           | Each maps one material parameter to its own attributes, and all of them run                                                                               |
|  Cluster States         | Each mutates one shared flags attribute, so ORed masks accumulate while Set, AND or XOR masks overwrite what came before                                  |
|  Point States           | Fold into one shared flags attribute, except the fold is unimplemented today and nothing is written                                                       |

Pickers, Vtx Properties, Partition Rules and Texture Params carry no priority at all, which costs nothing where their combination ignores order and is worth knowing where it does not.




> Figure: Two Filter : Bool Compare nodes and a Filter : Check Nearest node feed an AND filter group, whose output connects to the Filters pin of Uber Filter. One of the Bool Compare nodes also feeds the Point Filters input pin of Check Nearest.
> Three filters, one group, one pin. Filter : Check Nearest takes a filter of its own.


Where order matters it comes from **Priority**, lowest first, and a sub-node with a non-zero priority shows it as `[N]` in its subtitle so the ordering is readable from the graph. Equal priorities are not resolved by connection order, so give anything order-sensitive a priority rather than relying on how the wires were drawn.


> Figure: STILL | id: what-pcgex-adds-priority-subtitle | SHOWS: That the running order of a stack of sub-nodes can be read off the graph without opening a panel | FRAME: Three sub-nodes of one family wired into a single consumer pin, at least two of them carrying a non-zero Priority so the bracketed number appears in the subtitle | CALLOUTS: The bracketed priority number in each subtitle | SOURCE: example project, several Heuristics feeding a pathfinding node
> Priority is readable from the graph, with no panel open.



> **Warning.**
> **The editor accepts wiring the consumer will reject**
>
> Pin matching in the graph editor works by family, so any filter drops onto any filter pin and a Vtx filter connects to an Edge filter pin without complaint. The consumer applies the exact rule at execution, logs `Input is not supported by pin`, and carries on without it. A graph that looks correctly wired can be quietly running one condition short.


## One sub-node, many consumers

_A sub-node has no idea what it is being used for._

The same output can drive as many consumers as you like. Each one reads the configuration and applies it in its own context, which is why a filter never has to know whether it is selecting points, splitting a path or gating a transform.


> Figure: A single Filter : Bool Compare node routed to three consumers: the Filters pin of Uber Filter, the Split Conditions pin of Path : Split, and the Filters pin of Transform Points.
> One filter, three consumers. Each names the pin for its own job.


Change the sub-node and every consumer follows.


> **Note.**
> Inside a loop subgraph, sub-nodes that need no per-iteration override are better created outside the loop and passed in on an input pin. The wiring reads more clearly and the graph builds far fewer throwaway objects.


## What travels on the wire

_The configuration becomes a real piece of PCG data, which explains most of the behaviour above._

A sub-node emits a **factory**: an object carrying the settings you filled in, travelling on a `Param` pin like any other parameter data. That is why reroute nodes work on it, why one output reaches many inputs, and why it crosses a subgraph boundary like anything else on a wire.

**That last one is a design lever.** A reusable subgraph can expose a sub-node input of its own and leave it optional, so whoever places it can pass in extra intent: one more filter, a different heuristic, a sort rule. The subgraph gets refined from the outside without having to anticipate every variation as an exposed parameter.

Consumers never run the factory directly. Each one builds its own short-lived operation, per batch and per cluster, and those copies are plain C++ objects rather than anything the engine has to track. The shared configuration stays immutable while every worker holds private state, so a cluster batch spreads across threads with no locking in the hot path.

**The three layers**


The node you configure in the graph is a settings object. On execution it creates the factory, which is a `UPCGData` subclass and therefore real graph data, not a lightweight handle: it can hold caches, spatial octrees and loaded asset references built during its preparation step. Consumers then instantiate the third layer from it, one working instance per batch of data they process.

Instanced behaviours (below) share the shape but not the middle layer's lifetime, since they live inside the settings asset and get duplicated per execution instead of being created fresh.




> **Note.**
> **Sub-nodes live for one execution**
>
> Concrete data persists: point data and attribute sets can be serialized onto a PCG Component or written into a PCG Data Asset, then read back later. A factory cannot. It exists for the execution that created it and for nothing beyond it, so a graph generates the sub-nodes it needs rather than loading them from storage. Passing them through subgraph pins is the way they travel.


***

## The only data type PCGEx adds

_Vtx, Edges and paths are labels on ordinary point data, and vanilla nodes read them fine._

**Vtx**, **Edges**, a path, a staged point: none of these is a container type. Each one is standard PCG point data, and the name describes what PCGEx nodes assume about the attributes and tags it carries. The assumptions are PCGEx-specific. The data is not.

Pins follow from that. A cluster's **Vtx** and **Edges** pins are declared as ordinary point pins, so vanilla nodes connect in both directions with nothing to convert: move Vtx with a vanilla transform, thin a path with a density filter, merge two PCGEx outputs and carry on.


> Figure: STILL | id: what-pcgex-adds-vanilla-interop | SHOWS: A vanilla PCG node working on cluster data in the middle of a PCGEx chain | FRAME: A graph segment reading left to right, a PCGEx node outputting Vtx, a vanilla PCG node operating on those points, and the result going back into a PCGEx cluster node | CALLOUTS: The vanilla node sitting between the two PCGEx nodes | SOURCE: example project | NOTE: pick a vanilla operation that keeps the points intact, such as a transform, so the shot does not double as an example of breaking the pairing
> Nothing is converted going in, and nothing coming back out.


The factory is the exception, and the only one: the single kind of data PCGEx puts on a wire that vanilla PCG has no use for.


> **Warning.**
> **Identity lives in attributes and tags**
>
> A cluster's two halves are paired by reserved tags and by attributes carrying endpoint ids. A vanilla node that carries those through is safe, and one that drops them hands back a set of points PCGEx can no longer read as a cluster. Deleting Vtx does it from the other side, leaving edges that refer to endpoints which are gone. [Clusters](concept:working-with-pcgex/clusters) covers what each half has to keep.


## Instanced behaviours

_Some nodes embed the choice in a dropdown rather than taking a wire._

Where only one behaviour can be active anyway, the choice sits in the consumer's own details panel as a class dropdown with its settings underneath. Edge refinement, relaxation and orientation all work this way. It avoids a node for something that was never going to compose, at the cost of the two things wiring gives you: nothing else can reuse that configuration, and you cannot stack two.


> Figure: STILL | id: what-pcgex-adds-instanced-behaviour | SHOWS: Where an instanced behaviour is chosen, and the override pin that only exists once the node is expanded | FRAME: A node carrying an instanced behaviour in the graph editor, expanded so the override pin is visible, with the details panel beside it showing the class dropdown and the chosen behaviour settings nested beneath it | CALLOUTS: The class dropdown in the details panel, the settings nested under it, the override pin on the expanded node | SOURCE: example project, Cluster : Refine Edges or a Path node with an Orientation | NOTE: the node has to be expanded in the shot, since the override pin is hidden when it is collapsed
> The behaviour is chosen in the panel, and its override pin appears only once the node is expanded.


Driving their parameters from data takes a different route than a wired sub-node, whose settings are ordinary overridable properties fed by the node's own override pin. An instanced behaviour's properties sit one object deeper, so they get a pin of their own, which appears when the node is expanded:

1. Expand the instanced behaviour's settings, right-click the property, and choose **Copy Internal Name**.
2. Build an attribute set with an attribute of exactly that name. The match is on the internal name, character for character.
3. Connect it to the node's override pin.

The value is read from the attribute set's first entry, once, when the behaviour is set up. It configures a run, and does not vary per point.

## Related

* [Filters](concept:working-with-pcgex/filters) -- the largest sub-node family, and the section to read next
* [Additional Systems](concept:working-with-pcgex/additional-systems) -- blending, matching and the other transverse families
* [Pathfinding](concept:working-with-pcgex/pathfinding) -- where several heuristics score together

title: Authoring
description: Nearly all authoring happens inside one editor mode.
outline: Create can hand the new actor its assets
body:
## The Valency Editor Mode

Nearly all authoring happens inside one editor mode. You will find it in the **Modes** dropdown as **PCGEx | Valency**, and it is the first thing to turn on when you open an authoring level.

### Why it matters that you are in it

_Outside the mode, cages are actors with properties. Inside it, they are a design you can see._

The mode does three separate jobs at once, and each is worth knowing about:

* **It draws the design.** Connections between cages, orbital directions, connectors, volumes, mirror links. Without it you have a level full of actors and no way to see what is bonded to what.
* **It puts the authoring tools in reach.** A side panel appears with a rail of tools, and the viewport gains gestures that do the work property fields would otherwise do.
* **It keeps things in sync.** A pass runs while the mode is active that refreshes containers and rebuilds volumes as you author, and entering the mode re-syncs the PCG components registered against each level cache.

That third one is the reason to author from inside it rather than around it. Outside the mode, nothing is watching, and a scene that has drifted stays drifted.


> Figure: STILL | id: authoring-mode-overview | SHOWS: The editor mode active, so a reader can recognise every surface the page then names. | FRAME: Level viewport with several connected cages visible and their connections drawn, the Valency panel open on the right with its tool rail visible, and the Modes dropdown showing PCGEx Valency as the active mode. One cage selected so the panel has content. | CALLOUTS: The tool rail, the panel body, a drawn connection between two cages, an orbital line with no neighbour. | SOURCE: WFC 2D sample authoring level. | NOTE: Everything the page discusses should be identifiable in this one image. Prefer a slightly wider shot over a tight one.
> The mode active: connections drawn in the viewport, tools in the panel, and one cage selected.


## The pieces you place

_The Valency actors. Everything else is authored on them._

| Actor                      | Is                                                                                                |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Valency Cage (Simple)**  | The default cage, and the one you will place most. Authors one module.                            |
| **Valency Cage (Null)**    | A placeholder that authors no module: a boundary, a required neighbour, or space that is occupied and nothing more. |
| **Valency Cage (Pattern)** | One position in a pattern arrangement.                                                            |
| **Valency Module Cage**    | Declares the level it sits in as a single module. Self-aggregating, so it needs no volume.        |
| **Valency Assembly Cage**  | Declares everything attached to it as a single module. A cage in every other respect, so it needs a volume. |
| **Context Volume**         | Gathers the cages inside it into a library.                                                       |
| **Asset Palette**          | A reusable asset library that cages mirror from. Not a cage: no orbitals, no volume.              |

You do not need the Place Actors panel for any of them. The viewport action bar has a **Create** button that spawns any primitive at the viewport placement position, grouped into [Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages), **Containers** and **Level as Module** so the list reads as the two authoring workflows rather than a list of class names.

In practice you need two to start: a **Cage** and a **Context Volume**. The rest of a layout grows from that first cage with the expand gesture below.


> **Note.**
> **Create can hand the new actor its assets**
>
> Some primitives are inert until they reference something, so the Create menu offers that in the same gesture, with each binding letting you **pick an existing asset or create a new one**.
>
> * **Context Volume** takes [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) and **Pattern Assets**.
> * **Module Cage** takes a **Connector Set**, which it requires.
>
> Everything else spawns as a plain entry. A row also greys out when it does not apply, with the reason in its tooltip, rather than vanishing.


### The context volume is the entry point

_Valency only ever sees what a volume contains._

A context volume is not a grouping convenience. It is the thing that finds cages, gathers them, and hands them to a library, and **a cage outside every volume is ignored entirely**. It contributes nothing, it is not compiled, and no warning is raised about it, because there is nothing wrong with it.

That is deliberate. It leaves the level as a workspace: reference geometry, half-finished kits, a scratch corner of experiments and the pieces you are still deciding about can all sit next to your real cages without leaking into anything. What you want considered, you put in a volume.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: authoring-volume-scope | SHOWS: What a context volume gathers, what it ignores, and how nesting works. | ELEMENTS: A top-down level layout. One large volume outline containing several cages, drawn as included. Outside it, two cages and a stray mesh drawn greyed and marked ignored. Inside the large volume, a smaller nested volume outline containing three pattern cages, drawn as its own group. One cage straddling the large volume boundary, with a dot marking its origin clearly inside, so it reads as included. | MUST BE CLEAR: Membership is decided by the cage origin point, not its extent. Everything outside every outline is invisible to Valency rather than broken. The nested volume is a group in its own right.
> Inside a volume is considered. Outside is ignored, which is what keeps the rest of the level usable as a workspace.


Two things follow that are worth knowing before you lay a level out:

* **Membership is decided by the cage origin point**, not by its bounds. A cage overlapping the volume boundary is in or out according to where its origin sits, so a piece that looks half-contained is fully one or the other.
* **Volumes nest, and nesting recurses.** A volume inside another is a group in its own right, which is the usual way to keep a set of pattern cages together and separately targeted without moving them out of the layout they describe.


> **Note.**
> The exception is a **Valency Module Cage**, which declares its own level as a module and self-aggregates. It needs no volume, and putting one in a volume is not how it contributes.


## The tool rail

_Eight tools. Which ones are available depends on what you have selected._

| Tool                     | Authors                                                                           |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Bonding Settings**     | The module settings a cage produces: weight, limits, policy, placement conditions |
| **Orbitals**             | Which orbitals the cage has, which are enabled, and what an unconnected one means |
| **Assets**               | What the cage spawns. Absent on an assembly cage, whose subtree is the asset      |
| **Connectors**           | The sockets on the module, their types and polarities                             |
| **Footprint**            | The space the module occupies for overlap purposes                                |
| **Mirroring**            | Borrowing assets, connectors and properties from another container                |
| **Pattern Settings**     | Pattern-specific settings, on pattern cages                                       |
| **Placeholder Settings** | What a null cage asserts, on null cages                                           |

Only one tool is active at a time, and the rail only offers tools that apply to what is selected. **Orbitals** is the one tool a null cage shares with every other cage, because a placeholder still occupies a position and still connects, whatever else it does or does not author.

### The viewport does the authoring

_Most of the work is hovering and clicking, not typing into fields._

The mode adds gestures to the viewport. Each appears on hover, on a surface chosen so two gestures never compete for the same pixels.

| Hover                         | Offers                                                          |
| ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| An orbital with no neighbour  | Place something across it, into the empty cell beyond           |
| A container, with a selection | Attach the selection to it, or register references between them |
| A mirror, proxy or loose link | Delete that one link                                            |

The signature one is the first. An unconnected orbital shows a **(+)**, and clicking it duplicates the source cage into the cell across that orbital, emptied of its content, so you can lay out topology before deciding what fills it. Holding **Shift** opens a menu of the alternatives instead of taking the default.


> Figure: CLIP | id: authoring-expand-gesture | SHOWS: The expand gesture, which is how a layout gets built. | BEATS: 1) Cursor approaches a cage that has one orbital with no neighbour. A plus affordance fades in on that orbital line. 2) Click. A new cage appears in the cell beyond, already connected, empty of content. 3) Cursor moves to an orbital on the new cage and repeats, so a short chain of three or four cages builds up. 4) Shift is held over the next plus and a small menu opens instead, showing the alternative actions. | SOURCE: WFC 2D sample authoring level. | LENGTH: 10s, loops. | NOTE: The point is speed. Do not pause between clicks, and let the chain build faster than a viewer expects.
> Hover an unconnected orbital, click the plus, and the layout grows a cell at a time. Shift offers the alternatives.


That menu is where the less common actions live: duplicating a cage **with** its content rather than empty, dropping a placeholder that asserts the cell must stay empty or must hold something, and overriding what this one orbital means when it has no neighbour without changing the rest of the cage.

The attach gestures behave the same way. **Attach** moves each actor pivot onto the container origin, which is what placing a module usually means, and the menu offers variants that preserve the arrangement instead, or attach a copy and leave the originals where they are.

Alongside the hover gestures, a small action bar sits at the bottom of the viewport for actions with no hovered surface to attach to. It holds two: **Create**, covered above, and **Detach**, which removes the selected content from its container and leaves it exactly where it stands.

### What you can see, and what you can turn off

_Eight layers, each toggled independently. Dense scenes need this._

| Layer             | Draws                                       |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Connections**   | Bonds between cages                         |
| **Labels**        | Names on what is drawn                      |
| **Connectors**    | Sockets, with their orientation             |
| **Volumes**       | Context volume bounds                       |
| **Ghosts**        | Preview geometry for what a cage will spawn |
| **Links**         | Mirror and proxy arcs                       |
| **Constraints**   | Spatial connector constraint visualizations |
| **Expand**        | The (+) on unconnected orbitals             |

Two of these are worth turning off before the others. **Links** are the one visual that spans arbitrary distances, so a dense mirror setup is exactly when they stop helping. **Expand** is separated out because it is the only hover affordance that places something: the attach gestures need a deliberate selection before they appear at all, so they cannot fire by accident, and are not gated.

## Housekeeping

_Authored data can outlive what it referred to._

Cages accumulate references, and things they point at get deleted. The mode can sweep for authoring data that no longer refers to anything and report it by category before removing it: orbital variant choices whose symmetry the current orbital set no longer has, manual connections pointing at deleted cages, mirror entries with no source, and collection references with no collection.

Worth running after a round of restructuring, when the count tells you something useful about what you actually broke.

title: Authoring Connectors
description: A connector is a component on the cage.
outline: Identifiers must be unique within a cage
What a connector transform is relative to
Span pairs are a work in progress
body:
A connector is a component on the cage. You place it, move it with the ordinary transform gizmo, and set what it is. Most of the work is deciding where sockets sit and what types they carry, and the plugin has several ways of saving you from doing that by hand.

## Placing one

_Click it in the viewport, move it like anything else._

Connectors are picked directly in the viewport and manipulated with the standard editor transform gizmo, so positioning one is the same motion as positioning any actor. What you set on it:

| Field            | Decides                                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Identifier`     | Its name, unique within the cage.                          |
| `Connector Type` | Which type from the connector set it is an instance of.    |
| `Polarity`       | `Universal`, `Plug` or `Port`.                             |
| `Enabled`        | Off, it is ignored entirely at compile.                    |
| `Inheritable`    | Whether cages mirroring this one inherit it.               |
| `Priority`       | Frontier expansion order during growth.                    |
| `Spawn Capacity` | How many children this one socket may spawn.               |
| `Bridge Role`    | Whether it takes part in normal growth, bridging, or both. |


> **Note.**
> `Enabled` and `Inheritable` are easy to overlook and both have real uses. Disabling a connector keeps it in the level for reference while removing it from the compiled module, and marking one non-inheritable lets a template carry a socket that its mirrors deliberately do not get.


## Where connectors come from

_Four sources, and later ones win._

You rarely place every connector by hand. A cage assembles its list from up to four places, gathered in the order below, and **each one can override anything gathered before it**, matching by identifier. The further down the table a source sits, the more it wins.

| Gathered | Source                             | Notes                                                                                                        |
| -------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 1st      | **Mesh sockets** on the asset      | Opt-in per cage, and only when a connector set resolves. The cheapest route if your kit already has sockets. |
| 2nd      | **Mirrored from another cage**     | Only components marked inheritable, from an enabled mirror source.                                           |
| 3rd      | **The cage's own components**      | What you placed. Overrides a same-named entry from either source above, when told to.                        |
| 4th      | **Components on attached content** | Connector components sitting on the actors attached to the cage, rather than on the cage itself.             |

That ordering is what makes the mesh-socket route usable: take everything the kit provides, then place one component by hand to correct the one socket that is wrong.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: authoring-connector-sources | SHOWS: Four sources contributing connectors to one cage, and how a later source replaces an earlier one by name. | ELEMENTS: Four labelled input rows feeding a single cage, stacked in priority order: mesh sockets at the bottom, mirrored connectors, the cage own components, then components on attached content at the top. Each row carries two or three named socket chips. One name, MainDoor, appears in both the mesh-socket row and the cage own row, with the lower one visibly struck through and the upper one carried into the final list on the right. | MUST BE CLEAR: The final list is an override merge by name, not a concatenation. Only one MainDoor survives, and it is the one from the higher source.
> Sources merge by identifier, and the later one wins. Correcting a single bad socket does not mean abandoning the rest.



> **Warning.**
> **Identifiers must be unique within a cage**
>
> Two connectors on the same cage with the same identifier is not a merge. The second one is **dropped** and recorded as a duplicate.
>
