> Copying a connector component defends against this by renaming the copy, appending a number, so duplicating within a cage is safe. Duplicating the whole cage is also safe, because the copies land on a new owner and cannot collide. The case to watch is hand-typing a name that already exists.


### From mesh sockets

_The cheapest connectors are the ones your kit already has._

If the meshes in your kit carry sockets, a cage can read connectors straight off them. The socket name becomes the identifier, and its type is matched against the connector set.

Two things do not survive the trip, and both have to be set afterwards if you need them:

* **Polarity is always `Universal`.** A mesh socket has no way to express plug or port.
* **Nothing else is set either.** Priority, spawn capacity and bridge role all take their defaults.

Where the mesh sits off the cage origin, the socket transform is composed with the asset's own offset, so a socket lands where it visually appears rather than where it would be if the mesh were centred.

## What a connector transform is relative to

_One setting on the cage, and it decides more than it looks like it does._

All connector, growth and bridging maths runs in the **cage frame**. The visual asset is written in the **output frame**. The transform strategy is what relates the two, and it is set per cage.

| Strategy                          | Does                                                                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cage Relative**                 | The two frames are the same. Connectors and output both sit in cage space. The simplest, and the default place to start.                                                |
| **Asset Relative**                | The output takes the asset's full transform, position, rotation and scale. Use when the asset is deliberately posed inside its cage and that pose is part of the piece. |
| **Cage Relative (Scaled Bounds)** | Position and rotation stay cage-aligned, and only scale carries through, so bounds reflect a scaled asset without moving it.                                            |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: authoring-transform-strategy | SHOWS: How the three strategies relate the cage frame to the frame the asset is written in. | ELEMENTS: Three panels, each showing one cage with a mesh sitting inside it rotated and offset from the cage origin, and a connector on the cage. Left, Cage Relative: the output point sits on the cage origin, axes aligned to the cage. Middle, Asset Relative: the output point sits on the mesh, adopting its rotation and offset. Right, Cage Relative Scaled Bounds: the output point stays on the cage origin and axis-aligned, but its bounds box is visibly larger, matching the scaled mesh. In every panel the connector stays in exactly the same place. | MUST BE CLEAR: The connector never moves between panels. What changes is only where the visual asset is written and what its bounds are.
> The connector sits in the same place in all three. Only where the asset is written changes.


Choosing **Asset Relative** tells the editor to watch the asset transform for changes, so moving the mesh inside its cage is treated as an edit to the module rather than an incidental nudge.

## Span pairs

_Two connectors that define a stretchable axis._

A cage can declare two of its connectors as a span pair, naming them by identifier. That marks the axis between them as scalable, which is what lets a bridge module stretch to fit a gap of a size it was not authored at.

This only matters for modules meant to span variable distances. Everything else can ignore it, and how the scaling is chosen is covered under growth.


> **Warning.**
> **Span pairs are a work in progress**
>
> At the time of writing the wiring is largely in place but the feature is not finished. You can author a span pair, and generation will use it, but **the module will not scale to the gap correctly yet**.
>
> Treat it as something to set up and be aware of rather than something to rely on. A module authored with a span pair today will start behaving properly once the remaining work lands, with no re-authoring.

title: Authoring Orbitals
description: The orbital set decides which directions exist.
outline: Letting a module sit next to itself
body:
The orbital set decides which directions exist. Authoring decides which cages actually connect along them, and what an orbital with nothing across it is asserting. The second of those is the part people underestimate.

## Start from a shipped set

*Five topologies install with the plugin. Most projects never author one.*

| Set | Is |
|---|---|
| `VOS_Cardinal_XY` | Four directions on the XY plane |
| `VOS_Grid_XY` | Square grid on the XY plane |
| `VOS_Grid_XZ` | Square grid on the XZ plane |
| `VOS_Grid_XYZ` | Full 3D grid |
| `VOS_Hex_XY` | Hex grid on the XY plane |

Reach for a set of your own only when the topology genuinely differs. What goes into one, and why the set tolerates being edited later, is covered under [Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/orbitals) in Concepts.

## Connections come from proximity

*You position cages. Valency works out what that means.*

There is no wire to draw between two cages. Each cage reaches out by its probe radius, and two cages connect when their probes meet, which is why laying out a kit is mostly moving things until the connections you want appear.

Detected connections are transient. They are rebuilt when the level loads and whenever a cage moves, so they cannot go stale, and they are not something you maintain.

In practice you rarely position anything by hand either. Hovering an orbital with nothing across it offers a **(+)**, and clicking it drops a connected cage in the cell beyond, already bonded along that orbital. Most layouts are built by clicking outward from one cage.

## Manual connections

*For when proximity is the wrong answer.*

An orbital can also name cages explicitly, independent of where anything sits. That covers the cases proximity cannot: two pieces that belong together but are laid out far apart, or a connection you want regardless of how the layout gets rearranged later.


> **Warning.**
> Listing a cage manually on an orbital **excludes it from auto-detection** on that orbital. The two mechanisms do not stack, so a manual entry is a replacement for detection rather than an addition to it. That is what stops a cage acquiring a second, accidental version of the connection you just authored deliberately.


## What an unconnected orbital means

*The most consequential dial on a cage, and the one that is easy to leave wrong.*

An orbital with nothing across it is **not automatically unconstrained**. What it asserts is set by the cage, and every module compiled from that cage carries the assertion.

| Setting | The compiled module says |
|---|---|
| **Any** | Nothing. A neighbour here is acceptable, and so is none. The default. |
| **Boundary** | Nothing may sit here. This side faces outward. |
| **Wildcard** | Something must sit here, and it does not matter what. |

The dial is cage-wide, and any single orbital can override it. That combination is what you want in practice: a wall piece set to **Boundary** overall, with the two orbitals that face into the building overridden to **Any**.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: authoring-missing-behavior | SHOWS: How the same authored cage produces three different rules depending on what its unconnected orbitals are set to mean. | ELEMENTS: Three copies of one wall cage in a row, each with two connected orbitals drawn solid and two unconnected orbitals drawn open. Left, labelled Any, with the open orbitals drawn neutral and a result below showing the piece placed both at an edge and in the middle. Middle, labelled Boundary, open orbitals crossed out, result showing the piece only ever at an outer edge. Right, labelled Wildcard, open orbitals drawn with a required-neighbour marker, result showing the piece only ever surrounded. | MUST BE CLEAR: The cage is identical in all three. Only what its unconnected orbitals assert differs, and that alone decides where the module is allowed to appear.
> One cage, three dials, three completely different modules.


Setting an override does not need the details panel. Hovering an unconnected orbital and holding **Shift** offers the four choices directly: inherit the cage-wide setting, or pin this one orbital to Any, Boundary or Wildcard.

The same gesture panel carries the orbital's [Bond and Corner Tags](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bond-and-corner-tags): a seam identity narrowing who may sit across the orbital, separate from what the dial asserts about whether anything must.

## Letting a module sit next to itself

*Self-connection, for pieces that tile against copies of themselves.*

An orbital can be marked as self-connecting, which lets another copy of the same cage sit across it, presenting the opposite orbital back. A corridor section that continues into another corridor section is the obvious case.

This needs the orbital set to declare that opposite direction as the orbital's **reciprocal**, since Valency has to know which orbital the copy presents in return. It is also skipped where either side is a boundary, because a side asserting that nothing may sit there is not going to make an exception for itself.

## Turning an orbital off

An orbital can be disabled on a cage, which removes it from consideration entirely: it detects nothing, asserts nothing, and takes no part in what the module requires. That is different from setting it to **Boundary**, which is an active statement that the side must stay empty. Disabling says the direction is not part of this piece at all.

title: Authoring Patterns
description: A pattern is an arrangement that can be recognised in a result, and what one is belongs to patterns.md.
outline: Only cage-authored patterns can replace anything
body:
A pattern is an arrangement that can be recognised in a result, and what one is belongs to [Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/patterns). There are two ways to author one, and the choice is not stylistic: it decides what the pattern is able to do when it matches.

## Two routes

*In a level, or in the asset.*

**Pattern cages** are placed in a level like any other cage. Connect them, and the connected group is a pattern. Each cage is one position in it, and one of them is the **root** holding the settings.

**The pattern asset** holds the same topology authored directly: positions, the adjacencies between them, and the slot names those adjacencies run along. No level, no cages.

| | Pattern cages | Pattern asset |
|---|---|---|
| Authored in | A level | The asset |
| Positions carry | Real modules, from their own content | Names and adjacencies only |
| Can replace on match | Yes | No |
| Suits | Arrangements you can see and build | Topology you can describe |


> **Warning.**
> **Only cage-authored patterns can replace anything**
>
> **Swap** takes the module authored on each position's own pattern cage. **Substitute** takes the root cage's whole-arrangement module. Both need a cage carrying content, so a pattern authored in the asset has nothing to place.
>
> That is not a failure and nothing errors. A graph-authored pattern is a perfectly good **detector**, and annotating is a real outcome. What it cannot do is replace, and setting it to Substitute will not make it try.


## What a position asserts

*Active or constraint-only, and that is the distinction to get right.*

Every position in a pattern carries a flag deciding whether it takes part in the outcome.

| Position | Means |
|---|---|
| **Active** | Consumed by the pattern. It is part of what gets replaced or annotated. |
| **Constraint-only** | Must be present for the match, and is left alone |

That is how a pattern says "a stairwell with a wall on this side" without the wall becoming part of the stairwell. The wall is required for the match and untouched by the result.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: patterns-active-vs-constraint | SHOWS: That a constraint-only position is required for a match to happen and is left standing afterwards. | ELEMENTS: Three panels left to right, joined by flow arrows. Panel one headed Authored: three connected pattern positions drawn as squares linked by pattern connection lines, two of them filled and labelled active and the third drawn with a distinct outline and labelled constraint only. Panel two headed Matched: a larger result of many modules with those three positions found and highlighted in place, all three outlined together as one match. Panel three headed After Substitute: the two active positions replaced by a single larger hero piece spanning where they were, and the constraint-only module still standing unchanged beside it, drawn exactly as it was in panel two. | MUST BE CLEAR: All three positions were needed to find the match. Only the two active ones were consumed, and the third is untouched in the final panel.
> Three positions matched, two consumed. The constraint-only one had to be there and is still there.


A position can also require **absence**. Slots listed as boundaries must have no edges, and slots listed as wildcards must have some. Combined with [Placeholders](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/placeholders) in a cage-authored pattern, that is how an arrangement requires empty space as part of its shape.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: patterns-required-absence | SHOWS: That empty space can be part of what a pattern matches, so identical modules fail where the space is occupied. | ELEMENTS: A wide scene split into two halves by a vertical rule, with a small authored strip above both. The strip shows the pattern: two connected positions, and on the outer slot of one a boundary bead drawn as a dashed ring with a bar through it, labelled must be empty. Left half headed Matches: the two modules found in a result with nothing beyond that slot, the empty cell drawn as a faint dashed outline, and the match highlighted. Right half headed Does not match: the identical two modules in the identical arrangement, but with a third module occupying the cell beyond that slot, and the candidate match drawn refused, dimmed and struck. | MUST BE CLEAR: The two modules and their connection are the same on both sides. The only difference is whether the cell beyond the boundary slot is occupied, and that alone decides the match.
> Same two modules, same connection. The pattern fails on the right because the space it requires is filled.


A position can also require a **seam identity**. Bond-tag rows on a pattern position cage compile into a requirement on the slot: whatever module the match finds here must present those tags. Bond and Corner Tags owns the semantics.

## Adjacencies and slots

*An edge between two positions, named on both ends.*

An adjacency says two positions are connected, and it names the slot on each side: an orbital direction, or a connector type. A single pattern may mix both, because matching reads a finished result rather than driving placement.

`Index Pairs` list the specific pairs of slot indices that satisfy an adjacency, and they are **or** semantics: any listed pair is a match. That is what lets one authored adjacency cover several equivalent orientations.

An unnamed slot is a **wildcard**: the adjacency must exist, and which direction or type it runs along does not matter.

## What the asset carries

*Two sets, and either may be absent.*

A pattern asset holds an **Orbital Set** and a **Connector Set**, used to resolve slot names to indices. Leaving one null means the asset authors no slots in that domain, which is the ordinary case for a pattern that only cares about one of them.

Sources work the same way as for [Bonding Rules Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bonding-rules-settings): levels contribute their pattern cages, registered automatically by the [Context Volumes](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/context-volumes) targeting the asset, and collections are walked to their level-sourced entries at compile.

`Auto Rebuild On Stale` keeps the asset current when its upstream changes, and the last successful compile time is shown on the asset.

## Rotating a whole pattern

A pattern root can carry [Orbital Variants](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/orbital-variants), and there the setting rotates the **entire arrangement** rather than one module. The pattern is treated as a complex module whose rotation set is the orbital set's symmetry group.

Rotations whose constituent modules do not exist are dropped when the library builds, unless the root opts into forcing them. On a pattern **child** cage the field is inert and says so.

## Which to reach for

*Ask whether the pattern needs to place something.*

Reach for **pattern cages** whenever the pattern replaces or swaps, and whenever the arrangement is easier to build than to describe. That covers most real uses, because the reason to recognise an arrangement is usually to do something to it.

Reach for **the asset** when the pattern is a query: finding every T-junction to annotate, counting occurrences, or driving something downstream from where matches were. Describing topology directly is faster than building it, as long as nothing needs to be placed at the end.

title: Bond and Corner Tags
description: An orbital decides which direction two modules can bond along, and says nothing about whether the sides that meet there belong together.
outline: A partially stated orbital derives nothing
body:
An orbital decides which direction two modules can bond along, and says nothing about whether the sides that meet there belong together. On kits where sides carry an identity (grass continues into grass, road into road), that identity has to be authored somewhere. **Bond Tags** name it per orbital. **Corner Tags** state it per cell corner and derive the per-orbital form for you, which matters as soon as a side's identity varies along its length.

## What a bond tag says

_A bond tag narrows who may sit across an orbital, never whether anything must._

Each orbital on a cage carries a `Bond Tags` block with two gameplay tag containers:

| Container | Carries                                                                        |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Tags`    | What this seam presents: its identity, as one or more tags.                    |
| `Accepts` | What may face it. Empty means the same as `Tags`, which is symmetric matching. |

The boundary, wildcard and accept-any assertions from [Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/orbitals) are untouched. On an orbital that accepted anything, tagging replaces "anything" with "only matching seams", while whether a neighbour is required at all stays whatever the boundary or wildcard assertion, or the missing-connection dial, already said. On an orbital that already has authored connections, tag matches join the authored list instead of replacing it: physical adjacency stays authoritative.

Two consequences of that scope:

* A tag on a **Boundary** orbital is a contradiction, since a boundary demands no neighbour. The compile ignores the tag and warns, and the validation panel flags it at author time.
* An untagged seam presents nothing, so it never satisfies a tagged one. A tagged seam mates only with other tagged seams, or with neighbours authored by layout or by hand. The failure mode is closed: forgetting to tag one side of a kit produces missing bonds, never accidental ones.

## How two seams match

_Each module judges the facing seam from its own side, and a bond needs both judgements to pass._

When two modules face each other along an orbital, module A reads the seam module B presents at the **reciprocal** orbital, and accepts it if B's `Tags` satisfy A's effective `Accepts`. The same check runs from B's side against A's presented tags. Both must pass. Each module's neighbour list is written purely from its own perspective, which is what makes asymmetric relationships expressible with no pair bookkeeping anywhere.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: bond-and-corner-tags-matching | SHOWS: Two facing seams match only when each side, checked separately, accepts what the other presents. | ELEMENTS: Two rows. Top row, two modules facing across a gap, the East orbital of the left and the West orbital of the right drawn with beads and a bonded link between them. Under each module a card with Tags and Accepts rows in mono: left presents Terrain.Grass and accepts Terrain, right presents Terrain.Dirt and accepts Terrain. Two crossing hairlines tie each card Accepts row to the OTHER card Tags row, each landing on a pass mark. Bottom row, the same left module against an untagged module whose card reads none: the single hairline from the empty Tags row lands on a fail mark at the tagged side Accepts row, and the link is struck as refused. | MUST BE CLEAR: The check runs once FROM each side against the OTHER side presented tags, and an untagged facing seam fails a tagged one rather than passing it. | NOTE: The verdict ties are hairline apparatus, not arrows, so no fifth arrow kind is invented. One green, spent on the bonded link and the pass marks, which mean the same thing.
> Both directions are checked independently. The bottom pair fails on the direction the empty side cannot answer.


Tag hierarchy applies on the accept side only, with the engine's usual semantics: a specific presented tag satisfies a coarse query, never the reverse, and siblings never match. So a seam presenting `Terrain.Grass` satisfies an `Accepts` of `Terrain`, while a seam presenting bare `Terrain` does not satisfy an `Accepts` of `Terrain.Grass`.


> **Warning.**
> **Present specific, accept coarse**
>
> Under the symmetric default, a side tagged `Terrain` and a side tagged `Terrain.Grass` do **not** mate: the fine side's implied accepts is not satisfied by the coarse presented tag. A side meant to take a whole family is authored as `Accepts = Terrain`, never by presenting `Terrain`.


Matching runs over every module in the compile, the module itself included, so a seam that accepts what it presents tiles against copies of itself without needing the self-connection flag. It also runs after [Orbital Variants](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/orbital-variants) expand, with each rotation carrying its rotated tag table, so a match between one module rotated and another unrotated registers on its own merits. And none of it needs the cages wired together: a free-standing cage with a tag on each side is the normal shape of such a kit, and its connections exist only in the compiled result.

Three warnings close the loop at compile. A tagged orbital whose `Reciprocal` is unset warns, since matching reads the facing seam at the reciprocal orbital and nothing can face an unpaired one. A required orbital that still accepts nothing after annotation warns, naming the module and orbital, because that module can no longer be placed at any position with a cluster edge there. And annotations on modules whose [Module Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-settings) keeps them out of ordinary placement are ignored, with a warning.

## The mirror trap

_A seam whose identity varies along the side mates with its reverse, because the two cells read it in opposite directions._

Suppose a side is not one thing but an ordered profile, grass at one end and dirt at the other, read in the cell's own winding as `(a,b)`. This is the classic Wang-tile setup. Two facing cells traverse their shared side in opposite directions: the corners are the same physical corners, but what one cell reads as `(a,b)` the other reads as `(b,a)`. A mixed profile therefore mates with its mirror, never with itself.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: bond-and-corner-tags-mirror | SHOWS: Facing cells read their shared side in opposite winding directions, so a profile a,b faces b,a, and stating the corners once produces both readings automatically. | ELEMENTS: Two cells side by side sharing a vertical seam, the two SHARED corners drawn once as diamond markers carrying two different states a and b in two identity tints, each named in ink beside its diamond. Inside each cell a counter-clockwise winding arc, and along the shared side the reading each winding produces: an upward arrow on the left of the seam, a downward arrow on the right. Beside each cell a card with Presents and Accepts rows built from the same tinted diamonds: left presents a,b and accepts b,a, right presents b,a and accepts a,b. | MUST BE CLEAR: The two cells hold the SAME two corners in the same physical places. Only the reading direction differs, which is exactly why a,b must accept b,a, and why one state per corner gives both sides the right profile with nothing else authored. | NOTE: No green anywhere. The winding arcs and reading arrows are apparatus, never one of the four link kinds. Only the two shared corners are drawn, so the figure cannot read as a partially stated cage.
> Same two corners, opposite reading order. The mirror pairing is geometry, not a convention to memorise.


Bond tags can express this: mint a tag per ordered profile and hand-pair each mixed one with its mirror in `Accepts`, on every side and through every rotation. The trouble is that the authoring question, what do I accept here, and the geometric fact, my neighbour reads this side backwards, pull in opposite directions, so every wrong pairing looks plausible while it is being authored. That confusion is what corner tags exist to remove.

## Corner tags

_State each corner once. Every seam the corner touches follows, mirrors included._

The topology lives on the **Orbital Set**: which corners the cell has, and which corners flank each orbital, in winding order. **Populate Corners (Planar)** derives both from the cell polygon, one corner per pair of adjacent in-plane orbitals, and covers squares, hexes and any convex planar cell. **Clear Corners** switches the feature off for the set.

On a cage, each corner then takes one tag: its state. An orbital whose incident corners are **all** stated derives its seam automatically: the profile is the corner states in winding order, and what it accepts is that profile reversed. The mirror pairing from the previous section is handled by construction. Rotated and reflected [Orbital Variants](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/orbital-variants) permute the corners geometrically and re-derive their seams, so a reflected variant's profiles come out mirrored with nothing extra authored, which is also what makes kits with chiral pieces authorable at all.

Corner states are matched **exactly**. A corner is a state, not a query: it is shared by more than two cells (four, on a grid), so it has to be one thing every cell around it agrees on. There is no hierarchy on corners, and each corner carries a single tag by design.

A symmetric profile is its own reverse and self-matches; a mixed one matches only its mirror. Diagonal orbitals on grid-with-diagonals sets get a one-corner seam, since a diagonal touches the cell at exactly one corner: the profile is that single state, which is its own mirror, so two diagonal neighbours bond exactly when they agree on the shared corner. **Populate Corners (Planar)** handles that case on its own.


> **Warning.**
> **A partially stated orbital derives nothing**
>
> A seam derives only when every corner it touches is stated. Stating some corners of a side and not others is not a smaller constraint, it is no constraint, and both the compile and the validation panel warn about it. A cage with no corners stated at all has opted out.


Two more compile warnings are aimed at specific mistakes. An orbital carrying both a bond-tag row and a derived corner seam unions the two match lists, so the looser channel widens the stricter one, and the compile says so in case the kit is half-migrated rather than deliberately dual. And a derived seam that matches nothing anywhere in the compile gets its own advisory, because that is exactly how the hand-authored chirality mistake presents: a mixed profile authored expecting to mate with itself instead of its mirror.

## Authoring surfaces

_Details rows, the gesture menu's quick panel, and corner markers in the viewport._

In the details panel, each orbital's `Bond Tags` block carries the `Tags` and `Accepts` rows, and the cage's `Corners` array carries one `State` per corner. The set-side topology sits on the Orbital Set under its `Corners` category, next to the two buttons.

The faster route is the viewport. Hovering an orbital opens the gesture menu, actions at the top and a quick panel at the bottom that edits the side in place while the menu stays open: **Self Connect**, the missing-connection choice, the same `Tags` and `Accepts` fields the details panel has, and, when the set carries corner topology, the seam's two incident corners. Configuring `Bond Tag Menu Root` and `Corner Tag Menu Root` in the editor settings turns each vocabulary's tags into one-click pills above the fields.


> Figure: STILL | id: bond-and-corner-tags-quick-panel | SHOWS: The gesture menu on a hovered orbital, actions on top and the quick panel below editing the side in place. | FRAME: Viewport gesture menu open on an unconnected orbital of a selected Module-role cage, on a set with populated corners and both tag roots configured, so every panel row is present: Self Connect, the four-state missing-connection segment, the Bond Tags header with pills and the Tags and Accepts fields, and the Corners header with the two incident corner rows. | CALLOUTS: The action rows, the Bond Tags rows, the pills, the two corner rows. | SOURCE: Any planar sample kit with bond and corner tag roots configured in the editor settings.
> The panel edits in place and the menu stays open, so tagging a whole kit is hover, click, hover.


Corners are their own hover surface. Each set corner draws as a small diamond marker on the cage, filled and tinted when stated, hollow when not, with the state's short name as a label; hovering one opens a panel for that single corner. The two routes are complementary: the orbital panel edits a seam's two ends together, the corner panel edits one corner that several seams share. Marker and label visibility toggle in the editor settings alongside the other display options, and the tag line under an orbital's label reads presented first, accepted second, so `Grass` presents symmetrically and `Grass <- Terrain` presents `Terrain.Grass` while accepting the family.


> Figure: STILL | id: bond-and-corner-tags-corner-markers | SHOWS: Corner markers and labels on a stated cage, filled and tinted where stated, hollow where not. | FRAME: One selected cage on a planar set with populated corners, three corners stated and one not, corner markers and corner labels enabled, close enough that the diamond markers and their state labels read clearly. | CALLOUTS: One stated corner with its label, the unstated hollow corner. | SOURCE: Any planar sample kit with corner states authored.
> A hollow diamond is an unstated corner, and any seam it touches derives nothing until it is filled.


A **Valency Module Cage** has no orbitals of its own, so it authors both kinds of rows directly, keyed by orbital and corner **name** and resolved against the consuming rules asset's set at compile. Authoring one is also what opts the level-module into orbital adjacency at all: [Module Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-cages) are otherwise connector-only, and these rows are the first orbital-side thing they can carry.

## Bond tags on pattern positions

_On a pattern cage the same rows flip direction: they state what a module must present to sit here._

A pattern position cage's bond-tag rows, authored under [Authoring Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/authoring-patterns), do not author a module seam, because a pattern position is a slot, not a piece. They compile into a requirement on the slot: whatever module the match finds here must **present** these tags at these orbitals. The query is the row's effective accepts, `Accepts` when set and `Tags` otherwise, and the viewport label shows it accept-only, as `<- Tags`.

The requirement narrows what the slot can hold. A wildcard position with requirements stops being a wildcard and materialises into every module presenting the required seams, which is how a tag-driven slot is authored without naming modules at all. Requirements that no module in the active rules satisfies warn, and the position can never match: fail closed, same as everywhere else on this page.

title: Bonding Rules Settings
description: A bonding-rules.md asset is mostly output.
outline: A zero entry weight skips the entry, in every mode
Entry dedup is about the generated collection alone
The Modules list is editable, and every edit is temporary
body:
A [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) asset is mostly output. Its modules, limit groups and property registry are assembled by a compile, and there is nothing to gain from editing them.

This page is the other part: the inputs. What the asset draws from, what it does with what it builds, and what governs when it rebuilds.

## Sources

*Two kinds, and one of them registers itself.*

| Source | Is |
|---|---|
| **Level Contributors** | Levels the asset pulls cage contributions from |
| **Contribution Providers** | Instanced payload sources, of which the built-in importer is one |

Level contributors arrive two ways. [Context Volumes](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/context-volumes) targeting this asset register their levels automatically, and anything else you list by hand. [Module Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-cages) never register themselves, so a level carrying one is listed by hand or reached through a provider.

Each entry carries `Enabled`, which excludes it from compiles while keeping everything it has cached. Entries added by auto-registration are marked as such, and the distinction is not cosmetic: an auto-registered entry pointing at a deleted level is pruned silently, while one you added by hand warns and stays.

### The shadow, and why closed levels still compile

*Each contributor keeps a snapshot, and that is what makes an unopened level compilable.*

Every level contributor holds a **shadow**: the slice of that level's cache as of the last compile that could reach it. When the level is loaded, the compile reads it live and overwrites the shadow. When it is not, the shadow is what gets used.

That is why a rules asset spread across a dozen authoring levels compiles without opening any of them. It also means a level is loaded when it needs to be, which is when the shadow holds nothing or the level's package content changed on disk.


> **Note.**
> The comparison is on package **content**, not modification time, so a version control checkout that rewrites timestamps on unchanged files does not trigger a reload of every level.


### Collection Sources

*The built-in provider, for kits that already exist as collections.*

**Collection Sources** walks asset collections down to their level-sourced entries and ingests each of those levels. Any collection type qualifies, because leaf entries are asked whether they name a source level rather than assumed to be level-typed. Nesting is invisible: a level found three subcollections deep behaves exactly like a direct child.

Each collection in the list carries a weight policy, deciding how the entry's weight folds into the one its level authored.

| Weight Source | Result |
|---|---|
| **Cage x Entry** | The two multiplied. The default. |
| **Cage Weight** | The level's own weight. The entry's only decides inclusion. |
| **Entry Weight** | The entry's weight. The level's is ignored. |


> **Warning.**
> **A zero entry weight skips the entry, in every mode**
>
> That includes **Cage Weight**, where the entry's weight is otherwise unused. It is a Valency convention rather than a toolkit one: elsewhere in PCGEx a zero-weight entry is still pickable.


Providers are an extension point. Subclassing the provider base is how a studio pipeline feeds modules from somewhere Valency has never heard of, and the collection importer is one implementation of that seam rather than a special case. Providers are editor-only by contract and never reach a cooked build.

## Level Bounds

*Fallbacks, for modules that are whole levels.*

A module standing for an entire level has to get its bounds from somewhere, and two instanced objects on the asset supply the default answer.

| Setting | Decides |
|---|---|
| **Level Bounds Evaluator** | How a bounding box is measured from the actors in the level |
| **Level Content Filter** | Which actors count toward it |

Both are fallbacks. Bounds resolve in three tiers, and these are the last: a cage's explicit placement-bounds override wins first, then whatever the module measured when it was scanned, and only then the entry's own measurement. A collection contributing level entries brings its own evaluator and filter, and those take precedence over these.

## Default Properties

*Assembled shape, editable values.*

`Default Properties` is the union of every property the asset's modules declare, collapsed by name. The **shape** is not yours to edit: it follows the cages, and the panel renders it value-only for that reason. The **values** are yours, and they survive rebuilds.

Survival is by name. Renaming a property on the cage that declares it produces a new entry here with its default value, and the edit you made against the old name is gone.

Below it, the `Property Registry` is the flattened form. That is what [Reading Properties](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/reading-properties) imports its mapping from, which is the fastest way to fill that node in.

## External Storage

*Publishing the generated collection as a real asset.*

Compiling builds a generated collection alongside the modules, holding a row per module. Nothing in Valency needs it: connector geometry comes from [Write Connectors](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/write-connectors) and properties from Load Properties, both reading compiled data directly. The collection is there for legibility, and for anything you want to point at it yourself.

`Use External Assets` is how you point at it. It writes the collection out as a standalone asset under `Export Folder`, where a Variant Collection or anything else that consumes collections can source it.


> **Warning.**
> **The exported asset is pipeline-managed**
>
> It is overwritten on every rebuild. Editing it by hand is editing a build product, and the next compile will not preserve the change.
>
> An empty `Export Folder` with the toggle on warns and falls back to embedded storage for that rebuild rather than failing.


## Compilation

*Three options, two buttons, and two stamps.*

| Option | Effect |
|---|---|
| `Compile On Rebuild` | Compile whenever the asset rebuilds from its sources, and serialize the result. On by default. |
| `Auto Rebuild On Stale` | Refresh by itself when it loads or when a tracked dependency is saved. On by default. |
| `Entry Dedup Includes Module Name` | Keep differently-named modules in separate generated rows. Off by default. |

Leaving the first two on is the intended setup. The third is narrower than it looks.


> **Note.**
> **Entry dedup is about the generated collection alone**
>
> With it off, two modules whose entry content is identical share one generated row, and the first module's name wins for that row. The modules themselves stay separate, keep their own weights and limits, and generation is unaffected either way, because solvers read per-module data rather than collection rows.
>
> Turn it on when you consume the generated collection directly and need its rows to keep distinct names. The compile logs each merge it makes, naming both modules and the name it kept.


Two buttons force the issue.

| Button | Does |
|---|---|
| **Rebuild Stale** | Nothing at all unless the asset is stale. Then it re-pulls and compiles. |
| **Force Rebuild** | Re-pulls every contributor and compiles, regardless. |


> **Note.**
> Pressing either while a PCG graph is executing defers the work until generation is idle, rather than recompiling underneath a running graph. The button appearing to do nothing for a moment is that.


### What counts as stale

The asset carries `Last Rebuilt Utc` and compares it against everything upstream: the orbital set, the connector set, each enabled contributor's shadow, the on-disk content of each source level, and each provider's own answer. Any of those moving past the stamp makes it stale.

A loaded level counts too, and separately. Editing a module level and regenerating **without saving** moves nothing on disk, so the check also asks whether a loaded level's cache has been re-baked since the shadow captured it.

`Compiled Schema Version` is the other stamp, and it answers a question timestamps cannot: whether the compiled data was produced by a compiler speaking the current format. A plugin update that changes the format moves no data timestamp, so without this an asset compiled before the change would read as fresh forever. Finding everything stale after an update is this working.


> **Warning.**
> **The Modules list is editable, and every edit is temporary**
>
> Nothing stops you changing a module's asset or settings in the details panel, and the next compile overwrites it. Modules are assembled from sources; change the source.

title: Cages
description: A cage marks a position in your authoring layout and declares what may sit there.
outline: Type and role are different things
body:
A cage marks a position in your authoring layout and declares what may sit there. Its content becomes a module, its position states what it connects to, and almost everything else you author in Valency hangs off one.

## Type and role are different things

_Two independent axes, and a cage has both._

**Type** is which actor you placed. It decides what the cage fundamentally is, and you cannot change it afterwards.

| Type                       | Is                                                 |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| **Valency Cage (Simple)**  | An ordinary cage. Most of a layout.                |
| **Valency Cage (Null)**    | A placeholder that never carries content.          |
| **Valency Cage (Pattern)** | A position inside a pattern arrangement.           |
| **Valency Module Cage**    | A declaration that this whole level is one module. |
| **Valency Assembly Cage**  | A declaration that everything attached to it is one module. |

**Role** is a setting on the cage. It decides what that cage contributes to the compiled library, and you change it freely.

| Role          | Contributes                                                                                                                                 |
| ------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Module**    | A module, built from its content. The default.                                                                                              |
| **Template**  | Nothing. It exists to be mirrored, and its missing-content warnings are suppressed because having none is the point.                        |
| **Reference** | Nothing directly. It names modules authored elsewhere: its mirror sources and asset entries declare which modules may sit at this position. |

So an ordinary Simple Cage set to **Template** is a perfectly normal thing to build, and useful early. One cage carrying the settings, tags and connector layout your kit shares, mirrored by everything else, means changing the shared part once.

## Getting content onto a cage

_Four routes, and they coexist on the same cage._

| Route                        | Behaviour                                                                                                                         |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Attach it**                | Anything attached to the cage is scanned and registered automatically. The main route, and the fastest.                           |
| **Mirror another container** | Take another cage or palette's content, and optionally its settings and tags, without copying anything.                           |
| **Register it by hand**      | Explicit asset entries, persisted, and never touched by scanning. Use when the asset is not in the level.                         |
| **Reference a collection**   | An external asset collection, resolved by reference rather than copied into entries, so the collection stays the source of truth. |

Automatic scanning is on by default and can be turned off per cage, which discards whatever was detected and leaves the hand-registered entries alone. The two never fight: scanned entries are transient and rebuilt, authored ones are saved.

### Attaching, without the outliner

You do not attach content by dragging things around the outliner. Select the mesh or actor in the viewport, hover the cage, and take the **Attach** gesture. It attaches the selection and moves each actor pivot onto the cage origin, which is what placing a module usually means.

The menu on that gesture covers the cases where that default is wrong: preserving the arrangement instead of pivoting, or attaching a copy and leaving the originals where they are.

### Mirroring

_The mechanism that stops a kit becoming dozens of hand-maintained near-duplicates._

A cage can name other cages or **Asset Palettes** as mirror sources, and inherit from them. This is not a copy: the source stays authoritative, and changing it changes everything mirroring it.

What gets inherited is chosen per source, across five independent channels:

| Channel             | Inherits                                                                                          |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Assets**          | The source's asset entries, along with their local transforms                                     |
| **Connectors**      | Its connector definitions                                                                         |
| **Properties**      | Per-asset property overrides, such as material variants captured during scanning                  |
| **Tags**            | Its gameplay tags                                                                                 |
| [Module Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-settings) | Its weight, spawn limits and the rest. Off, mirrored entries use this cage's own settings instead |

Each source also declares, separately, **which of those channels resolve recursively** through its own mirror sources. So a cage can inherit assets from a chain several deep while taking tags only from its immediate source, which is what makes deep kit hierarchies stay predictable.

Both selections default to everything, so a mirror source pointed at a palette and left alone inherits all five channels, all the way down.


> **Note.**
> Mirror sources are added by gesture too: select the cages or palettes to mirror from, hover the cage that should mirror them, and take the action. Hovering the arc that appears between them offers to remove it.
>
> Mirroring, palettes and the way they compose get their own page.



> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: cages-content-routes | SHOWS: The four ways content arrives on a cage, and which of them store anything. | ELEMENTS: A cage in the centre. From the left, an attached mesh actor feeding in, labelled scanned and marked transient. From below, a list of hand-entered asset rows feeding in, labelled authored and marked saved. From the right, an asset collection feeding in by an arrow labelled by reference, drawn as a link rather than a copy. From above, another cage feeding in by an arrow labelled mirrored, also drawn as a link, with five small channel pips on it for assets, connectors, properties, tags and settings. All four converge on the same cage, and one module list leaves it. | MUST BE CLEAR: All four can be present at once and produce one combined result. Two of the arrows are links to something that stays authoritative elsewhere, and only the hand-entered route is stored on the cage itself.
> Four routes in, one set of modules out. Only the hand-entered one is stored on the cage.


## What a scanned actor becomes

_Decided from the actor class, never from what components it happens to carry._

| Actor                     | Registers as                                                   |
| ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A Level Instance          | A **level** module                                             |
| A plain static mesh actor | A **mesh** module                                              |
| Anything else             | An **actor** module, using its Blueprint asset when it has one |

Reading the class rather than the components is deliberate. Instanced mesh components derive from static mesh components, so "carries a mesh component" is true of nearly anything that renders, and collapsing on that would reduce a whole instanced actor to the single mesh its instances share, at the actor transform, discarding every instance.

There is a per-cage option to reduce scanned actors to the static mesh they carry, for actors that carry nothing but a mesh. Instanced components never qualify even then.

On a **Valency Assembly Cage** the table above never applies: its whole subtree is exported as one module, covered under [Assembly Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/assembly-cages).


> **Warning.**
> **Every scanned actor becomes something**
>
> A light, a trigger volume, a note: if it is attached to a cage and scanning is on, it registers as an actor module. Nothing filters by usefulness.
>
> The context volume carries ignore lists, by actor and by tag, and they are the intended way to keep incidental actors out of a library.


## What a cage transform means

_Its position states what it connects to. Nothing about it travels into the module._

Where a cage sits decides which other cages it is near enough to bond with, and that is the whole of its job. **Modules carry no world transform.** Two cages holding the same content with the same connections produce one module however far apart they sit, and the layout you built to express the relationships does not survive into it.

One exception is opt-in. A cage can preserve the local transforms of its content, keeping each asset positioned relative to the cage centre for when placement inside the cage matters, and you choose which of translation, rotation and scale are preserved.


> **Warning.**
> Preserving local transforms changes what counts as a distinct module. Every distinct asset and transform pair becomes its own module variant, so a cage holding the same mesh at four offsets produces four modules rather than one.


## Reach

_How far a cage looks for neighbours._

Connections between cages are detected by proximity, and each cage carries a probe radius that decides how far it reaches. Two cages connect when their probes meet, so what matters is the sum of both radii against the distance between their centres. In the viewport, probe tips touching means connected.

| Value         | Means                                                                                                                   |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `-1`          | Use the containing volume's default. The usual setting.                                                                 |
| `0`           | Receive-only. This cage detects nothing, and a neighbour must cover the whole distance with its own radius to reach it. |
| Anything else | This cage's own reach, overriding the volume.                                                                           |


> Figure: CLIP | id: cages-probe-reach | SHOWS: That a connection depends on both probe radii meeting, not on one cage reaching the other. | BEATS: 1) Two cages close together, each drawing its probe sphere, the spheres overlapping and a connection line drawn solid between them. 2) One cage is dragged slowly away. The spheres separate, and at the moment they stop touching the connection line disappears. 3) The stationary cage probe radius is increased until the spheres touch again, and the connection returns without either cage having moved. 4) The moved cage radius is set to zero, its sphere vanishes, and the connection holds because the other cage now covers the whole gap alone. | SOURCE: WFC 2D sample authoring level, two cages isolated. | LENGTH: 10s, loops. | NOTE: Beat 4 is the point of the clip. Hold on it slightly longer than the others.
> Probes meet in the middle. Either cage can cover the gap, or they can share it.


Authoring which orbitals those connections land on, and what a cage asserts where it has no neighbour, is covered under [Authoring Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/authoring-orbitals).

title: Assembly Cages
description: A Valency Assembly Cage says: everything attached to this cage is one module.
outline: The cage must be reachable when the library stages
body:
A **Valency Assembly Cage** says: everything attached to this cage is one module. The attached subtree is exported, as if it were a level, into a PCG data asset, and that asset is what the module spawns as. A hand-built arrangement of several meshes and actors becomes one placeable piece without getting a level of its own, and without giving up any of what a cage authors.

## One module from the subtree

_The cage exports what it owns, relative to itself._

An ordinary cage registers one module per attached actor. An assembly cage registers one module, and the asset behind it is the cage itself: when the library stages, the cage's attached subtree is exported the way the PCGEx book's [PCG Data Asset Collection](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/node-library/staging/collections/pcg-data-asset-collection) exports a level. Mesh actors become mesh points, other actors become actor points carrying their property deltas, a Level Instance becomes a level point, and the export carries its own Collection Map so all of them resolve.

The cage is never part of the export, and every point is expressed relative to the cage's transform. Where the cage stands in the authoring level leaves no trace in the module, which is the rule every cage follows; here it also decides where the arrangement's origin sits when it is placed.

What the export descends is what the cage owns, bounded the same way the regular scan is bounded:

| Pruned                                           | Because                                                                                     |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Owned actors: child-actor components, PCG output | They belong to someone else's composition, and so does anything parented under them.        |
| A nested cage or palette                         | It owns its own subtree, so this one ends at its boundary.                                  |
| The interior of a Level Instance                 | The instance itself is one level point; what is inside it stays inside it.                  |
| Ignored actors                                   | The volume's ignore lists apply, along with everything attached to them.                    |

A grouping pivot is walked through: an empty actor used to organise the subtree does not cut off what is attached under it. The exporter's own content filter then decides which of the remaining actors become points, with the rules the PCGEx book's [Default Level Data Exporter](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/node-library/staging/collections/pcg-data-asset-collection/level-data-exporter-default) page describes.

An assembly cage with nothing attached registers no module, and is skipped the way an empty cage is.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: assembly-cages-subtree-to-module | SHOWS: That an attached subtree exports as one module whose points are relative to the cage, with the cage itself and the pruned branches left out. | ELEMENTS: Left, an assembly cage in an authoring level with a small tree of actors attached under it: two mesh actors, one actor with a property badge, one grouping pivot holding two more meshes, and one greyed branch marked owned hanging off a child actor component. A frame marker at the cage origin. Right, one module drawn as a PCG data asset holding the same actors as points, laid out around a shared origin that matches the cage frame, the pivot absent and the greyed branch absent. An arrow from the cage to the module labelled exported at staging. | MUST BE CLEAR: The whole subtree is one module, the cage transform is the origin of the exported points rather than a point itself, and the owned branch never crosses over.
> What is attached is the module. The cage is its origin, never its content.


## Against a Module Cage

_Both turn a hand-built arrangement into one piece. Only one of them is a cage in the ordinary sense._

|                             | A module cage                                               | An assembly cage                                        |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **What becomes the module** | The level it sits in                                        | What is attached to it                                  |
| **Needs a volume**          | No. It aggregates itself.                                   | Yes, like any cage.                                     |
| **Names its target**        | Never. It publishes and stops.                              | Through its volume, like any cage.                      |
| **Connection model**        | Connectors, unless bond or corner tags opt it into orbitals | Orbitals, connectors, or both, authored on the cage     |
| **Requires**                | A Connector Set                                             | Nothing in particular                                   |
| **Shares its level with**   | Other module cages and palettes only                        | Anything. It is part of a kit.                          |

The last row is the practical one. An assembly cage lives inside a kit, next to ordinary cages, inside the same volume, and contributes to whatever that volume targets. Several can share a level. It also counts as an ordinary cage for the kit-or-module rule on [Module Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-cages): once one is placed, the **Module Cage** entry in the Create menu greys out.

## Against an ordinary cage

_The asset side is fixed. Everything else is the same cage._

The subtree is the asset, so the settings that would author a second one are greyed out: `Manual Asset Entries`, `Collection References`, `Auto Register Contained Assets`, `Reduce Actors To Meshes`, `Preserve Local Transforms` and its `Local Transform Flags`. The **Assets** tool is not offered on the rail. `Cage Role` is greyed out too, held at **Module**: an assembly that authored nothing would carry a subtree that never exports.

Everything else applies unchanged. Orbitals, connectors, footprints, placement conditions, module settings, properties, tags, mirroring and loose neighbours are authored on it the way they are on any cage, and the module they produce takes part in solving and growth like any other.

## Creating one

_One Create entry, then attach._

The viewport **Create** button lists **Assembly Cage** under **Cages**. Attach content to it the way you attach content to any cage, with the **Attach** gesture, and nest as deep as the arrangement needs: a prop parented to a wall parented to the cage is still the cage's content, at its own place in the arrangement.

## Spawning it

_One more node than a mesh module._

The module's asset type is a PCG data asset. In the library's generated collection it is a PCG Data Asset entry whose `Source` is **Actor**, pointing back at the cage, and **Valency : Staging** writes a pick for it like any other module. The PCGEx spawners for meshes and actors do not read that pick: **[Staging : Load PCGData](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/node-library/staging/staging-load-pcgdata)** does. It loads the exported asset, unpacks its mesh, actor and level points, and merges the maps they carry, so the ordinary spawners take over from there. Put it after **Valency : Staging** and before whatever spawns; [Output](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output) covers the rest of the chain.


> **Warning.**
> **The cage must be reachable when the library stages**
>
> The export reads the cage's subtree when the library's generated collection stages. With the authoring level open, that is the live cage. A closed level is loaded on demand, except a World Partition level, which cannot be read closed: the export is refused with a warning. Keep assemblies in levels that are not World Partition.


## When to reach for one

_When the piece is bigger than a mesh and smaller than a level._

A small arrangement with internal structure: a lamp post with its fixtures, a doorway with its frame and trim, a stack of crates. Anything that should place as one piece, keep its orbitals, and sit in a kit beside single meshes. When the piece is a whole room with its own lighting and interior, and nothing else lives in its level, a module cage is the better fit. Both pages close on the same trade: authored quality, at the cost of recombination.

title: Footprints
description: A footprint is the space a module occupies, described by marker components attached to its cage.
outline: A footprint on its own does nothing
Footprints are a growth and grammar concern only
A Polygon marker turns Footprint Penetration into plain overlap
body:
A **footprint** is the space a module occupies, described by marker components attached to its cage. It is what lets generation ask "would this piece land inside something already there".

Most readers arrive here from one of two results, and they are opposites: pieces growing straight through each other, or growth stopping far short of its budget with nothing visibly in the way. Both are footprint problems and this page covers both.

## A footprint on its own does nothing

_It describes a shape. Something else has to decide to care._

Authoring a footprint does not make anything avoid anything. It supplies a shape, and a **placement condition** on the module is what reads that shape and refuses a placement over it.

A module with an empty placement-condition stack refuses nothing of its own on spatial grounds, whatever footprint it carries, and a grammar rule is then the only thing that could. That is deliberate rather than an oversight: plenty of modules are decoration that should sit inside other things, and a system that refused every intersection by default would make them impossible.

Empty is the shipped default rather than a fixed rule. A project where pieces should collide unless told otherwise can put a condition into `Default Placement Conditions` under **Project Settings**, and every cage created afterwards starts with it. See [Module Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-settings).

So the first symptom, **pieces growing through each other**, is usually not a footprint that is wrong. It is a module nobody asked to check.


> **Warning.**
> **Footprints are a growth and grammar concern only**
>
> A solve fills positions that already exist. It never invents a place to put something, so there is nothing for it to reject on spatial grounds and no footprint is consulted anywhere in solving.
>
> If a solved layout has pieces interpenetrating, the cluster put them there. The fix is the cluster or the bonding rules, not a footprint.


## Building one

_Three markers, and as many of each as the shape needs._

| Marker                                     | Bakes                                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Valency Spatial Footprint Box**          | One oriented box, where you put it                                    |
| **Valency Spatial Footprint Spline**       | A curve you author on the component, as a prism or as a run of boxes  |
| **Valency Spatial Footprint Gather Box**   | One box per level actor found inside it. Contributes no shape itself. |

Attach as many as the shape needs. Every active one bakes into the module's footprint on rebuild, and adding, moving, editing or deleting one triggers a rescan on its own.

### Boxes

_The default, and several rather than one is the normal case._

A single box around an L-shaped room, a corridor with a bend, or anything with a courtyard swallows the empty parts, and that empty space then refuses placements that should have been fine. That is the second symptom, **growth stopping short of its budget**: footprints authored larger than the pieces they describe, so every candidate collides with its own neighbours.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: footprints-one-box-vs-many | SHOWS: That one box around an L-shaped piece claims the empty corner, and that empty corner is what refuses the neighbours. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same L-shaped module, an outline with an inside corner, and the same second module offered into the notch of the L. Left panel headed One box: a single footprint rectangle drawn around the whole L, visibly covering the empty notch as well as the geometry; the offered module sits inside that empty notch and is drawn refused, dimmed and struck. Right panel headed Boxes following the shape: two footprint rectangles, one along each arm of the L, leaving the notch uncovered; the same offered module sits in the notch and is drawn accepted, its own footprint interlocking with the two without touching them. | MUST BE CLEAR: The geometry is identical in both panels and so is the offered placement. The only difference is whether the footprint covers the empty notch, and that is what turns a legal placement into a refused one.
> The piece did not change. One box claims the empty corner, and the refusal follows from that alone.


### A curve

_For shapes that are easier to draw than to stack boxes around._

A **Valency Spatial Footprint Spline** carries its own curve, authored on the component rather than referencing a spline actor. Editing a spline point rescans the cage like any other change. `Mode` decides what the curve becomes, and the two answers are not interchangeable.

| Mode         | Bakes                                                                     |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Polygon**  | One extruded prism from the curve's outline, between `Extrusion Min` and `Extrusion Max` |
| **Solidify** | One oriented box per sampled segment, so the shape stair-steps the curve  |

**Polygon** is the exact one, and the one that handles a concave outline without stacking boxes into it: a courtyard, an L, a room with an alcove. **Solidify** walks the curve instead, sizing each box by `Step Distance` or by `Segment Count` and shaping it with `Half Width`, `Half Height` and `Cross Section Offset`. That is the mode for a wall, a fence line or a pipe run, where the footprint is a ribbon along a path rather than an area.


> **Warning.**
> **A Polygon marker turns Footprint Penetration into plain overlap**
>
> Penetration depth is measured against boxes. A **Polygon** element has no depth test of its own, so a **Footprint Penetration** condition falls back to rejecting any overlap at all against it, whatever `Max Penetration` says.
>
> Nothing warns, and the symptom is a piece meant to bed slightly into a wall being refused outright. Use **Solidify** for anything a penetration condition is going to test, and keep **Polygon** for shapes that only ever need plain overlap.


### A gather box

_For a whole level, where hand-placing markers stops being practical._

A **Valency Spatial Footprint Gather Box** contributes no shape of its own and is purely a search region: every actor whose bounds fall inside it is captured, and each one bakes as a box oriented to that actor. Drop one over a room and the footprint follows the geometry you built.


> **Warning.**
> Editing an actor a gather box already captured triggers a rescan. **Adding a new actor** into the region does not, so geometry added after the fact is missing from the footprint until you rescan.


### Two channels per marker

_The space a module needs free, and the space it claims._

Every marker declares what it contributes to, whichever kind it is, and the two are independent.

| Setting                     | Means                                                              |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `Contributes To Overlap`    | Include this marker in the space the module **needs free to fit**  |
| `Contributes To Occupation` | Include this marker in the space the module **claims once placed** |

Both are on by default, which is the ordinary case: a piece needs its own volume free, and once placed it occupies that volume.

Turning one off expresses things a single shape cannot. A marker on overlap only is clearance the module needs on the way in but does not keep, like the swing of a door. A marker on occupation only is space the module blocks without needing it free first, like an overhang something may pass under during placement but must not end up inside.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: footprints-two-channels | SHOWS: That the space a module needs free and the space it claims are two different shapes on the same module. | ELEMENTS: One annotated scene, three stages left to right joined by flow arrows. A door module drawn as an outline with an inside corner, carrying two footprint rectangles distinguished by fill pattern and keyed: a solid one over the door leaf itself marked both channels, and a quarter-circle-shaped one over the swing area marked overlap only. Stage one, the candidate offered into a gap with both rectangles shown and a second module sitting inside the swing area, the placement drawn refused. Stage two, the same candidate offered where the swing area is clear, drawn accepted. Stage three, the door now placed, with the swing rectangle drawn faded away and gone, and a new module placed inside that swing area drawn accepted. | MUST BE CLEAR: The swing area blocks the door from being placed, and then stops existing. Something else may occupy it afterwards, because the swing box never contributed to occupation.
> The swing has to be clear for the door to fit, and stops mattering once it is in. That is one box on overlap and not on occupation.


A marker with both off is inert, which is worth knowing when a footprint mysteriously does nothing.

## Channels

_Footprints can be kept in separate namespaces._

Every marker carries a `Channel Key`, defaulting to the standard one. Markers on different channels do not test against each other, which is how one module can have a physical footprint and a separate abstract one, tested by different conditions.

Most libraries never leave the default. Reach for a second channel only when two genuinely different spatial questions are being asked about the same modules.

### Turning a marker off

`Active` leaves a component in place while excluding it from the cage scan. That is the tool for trying a footprint variation without deleting the work, and for keeping a marker around that is not currently wanted.

### The other half

Authoring the shape is half the subject. Which condition reads it, how strictly, and what a placement is tested against are covered under [Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap).

title: Loose Neighbors
description: Authoring orbital connections is precise: this cage bonds to that one, along this direction.
outline: Two ways to name a target
The grant is mutual by default
It grants in bulk, including sides you narrowed
body:
Authoring orbital connections is precise: this cage bonds to that one, along this direction. Sometimes the statement you want has no direction in it. *These pieces go together.* *Rubble may sit next to any wall.*

**Loose Neighbors** is that statement. A cage names targets its modules may sit beside, and the grant is applied to every eligible side at once.

## Two ways to name a target

| Field | Names |
|---|---|
| `Loose Neighbor Cages` | Another cage, resolved through its asset-mirror group |
| `Loose Neighbor Assets` | Asset paths, matching every module built from them |

The cage form follows mirroring, so pointing at one cage reaches the family it belongs to. The asset form reaches anything built from the named assets regardless of which cage authored it, which is what you want when the target lives in another kit.

Both are available only when the cage's role is **Module**. A reference cage, covered in [Reference Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/reference-cages), is already a positional statement and has no use for a bulk one.

## The grant is mutual by default

*`Mutual`, on by default, grants the reverse as well.*

Naming a target says the owner's modules may sit beside it. `Mutual` additionally says the target accepts the owner's modules on any of **its** open sides.

Leaving it on is usually right, since "these go together" is rarely one-directional. Turning it off expresses a one-way tolerance: rubble may sit beside a wall without the wall's own authoring gaining rubble as an acceptable neighbour everywhere it appears.

## Where the grant lands

*Every list-governed orbital, and only those.*

At compile the grant fans out into the neighbour list of every orbital that is governed by a list. Two kinds of orbital are deliberately untouched.

| Orbital | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Boundary** | Stays empty. Authored intent wins: a side declared as facing nothing keeps facing nothing. |
| **Accept-any** | Gains nothing. It already accepts everything, so a list there is inert. |


> **Warning.**
> **It grants in bulk, including sides you narrowed**
>
> The fan-out reaches **every** list-governed orbital, and that includes one a proxy exception had narrowed. Bulk is the design, and per-side exceptions are not its job.
>
> When one particular side needs to differ, author a per-orbital connection there instead. A loose neighbour cannot be locally overridden.


## Narrowing by tag

`Loose Neighbor Default Predicate` applies a tag predicate to every entry that does not set its own override. That narrows a bulk grant without listing targets individually: "any wall, but only the exterior ones".

It is the pressure valve on a feature that is otherwise deliberately broad, and worth reaching for before a loose neighbour is abandoned as too coarse.

## When to use which

*Ask whether the direction carries meaning.*

| The statement | Use |
|---|---|
| "This side connects to that" | A per-orbital connection |
| "These may be adjacent, any side" | A loose neighbour |
| "On this side, one of these specific things" | A [Reference Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/reference-cages) |

Loose neighbours are the widest of the three and the cheapest to author. That is also the reason to be deliberate with them: a kit where everything loosely neighbours everything has expressed nothing, and lost the constraint that made the bonding rules worth having.

title: Module Cages
description: A Valency Module Cage says: this entire level is one module.
outline: A level is a kit or a module
Duplicating a level with a module cage in it
Duplicate a level, then Shift+click Rebuild All
body:
A **Valency Module Cage** says: this entire level is one module. Everything in the level travels together as a single piece, so the thing generation places can be a hand-built room with its own interior rather than a mesh.

It is the same idea as a cage, applied at a different scale, and almost every rule about ordinary cages stops applying.

### How it differs from every other cage

_Five ways, and each one follows from the level being the module._

|                      | An ordinary cage                | A module cage                  |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| **Needs a volume**   | Yes. Outside one it is ignored. | No. It aggregates itself.      |
| **What it contains** | Assets attached to it           | The level it sits in           |
| **Connection model** | Orbitals, connectors, or both   | Connectors, unless bond or corner tags opt it into orbitals |
| **Names its target** | Through its volume              | Never. It publishes and stops. |
| **Requires**         | Nothing in particular           | A **Connector Set**            |

The Connector Set is not optional and not a default you can leave empty. It is the only match key the contribution carries, so a module cage without one publishes something no rules asset can ever find.


> **Note.**
> A module cage authors no orbitals, and its module defaults to the **Connector Only** placement policy, so orbital placement never draws it. Authoring [Bond and Corner Tags](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bond-and-corner-tags) on the cage is what opts it in: the policy becomes Normal, the named seams take part in tag matching against the consuming rules asset's orbital set, and every side without a stated requirement compiles as accept-any.


For an arrangement smaller than a level, an [Assembly Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/assembly-cages) makes one module out of what is attached to it and stays an ordinary cage in every other respect: it needs a volume, keeps its orbitals, and shares a level with a kit.
