> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: module-cages-scale | SHOWS: That an entire authored level becomes a single placeable piece. | ELEMENTS: Left, one level viewed from above: a room with walls, furniture, a doorway, and a module cage marker at its origin with two connectors on the doorways. A dashed outline encloses the whole thing, labelled one module. Right, a much larger generated structure in which three copies of that same room appear, each drawn small and identical, connected to corridors and other pieces. An arrow runs from the dashed outline on the left to one of the copies on the right. | MUST BE CLEAR: Everything inside the dashed outline on the left is one item on the right. The internal detail is authored once and repeats intact, unchanged and unrecombined.
> Everything on the left is one piece on the right. The interior is authored once and travels whole.


### It publishes, and stops there

_You cannot point a module cage at a rules asset, and that is deliberate._

Every other authoring path lets you name a target. A module cage does not. It bakes its contribution into the level cache that [Context Volumes](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/context-volumes) describes, and takes no further interest in who consumes it.

Consumption is entirely the rules asset's decision, by listing the level as a contributor or by reaching it through a collection it draws from.

The reason is worth understanding, because it explains a whole class of things that would otherwise look like missing features. A module cage's level gets spawned, repeatedly, as instances of the module it declares. If the cage registered itself with a rules asset, every one of those spawned copies would register again, and the library would fill with duplicates of itself. Publishing only, and never subscribing, is what stops that.

## A level is a kit or a module

_Not both, and the Create menu enforces it._

The **Module Cage** entry greys out once the level holds a Context Volume, or any ordinary, null, pattern or assembly cage. Those are the two incompatible ways to use a level, and mixing them produces a level that is simultaneously a set of pieces and a single piece.

Existing module cages and asset palettes do not count against it, so a level can hold **several** module cages. That is supported deliberately: contributions are keyed per actor, so more than one is a normal thing rather than a workaround.

Loose Neighbors are greyed out on a module cage for a related reason: the level-as-module bake carries no channel for those declarations, so the field would be inert rather than merely unusual.

### Describing the space it occupies

_The one thing you will want immediately, and the reason gather boxes exist._

Growth can refuse a placement that would overlap something already placed, but only for modules that ask it to, and only if it knows what shape they occupy. Both halves matter for a level-as-module: it needs a footprint, and it needs a placement condition that uses one. Since a module cage is ordinarily connector-only, and connectors are what growth places with, this is always the relevant question for it.

For a mesh in a cage, a box around it is usually close enough. For a whole level it usually is not: an L-shaped room, a corridor with a bend, or anything with a courtyard is badly served by a single box that swallows the empty parts.

So a cage's footprint is built from as many of the markers in [Footprints](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/footprints) as you like. Attach **Valency Spatial Footprint Box** components, position them, and each active one bakes into the footprint. A **Valency Spatial Footprint Spline** covers the same ground with a drawn outline where a room is concave enough that boxes get tedious. Adding, moving, editing or deleting one triggers a rescan by itself, with no manual step.

For a level-as-module that is still a lot of authoring, which is what the third component is for.

A **Valency Spatial Footprint Gather Box** does not contribute its own shape at all. It is purely a search region: every actor whose bounds fall inside it is captured, and each one bakes as a box oriented to that actor. Drop one over your room and the footprint follows the geometry you actually built.

| Setting              | Does                                                                                                  |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Selection Mode**   | `Overlap` captures anything touching the region. `Contained` captures only actors entirely inside it. |
| **Content Filter**   | Narrows what is eligible, so scenery and decoration can be skipped.                                   |
| **Bounds Evaluator** | Chooses where each candidate's bounds come from, for both the selection test and the baked box.       |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: module-cages-gather-footprint | SHOWS: How a gather box turns built geometry into a multi-box footprint without hand-authoring it. | ELEMENTS: Three panels left to right. One, an L-shaped room with walls and furniture, and a single large gather box outline drawn loosely around all of it, the outline dashed to read as a region rather than a shape. Two, the same room with the gather box gone and instead one tight oriented box around each captured wall and object, following the L shape and leaving the courtyard empty. Three, two copies of the room placed near each other in a generated result, their footprints visibly interlocking without overlapping, with a third rejected placement greyed out where a footprint would have collided. | MUST BE CLEAR: The gather box contributes no geometry of its own, it only selects. The resulting footprint follows the built shape rather than enclosing it, and that is what makes the rejection in panel three correct.
> The gather box only selects. What ends up in the footprint is one box per captured actor, following the shape you built.



> **Warning.**
> Editing an actor that a gather box already captured triggers a rescan. **Adding a new actor** into the region does not, so a piece of geometry added after the fact is missing from the footprint until you rescan.


## Duplicating a level with a module cage in it

_The one trap on this page, and it is silent._


> **Danger.**
> **Duplicate a level, then Shift+click Rebuild All**
>
> Contributions are stored in a per-level cache that survives being copied. Duplicate a level containing a module cage and the copy arrives carrying **the original level's baked contribution**, which is not the same thing as the copy you now want.
>
> An ordinary rebuild will not clear it, because a rebuild re-bakes **on top of** what is already stored. The stale entry is not contradicted by anything, so it survives and reads back as authored truth.
>
> The fix, and it has to be done deliberately:
>
> 1. Open the **Valency editor mode**.
> 2. **Shift+click Rebuild All** in the panel header.
>
> That empties every level cache and every stored shadow snapshot first, then rebuilds from nothing. It is slow, because the next compile re-loads every contributing level to refill what was purged, and it is the only thing that clears a contribution nothing else will overwrite.


The same applies to anything else that leaves a cache entry with no live source behind it: a deleted cage whose contribution was never superseded, or a level nobody has opened since something about the bake format changed. Symptoms look like modules you did not author, or results that differ between editor sessions on a scene nobody touched.

## When to reach for one

_When the piece is bigger than a mesh._

Module cages suit pieces with internal structure that is authored rather than generated: a room with furniture, lighting and a door in the right place; a junction with its own detail; a prefab that would be tedious to describe as a kit and pointless to let vary.

The trade is the usual one. A level-as-module places as a unit and cannot be recombined, so it buys authored quality at the cost of variety. Kits of small pieces give the opposite. Most projects that use both put the structure in a kit and the set pieces in levels.

title: Module Properties
description: A module can carry data of your own: a material index, a gameplay value, a number some later stage reads.
body:
A module can carry data of your own: a material index, a gameplay value, a number some later stage reads. **Properties** are how that data is attached at authoring time and recovered at the far end.

They travel the whole way. Authored on the cage, baked into the module at compile, resolved back onto points by [Reading Properties](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/reading-properties). Nothing in between needs to know what they mean.

## Authoring them

*A property collection component on the cage.*

Properties are held by a **property collection** on the actor, which is the PCGEx property system rather than anything Valency-specific. A cage exposes whatever that collection defines, so the types available and the way values are edited are the same as anywhere else PCGEx uses properties.

What Valency adds is the journey: it gathers the cage's effective properties at compile and stores them on the module.

`Property Schema` assets are the reusable half. A schema is a composable, inheritable library of property definitions, so a kit declares its shape once and every cage in it carries the same set with its own values. That is worth doing early, because it is what stops twenty cages disagreeing about whether the field is called `Variant` or `VariantIndex`.

## Properties and mirroring

*Gathered from every source, and the cage wins collisions.*

Properties are one of the five mirror channels in [Palettes and Mirroring](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/palettes-and-mirroring), so a cage can inherit them from a palette or a template instead of restating them.

Where the same property name arrives from more than one place, the resolution is **first wins**, in traversal order, with the cage's own properties first. A cage that defines a property overrides whatever its mirror sources say about it, and a mirror source only fills what the cage left unsaid.

That is the useful direction. A template carries the defaults, each cage overrides the handful it cares about, and nothing has to restate the rest.

## Tags are a different thing

*Both live on the cage. Only one of them is data.*

`Module Tags` sit alongside properties on the same cage and do a different job. A property is a **value carried through to the output**. A tag is an **identity used for matching**, read by tag predicates, patterns, grammar rules and filters throughout generation.

The practical difference is where each one is consumed. Nothing during generation reads a property, and nothing at the far end matches on a tag unless you ask for the tags to be written out as an attribute.

Tags also merge differently: mirror sources **union** their tags into the cage's, rather than the cage overriding them. Tags accumulate, properties override.

What tags are and how predicates read them is covered under [Selecting Modules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/selecting-modules).

## Getting them back

*One node, and it writes nothing until told what to write.*

[Reading Properties](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/reading-properties) resolves each point's module and writes the properties you name onto it as attributes. Nothing comes out that is not listed in its mapping, and the fastest way to fill that mapping is to import it from the [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) asset the properties were compiled into.

That node can also write the module's name and its tags, the latter as a single comma-separated string, which is how a tag reaches the output side at all.

Placements made by a structural grammar can carry one more layer: the placing grammar node may override property values per node, and Load Properties resolves that override ahead of what the cage authored. Authoring those overrides belongs to [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar), not to the cage.

title: Module Settings
description: Everything else about a cage says what the module is.
outline: Reload your levels after changing it
Where these come from when mirroring
body:
Everything else about a cage says *what* the module is. These settings say how generation is allowed to treat it.

They travel with the module through compilation, so they apply wherever it ends up, and every consumer of the library respects them.

## Weight

*Relative likelihood, and nothing else.*

`Weight` is how often this module is drawn relative to its competitors. It is a ratio rather than a probability: doubling one module's weight makes it twice as likely as it was against the same alternatives, and says nothing on its own.

In growth it does a second job. Weight is the currency a per-seed budget spends, so a heavy module is both more likely and more expensive, and a budget expressed in weight naturally produces fewer of the expensive pieces without capping any of them.

## Placement policy

*Which mechanisms may place this module at all.*

| Policy | Placed by |
|---|---|
| **Normal** | Everything. The default. |
| **Filler** | Solving, as a last resort, without propagating constraints |
| **Excluded** | Nothing. It contributes sockets and metadata and is never placed. |
| **Bridge Only** | Only as a bridge between branches, never by ordinary growth |
| **Connector Only** | Connector compatibility only, outside orbital constraint propagation |
| **Pattern Only** | Only as a pattern substitution, never by a solver, growth, grammar or bridge |

**Filler** is the one that saves a solve. A filler is available when nothing else fits, and because it propagates no constraints it cannot make its neighbours harder to solve. That is what turns an unsolvable position into a plain one.

**Excluded** sounds useless and is not. A module that is never placed can still be referenced, still carries connectors and properties, and still takes part in patterns.

**Pattern Only** is what a pattern cage's own module gets automatically, which is why a piece authored inside a pattern does not start appearing on its own.

## Spawn limits

*Caps, and a floor that leans rather than guarantees.*

`Spawn Limits` holds the minimum and maximum for this module, along with whether the maximum is an absolute count or a proportion of a population.

The asymmetry between the two halves is the thing to know: a maximum is enforced by removing the module from the candidate pool, while a minimum only weights it upward. That is covered in full under [Spawn Limits](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spawn-limits).

## Placement conditions

*What refuses this module on spatial grounds.*

`Placement Conditions` is a stack, all of which must pass, and an empty stack means the module carries no spatial refusal of its own.

These are what read the module's footprint, authored under [Footprints](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/footprints), and they only apply during growth and grammar: a solve fills positions that already exist and has nothing to reject. The conditions themselves are covered under [Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap).

### The empty stack is a project default

*Set it once and every new cage starts with a condition already on it.*

**Project Settings → Plugins → PCGEx | Valency** carries `Default Placement Conditions`, handed to new cages and asset palettes as they are created. Leave it empty and cages start with no spatial test, which is the shipped behaviour. Put a **Footprint Overlap** in it and every cage authored from then on starts checking.

That is the right lever for a project where pieces should collide by default and the exceptions are the decoration. Setting it per cage across a kit of eighty is the wrong one.


> **Danger.**
> **Reload your levels after changing it**
>
> The default reaches containers **loaded after the change**. Cages in a level that is already open keep the previous value, and **saving that level bakes the old value into them permanently**.
>
> So the sequence matters: change the setting, then reopen the levels you want it to apply to. A level saved in between has opted out for good, and no later edit to the project default will reach it.


Two other project-wide defaults sit alongside it, `Default Orbital Set` and `Default Connector Set`, given to new Valency assets and nodes. The orbital one behaves differently: editing it also re-points any node still sitting on the previous default, rather than affecting only what is created next.

## Bounds modifier

*Adjusting the bounds without touching the asset.*

`Bounds Modifier` changes the bounds used for fitting and overlap, leaving unset to use whatever the asset reports. It is the adjustment for an asset whose own bounds are wrong for the purpose: padded meshes, assets with decorative overhang, anything where the useful volume and the reported volume differ.

## Merge branches on bridge

*Only meaningful on a bridge module.*

`Merge Branches On Bridge` folds the two branches a bridge joined into one, so later bridge checks treat them as the same branch and stop looking for more connections between them.

Leave it off for a mesh of connections between two regions, turn it on when a single link between them is the point. It is covered alongside the rest of bridging under [Branches and Bridges](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow/branches-and-bridges).

## Where these come from when mirroring

A cage that mirrors another can inherit its module settings as one of the five channels covered in [Palettes and Mirroring](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/palettes-and-mirroring), or keep its own. That choice is per mirror source, which is what lets a family of variants share an asset list while each keeps its own weight.

title: Orbital Variants
description: A corner piece authored once faces one way.
outline: Plane flips are an explicit opt-in
What a rotation does to an authored neighbour
body:
A corner piece authored once faces one way. A grid needs it facing four. Authoring the other three means three more cages carrying the same asset with the same connectors, rotated.

**Orbital Variants** produce them at compile instead. Turn them on for a module and it expands into one rotated variant per symmetry of the orbital set, each a real module with correctly rotated bonding data.

## Where the rotations come from

*The orbital set, not the cage.*

An orbital set has symmetries: the rotations that map its directions onto themselves. A square grid has four, a hex has six, a cube set has considerably more. Those are detected from the set and offered as the variants a module may expand into.

That is why this is an orbital feature rather than a transform one. The rotations available are exactly the ones under which the set's own directions are interchangeable, so a rotated module's bonding data stays meaningful.

The editor presents them as a grid of glyph tiles, one per detected symmetry, with group shortcuts for whole axes. Hovering a tile ghost-draws the cage's orbital arrows in that pose, so the rotation can be seen before it is chosen.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: variants-what-a-rotation-is | SHOWS: That a variant is the same module with its orbitals rotated onto other directions of the same set, drawn the way the editor draws it. | ELEMENTS: Follow the SValencyOrbitalGlyph vocabulary in DIAGRAMS.md exactly. One wide panel holding three glyphs in a row above a shared caption strip. Each glyph is a common centre with spokes for the orbital directions, in isometric with Z up, X down-right, Y down-left, each spoke in its orbital colour and back-facing spokes faded. First glyph headed Authored: the base pose alone, solid, no ghost. Second headed One rotation: the base pose as a faint ghost underneath, the rotated pose solid on top, and a motion arc per moving spoke tracing base to rotated in that spoke colour. Third headed The family: four small glyphs tiled together showing the four resulting poses, each solid, labelled as four modules in the library. Beneath the first two glyphs, the same L-shaped module drawn once and then rotated to match, so the geometry and the spokes turn together. | MUST BE CLEAR: The rotation moves the orbitals onto OTHER directions of the same set, which is why the bonding data stays meaningful. The third glyph is four separate library entries, not one module with options. | NOTE: This figure and its siblings are the book's only isometric drawings, matching the editor widget by design.
> A variant is a delta: the authored pose ghosted, the rotated pose solid, and an arc per orbital showing where it went.


## Choosing which

*`Enable Variants` first, then optionally narrow.*

The master toggle is off by default: a module produces no variants until asked.

Turned on with no explicit choices, **every detected rotation is enabled**, with one exception below. Making any change materialises an explicit list, so from then on the set is exactly what the tiles show.


> **Warning.**
> **Plane flips are an explicit opt-in**
>
> The implicit "all variants" set includes rotations and **excludes plane flips**. A flip only expands when it is explicitly picked.
>
> That is deliberate: a flipped module is a mirror image, which is right for some assets and visibly wrong for anything with text, handedness or asymmetric detail. Opting in per module keeps the accident from happening at scale.



> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: variants-rotation-vs-flip | SHOWS: Why rotations are safe to enable implicitly and flips are not. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same asset, a wall piece carrying an obviously handed detail: a stair rail on one side and a readable sign on the wall. Left panel headed Rotation: the piece shown in four poses around a centre, each turned, with the sign still readable and the rail always on the same side of the piece relative to its own body. Above them a strip of four glyph tiles in the SValencyOrbitalGlyph style, all shown enabled. Right panel headed Plane flip: the same piece mirrored, with the sign reversed and the rail swapped to the opposite side, and one glyph tile above it drawn unselected with a marker showing it must be picked by hand. | MUST BE CLEAR: Rotation preserves the piece and only turns it. A flip produces a mirror image, which is what the reversed sign and swapped rail show, and is why it never expands unless explicitly chosen.
> A rotation turns the piece. A flip mirrors it, which is why one is implicit and the other never is.


## What variants do to weight

*`Normalize Family Weight`, on by default, and it decides whether a variant is a piece or a family.*

A module expanded into four rotations is four modules in the library. Left alone, each would carry the authored weight, so the family as a whole would be four times as likely to appear as the single authored piece was.

`Normalize Family Weight` divides the weight by the family size so the family's total frequency matches what was authored. That is almost always what you want: rotating a piece should not make it more common.

Turn it off when the variants genuinely are extra content rather than the same piece seen from different angles.

`Weight Scale` on an individual variant multiplies that variant's share, which is how one rotation is made rarer than its siblings without touching the others.


> **Note.**
> Spawn limits count per **family**, not per variant. A cap of one places one piece, whichever rotation wins, rather than one of each. See [Spawn Limits](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spawn-limits).


## What a rotation does to an authored neighbour

*What happens when a variant's authored relationship does not survive the rotation.*

A module's authored neighbours are rotated with it. Where a neighbour has no matching rotated variant of its own, that relationship has nowhere to point and is dropped by default.

`Loose Neighbor Closure` keeps the base neighbour instead. That preserves the relationship at the cost of exactness: the seam that was authored is not the seam that results, because the neighbour is not in the pose the rotation implies.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: variants-loose-neighbor-closure | SHOWS: What happens to an authored neighbour relationship that has no rotated counterpart. | ELEMENTS: Three panels left to right, separated by vertical rules. Panel one headed Authored: two modules side by side, a corner piece and its neighbour, meeting at a seam drawn as a clean flush contact and marked as the authored fit. Panel two headed Rotated, closure off: the corner piece turned ninety degrees, the neighbour absent entirely, and the relationship drawn as a dropped link, dimmed and struck, with the rotated piece having nothing on that side. Panel three headed Rotated, closure on: the same rotated corner with the ORIGINAL unrotated neighbour kept beside it, their contact drawn as a visibly imperfect seam with a small gap-and-overlap marker, annotated as kept but not the authored fit. | MUST BE CLEAR: Closure off loses the neighbour. Closure on keeps it at the cost of the seam, which is the trade the setting makes and the reason it is a trade rather than an improvement.
> Off drops the relationship. On keeps it and gives up the authored seam.


Reach for it when the relationship matters more than the alignment, and leave it off when the authored fit is the point.

Tagged seams have none of this trouble: [Bond and Corner Tags](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bond-and-corner-tags) permute with the variant and re-match after expansion, so a rotated seam pairs on its own merits rather than through a rotated copy of its authored list.

## Patterns rotate too

*The same control, on a pattern root, means something larger.*

On a **pattern root cage** the same setting rotates the **whole pattern** rather than one module. The pattern is treated as a complex module whose rotation set is the orbital set's symmetry group, independent of what its constituent cages individually support.

Rotations whose constituent modules do not exist are dropped when the library is built, unless the root opts into forcing them.

On a pattern **child** cage the field is inert and says so: rotations for a pattern are controlled on its root.


> **Warning.**
> Choices are stored against each symmetry's stable key, so swapping the orbital set for one with different symmetries leaves choices pointing at rotations that no longer exist. Those surface as a single warning row with a Clear action rather than one row per orphaned key.

title: Palettes and Mirroring
description: A kit repeats itself.
body:
A kit repeats itself. Twenty wall pieces share one set of connectors; a dozen variants share one asset list with one thing swapped. **Mirroring** is how a cage borrows that from somewhere else rather than restating it.

The source stays authoritative. A mirror is a live reference, not a copy taken once, so editing the source updates everything mirroring from it.

## Five channels, chosen per source

*A mirror is not all-or-nothing.*

Each mirror source declares which kinds of content it brings across.

| Channel | Inherits |
|---|---|
| **Assets** | The source's asset entries, with their local transforms |
| **Connectors** | Its connector definitions |
| **Properties** | Per-asset property overrides, such as material variants captured while scanning |
| **Tags** | Its gameplay tags |
| [Module Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-settings) | Its weight, spawn limits and the rest. Off, mirrored entries use this cage's own settings. |

All five are on by default, so a source pointed at and otherwise left alone brings everything.

Turning individual channels off is what makes mirroring precise. Borrow connectors from a shared template while keeping your own assets; borrow assets from a palette while keeping your own tags. A cage can carry several sources, each contributing a different channel.

## How far a channel reaches

*Every source declares recursion separately.*

Mirror sources chain: a cage mirrors a cage that mirrors a palette. `Recursive Flags` decides, per channel, whether inheritance follows that chain or stops at the immediate source.

That is what keeps deep kit hierarchies predictable. A cage can inherit assets from several links up while taking tags only from the cage it points at directly, so a shared asset library reaches everywhere while local identity stays local.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: palettes-and-mirroring-channel-reach | SHOWS: That each channel reaches a different distance along the same chain of mirror sources, decided per source rather than per cage. | ELEMENTS: A chain of three containers drawn left to right and joined by mirror arcs: an Asset Palette at the right, a template cage in the middle, and the borrowing cage at the left. Each arc is a tapered quadratic bezier in CC7CE8, heavy at the source end and line weight at the borrower end, so inheritance direction reads without a label. Above the chain, five labelled channel lanes run right to left: Assets, Connectors, Properties, Tags, Module Settings. The Assets, Connectors and Properties lanes run the full width from the palette to the borrowing cage. The Tags and Module Settings lanes stop at the middle cage, their ends drawn as a short stop bar rather than fading out. Beside each of the two mirror sources, a small five-pip strip shows which channels that source declares recursive, the pips matching the lanes above. | MUST BE CLEAR: One chain, five different reaches. The Tags lane stopping at the middle cage is the whole reading: the borrowing cage takes its tags from the cage it points at and nothing further, while its assets come from two links away. | NOTE: Mirror arcs lift straight up and draw solid per DIAGRAMS.md. The palette is drawn without orbitals, since it has none.
> One chain of sources, five reaches. Recursion is declared per channel, so assets can come from two links away while tags stop at one.


Both flag sets default to everything, so a source pointed at a palette and left alone inherits all five channels, all the way down.

## Asset palettes

*A library that exists only to be mirrored from.*

An **Asset Palette** holds asset entries the way a cage does and is not a cage. It has no orbitals, belongs to no context volume, and contributes nothing to a library on its own.

That is the whole point of it. A palette is where a set of wall meshes or a family of material variants lives, so that no single cage owns the list and every cage that needs it mirrors it. Deleting the cage that happened to hold the assets stops being a problem.

Palettes also sidestep the kit-or-module exclusivity that governs levels: they do not count as cages for that rule, so a level holding [Module Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-cages) may still hold palettes.

## Adding a source

*By gesture, in the viewport.*

Select the cages or palettes to mirror from, hover the cage that should mirror them, and take the action. An arc appears between them, drawn heavy at the source end and light at the borrower's, so the direction of inheritance is readable without selecting anything.

Hovering that arc offers to remove it.


> **Note.**
> The arc's taper is the notation for inheritance throughout the editor. Heavy end is the authority, light end is the borrower, which is the same in reverse of what an arrow would suggest.


## When to reach for it

*Whenever the same list would otherwise be typed twice.*

Mirroring earns its place at the point where a second cage needs what the first one has. Below that it is overhead, and above it the alternative is keeping several lists in sync by hand, which fails quietly the first time one is edited and the others are not.

The one thing to keep local is whatever makes a module itself. A kit where every cage mirrors its tags from one template is a kit where every module carries the same tags, which is rarely what a tag is for.

title: Placeholders
description: A Valency Cage (Null) stands at a position and asserts something about it without contributing a module.
body:
A **Valency Cage (Null)** stands at a position and asserts something about it without contributing a module. It is how a layout says "nothing may be here", "something must be here", or "a neighbour sits here, and I am only telling you where".

It is a cage in every other respect. It has orbitals, it takes part in detection, and other cages connect to it exactly as they would to a real one. What it never does is author a module: it collects no assets from the level, so nothing it contains is ever placed.

## Three things it can assert

_`Placeholder Mode`, and the choice changes what the neighbouring cages mean._

| Mode         | Asserts                                                  | Drawn          |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| **Boundary** | Nothing may sit here. The cell must stay empty.          | Red sphere     |
| **Wildcard** | Something must sit here, and it does not matter what.    | Magenta sphere |
| **Any**      | Nothing. A neighbour here is acceptable, and so is none. | Cyan sphere    |

The colours are worth learning, because a level full of placeholders is read at a glance and the mode is the only thing distinguishing them.

**Boundary** is the default and the common case. Put one where a structure should end, and every module authored against it declares that side as facing outward.

**Wildcard** is its opposite: the position must be filled, by anything at all. It expresses "this side must connect to something" without naming what, which is what you want for a doorway that must lead somewhere.

**Any** asserts nothing. Its whole purpose is to occupy a position so that neighbouring cages can be authored relative to it, and then to get out of the way.


> **Note.**
> **Boundary and Wildcard are opposites, and neither is the absence of the other.** A module orbital set to **Any** makes no such demand: a neighbour there is acceptable, and so is none. Boundary forbids one, Wildcard requires one, and most orbitals want neither.


### Why a spatial-only placeholder is useful

_Authoring a relationship needs both ends to exist._

Connections between cages are detected from where they sit. To author "this piece connects along here", something has to be at the other end of "here" for the connection to be detected at all.

An **Any** placeholder is that something. It fills the position, the connection is detected, the module records the orbital it bonds along, and the placeholder itself contributes nothing to the library. The relationship survives; the stand-in does not.

That is also the tool for authoring against a neighbour you have not built yet, or one that belongs to a different kit entirely.

### Placeholders in patterns

_A pattern can require a position to be empty._

Null cages can join pattern networks, which lets a pattern describe absence as well as presence. A pattern matching "two of these with nothing between them" needs a way to say _nothing_, and a null cage in the network is it.

That works in both directions: a **Wildcard** in a pattern requires an occupied neighbour without caring which module fills it, so a pattern can match a shape rather than a specific arrangement of pieces.

### What a null cage authors

A null cage authors no module, so most of the cage tooling does not apply to it. It collects no assets, carries no connectors worth speaking of, and contributes no weight or spawn limits.

In the editor mode this shows up as a much shorter rail: **Orbitals** is the only tool a null cage shares with every other kind of cage, alongside its own **Placeholder Settings**.

title: Reference Cages
description: A cage authors a module from its own content.
body:
A cage authors a module from its own content. Sometimes the thing you need at a position was authored somewhere else entirely, in another level or another kit, and copying it here would put a duplicate in the library.

A **Reference** cage is the alternative. It occupies the position and **names** modules rather than authoring one, so a relationship can be authored against them while they stay where they are.

## Cage role

*One property, three ways a cage can contribute.*

Every cage carries a `Cage Role`, and it decides what the cage puts into the compiled rules.

| Role | Contributes |
|---|---|
| **Module** | A module built from its own content. The default. |
| **Template** | Nothing. It exists to be mirrored from, and its "no assets" warnings are suppressed. |
| **Reference** | Nothing of its own. It names modules authored elsewhere. |

**Template** is worth knowing about alongside Reference because the two solve different halves of the same problem. A template is boilerplate other cages borrow *from*; a reference is a stand-in for content that lives *elsewhere*.

The role also gates the details panel. Most of a cage's settings are meaningful only for **Module**, so switching to **Reference** hides them rather than leaving inert fields on screen.

## What a reference names

*Its asset entries and its mirror sources, read as a list of candidates.*

A reference cage's asset entries do not become a module. They declare **which modules may sit at this position**, the same way a pattern position's proxies do, and its mirror sources contribute candidates in the same way.

Those candidates travel as **asset paths**, which is what lets them refer to modules built elsewhere. The reference does not need the other kit loaded, or the other level open: it names the assets, and whatever module in the library was built from them is what the relationship resolves to.

## Why author against one

*A relationship needs both ends to exist somewhere.*

Connections are detected from where cages sit, so authoring "this piece connects to that one" needs something at the far end. When the far end belongs to another kit, three options exist and only one of them is right:

| Option | Cost |
|---|---|
| Copy the other cage in | A duplicate module in the library, and two things to keep in sync |
| Use a [Placeholders](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/placeholders) | The relationship is recorded, but it says nothing about *what* may sit there |
| Use a **Reference** | The relationship is recorded and constrained to the named modules |

The middle one is right when any neighbour will do. The reference is for when the neighbour must be one of a specific set that you are not authoring here.

## Reference and Loose Neighbors

*Two ways to say "these may be adjacent", with different reach.*

A **Module** cage can also declare [Loose Neighbors](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/loose-neighbors): cages or asset paths that its modules may sit beside. That is a bulk grant, applied to every side at once, and it is the tool when the adjacency is not about a particular direction.

A reference cage is the opposite. It sits at one position, so the relationship it carries is directional: it says what may be *there*, along the orbital pointing at it.

Reach for loose neighbours when the answer is "these things go together" and a reference when it is "on this side, one of these".


> **Note.**
> Loose-neighbour fields are hidden unless the cage's role is **Module**, which is the panel telling you the same thing: a reference cage is already a positional statement and has no use for a bulk one.

title: Connector Constraints
description: Attachment is exact.
body:
Attachment is exact. Two connector frames mate, and the child lands in precisely one place, which is where [Connectors](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/connectors) leaves it.

**Connector constraints** are what make that interesting. They take the one exact placement and turn it into a set of **variants**, then shape, offset and thin that set. Where a module ends up is whatever survives.

## A pipeline of three kinds

*Each constraint plays one of three roles, and order matters.*

| Role | Does |
|---|---|
| **Generator** | Produces several transform variants from the base placement |
| **Modifier** | Offsets or re-orients each variant |
| **Filter** | Rejects variants |

Constraints run in list order, so the pipeline reads top to bottom: generate a spread of candidates, nudge them, throw some away. A modifier before any generator adjusts the single base placement; the same modifier after one adjusts every variant it produced.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connector-constraints-pipeline | SHOWS: One exact attachment becoming a set of candidate placements, and that moving a modifier past a generator changes what it acts on. | ELEMENTS: Two rows sharing one setup drawn at the left of each. The setup is a parent module as an outline with an inside corner, one connector on it in FFA627, and a child module outline offered onto it. Row one headed Modifier after the generator: four stages left to right joined by flow arrows, labelled Base, Generator, Modifier, Filter. Base shows the single exact placement. Generator shows five child placements fanned across an arc from that connector. Modifier shows the same five, each pushed out along the arc normal by the same amount, the shift marked once with a short offset tick. Filter shows two of the five struck with the refusal cross and three surviving solid. Row two headed Modifier before the generator: the same four stage labels in the order Base, Modifier, Generator, Filter, and the drawing shows the modifier displacing the ONE base placement, the generator then fanning five variants from that displaced origin, so the whole arc sits offset rather than the variants sitting offset from the arc. A count strip under each stage reads 1, 5, 5, 3 in row one and 1, 1, 5, 3 in row two. | MUST BE CLEAR: The list is identical in both rows and only the order differs. In row one the offset is applied five times to five variants; in row two it is applied once, to the origin they are generated from, and the resulting spreads do not coincide. | NOTE: Modules get inside corners per DIAGRAMS.md, connectors are FFA627 since no type distinction is being made, and the figure carries no green.
> Generate, nudge, discard. The same modifier one row higher moves the origin the variants come from instead of the variants.


## The fifteen

*Grouped by what they do rather than by role.*

**Spreading placements out**

| Constraint | Produces |
|---|---|
| **Angular Range** | Evenly-spaced rotations around a frame axis, across an angular range |
| **Conic Range** | A spread over a cone surface, tilting rather than rotating in-plane |
| **Arc Repeat** | Evenly-spaced variants along an arc at a radius, each rotated to follow it |
| **Spiral** | A helix: rotation plus progressive forward offset |
| [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) | A 2D grid across the frame's right and up plane, for panels and window arrays |

**Moving the attachment point**

| Constraint | Moves it |
|---|---|
| **Surface Offset** | To a random spot in a rectangular region on the right/up plane |
| **Arc Surface** | To a random spot in an arc-shaped area on that plane |
| **Volume Offset** | By a random offset within a box around the frame origin |
| **Hemisphere Offset** | By a random offset within a dome facing along the frame's forward axis |
| **Snap To Grid** | Onto a grid anchored at the frame origin |

**Re-orienting and scaling**

| Constraint | Does |
|---|---|
| **Look At** | Aims a chosen local axis toward, or away from, a target |
| **Scale Ramp** | Scales by a growth-context value, mapping a source range onto a scale range |

**Thinning the set**

| Constraint | Rejects |
|---|---|
| **Probability** | A fraction of variants, hashed from the candidate so results reproduce |
| **Context Condition** | Every variant, when a growth-context property fails a threshold |
| **Branch** | Nothing itself. It splits the pool on a condition, runs a sub-pipeline per side, and rejoins. |

**Branch** is the one that makes the pipeline more than a list. It is a fork-join, so two halves of the candidate pool can be shaped differently and then merged, which is how one connector expresses "near the ground, do this; higher up, do that".


> **Note.**
> **Probability** hashes from the candidate rather than drawing freely, so the same inputs always thin the same way. Randomness here is reproducible by construction.


## The working frame

*Every constraint resolves in a frame, and which one is a setting.*

Positions, axes and rotations are all expressed relative to a **working frame** rather than to the world. `Frame Source` chooses it.

| Frame | Is |
|---|---|
| **Parent Connector** | The open connector being expanded. The default. |
| **Child Connector** | The mated child connector: same origin, flipped 180 degrees about the parent's up axis |
| **Child Module** | The placed child module's base frame, with its origin at the module pivot |

That choice changes what "right", "up" and "forward" mean for everything downstream of it, which is why the same constraint produces different results with nothing else altered.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connector-constraints-frame-source | SHOWS: The same constraint resolving in three different frames, producing three different spreads from one unchanged setup. | ELEMENTS: Three panels compared, separated by vertical rules, sharing one setup drawn identically at the top of each. The setup is a parent module as an outline with an inside corner, a connector on it drawn as an axis triad with its forward and up arrows labelled, and a child module outline whose pivot sits well away from its own mating connector so the two origins are visibly different. Each panel applies one Surface Offset scatter, drawn as eight small candidate markers over a shaded rectangular region. Panel one headed Parent Connector: the triad and the region sit on the parent socket. Panel two headed Child Connector: the region sits at the same origin but its axes are turned 180 degrees about the parent up, so the region extends the opposite way. Panel three headed Child Module: the triad has moved off the socket onto the child module pivot and the region is spread over the child body instead. In every panel the parent, the socket and the constraint settings are drawn unchanged. | MUST BE CLEAR: Nothing about the authoring differs between the three panels. The region moves and turns because right, up and forward were re-read from a different frame, and Child Module is the only one whose origin is not the socket. | NOTE: Child Connector shares the parent origin and differs only in orientation, so the two regions must overlap at their corner rather than being drawn apart.
> One constraint, one setup, three frames. Child Connector turns the region; Child Module moves it off the socket entirely.


**Child Module** is the one to reach for when the shaping is about the piece rather than the joint: scattering across a module's own extent wants its pivot as the origin, not the socket it happens to be hanging from.

## Type defaults and instance overrides

*Constraints are authored twice over, and the second decides how they combine.*

A **connector type** on the set carries default constraints, inherited by every instance of that type. A connector **instance** on a module can carry its own, and `Override Mode` decides what happens.

| Mode | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Append** | Type defaults run first, then the instance's constraints continue the pipeline. The default. |
| **Replace** | Type defaults are skipped entirely |

**Append** is what makes type defaults worth having: the type establishes the house behaviour, and an instance adds to it without restating it. Reach for **Replace** when one socket genuinely needs to opt out of everything its type does.

## Presets

*A reusable fragment of pipeline.*

A **Constraint Preset** is a data asset holding a list of constraints, expanded inline where it is referenced. It behaves exactly as though its contents had been typed in at that point in the list.

That is the tool for a shaping recipe used in several places: define "scatter across the face with a slight tilt" once, and reference it from every connector type that wants it.

## Where to see them

Constraints draw in the viewport under the **Valency editor mode**, which is the only practical way to author them. Each has an indicator at the connector and a zone showing the region it acts over, and the one being edited is highlighted.

Reading a pipeline from the details panel alone is possible and slow. Reading it from the viewport, where the candidate spread is visible, is what the visualisation exists for.

title: Context Volumes
description: A context volume is the entry point: it gathers the cages inside it and publishes them to the assets you point it at.
outline: Where the volume's sets come from
body:
A context volume is the entry point: it gathers the cages inside it and publishes them to the assets you point it at. It also quietly supplies most of what those cages need, which is why a well-set-up volume means cages carrying almost no settings of their own.

Everything about what a volume contains, and the fact that a cage outside every volume is ignored entirely, is covered under [Authoring](concept:working-with-valency/authoring). This page is what a volume does with what it found.

### What it publishes to

_Targets, and there can be more than one of each._

| Target             | Receives                                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules)  | The modules its cages author                |
| **Pattern Assets** | The arrangements its pattern cages describe |

Both are sets rather than single references, so one volume can feed several rules assets and several pattern assets at once. Publishing is one-way: the volume pushes contributions, and each target picks them up when it compiles.


> **Warning.**
> **Where the volume's sets come from**
>
> It derives them from the **first** target Bonding Rules asset, and hands them down to every cage inside it. Nothing on the volume lets you set them directly.
>
> The consequence matters when a volume targets several rules assets: those assets must agree about their orbital and connector sets. A module is tied to exactly one of each, so targeting rules that disagree is a configuration error, and it is reported at compile rather than silently picking one.


### Where contributions actually go

_Publishing is indirect, and the thing in the middle is worth knowing about._

A volume does not write into your Bonding Rules asset. It writes into a **Valency Editor Cache**, one per level, and the rules asset pulls from that when it compiles.

The cache is an invisible, locked actor that appears by itself the first time something in the level needs it. You do not create it, you cannot place it, and deleting it does not stick: it respawns. It lives in the always-loaded layer so World Partition streaming cannot hide contributions from a compile.

That indirection is what makes several things possible at once. A rules asset can draw from levels that are not open. Several volumes across several levels can feed one asset. A level can publish without knowing or caring who consumes it, which is exactly how [Module Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-cages) work.


> **Note.**
> The cache stores what was baked, not what is currently in the level, and it is not rebuilt when a level is merely opened. That is what makes it fast, and also what makes a stale entry possible. **Rebuild All** in the panel header re-bakes on top of it; **Shift+click Rebuild All** empties it first and rebuilds from nothing.
>
> Reach for the Shift version when results differ between editor sessions on a scene nobody edited.


### What it supplies to the cages inside it

_Defaults, so a cage only carries what actually differs._

| Supplied                                       | Cage-side override                                          |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| The bonding rules to resolve against           | None. This comes from the volume.                           |
| The orbital set and connector set              | None. Derived, as above.                                    |
| **Default Probe Radius**, `100` out of the box | A cage sets its own radius to override, or `-1` to inherit  |
| **Display Cell Size**, purely visual           | A cage inherits it, and the orbital set supplies a fallback |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: volumes-publish-and-supply | SHOWS: That a volume moves data in two directions at once. | ELEMENTS: A volume outline in the centre containing four cages. Upward arrows from the volume to two target assets above it, one Bonding Rules and one Pattern Asset, labelled publishes. Downward arrows from the volume to the cages inside it, labelled supplies, carrying small chips reading rules, orbital set, connector set, probe radius. A side arrow from the first Bonding Rules asset back into the volume, labelled derives its sets from, drawn distinctly. | MUST BE CLEAR: Contributions go up to the targets, defaults come down to the cages, and the sets the volume hands down were themselves read off the first target.
> Contributions go up to the targets. Defaults come down to the cages. The sets going down were read off the first target going up.


Volumes nest, so a cage can be inside more than one at a time. Where that happens, resolution is **first match wins**: the first containing volume that supplies a non-null rules asset, a probe radius, or a cell size is the one used. Nesting is for grouping and separate targeting, and is not a way to layer settings on top of each other.

Separate targeting is the useful half. A nested volume inside your main one, holding a set of pattern cages and pointing at its own **Pattern Asset**, keeps those patterns in their own asset without moving the cages out of the layout they describe. Splitting patterns across several assets is mostly done this way.


> **Note.**
> **Display Cell Size** is worth setting even though nothing reads it at compile or runtime. It controls the spacing of the orbital-cell display on contained cages, and matching it to the Cell Size on the Lattice node this layout feeds means the cells you author against are the cells that get built.


## Keeping incidental actors out

_Scanning takes everything, so the volume is where you say what to skip._

Anything attached to a cage gets registered, including lights, triggers and notes. Three settings on the volume decide what is exempt, and they apply to scanning, detection and building alike.

| Setting                            | Excludes                                                                             |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Ignored Actor Tags**             | Any actor carrying one of these tags. Ships with `PCGEx_Ignore` already in the list. |
| **Ignored Actors**                 | Specific actors, along with everything attached to them.                             |
| **Auto Ignore PCG Spawned Actors** | Actors spawned by the level cache's regenerated PCG. On by default.                  |

The tag is the one to reach for. Tagging a prop `PCGEx_Ignore` keeps it visible in the level and out of every library, with no per-cage configuration, and the tag is in the list out of the box so it works immediately.

The third setting earns its place: generated output can land in the same level as the cages that produced it, and without it a volume would scan its own results back in as new modules.

## When it rebuilds

_Mostly by itself, and deliberately quiet about it._

Editing a cage, moving a volume, or changing a target all trigger a re-aggregation. Several things stop that becoming noise:

* **Edits coalesce.** A burst of changes produces one bake per volume rather than one per change.
* **A no-op bake changes nothing downstream.** The volume compares what it just gathered against what it published last time, and only marks a target for recompile when the contribution actually differs. Authoring does not dirty-spam your assets.
* **It works with the editor mode off.** Cache correctness does not depend on the mode being active. What the mode adds is per-tick coalescing rather than a deferred pass on the next editor tick.

Two explicit actions sit on the volume for when you want the unconditional version:

| Action                         | Does                                                                                                                                             |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Build Rules From Cages**     | Re-aggregates and updates every target Bonding Rules asset in place, whether or not anything changed.                                            |
| **Refresh Cage Relationships** | Re-runs connection detection across the cages in this volume. Useful after cages have been moved or edited by something outside the normal path. |


> **Note.**
> Because a no-op bake is deliberately silent, "nothing happened" after an edit usually means nothing needed to. When you want certainty rather than inference, **Build Rules From Cages** is the button that always does the work.


## Automatic asset tracking

_Rescan as content moves in and out._

**Auto Track Asset Placement**, on by default, rescans a cage's assets as actors are moved into and out of it, so dragging a mesh into a cage registers it without any further action.

This one is genuinely mode-dependent: it is only active while the Valency editor mode is on. Moving content around with the mode off leaves the cage's asset list as it was until something else triggers a rescan.

title: Gestures
description: Most cage authoring happens in the viewport rather than the details panel.
outline: Dropping a selection into a container
body:
Most cage authoring happens in the viewport rather than the details panel. Hovering a cage or one of its orbitals offers an action, clicking takes it, and holding **Shift** either takes a second one or opens a menu of the rest.

[Authoring](concept:working-with-valency/authoring) covers the three you will use constantly. This is the whole vocabulary, in the order the menu presents it.

## Two hover surfaces

*Where you hover decides which family of actions you get.*

| Surface | Offers |
|---|---|
| An orbital's outward line | Expanding across it into the empty cell beyond |
| The container's own body | Dropping the selection into it, or registering references on it |

They are separate pixels, so there is never a guess about which gesture a click means.

The body surface serves two different families depending on **what is selected**, and the two selections are disjoint by construction: non-Valency actors mean you are placing content, Valency actors mean you are registering references.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: gestures-two-surfaces | SHOWS: Which pixels offer which family of actions, and that the body surface answers to what is selected rather than to where the cursor is. | ELEMENTS: One cage drawn as a square with a dot at its origin, four orbital arrows out of it, two of them connected to neighbours and two unconnected. Two hover zones are shaded and keyed, and they do not touch: a band along each unconnected orbital line, and the cage body itself. Beside the orbital band, a list of the four rows it offers, headed Expand Into This Cell. Beside the body, TWO lists stacked and bracketed together, headed by what is selected: an upper one headed Non-Valency actors selected listing the three Attach rows, and a lower one headed Valency actors selected listing the three reference rows. A cursor glyph sits on the orbital band, and a second faint cursor glyph sits on the body, so both surfaces are shown as reachable. | MUST BE CLEAR: The two shaded zones never overlap, which is why a click is never ambiguous. The body zone alone has two possible answers, and the selection is what picks between them, not the position of the cursor. | NOTE: The connected orbitals carry no expand band, which is what makes the band an unconnected-only affordance.
> Two zones that never share a pixel. Only the body has two answers, and the selection decides which.


## Expanding across an orbital

*Hovering the line out of an unconnected orbital. Menu section: **Expand Into This Cell**.*

| Action | Does |
|---|---|
| **New Copy** | Duplicates the source cage into the empty cell, without the assets it currently contains |
| **New Copy (With Contents)** | Duplicates it with the attached content, offsets intact |
| **New Null** | Places a [Placeholders](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/placeholders): the cell must stay empty |
| **New Wild** | Places a Wildcard placeholder: the cell must hold something |

**New Copy** is the default rather than **New Copy (With Contents)**, and that is deliberate: an empty stamp is the right tool for laying out topology before deciding what fills it. Copying with contents works only because content is attached, so the whole subtree duplicates with its offsets.

### Annotating the orbital instead

*Four states in one row, at the bottom of the same menu. Menu section: **This Side**.*

The same hover carries a per-orbital override of the cage's missing-connection dial. It places nothing: it annotates the orbital being hovered. The four states are one exclusive choice drawn as a row of icons, and it edits in place while the menu stays open.

| State | Means |
|---|---|
| **Use Cage Default** | Whatever the cage's `Missing Connection Behavior` says. No override. |
| **Any** | A neighbour here is acceptable, and so is none. |
| **Boundary** | Nothing may sit here. This side faces outward. |
| **Wildcard** | Something must sit here, and it does not matter what. |

Picking one of the three enables the override in the same click, so there is nothing to arm first. **Use Cage Default** is the fourth state of that same row, and it is genuinely different from **Any**: the first follows whatever the cage says, the second pins this side to Any even on a cage whose dial is Boundary.

**Boundary** and **Wildcard** here mark the cage's own orbital. **New Null** and **New Wild**, above, place a placeholder cage in the cell beyond instead.

**This Side** carries the orbital's other per-side settings in the same panel: its **Self Connect** toggle, and its [Bond and Corner Tags](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bond-and-corner-tags).

## Dropping a selection into a container

*Hovering the body with non-Valency actors selected. Menu section: **Attach The Selection**.*

| Action | Does |
|---|---|
| **Attach** | Attaches, moving each actor's **pivot** onto the container's origin, keeping rotation and scale |
| **Attach (Preserve Placement)** | Attaches without moving anything |
| **Attach a Copy** | Leaves the originals alone and attaches a copy, pivot-aligned |

**Attach** is the default because it is what placing a module means: a kit mesh belongs at its cage's origin. It only moves position, so an asset you turned or resized keeps that.


> **Warning.**
> Attaching is **per actor**, so attaching several at once stacks all their pivots on the same origin. A selection whose internal arrangement matters wants **Attach (Preserve Placement)** instead.


**Preserve Placement** is subtler than "do not move". Content coming from another container is re-anchored between the two origins, so the placement it had *inside that container* is the placement it keeps. Content coming from nowhere stays exactly put, because there is no frame to re-anchor between.

## Registering references

*Hovering the body with Valency actors selected. Two menu sections, and which one appears depends on which end can hold the reference.*

| Menu section | Action | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| **Reference The Selection** | **Add As Mirror Sources** | The selection onto the hovered cage's mirror sources |
| **Reference The Selection** | **Add As Proxies** | The selection onto the hovered **pattern** cage's proxied cages |
| **Reference From Here** | **Mirror Into Selection** | The hovered container onto each **selected** cage's mirror sources |

**Mirror Into Selection** reverses the write direction, and it exists for containers that can *be* a mirror source but cannot *host* one. An asset palette is exactly that, so without this row, hovering a palette with cages selected would offer nothing at all.

The direction is never a guess, which is what the two section names say. Where both ends could host the reference, the hovered one does. Where only the selection can, it does.

## Removing a link

*Hovering the arc itself.*

| Action | Removes |
|---|---|
| **Remove Mirror Source** | One entry from the owner cage's mirror sources |
| **Remove Proxy** | One entry from the owner pattern cage's proxied cages |
| **Remove Loose Neighbor** | One entry from the owner cage's [Loose Neighbors](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/loose-neighbors) |

Links are drawn as arcs between the two cages, so removing one is a matter of hovering the arc rather than finding the entry in a list.

## Primary, Shift, and the menu

*Which action a click fires depends on the surface and on what is being hovered.*

Every gesture kind resolves a **primary** action for a plain click. Shift then does one of two things depending on the kind: it fires a second declared action directly, or it opens a menu of everything applicable.

That resolution is driven by facts about the target, so the offered action changes with context: what kind of cage is hovered, what is selected, whether the orbital already carries an override. A gesture with nothing sensible to fire offers nothing and refuses the click, rather than consuming it on an action that does nothing.


> **Note.**
> This is why the same click does different things on different cages, and why a row you expected can be absent. The vocabulary is fixed; which parts of it apply is decided per target.

title: Concepts
description: These pages are the vocabulary.
body:
These pages are the vocabulary. Everything in Authoring and Generating is written in terms defined here, which is the difference between the rest of the book reading as instructions and reading as a list of settings. ## Read in this order _The first page decides how much of the next two you need._
PageAnswers
[Connection Models](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/connection-models)Orbitals and connectors: which one carries your structure
[Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/orbitals)Bonding by direction, and what a module asserts along each one
[Connectors](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/connectors)Bonding by socket: types, polarity, and what happens when two mate
[Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules)The module library, what can fill it, and what a module is
[Selecting Modules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/selecting-modules)How you tell Valency which modules you mean
[Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/patterns)Recognising an arrangement in a finished result, and acting on it
**Connection models earns its place at the front.** Most setups end up using both models, so it is rarely a choice between reading Orbitals and reading Connectors. What it settles is which of the two carries your structure and which one plays the supporting role, and reading the next two pages with that already decided is what stops them blurring together. The last three apply whatever you settled on, and can be read in any order. ### Where the rest lives _This section is what both halves of the plugin share._
SectionCovers
[Authoring](concept:working-with-valency/authoring)Level and asset editor work: cages, sets, volumes, the Valency editor mode
[Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating)PCG graph work: solving, growing, grammars, patterns, output
[Systems](concept:working-with-valency/systems)Machinery reached from several places: biases, limits, facts, filters, debugging
If you are looking for which button does what, those are the sections you want. Nothing here tells you where anything is.

title: Bonding Rules
description: Everything in it is assembled rather than written by hand, from whichever sources you point it at.
outline: What you configure, and what is assembled
Author from inside the editor mode
body:
> Figure: The Bonding Rules asset icon

A **Bonding Rules** asset is a library of modules, and the only Valency asset a PCG graph consumes directly.

Everything in it is assembled rather than written by hand, from whichever sources you point it at. Laying out cages in a level is the most direct of those, and far from the only one.
## It is a library

_The asset is the set of pieces you can build from. Where they were authored stops mattering once they are in it._

A Bonding Rules asset holds a flat set of modules, each knowing its own asset, its connections and its rules, with no memory of how it got there. Most people fill their first one entirely from cages, which makes that route easy to mistake for the whole story.

Reading it as a library is what makes the sources interchangeable. A module contributed by a hand-authored cage, a module standing for an entire level, and a module imported from an asset collection are the same kind of thing once compiled, and generation cannot tell them apart.

### Why it is a separate asset

_Generation runs off compiled data, never off the actors you authored._

Cages are editor actors sitting in levels. Generation runs in a PCG graph, off the game thread, with none of those levels necessarily in memory. Nothing about a cage is reachable from there, so authoring has to be frozen into something that is: a flat dataset of modules, masks, connectors and properties, serialized on an asset a graph can hold a reference to.

One library draws from as many levels as you point it at. A ruleset can be spread across several authoring levels, split by kit, by theme, or by whoever is working on it, with each level's volume registering itself on the same asset. They converge into one library, and the modules that arrive carry no trace of which level supplied them.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: bonding-rules-sources-to-library | SHOWS: Several unlike sources converging into one module library, which a PCG graph then reads. | ELEMENTS: Left column, three dissimilar sources stacked: a level containing cages and a Context Volume, a second level marked as being a single module in its own right, and an asset collection. Middle, the Bonding Rules asset drawn as one flat table of module rows, the rows visually identical regardless of which source fed them. Right, a PCG graph with a Valency node reading the table. Arrows go left to middle labelled contribute, and middle to right labelled read. No arrow bypasses the middle. | MUST BE CLEAR: The sources look nothing like each other. The rows they produce are indistinguishable. The graph only ever sees the table.
> Unlike sources, identical results. Once a module is in the library, where it came from stops mattering.


## What a module is

_One asset, plus everything the rules need in order to place it._

A **module** is the compiled unit. It pairs an asset to spawn with everything decided about how it may sit in the world:

| Carries                                 | Meaning                                                     |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| An asset reference, and its type        | A mesh, an actor, a whole level, or a PCG data asset holding an exported arrangement |
| An orbital mask, or connectors, or both | How it is allowed to bond                                   |
| Properties and tags                     | Data and identity that travel to the spawned point          |
| A weight                                | Relative likelihood when something picks between candidates |
| Spawn limits                            | Caps on how often it may be placed                          |
| A placement policy                      | Whether, and how, it may participate at all                 |

Modules are what every part of generation actually works with. A solve assigns modules to positions, growth attaches modules to connectors, a grammar asks for modules by signature. Cages are an authoring convenience; after compilation they do not exist.

The last three rows are a family of their own, authored per module and covered under module settings. The rest of this page is about how modules get into the library, and what happens when several sources describe the same one.

### Where modules come from

_Several unlike sources, and the list is meant to grow._

| Source                                                 | Contributes                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Cages in a level**, gathered by a **Context Volume** | The direct route. Each cage authors one module, and the volume registers its level on the rules asset automatically.                                                                                                          |
| A **Valency Module Cage**                              | Declares the level it sits in as a single module. It needs no containing volume, and requires a **Connector Set**, which is the only key its contribution carries. |
| A **Valency Assembly Cage**                            | One module from everything attached to the cage, exported to a PCG data asset at staging. An ordinary cage otherwise, gathered by a volume like the rest. |
| The **Collection Sources** provider                    | Imports modules out of existing asset collections, so a kit already built for PCGEx can be brought in without re-authoring it as cages.                                                                                       |
| Any other provider                                     | Contribution providers are an extension point, and the built-in importer is one implementation of it.                                                                                                                         |

**Module Cages are worth understanding early**, because they change what a module can be. A cage normally wraps a mesh or an actor. A module cage instead says _this entire level is one module_, so an elaborate hand-built structure with its own interior detail becomes a single library entry that generation places as one piece. Those modules carry connectors and no orbitals, so they belong to the connector connection model. An assembly cage covers the ground between the two: one module from the arrangement attached to it, keeping its orbitals and its place in a kit.


> **Note.**
> A module cage never registers itself anywhere. It publishes its contribution and stops, and which rules asset consumes it is that asset's decision, made by listing the level or by reaching it through a provider. That is deliberate: a self-registering one would re-register through every copy of the level that generation spawns.


### Identical content becomes one module

_Deduplication is by content, and it decides what counts as one module._

Two contributions that describe the same module produce **one** module. Identity is content-based: the asset, how it bonds, its material variant, its property overrides and a few related details. Two cages holding the same mesh with the same connections are one module, however far apart they sit and however many of them you laid out.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: bonding-rules-dedup | SHOWS: Several separately authored cages resolving to a single library entry. | ELEMENTS: Left, four cages scattered across a level at different positions and rotations, all holding the same mesh and all wired the same way. Right, a single module row in the library, holding one asset reference and one set of connections, with no position anywhere on it. Thin lines run from all four cages to that one row. | MUST BE CLEAR: Four cages, one module. The scatter and rotation visible on the left has no counterpart on the right, because none of it is part of a module.
> Four cages, one module. Their positions said what connects to what, then stopped mattering.


Settings are a separate matter. Because two contributions can describe the same module while disagreeing about what to do with it, dedup keeps the **first** source's settings wholesale.


> **Warning.**
> **The first source's settings win**
>
> If two sources produce the same module but differ on weight, spawn limits, limit group, module name or placement policy, one set of values is kept and the other is discarded silently as far as the result is concerned.
>
> It is not silent in the log. Valency warns for each of those cases individually, naming what was kept and what was ignored. A compile log is the fastest way to find two pieces you believed were identical and are not, or two you believed were distinct and are not.


## What you configure, and what is assembled

_The asset is mostly output. A short list of things on it are inputs._

| Yours to set                                                                                                         | Assembled by compile                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| The **Orbital Set** and **Connector Set** this ruleset speaks | Every module, and everything on it           |
| Its sources: level contributors and contribution providers                                                           | Their masks, connectors, properties and tags |
| Default properties, as a schema                                                                                      | Their weights, limits and policies           |
