| Compilation options                                                                                                  | The asset collection modules resolve through |

The `Modules` list is editable in the details panel and editing it achieves nothing, because the next compile reassembles it. Changing a module means changing the source it came from. The [Bonding Rules Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bonding-rules-settings) are the part that is genuinely yours.

## Keeping it current

_The editor works hard at this, and most of that work happens inside the Valency editor mode._

The asset stamps itself whenever a compile succeeds, and compares that stamp against its sources to know when it has fallen behind. Around that sits a good deal of automation: the rules asset can refresh itself when it is loaded and finds itself stale, and while you are in the **Valency editor mode** a per-tick pass keeps containers refreshed and volumes rebuilt as you author. Entering the mode also re-syncs the PCG components registered against each level's cache, so a scene that drifted while you were elsewhere is brought back into line on the way in.

Two options govern how eager any of that is:

| Option               | Effect                                                                                    |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Compile On Rebuild` | Compile whenever the asset is rebuilt from its sources, and serialize the result with it. |
| `Auto Refresh`       | Refresh by itself when upstream dependencies are seen to have changed.                    |

Leaving both on is the intended setup, and in ordinary authoring you should not have to think about any of this.


> **Note.**
> **Author from inside the editor mode**
>
> Much of the automation above is gated on the Valency editor mode being active. Editing cages from outside it is not forbidden, but it is the state in which things most plausibly look stale, because the machinery that would have noticed is not running.

title: Connection Models
description: Valency has two ways of stating how modules connect: orbitals and connectors.
body:
Valency has two ways of stating how modules connect: **orbitals** and **connectors**. The choice is not a style preference. It decides which nodes you use, whether you bring a topology or generate one, and what counts as a valid result.

## The two models

_Orbitals bond by direction. Connectors bond by socket._

An **orbital** is a named direction. A module states which directions it can bond along, and matching compares directions only, never positions. That is what lets one set of rules serve a grid, a hex field and an irregular graph without change.

A **connector** is a socket: a position, an orientation, and a type. Matching pairs a connector with a compatible one and derives a transform from that pairing, so the sockets line up.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connection-models-side-by-side | SHOWS: The same module expressed in both connection models. | ELEMENTS: Two copies of one module box. Left, arrows radiating from its center with no surface contact, and a neighbour box sitting where an arrow points. Right, oriented frames on its surface, with a neighbour box mated flush to one frame. | MUST BE CLEAR: Left, the neighbour position was already decided and the arrow only says whether it is allowed. Right, the mating produced the position.
> Orbitals say whether a neighbour is allowed. Connectors decide where it lands.


### Orbitals: you bring the topology

_The positions already exist. Valency decides what goes in them._

You supply a cluster. Every node is a position, every edge is a connection that already exists. **Valency : Solve** assigns a module to each node so that every edge is legal under your rules. This is Wave Function Collapse, generalised off the grid.

Solving cannot move anything, and it cannot add or remove a position. It answers one question per node, which is _what goes here_. If the shape is wrong, the shape was wrong before Valency saw it.

Directions are matched within a tolerance, so a cluster does not need to be perfectly regular for its edges to register as bonds. An orbital set holds up to 63 directions.

### Connectors: the topology is the output

_You supply a starting point. Valency produces the positions._

You supply seeds. Growth attaches a compatible module to an open connector, which exposes that module's remaining connectors, and repeats. Each attachment creates the next position, so the result is a structure that did not exist in any form beforehand.

**Valency : Grow Points** grows from seed points. **Valency : Grow Cluster** grows outward from an existing result.

Connectors carry a type and a polarity. Polarity is `Plug` (outward), `Port` (inward), or `Universal`. Compatibility is stated between types, so a module cannot attach somewhere it has no business attaching, however well the geometry happens to line up.

What decides _which_ compatible module attaches next is a separate choice: a traversal strategy, or an authored **Structural Grammar** that dictates the sequence. Both are ways of driving the connector model, not a third model alongside it.

## A module can carry both

_Placement is always one model. Influence is not._

A module may declare orbitals, connectors, or both. What never happens is a single pass _placing_ with both: a solve places using orbitals, growth places using connectors.

They meet through their output. Both end in placed modules, so a solved layout is a valid input to growth, and **Valency : Grow Cluster** consumes a solved cluster and grows from the open connectors of the modules that resolved into it. Blocking out a floor plan by solving, then growing its fixtures onto that result, is one pipeline and two passes. Reach for it when a problem has a constrained skeleton and an open-ended remainder.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connection-models-combined | SHOWS: One module carrying both, and the two passes reading it in turn. | ELEMENTS: The same module box from the earlier diagram, now drawn with both its orbital arrows and its surface connectors at once. Left half, a solved cluster where the module sits at a node, orbital arrows lit, connectors idle. Right half, the same placed module with its connectors now growing new modules outward, orbital arrows dimmed. One arrow between the halves labelled as the second pass. | MUST BE CLEAR: It is one module and one set of authored data throughout. What changes between halves is which pass is reading it, never the module.
> Same module, same authoring. The solve reads its arrows, then the grow reads its sockets.


**How orbital state constrains connector growth**


Placement is single-model. Eligibility is not. Orbital state can decide what growth is allowed to place, and which connectors are available to grow from at all:

* A connector can be **gated on an orbital fact** of the module hosting it, so that it only exists where the orbitals you name are occupied, or where they are vacant. A gated connector that fails its check is not skipped, it is not there at all.
* A grammar **Orbital Facts** constraint vetoes placement candidates by an orbital fact of either the module being grown from or the module being considered.

Facts about a _module_ are compiled into the rules and can always be answered. Facts about live orbital state, `Occupancy` and `Vacant`, need an actual orbital substrate to read, which exists when growing from a solved cluster and not otherwise. Where it is absent, an authored fallback answers.

This is what makes solve-then-grow more than sequencing. The solve leaves a record of what bonded where, and growth can be authored to respect it.




> **Note.**
> Patterns are the other crossover. A single pattern may match a mix of orbital and connector relationships, because matching reads a finished result rather than driving placement.


## Which model carries the structure

_Most setups use both. The real question is which one the structure hangs off._

Two shapes cover most of what gets built:

| Shape                                      | Looks like                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Connectors throughout**                  | Everything grows. No cluster is supplied, and the structure is produced entirely by mating sockets.                                                              |
| **Orbitals, with a handful of connectors** | A solve decides the structure, and a few sockets carry whatever attaches to it: fixtures, trim, props, the things that hang off a layout rather than forming it. |

Pure orbital kits exist, and so do problems that only ever grow. Most work sits between the two, and adding a couple of connectors to an otherwise orbital kit costs nothing.

What decides which one carries the structure:

| If                                                                                              | Then           | Because                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| You have a grid, a graph, a floor plan, a road network, anything whose shape is already decided | **Orbitals**   | The positions exist. You need the right module in each.      |
| You have a starting point and want structure to emerge from it                                  | **Connectors** | The positions do not exist. Attachment is what creates them. |
| The shape must satisfy global constraints you can express as a layout                           | **Orbitals**   | Solving sees every position at once. Growth sees a frontier. |
| Pieces must physically mate, with sockets aligning exactly                                      | **Connectors** | Orbitals constrain direction, not contact.                   |

If you would have to author the cluster by hand to give the solver something to work on, you wanted growth.

title: Connectors
description: Where an orbital is matched by direction, a connector is matched by identity, so two connectors can meet at any angle in space as long as their types accept each other and they face each other.
outline: Joining two things that already exist needs both directions
Two connectors in the same place do not necessarily meet
The cost of changing a set
body:
> Figure: The Connector Set asset icon A connector is a socket on a module: a place, a facing, a type and a polarity. Where an orbital is matched by direction, a connector is matched by **identity**, so two connectors can meet at any angle in space as long as their types accept each other and they face each other. Attaching one to another is what produces the next position, which is why the connector model generates structure rather than filling it in. ## What a connector is _Type and polarity decide what may attach. Everything else decides where it lands._ Connector **instances** live on modules. Each carries: | Field | Meaning | | ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `Connector Type` | Which type from the **Connector Set** this is an instance of. All compatibility is decided by type. | | `Polarity` | `Universal`, `Plug` or `Port`. Set per instance, not per type. | | `Local Offset` | Where the socket sits and which way it faces, relative to the module. Used when `Override Offset` is on, otherwise the type's default offset applies. | | `Identifier` | Names this socket uniquely within its module. | **Type and polarity are the working pair.** Together they answer every question generation asks: what may attach here, and what may this attach onto. A whole system can be built without ever thinking about a specific socket by name. `Identifier` is narrow by design. It is the tool for addressing one specific socket when a problem genuinely calls for that, and it is what gives sockets meaningful names on the way out of the pipeline. It takes no part in ordinary matching: growth expands a frontier of connectors carrying type, polarity, transform, priority, spawn capacity and bridge role, with no identifier among them. Keep identifiers unique within a module, reach for them when a problem is specific enough to warrant it, and build everything else out of types and polarity. > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connectors-set-and-instances | SHOWS: The split between a connector set and the connector instances on modules. | ELEMENTS: Left, a connector set drawn as a short list of named types, each with a colour and an icon. Right, three modules, each carrying several sockets drawn at their own positions and facings, colour-matched back to the types on the left. One module carries two sockets of the same type at different places, and one carries the same type as both a plug and a port. | MUST BE CLEAR: Types are shared and few. Instances are per module, many, positioned, and each picks its own polarity. > The set defines a small vocabulary of types. Modules place as many instances of them as they need, in whichever polarity each one needs. ## The connector set _Types live on the set. Instances live on modules._ A **Connector Set** defines the type vocabulary and how those types relate. It is the non-directional counterpart to an **Orbital Set**, and like an orbital set it holds at most **63** entries, bit 63 being reserved. Each type carries a name, a default offset that instances inherit unless they override it, a debug colour and icon, and a list of **default connector constraints** that every instance of the type inherits. Those constraints are where placement variation comes from, and are covered under attachment below. > **Note.** > A connector set carries a `Layer Name`, defaulting to `Main`, which names the attributes it writes. Changing it lets several independent connector systems coexist on one cluster. That is an advanced setup with a narrow set of uses, and everything in this book assumes the default. ## Compatibility is directional _A type's list says what it may attach **onto**. It says nothing about what may attach onto it._ Each type holds a list of types it may attach onto, and that list is one-way. Putting `Pillar` in `Beam`'s list means a beam may grow onto a pillar. It does not mean a pillar may grow onto a beam. Growth reads the **candidate's** list against the type of the open connector it is growing from, so the direction that matters is the direction growth travels. The list belongs to the thing being placed. > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connectors-directional-compatibility | SHOWS: Why a one-way compatibility list is not a mistake. | ELEMENTS: Two types, Beam and Pillar, as two rows of a small table with ticks. Beam's row ticks Pillar. Pillar's row does not tick Beam. Below, two growth attempts: a beam growing onto a placed pillar, marked allowed, and a pillar growing onto a placed beam, marked refused. | MUST BE CLEAR: The same pair of types gives opposite answers depending on which one is being placed. The row belongs to the module being placed, not to the one already there. > The row belongs to the thing being placed, not to the thing already there. That asymmetry is the point. A fallback type, filling whatever is left over, can list every other type so it attaches anywhere, while no regular type lists it in return so nothing ever grows out of it. Only the fallback needs authoring. This is how terminators are built, and it is why module behaviour flags for dead ends do not exist. > **Warning.** > **Joining two things that already exist needs both directions** > > Growth reads one list because one side is being placed and the other is already there. Sometimes neither side is being placed, and two pieces that both already exist are being joined to each other instead. There is no candidate to read then, so both types have to accept each other. > > A one-way pair steers growth perfectly well while being unable to close a joint between two things that are already there. > **Note.** > A newly created type lists **itself**, so its instances attach to each other out of the box. Clear `Self` in its compatibility list to opt out. In the editor, the compatibility column shows the relation from both sides at once, distinguishing "we accept them", "they accept us" and mutual. ## Polarity _A second gate, independent of type, decided per instance._
PolarityIconAttaches to
UniversalAny polarity.
PlugOutward. Connects to Port or Universal.
PortInward. Connects to Plug or Universal.
`Universal` pairs with anything. Otherwise the two polarities must differ, so two plugs never mate and neither do two ports. Because polarity is per instance rather than per type, one type can be a plug on one module and a port on another. That is what lets a single type describe both halves of a joint. It is also the mechanism that stops a module from attaching to a copy of itself when you do not want it to, without needing a second type for the purpose. Polarity is also a first-class part of how a **grammar** describes what it wants. A grammar does not name modules: it asks for a module carrying, say, at least two `Socket` connectors of polarity `Port`, and any module in the ruleset satisfying that signature is a candidate. Type and polarity are the vocabulary that request is written in. ## When two connectors mate _Three tests, all of which must pass, plus a distance check owned by whoever is asking._ 1. **Their types accept each other**, in both directions. 2. **Their polarities are compatible.** 3. **They face each other.** The two forward axes must be roughly antiparallel, within about 60 degrees of exactly opposed. Distance is checked separately by whatever is asking, because "close enough" means something different to a bridge search than to a cage link. > Figure: CLIP | id: connectors-mating-tests | SHOWS: Each of the three tests failing in turn, then all three passing. | BEATS: 1) Two connectors face each other at a good distance. A three-item checklist reads types, polarity, facing. Types is red because one list does not accept the other, and the joint reads as refused. 2) The compatibility list is corrected. Types goes green, polarity goes red because both sockets are plugs, still refused. 3) One socket is switched to port. Polarity goes green, facing goes red as one socket rotates away from the other. 4) The rotated socket swings back. Facing goes green, all three tick, and the two modules snap together. | SOURCE: Connectors sample, two modules with one socket each. | LENGTH: 9s, loops. | NOTE: Keep all three checklist items visible throughout. The point is that any one alone refuses the joint. > Any single failing test refuses the joint, and only the third one is visible in the geometry. > **Warning.** > **Two connectors in the same place do not necessarily meet** > > The facing test is what makes a joint a joint. Two connectors sitting at the same position but pointing the same way never mate, however compatible their types and polarities are. If two pieces refuse to join where they visually touch, check which way their sockets point before suspecting the compatibility table. ## What attaching actually does _The child's socket is mated onto the parent's socket, and the module comes along for the ride._ Attachment is full-frame. The child connector's frame is snapped onto the parent connector's frame, turned 180 degrees so the two forwards oppose and the two ups align. The child module's transform is then whatever places its socket there. > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: connectors-attachment-frame | SHOWS: That the child module is positioned by mating connector frames, and follows wherever that puts it. | ELEMENTS: Left, two modules apart. Each carries one connector drawn as a small axis triad, a forward arrow and an up arrow, clearly labelled. Right, the child has moved so its triad sits exactly on the parent triad, with the two forward arrows drawn opposed and the two up arrows drawn aligned, and the child module body carried into whatever position and orientation that implies. Two small callouts below: one where the parent connector is rolled about its forward axis and the child arrives rolled to match, one where the parent connector is scaled and the child arrives scaled. | MUST BE CLEAR: The child module never chose its own position. The two frames were mated and the module came along, which is why roll and scale authored on the parent transfer to everything grown from it. > The frames mate and the module follows. Roll and scale on the parent are inherited because of it. Two consequences follow, and both surprise people: * **Roll is inherited exactly as authored.** Connectors mate the way you built them, with no incidental spin introduced along the way. If a piece lands rotated oddly about the joint axis, that roll was authored into one of the two sockets. * **Scale flows down the joint.** The child module takes the parent connector's scale, so scaling a parent scales everything grown from it. Deliberate variation is a separate system. **Connector constraints**, authored per type on the set and overridable per instance, shape where a connector's attachment may actually land: arcs, angular ranges, offsets, snapping, probability. Attachment itself is exact, and constraints are what make it interesting. ## How growth treats an instance _Three settings change a socket's behaviour during growth without affecting whether it mates._ | Field | Effect | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `Priority` | Frontier expansion order. Higher is expanded sooner. Defaults to `0`. | | `Spawn Capacity` | How many children this one socket may spawn. `1` is a normal socket. Above `1` it is a multi-spawn point, up to `16`. | | `Bridge Role` | `Can Bridge`, the default, takes part in both normal growth and bridging. `No Bridge` never bridges. `Bridge Only` is skipped during normal expansion entirely and exists only to join branches. | A connector used to attach a module is consumed, and so is the socket it attached to. Everything else on a newly placed module joins the frontier as an open connector. **Bridging** is the case where two things that already exist get joined to each other, closing a loop between separate lines of growth instead of extending one. It is the main place the both-directions rule above bites: a pair of types that only accepts one way will grow happily and never bridge. If two branches refuse to meet where you expect them to, that asymmetry is the first thing to check. Bridging is covered in full under growth. ## Settle the set early _Of the two connection models, this is the one that rewards deciding up front._ An orbital set is largely re-derived on recompile. A connector set accumulates authored structure that only a person can supply: a compatibility decision for every ordered pair of types, and connector instances placed by hand on every module. > **Warning.** > **The cost of changing a set** > > * **Renaming and reordering types is safe.** Compatibility is stored against a stable internal id that survives both, so references do not break. > * **Adding a type is not free.** Every existing type needs a decision about whether it accepts the new one, and the new one needs a decision about each of them. That work grows with the square of the vocabulary, and it is judgement rather than mechanics. > * **Every module already authored** may need instances of the new type placed on it. > > Keep the vocabulary small and decide it early. Six well-chosen types will carry a project further than twenty added one problem at a time.

title: Orbitals
description: Modules declare which directions they can bond along, and the solve matches the edges of your cluster against those directions.
outline: How an edge becomes a bond
An edge outside every orbital's tolerance
What a module asserts on an orbital
One set, for the whole project
Orbital sets tolerate being changed later
body:
> Figure: The Orbital Set asset icon

An orbital is a named direction.

Modules declare which directions they can bond along, and the solve matches the edges of your cluster against those directions. Nothing here is positional, which is why one orbital set serves a grid, a hex field and an irregular graph without change.
## What an orbital is

_A direction, a name, and a bit._

Orbitals live on an **Orbital Set** asset, in an ordered array. Each entry carries:

| Field               | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Direction`         | The direction the orbital points.                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `Display Name`      | The orbital's name. Names are how modules and rules refer to orbitals.                                                                                                                                   |
| `Normalized Length` | Step multiplier on the consumer's cell size, so `1.0` is one full cell. Above `1.0` it also extends this orbital's probe reach by the same factor. Below `1.0` it shortens the step but never the reach. |
| `Reciprocal`        | The orbital facing this one across an aligned edge, so West names East. `None` leaves it unpaired.                                                                                                       |
| `Debug Color`       | Visualization only.                                                                                                                                                                                      |

The bit each orbital occupies in a mask is its **array index**. A set holds at most **63** orbitals, because bit 63 is reserved.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: orbitals-set-and-mask | SHOWS: How an orbital set becomes a per-module mask. | ELEMENTS: Left, an orbital set as a numbered list of named directions, drawn as arrows from a common origin. Right, three different modules, each with a subset of those same arrows lit and the rest greyed. Beneath each module, its mask as a row of bits, lit bits aligning with lit arrows. | MUST BE CLEAR: The arrow layout is identical for all three modules because the set is shared. Only which arrows are lit differs, and that is exactly what the mask records.
> One shared set of directions. A module is defined by which of them it claims.



> **Warning.**
> `Reciprocal` is **directed**. Setting West's reciprocal to East does not set East's reciprocal to West. Pairs that should be mutual have to be authored from both ends.



> Figure: CLIP | id: orbitals-angle-threshold | SHOWS: Why an edge falling outside the threshold stops being a bond. | BEATS: 1) Two nodes, one edge, with the left node's East orbital drawn and its threshold cone visible. 2) The right node swings around the left one. While the edge stays inside the cone it draws solid and the East bit reads as set. 3) The right node passes outside the cone. The edge goes dashed, the East bit clears, and the right node drops out of the left node's neighbour list. 4) Angle Threshold widens. Nothing moves, and the edge goes solid again. | SOURCE: Orbitals sample, flat 4-direction set. | LENGTH: 8s, loops. | NOTE: Keep the bit readout on screen for every beat, it is the point of the clip.
> Nothing moved in the last beat. Only the tolerance changed.


## How an edge becomes a bond

_Every edge is resolved to an orbital on each of its ends, or to nothing at all._

Given an edge between two nodes, Valency takes the direction from one to the other, finds the orbital whose direction best matches it, and checks that the match is close enough. The same happens from the other end, against the reversed direction. Both ends must land on an orbital for the edge to mean anything.

Two settings on the orbital set govern this:

| Setting               | Default        | Effect                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| --------------------- | -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Angle Threshold`     | `22.5` degrees | How far an edge may deviate from an orbital's direction and still match it.                                                                                                                                               |
| `Transform Direction` | On             | Orbital directions are rotated by the vertex's own transform, so a rotated point carries a rotated set of directions. Off, directions are absolute and a point's rotation does not affect which orbital an edge lands on. |


> **Warning.**
> **An edge outside every orbital's tolerance**
>
> An edge whose direction falls outside `Angle Threshold` on either end does not become a bond. The two Vtx stop seeing each other as neighbours, and the solve proceeds as though the edge were not there.
>
> **Valency : Write Orbitals** counts them and warns, naming the number of edge directions that matched no orbital. That warning is on by default, under `Warn On No Match`. A non-zero count is the first thing to check when a solve produces impossible adjacencies, or places modules as though they were isolated.


## What a module asserts on an orbital

_Four statements, two of which read alike and are not._

Per orbital, a module states one of four things:

| Assertion            | Means                                                 |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| **A neighbour list** | Only these modules may sit here.                      |
| **Boundary**         | Nothing may sit here.                                 |
| **Wildcard**         | Something must sit here, and it does not matter what. |
| **Accept any**       | Whatever sits here is acceptable.                     |

**Boundary** is how a module declares which of its sides face outward. A wall piece with a boundary on its back is stating that it belongs against the outside of a structure and must never have anything behind it. It is a positive assertion about emptiness, not an absence of rules: a solve will refuse to place that module anywhere its boundary orbital has a neighbour.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: orbitals-assertions | SHOWS: The four assertions a module can make, on one module. | ELEMENTS: A single module at center with four orbitals drawn outward, each annotated differently. One carries a short list of allowed neighbour thumbnails. One is a boundary, drawn crossed out with empty space beyond it. One is a wildcard, drawn with a question-mark neighbour that is present but unidentified. One is accept-any, drawn with several candidate neighbours stacked and all acceptable. | MUST BE CLEAR: The boundary and the wildcard differ on whether a neighbour exists at all. The wildcard and the accept-any differ on whether one is required. Show presence and absence, not just permission.
> Boundary and wildcard disagree about whether anything is there. Wildcard and accept-any disagree about whether anything has to be.


Wildcard and accept-any are the pair worth separating. **Wildcard is about existence**: it fails if the orbital has no neighbour. **Accept-any is about acceptance**: it says nothing about whether a neighbour is required, only that any of them would do.

The consequence is in the negative case. Where accept-any is _not_ set, the neighbour list is authoritative, and a list that has lost its last entry accepts nothing rather than becoming permissive.

Neighbour lists are also where [Bond and Corner Tags](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/bond-and-corner-tags) land: seam identities authored per orbital, or derived per corner, compile into these same lists and narrow the acceptance to match.

## One set, for the whole project

_Most projects need exactly one orbital set, and one connector set, for everything they ever build._

Every module in a rules asset resolves against the same orbital set, which is what makes their masks comparable. A second set is warranted when the topology genuinely differs, not when a new kind of module appears. Wall pieces, props, roofs and stairs all coexist happily in one topology.


> **Tip.**
> **Orbital sets tolerate being changed later**
>
> A cage does not author orbital identity. Its orbital index and name are read from the set, and what it actually authors is spatial: which neighbours it connects to, and which orbitals are enabled. Connections are detected from the layout. So a set can gain directions, or have them rearranged, and a recompile re-derives every mask from where the cages actually sit.
>
> The exceptions are the places that name an orbital explicitly, such as a connector gated on a named orbital or a filter given raw orbital indices. Renaming or reordering leaves those pointing elsewhere, and they warn at compile rather than failing silently.
>
> Do not generalise this to **Connector Sets**. Those carry a directional compatibility relation between every pair of types, plus connector instances authored individually on each module. They are the asset to settle early.


**How rotated modules are handled without authoring them twice**


An orbital set knows its own rotational symmetries. Valency detects every proper rotation that maps the direction set onto itself, and records the orbital permutation each one induces. A module can then be registered in several rotations without you authoring a variant per rotation: its mask is permuted rather than rebuilt.

`Symmetry Tolerance Degrees` (default `0.5`) governs detection only, absorbing floating-point error. Keep it far tighter than `Angle Threshold`. A loose value invents symmetries that do not exist, and the modules placed through them will be wrong in ways that are hard to trace back here.

For planar sets, a rotation that maps the plane onto itself but reverses its normal is flagged separately. It reads as a mirror and places content upside down, so implicit "all symmetries" selections leave those out. Picking one explicitly still enables it.




> **Note.**
> An orbital set carries an `Identifier`, defaulting to `Main`, which names the attributes it writes. Changing it lets several independent orbital resolutions coexist on one cluster. That is an advanced setup with a narrow set of uses, and everything in this book assumes the default.

title: Patterns
description: Valency finds every occurrence of that arrangement in a result and can then act on it, most usefully by collapsing the whole thing into one larger asset.
outline: What a pattern is made of
Replacing anything requires a pattern built from cages
Biases can take the decision over
body:
> Figure: The Pattern asset icon

A **pattern** is a named arrangement: a handful of positions, what each accepts, and how they connect to one another.

Valency finds every occurrence of that arrangement in a result and can then act on it, most usefully by collapsing the whole thing into one larger asset. Patterns run over a result that already exists, which is what lets them see structure no single placement decision could.
## What a pattern is made of

_Positions, what each accepts, and the connections between them._

| Part                                                     | Is                                                                            |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Entries**                                              | The positions in the arrangement. Entry 0 is the root.                        |
| [Targets](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/targets) | What each entry accepts, written exactly like any other module selection.     |
| **Adjacencies**                                          | Which slot on one entry faces which slot on another. This is the arrangement. |
| **Slot constraints**                                     | Per entry, slots required to have no neighbour, or required to have one.      |

Targets follow the same rules as everywhere else: criteria are combined with AND inside one target, a position offering several targets accepts any of them, and a position with no targets accepts anything.

An entry can also be marked inactive, which makes it **constraint-only**. It has to be there for the pattern to match, and the match does nothing to it. That is how you say "a corner piece, but only where a wall continues past it" without the wall becoming part of what gets replaced.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: patterns-anatomy | SHOWS: A three-position pattern, and the same arrangement located inside a larger result. | ELEMENTS: Left, a small pattern: three entry circles, the root marked, lines between them labelled with the slots they connect, one entry drawn hollow to mark it constraint-only. Right, a much larger solved structure of many modules, with one triplet highlighted where the pattern matches, its constraint-only member outlined rather than filled. | MUST BE CLEAR: The pattern is small and abstract, the result is large and concrete, and the match is a subgraph of the result. The hollow entry participates in the match without being part of what the match acts on.
> The pattern describes a shape. Matching finds every place that shape occurs.


## Matching is about arrangement

_What matters is what connects to what, never where anything sits in space._

A pattern match asks whether these modules are related in this way. Distances, angles and world positions play no part. The same pattern finds its arrangement wherever it occurs, at any scale, anywhere in the result, however the structure around it is oriented.

Because slots are named per connection model, a single pattern can describe orbital adjacencies, connector adjacencies, or a mix of both in one arrangement. Which models a pattern addresses is worked out from the slots its entries actually name rather than declared up front, so a pattern only needs the set references for the models it uses.

### What a match does

_Three outcomes, and the one you probably want is the third._

| Outcome        | Effect                                                                                                                                                           |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Annotate**   | The match is recorded and nothing changes. Every matched point is tagged with the pattern's name and which occurrence it belongs to.                             |
| **Swap**       | Each matched position takes the module authored on its own pattern position. The arrangement keeps its shape, and its pieces are exchanged for specialised ones. |
| **Substitute** | The whole arrangement collapses. The root takes a module standing for the entire arrangement, and every other matched position is consumed.                      |

**Substitute is the headline case.** Solve a pipe network, find every T-junction, and replace each one with a single purpose-built junction mesh. Nine facade modules become one hero piece. Consumed positions place nothing, so the detail asset takes over the space the pieces occupied.

Annotation happens on every match regardless of outcome, so even a pattern that changes nothing leaves behind a record downstream can partition on.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: patterns-outcomes | SHOWS: The same three-module match under each of the three outcomes. | ELEMENTS: One matched triplet repeated in three rows. Row one, annotate: unchanged pieces, each carrying a small tag marker. Row two, swap: same three positions, same shape, each piece visibly replaced by a more detailed version of itself. Row three, substitute: the three positions replaced by one larger asset spanning all of them, with two of the original positions greyed to show they now place nothing. | MUST BE CLEAR: Annotate changes nothing visible, swap preserves the count and changes the pieces, substitute reduces three placements to one.
> Same match, three outcomes. Only substitute changes how many things get placed.



> **Warning.**
> **Replacing anything requires a pattern built from cages**
>
> Swap and Substitute both work by taking the module authored on a pattern position, which means the pattern has to have been built from pattern cages in a level. A pattern authored purely as a graph has no cages behind it, therefore no modules to hand over, and every outcome behaves as Annotate.
>
> That is not a failure and nothing errors: a graph-authored pattern is a perfectly good detector. What it cannot do is replace anything, and setting it to Substitute will not make it try.


### When matches compete

_Several patterns can want the same modules, and by default the first one to claim them keeps them._

Real libraries have overlapping patterns, and one arrangement often satisfies several. Four settings decide what happens:

| Setting          | Does                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Weight**       | Relative likelihood when patterns compete for the same modules.                                                                                                     |
| **Exclusive**    | On by default. A pattern's matched positions are claimed, so nothing else can match them. Turning it off lets other patterns overlap the same modules.              |
| **Match limits** | A minimum and maximum number of times the pattern may match. A relative maximum is a proportion of the candidate matches actually found, rather than a fixed count. |
| `Claim`          | On the node rather than the pattern. Reserves matched positions from later matchers in a chain, so you can run a specialised pass before a general one.             |

The useful shape is a chain: run the specific, high-value patterns first with exclusivity on, then run broader ones over whatever remains.


> **Note.**
> **Biases can take the decision over**
>
> Everything above is authored on the patterns themselves. Matching also accepts **biases**, and connecting them changes the hierarchy rather than adding to it: each candidate match gets a bias score, that score becomes the primary key for resolving overlaps and for deciding which matches survive the maximum, and the settings above drop to breaking ties. Where a position accepts several modules, the bias weighs that draw too.
>
> Worth knowing exists before trying to solve an ordering problem with weights alone. Biases are covered under Systems.


## Rotated arrangements

_One authored pattern can match its own rotations._

An arrangement authored facing one way will not, by default, match the same arrangement rotated. Two settings address that, and they answer different questions.

**Matching rotated variants** clones the pattern once per rotational symmetry the orbital set has, so the whole arrangement is looked for in every orientation the topology allows. The match limits budget the entire rotated family rather than each clone, and the weight is split across it, so turning it on does not quietly multiply how often the pattern fires.

**Variant matching** answers a different question: how each position treats rotated versions of the modules it accepts. Rotation-aware means each position wants the rotation implied by its place in the arrangement. Orientation-agnostic means each position accepts any rotation, so the arrangement matches regardless of how individual pieces within it are turned.

## Rejection and seed patterns

_Recognition is useful on its own, and generation uses it while it runs._

Growth can be handed patterns for two other purposes. **Rejection patterns** describe arrangements that must not be created, and a placement that would complete one is refused. **Seed patterns** describe arrangements growth should start from.

Both use the same authored patterns as replacement does. An arrangement worth detecting after the fact is often an arrangement worth avoiding, or seeking, while the structure is still being built.

title: Selecting Modules
description: Almost nothing in Valency asks for a module by name.
outline: A misspelled tag fails differently in each clause
body:
Almost nothing in Valency asks for a module by name. Rules, patterns and grammars describe the module they want and take whatever matches, which is what lets one grammar drive several kits and one pattern survive a library growing underneath it. Tags are how that description is written.

## Three handles

_Tags describe, names group, assets pin down._

| Handle          | Answers                      | Reach                                             |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| **Module tags** | What kind of thing is this   | Every selection mechanism in the plugin           |
| **Module name** | Which named group is this in | Fixed picks, and targets that name a group        |
| **The asset**   | Which exact content is this  | Pattern targets, and anything matching on content |

Tags carry nearly all of the weight. The others exist for the cases where you need to be specific, and reaching for them first is the usual sign that a description would have worked better.

### Tags

_Authored on the container, propagated to every module it produces._

Module tags are gameplay tags, set on a cage or palette and copied onto every module that container authors. Mirror sources merge theirs in, so a cage borrowing from another inherits its tags along with its assets.

**Valency ships a structural vocabulary, registered natively and appearing in the tag picker as the default set**


| Family          | Describes                              | Examples                                                               |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Topology**    | Where the module sits in the structure | `Endpoint`, `Junction`, `Span`, `Branch`, `Loop`                       |
| **Function**    | What it is for                         | `Standard`, `Filler`, `Bridging`, `Decorative`                         |
| **Phase**       | When during generation it belongs      | `Seed`, `Expansion`, `Closure`                                         |
| **Geometry**    | How it responds to sizing              | `FixedSize`, `Scalable`, and scalable's axis-aligned and uniform kinds |
| **Frequency**   | How often it should show up            | `Common`, `Rare`                                                       |
| **Cardinality** | How many may exist                     | `Singleton`, `Unique`, `Repeatable`                                    |
| **Slot**        | How its connectors should be treated   | `Required`, `Optional`, `Forbidden`                                    |

These are a starting vocabulary rather than a fixed one, and describe structure rather than content on purpose: nothing in the shipped set knows what a wall is. Projects add their own tags under the Valency root, or any root they like, through Project Settings.


> **Note.**
> The shipped tags carry no built-in behaviour. Tagging a module `Topology.Junction` does not make anything treat it as a junction. They are a shared vocabulary so that rules written by one person read the same way to another, and every one of them only does something once a predicate asks for it.




### Predicates

_Three clauses. Each one is unconstrained while it is empty._

A **tag predicate** is how a rule states which modules it means:

| Clause        | Passes a module that               |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `Require All` | carries every one of these tags    |
| `Require Any` | carries at least one of these tags |
| `Exclude`     | carries none of these tags         |
| `Invert`      | flips the final result             |

An empty predicate matches everything, so a rule with nothing filled in constrains nothing. `Invert` is the exception worth noting: inverting an empty predicate turns match-everything into match-nothing, which is a useful way to write "never" and a confusing way to arrive at one by accident.

Tags are hierarchical, and matching honours that. A clause asking for a parent tag matches a module carrying any of its children, so you can select a whole family without listing it.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: selecting-modules-predicate | SHOWS: How the three clauses narrow a library down to a candidate set. | ELEMENTS: Left, a row of eight modules each showing two or three tags. Middle, three stacked clause boxes: Require All, Require Any, Exclude, each with a tag or two in it. Right, the two or three modules that survive. Modules eliminated by each clause are greyed at the point they drop out, so it is visible which clause removed which. | MUST BE CLEAR: The clauses narrow in sequence and every module either survives all three or is named by the one that removed it. An empty clause removes nothing.
> Each clause only ever narrows. An empty one lets everything through.



> **Warning.**
> **A misspelled tag fails differently in each clause**
>
> A tag that no module in the library carries, whether misspelled or never used, is not an error. What it does depends on which clause it sits in:
>
> * In `Require Any`, it matches **nothing**. The clause is asking for a tag that does not exist, and no module can satisfy it.
> * In `Require All` or `Exclude`, it is **trivially satisfied** and changes nothing.
>
> This asymmetry is deliberate. The alternative would be an unknown tag quietly relaxing a constraint to match-everything, which is far harder to notice than a rule that suddenly selects nothing. If a rule stops matching entirely after an edit, check `Require Any` for a typo first.


### Names are a group label

_Several modules can share one, and a name is not a unique key._

A name is not a unique key. Several modules may carry the same one, and a pick that asks for that name chooses among them by weight. That is the intended use: name a group `Doorway`, let five doorway variants share it, and ask for `Doorway` when you need one.

Two consequences follow:

* **Names are authored, with no fallback.** A module whose cage left the name blank is unreachable by anything that selects on names. Nothing derives a name from the actor label.
* **Names are not part of a module's identity.** Two contributions that describe the same module but disagree about its name still merge into one, and the first source's name wins. Valency warns when that happens, because fixed picks and name targets will then resolve against a name you may not have expected.

### Asking by description

_The most useful selections never mention a specific module at all._

A **module descriptor** describes the module a rule wants and lets the library answer. It combines a tag predicate with a **connector signature**: how many connectors of which type and which polarity the module must carry, with optional minimum and maximum counts, and an option requiring that the module carry nothing beyond what was asked for.

A grammar asking for "a module with at least two `Socket` connectors of polarity `Port`, tagged `Function.Standard`" works against any library that can satisfy it. This is why grammars are portable across kits: they never name the modules they place.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: selecting-modules-descriptor | SHOWS: A description resolving to a set of candidate modules rather than to one. | ELEMENTS: Left, a descriptor card listing a tag predicate and a connector signature reading two Port connectors of type Socket. Right, a library of eight modules, three of them highlighted as satisfying the card, each visibly different from the others in shape and content. An arrow from the card fans out to all three. | MUST BE CLEAR: The description resolves to a set, not a winner, and the three that match do not resemble each other. Choosing between them happens later, by weight and bias.
> A description resolves to every module that satisfies it. Picking one of them is a separate step.


Pattern targets work the same way, with a small twist worth knowing: within one target the criteria are combined with AND, while a position offering several targets accepts any of them. An empty target matches anything, so leaving one blank makes that pattern position a wildcard.

title: Generating
description: Generation is where the library gets used.
outline: An older map costs you the newest modules, silently
body:
Generation is where the library gets used. A handful of nodes resolve modules onto points, and everything after that is ordinary PCG.

Valency moves three separate things between nodes, and only one of them is the points. Knowing what the other two are, and that they have to be carried, accounts for most of the plumbing in a Valency graph.

## What actually flows

_Three things travel, and two of them are pins you have to remember._

| Carried as                      | What it is                                     | Why it exists                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **An attribute on every point** | The **entry**, written as `PCGEx/V/Entry/Main` | Says which module this point resolved to. Opaque by design: nothing downstream should read it directly. |
| **A parameter pin**             | The **Valency Map**                            | Says which library those entries belong to, and how to reach it.                                        |
| **A parameter pin**             | The **Collection Map**                         | The PCGEx transport that resolves a point to the asset entry it should spawn.                           |

The entry is a compact value, not a name or a path. On its own it means nothing at all: it only resolves against the Valency Map that produced it. That is the single fact that explains most of the plumbing on this page.

### Each node can emit a new map

_A node that adds modules emits a new map that includes them. Chain that one._

Where a Valency Map is needed the pin is marked required, so it is hard to leave one off by accident. The mistake that does happen is subtler: taking the map from the wrong place.

Many nodes both consume a map and emit one, and the map they emit supersedes the one they were given. **Grow Cluster** emits a map with its grown module entries included. **Find Bridges** emits one with its bridge modules included. Anything that puts new modules into a result also puts them into the map, and the entries on those points only resolve against that newer map.

The rule that follows is short: **take the map from the last node that touched the points.**


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: generating-chain-the-map | SHOWS: That chaining an older map silently loses everything added after it. | ELEMENTS: Two versions of the same three-node chain, a solve into a grow cluster into a staging. Top version, the map line runs solve to grow cluster, then grow cluster to staging, and the staged result shows both the solved pieces and the grown pieces present. Bottom version, the map line runs solve to grow cluster as before, but staging is fed from the solve output instead, drawn as a long line reaching back past the grow node. Its staged result shows the solved pieces present and the grown pieces missing, drawn as empty outlines. | MUST BE CLEAR: Both chains are wired, complete and error-free. The only difference is which node the staging map came from, and it costs exactly the modules added after that point.
> Both graphs run clean. The lower one is missing everything the grow pass added, because staging was handed the solve map.



> **Warning.**
> **An older map costs you the newest modules, silently**
>
> Feeding a downstream node a map from earlier in the chain does not fail. The points still arrive and the older modules still resolve. Only the entries added since that map was made come out as nothing.
>
> The symptom is a partial result: the solved structure appears, the grown pieces do not. When part of a result is missing rather than all of it, the map wiring is the first thing to check.


For reference, which nodes sit on which side:

| Emits a map                                                                                     | Needs one                                                                      |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Solve**, **Grow Points**, **Grow Cluster**, **Find Bridges**, [Write Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/write-orbitals), [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) | **Staging**, **Load Properties**, **Find Patterns**, the Valency point filters |

## The shape of a graph

_Prepare, resolve, refine, stage._

Most Valency graphs are four stages, and only the middle two are Valency-specific.

| Stage       | Does                                                     | Nodes                                                                                             |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Prepare** | Produce the structure a solve will fill, and describe it | **Lattice**, or a cluster you build plus **Write Orbitals**. Then optionally [Planar Partition](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/planar-partition) |
| **Resolve** | Decide which module goes where                           | **Solve**, or **Grow Points** / **Grow Cluster**                                                  |
| **Refine**  | Optional passes over the result                          | **Find Patterns**, **Find Bridges**                                                               |
| **Stage**   | Turn resolved modules into spawnable points              | **Staging**, then ordinary PCG spawning                                                           |

Preparation is where the two connection models differ, and it is the only place they do.

### Solving needs a cluster, and Lattice will make you one

A solve fills positions that already exist, so something has to supply them. There are two routes, and the first is much easier than it looks from the node list.

**Valency : Lattice** takes spatial data and quantizes it onto the orbital lattice, producing an orbital-aligned cluster directly. Give it shapes to trace as spines, closed surfaces to fill, volumes to occupy, or a combination, and it hands back vtx, edges and a Valency Map with the orbital data already written. There is no cluster to author and no **Write Orbitals** pass, because it does that part itself. It needs only an orbital set, and will take one from a Bonding Rules asset if you would rather point at that.

The other route is to build the cluster yourself with ordinary PCGEx nodes and run **Write Orbitals** over it, which works out which orbital each connection lands on. Reach for this when the shape comes from somewhere Lattice cannot produce it.

### Planar Partition describes a structure before it is filled

**Valency : Planar Partition** decomposes a cluster into floors, and within each floor into regions connected through in-plane orbitals. It writes that onto the vtx: which floor each one sits on, which region within that floor, a packed key combining the two, and how many regions above and below each region connects to.

None of that places anything. It exists so that resolution can use it. Feed the region key to **Partitioned Limits** on a solve or on Find Patterns and a spawn cap applies per floor or per room rather than across the whole result, which is the difference between "three of these" and "three of these on every floor". The floor and adjacency values are equally usable to drive biases and filters.

It also emits one point per region on a secondary pin, at the region centroid, which is a convenient handle for anything you want to place once per room.

### Growth brings its own positions

**Valency : Grow Points** takes seed points and produces its own positions, so there is no preparation stage. Seeds in, structure out.

### Grow Cluster is where the two models meet

**Valency : Grow Cluster** is the interop node, and the reason a project rarely has to choose between the models. It takes a cluster whose modules are already resolved, typically from a solve, and runs a growth pass using those placed modules as its roots, growing outward from their open connectors.

That is the concrete form of "a solve can feed a grow". Block out a floor plan by solving it on a lattice, then grow the fixtures, trim and attachments onto the result. The solved structure is extended in place rather than replaced, and newly grown vtx are flagged so downstream nodes can tell them apart.

## Reading the result back

_Everything you authored is available, and none of it comes out automatically._

A staged point carries what it needs to spawn, but the properties and connector data you authored are fetched deliberately:

| Node                           | Gives you                                                                       |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Valency : Load Properties**  | The typed properties authored on the cage, as attributes                        |
| **Valency : Write Connectors** | Connector positions and orientations as points, for attaching things to sockets |
| **Valency : Write Orbitals**   | Orbital data on an existing cluster                                             |

After staging, the result is ordinary point data. Filter it, partition it, sample it, or hand it to something that has never heard of Valency. There is no Valency-specific spawning step.

title: Finding Patterns
description: Because it reads a finished result rather than driving placement, it works on anything that produced modules: a solve, a growth, a grammar, or a mixture.
body:
**Valency : Find Patterns** looks through a result for arrangements you authored, and does something to each occurrence it finds. It is the only node that consumes [Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/patterns), and the whole reason for authoring one.

Because it reads a finished result rather than driving placement, it works on anything that produced modules: a solve, a growth, a grammar, or a mixture.

## What a match can do

*Four outcomes, decided by the pattern rather than by this node.*

| Outcome | The matched points |
|---|---|
| **Consumed** | Place nothing. A larger asset placed at the root represents them. |
| **Substituted** | Carry the pattern root's whole-arrangement module |
| **Swapped** | Carry the module authored on their own pattern cage |
| **Annotated** | Are tagged for downstream use and otherwise unchanged |

**Substituted** is the headline case, and the one that makes patterns worth having: nine facade modules become one hero piece, a T-junction of pipes becomes a purpose-built junction mesh. The positions the replacement covers are consumed so nothing spawns twice.

**Annotated** changes nothing about what is placed. It is how a pattern becomes a query, marking every stairwell or every corner so that something later can act on them.

## Narrowing what is looked for

*Two filters on the patterns, one on the positions.*

`Pattern Names` restricts matching to named patterns, and `Tag Predicate` restricts it by the tags on each pattern's root cage. Leave both empty and every pattern the library carries is looked for.

Positions are gated separately, by vertex filters on their own pin, and `Vtx Filter Mode` decides what the gate means.

| Mode | A filtered-out vertex |
|---|---|
| **Exclude From Matches** | Cannot take part at all, as root or as member. The default. |
| **Exclude As Root** | Cannot start a match, but can still be claimed as a member |

The second is the subtler and often the one wanted. "Do not start a stairwell here, but this position may be part of one" is a different rule from "this position is off limits".

## Overlapping matches

*Claiming is what stops two patterns fighting over the same positions.*

Two patterns can both match at overlapping positions, and only one of them can have them. `Claim` decides whether a match reserves the positions it took.

Left on, which is the default, a matched position is reserved and later matchers in the chain cannot use it. Turned off, every valid match is emitted with nothing reserved, which is what you want when matching is being used to *find* things rather than to replace them.

That makes chained Find Patterns nodes ordered: the first has first refusal, and later ones work on what is left.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: patterns-claim-contention | SHOWS: That claiming is what decides whether two patterns competing for the same positions can both win. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same solved result, a grid of resolved positions, with two candidate matches outlined over it in different colours: a three-position L-shaped match and a three-position straight match, sharing one position where they cross. Left panel headed Claim on: the first match drawn solid and its three positions marked as taken, the second match drawn dimmed and struck with its shared position marked as already claimed. Right panel headed Claim off: both matches drawn solid, the shared position shown as belonging to both, and both listed as emitted. | MUST BE CLEAR: The two candidate matches are identical in both panels. Claiming decides only whether the second one survives, which is what makes a chain of matchers ordered rather than simultaneous.
> Same two candidates. Claiming is what makes the first matcher win the contested position and the second lose it.


## Steering which matches survive

*Biases turn match selection into a weighted decision.*

Connect [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases) and the bias score of each candidate match becomes the **primary selection key**. It orders overlap resolution, decides which matches survive a cap, and weighs the placement draw where a matched position could take several modules.

That is a lot of leverage for one pin. It is how "prefer the hero piece near the entrance" is expressed without hand-placing anything, and it is the reason the same bias assets serve both guidance and pattern matching.

## Limits, per region

*The same partitioned-limits machinery, with one extra decision.*

Match counts respect [Spawn Limits](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spawn-limits), and those limits can be partitioned by [Planar Partition](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/planar-partition) so a cap means "per building" rather than "per result".

A pattern covers several positions, so a multi-node match has to be assigned to one partition. `Partition Mode` decides how.

| Mode | A match |
|---|---|
| **Root Key** | Belongs to its root's partition, and may straddle a boundary |
| **Require Uniform** | Is rejected unless every one of its active nodes shares a partition |

**Require Uniform** is the stricter reading and the one for arrangements that should never span two regions. **Root Key** allows a pattern to bridge, which for something like a staircase between floors is exactly right.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: patterns-partition-straddle | SHOWS: What the two partition modes do with one match whose positions fall in two different regions. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same structure of two stacked floors, each floor tinted its own colour as its own partition, with a three-position staircase match outlined across them: its root position and one member on the lower floor, one member on the upper. A small counter beside each partition shows how many matches it has been charged. Left panel headed Root Key: the match drawn accepted, an arrow from it to the LOWER partition counter which increments, and the upper counter unchanged. Right panel headed Require Uniform: the same match drawn refused, dimmed and struck, and neither counter incrementing. | MUST BE CLEAR: The match is identical in both panels. Root Key allows the straddle and charges it to the root position's partition alone; Require Uniform refuses it for straddling at all.
> One match across two floors. Root Key allows it and bills the root's region; Require Uniform refuses it outright.


## What comes out

*The main output is never thinned.*

The cluster passes through with matched points carrying whatever their outcome gave them. Nothing is removed, so the result stays the same shape as the input.

A secondary **Matched** pin is purely additive, and `Matched Output` chooses its shape.

| Shape | Emits |
|---|---|
| **Matched Points** | One point per active matched vertex, deduplicated across overlapping matches. The default. |
| **Match Roots** | One point per match, at the pattern root, bounded to that match's active points |
| **Off** | Nothing, and the pin is not emitted |

**Match Roots** is the one to reach for when something should happen once per occurrence rather than once per position: labelling, scattering, or driving a second pass.


> **Note.**
> The bonding rules and orbital set come from the **Valency Map** described in [Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating), so there is nothing to pick on the node. A **Pattern Matcher** is required though, and the node errors without one.

title: Grammar
description: A grammar replaces that decision with an authored one.
outline: A grammar is a growth strategy
Asking for a module without naming one
A descriptor that resolves to nothing places nothing
Two different things are called scope
Values can come from the points
body:
> Figure: The Structural Grammar asset icon A growth strategy makes one decision, over and over: which open connector to expand next. That single decision produces the entire silhouette, which is why swapping BFS for DFS changes a result more than any amount of rule tuning. A **Structural Grammar** replaces that decision with an authored one. ## A grammar is a growth strategy _It occupies the same slot as the other three, and takes it over._ **Grammar Growth** is an option on a growth node's `Growth Strategy`, alongside **BFS Growth**, **DFS Growth** and **Random Growth**. Choosing it replaces them. A grammar and a strategy never run together. Everything around that choice is unchanged. Same [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules), same seed points, same budgets, same placement conditions, same bridges. A grammar decides which connector is expanded and what goes on it, and the budget that eventually stops the run is the growth node's as before. Legality is the one place a grammar reaches further than a strategy does. The module's own placement conditions still run on every candidate, and a grammar rule can add a spatial test of its own on top of them, so a placement can be refused by something no module authored. See [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules). > One setting disappears. **Seed Patterns** are hidden on **Grammar Growth**, because a grammar already describes the arrangement a run starts with. **Rejection Patterns** are unaffected and still forbid what they forbid. ## What it buys _Strategies shape a silhouette. Grammars express a sequence._ | A strategy can express | A grammar can also express | | ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Expand evenly, or deeply, or randomly | Place this, then that, then repeat the pair three to five times | | Prefer these modules everywhere, by weight | Prefer these modules **here**, and different ones after the third one lands | | Stop after so many modules | Stop this part after so many, then start a different part | | Nothing about relationships between placements | Never put these two next to each other. Require a stairwell before a second floor. | | Nothing about where growth is heading | Grow toward that connector over there and join onto it | | The same numbers at every seed point | Numbers read from each seed point, so one grammar grows five storeys here and two there | > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-vs-strategy | SHOWS: The same library producing an arbitrary shape under a strategy and a deliberate one under a grammar. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Same seed marker and same small set of module outlines with inside corners in both. Left panel headed DFS Growth: one long wandering run of modules, module kinds interleaved with no discernible pattern, drawn plainly. Right panel headed Grammar Growth: the same module count arranged as a readable structure, a repeated two-module unit occurring three times along a spine and terminating in a distinct end piece. Above the right panel, a small strip of the grammar that produced it: four linked node boxes labelled Seed, Sequence, Repeat, Module, drawn in the grammar node style rather than as generic boxes. | MUST BE CLEAR: The library and the module count are identical. What differs is that the right-hand result has structure a reader can name, and the strip above shows the structure was authored rather than emergent. > Same library, same budget. The strategy produces a silhouette; the grammar produces an arrangement you can name. The cost is authoring. A grammar is a graph someone has to build and maintain, and for a result whose shape is the whole requirement, a strategy and some weights get there sooner. Reach for a grammar when the **order** matters, when parts of the structure need different rules, or when placements need to know about each other. ## Asking for a module without naming one _A placement node describes what it wants, and the library answers._ Placement nodes carry a **module descriptor** rather than a module. A descriptor combines three optional narrowings: | Narrowing | Matches on | | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Connector Requirements** | Connector type, polarity, and a count range. "At least two `Corridor` sockets." | | **Tag Predicate** | Module tags, through the usual require-all, require-any and exclude clauses | | **Module Names** | An explicit name list, when nothing else will do | Leave all three empty and the descriptor matches anything. Set `Exact Match` and the module may carry no connectors beyond what the requirements name. This is what keeps a grammar portable. The same graph drives a sci-fi kit and a medieval one, as long as both libraries tag and socket their pieces consistently, because nothing in the grammar names a module the library has to contain. > **Warning.** > **A descriptor that resolves to nothing places nothing** > > A descriptor is resolved against the library once per run. If it matches no module, that placement node has no candidates and the subtree hanging off it never runs, which reads exactly like a broken wire. > > `Allow Placeholders` on the strategy substitutes a synthetic stand-in so structural expansion continues and the shape of the run is still visible. Off by default, and worth turning on the first time a grammar produces less than expected. ## Execution starts at a Seed _The only entry point, and there can be more than one._ A grammar runs from **Seed** nodes and nowhere else. Nothing is inferred from connectivity, an unreachable node never runs, and a grammar with no Seed node fails to compile rather than doing nothing quietly. A Seed node adopts a seed module that growth already placed, matching its own descriptor, and grows its subtree from there. Several Seed nodes in one grammar are normal: each seed point is assigned one, either by a weighted draw or by a per-point name override, so one graph can carry the recipes for a tower, a bridge and a courtyard and let the input points choose. When there is more than one assignment, `Execution Mode` decides how they run. | Mode | Runs | Use when | | -------------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Parallel** | Every assignment in one pass | Structures should interact: **Merge** and **Join** work across seeds, and anything after a Merge runs once | | **Sequential** | One assignment at a time | Structures are independent, or should be built in order. Spatial data and the frontier can still be shared across runs by two toggles. | ## What each step sees _The single idea that makes a grammar behave, or not._ Every wire in a grammar carries an **edge scope**: which open connectors the node at the far end is allowed to work with. It is set per wire, not per node, so the same node reached by two different wires can see two different things.
Edge scopeIconThe consumer sees
InheritedWhatever the upstream node left available. The default for most wires.
