ProducedThe connectors of everything the upstream node just produced: every placement of a Growth pass, the module a Join spanned with, the sockets a Prune freed, the connectors a Filter passed
FrontierEverything still open anywhere in the run
A wire left alone does not resolve to one fixed value. It takes the default of the node it leaves, settled at compile time, so the same untouched wire means different things depending on where it starts. | A wire leaving | Defaults to | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | **Module**, **Growth**, **Fill**, **Prune**, **Seek**, **Route** | **Produced** | | **Sequence** | **Frontier**, so each step sees everything still open | | A continuation output, on any node | **Frontier** | | Everything else | **Inherited** | **Inherited** and **Produced** are the same answer on a node that publishes without placing anything. What a **Filter** produces is the connectors that survived it, what a **Merge** produces is the union it fired with, and what an **Unstash** produces is the part of its bank still open, so an untouched wire and a **Produced** wire leaving one of them carry the same set. A publisher that ended up with nothing passes nothing on. A Filter that dropped every connector, or a union whose connectors have all been built on since, hands its children an exhausted scope, and the section below stops rather than spreading across the whole structure. ### Chaining narrows. A Sequence step resets. _Produced compounds, and that is the most useful thing to know about wiring a grammar._ Wire one placement node into another and the second sees only what the first produced. Add a third and it sees only what the second produced. A chain is a **narrowing pipeline**: at every link the view shrinks to whatever the node before it just made. That is what makes chains worth having. It is how a grammar says "and now, on the piece you have just placed, do this", without naming the piece or tracking it by hand. A **Sequence** does the opposite. Its steps default to **Frontier**, so each one starts from everything still open, whatever the step before it built. | You want the next node to | Wire it as | | ------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | Continue from what the previous node built | A chain. The defaults already do this. | | Act on the whole structure built so far | A step of a **Sequence**, or set the wire to **Frontier** by hand | > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-scope-compounding | SHOWS: That a chain of placement nodes narrows what each successive node can see, while a Sequence step restores the whole frontier. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both produce the identical structure below them, a hub with several chains grown from it, some ending in dead ends and some not. Panel one headed Chained: a grammar strip of four boxes wired in a line, Growth then Module then Growth then Prune, and under each box the set of open sockets that box can see, drawn on a small copy of the structure, shrinking left to right until the last copy highlights only the two sockets the second Growth just made. Panel two headed Sequence: a Sequence box with two steps, the first step holding the same Growth-Module-Growth chain and the second holding the Prune, and under the Prune a copy of the structure with every open socket in the whole thing highlighted. | MUST BE CLEAR: The structure is identical in both panels. What differs is how much of it the final Prune can see, and the chain narrows to a keyhole purely by passing Produced along three times. > Same structure, same nodes. Three Produced wires in a row leave the last node looking through a keyhole. The nodes this catches are the ones that reason about the structure rather than extend it. A **Prune** chained onto a Growth considers only the placements that Growth just made, so dead ends anywhere else are invisible to it. As a Sequence step it sees all of them. Neither behaviour is wrong: the chain is answering a narrower question than it appears to be asking. > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-edge-scope | SHOWS: How the three edge scopes select different open connectors from the same moment in a run. | ELEMENTS: One shared structure drawn three times in a row, identical in each: a seed module with a short chain grown from it, three modules deep, plus a second older chain elsewhere that is not part of the recent work. Open connectors are drawn as small sockets throughout. In each copy a different subset is highlighted and the rest dimmed. First, headed Inherited: the connectors the upstream step was working with, a mid-chain slice. Second, headed Produced: only the sockets on the last modules placed, at the growing end. Third, headed Frontier: every open socket in the whole picture including the older unrelated chain. | MUST BE CLEAR: Nothing about the structure changes between the three. Only which sockets the next node is allowed to touch changes, and Frontier is the only one that reaches the older chain. > One moment in a run, three answers to what happens next. The structure is identical in all three. The failure this prevents is a common one. A chain that stops producing after its first step is usually a wire passing **Inherited** where the author meant **Produced**: the downstream node is looking at connectors that have already been used rather than at what its parent just built. > **Danger.** > **Two different things are called scope** > > **Edge scope**, above, selects open connectors and lives on a wire. > > **Placement scope**, on a rule, selects already-placed modules: the owning module, the ancestor chain, the current region, the same branch, the same seed, or everything placed so far. It answers questions like "how many of these are already here", never "where may I build next". > > The editor labels both of them scope. They are separate axes and neither substitutes for the other. ## Rules reshape and refuse _Biases prefer. Constraints forbid. Regions decide where either applies._ A **rule** is either a **bias**, which reweights candidates, or a **constraint**, which rejects them. Fourteen biases and nine constraints ship, covering tags, connector types and identifiers, depth, distance, quotas, cooldowns, affinity, field alignment, target proximity, position against a spatial channel, and hard conditions on counts, uniqueness, dependency, pairings and facts. Rules attach in two places. Inline on a single node, applying to that node alone, or on a **Begin Region**, applying to everything downstream until the matching **End Region**. A region left unclosed runs to the end of the grammar, which is intended rather than an error. > Where regions nest, each one declares how it combines with what it inherited, separately for biases and for constraints: stack them, replace them, or mute inherited rules by name. A constraint that fails does not merely skip a candidate. Its **severity** decides the consequence, from warning and continuing, through retrying the module, undoing back to the last **Branch** or **Choice**, or restarting the run with a different draw. That is what makes a grammar able to express requirements it cannot satisfy greedily, and it is also the setting that turns a slow grammar into a very slow one. ## Values can come from the points _A number typed on a node is the default. The seed points can supply it instead._ Almost every number and switch on a grammar node or rule, a Growth's `Growth Max`, a Repeat's bounds, an Optional's `Probability`, a bias's `Influence`, is the same Constant or Attribute row PCGEx nodes use for their own inputs. Set to **Attribute**, it reads from the seed point data: a `@Data` attribute gives one value per input, and a point attribute or property gives one value per seed point, followed by everything grown from that seed. That is what lets one grammar build differently per seed with no second asset. A height attribute on the seed points becomes the number of storeys, and a density attribute becomes an Optional's odds. A missing attribute falls back to the typed value and warns on the growth node. Which seed a value follows, and what is corrected as it is read, is on [Data Bindings](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/data-bindings). ## Overriding properties per node _One schema on the asset, values per placing node, read back at the far end._ Modules carry [Module Properties](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-properties) authored on their cages, and every placement of a module comes out with the same values. A grammar can vary them by placement site. The asset declares `Grammar Properties`, a property schema of its own (inline declarations plus imported schema assets, the same machinery module properties use), and every module-placing node, **Module**, **Seed**, **Growth**, **Fill**, **Seek**, **Route** and **Join**, carries a `Property Overrides` block authored against it. The block lists what the schema declares; a row does nothing until enabled, and an enabled row applies to every placement that node makes. That is what makes placements distinguishable by their place in the recipe. Two Module nodes drawing on the same pool can stamp different values on what they place, so a downstream stage can treat the pieces the entrance placed differently from the pieces the towers did, with nothing extra authored on any module. To be resolvable later, grammar growth records which node placed each point: an opaque attribute at `PCGEx/V/Grammar/{Suffix}` travels alongside the entry, and a seed point adopted by a **Seed** node records that Seed node. [Reading Properties](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/reading-properties) is the consumer, resolving each property from the placing node's override first, then the module, then the defaults. The resolution order and its one trap live on that page. In the graph editor a node with enabled overrides shows a coral count badge above it, next to the teal count that inline rules show. **Seed** renders as a pill and shows neither badge, so overrides on a Seed are in force without being visible on the canvas.

title: Backtracking
description: A grammar can express requirements it cannot satisfy by building greedily.
outline: The symptom is a constraint that appears to be ignored
body:
A grammar can express requirements it cannot satisfy by building greedily. **Backtracking** is what makes those requirements enforceable: when something fails, the run takes placements back and tries a different way.

It is also the setting most able to turn a slow grammar into a very slow one, so it is worth knowing what actually rolls back and where the mechanism stops working.

## Three constructs that undo themselves

*Before any backtracking setting is involved.*

Before any backtracking setting is involved, three constructs already restore what they touched:

| Construct | On failure |
|---|---|
| A **Choice** option | Rolled back before the next option is tried |
| A **Repeat** iteration | Rolled back, and the loop stops |
| An **Optional** body | Rolled back, and the node still reports success |

None of them can leave half-built work in the result, which is what makes a Choice cheap to author with risky options in it. That is a different mechanism from what follows: those are local rollbacks a node performs on itself, not a failure propagating outward.

## Three scopes

*How far back a failure reaches.*

When a constraint fails, its `Severity` names one of these, or **Skip**, which warns and changes nothing. A constraint answering on the **Placement** channel is the exception: a refusal there moves to the next pose with nothing committed, so it never reaches severity at all. See [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules).

| Scope | Undoes |
|---|---|
| **Local** | The offending placement, so the node retries with a different candidate |
| **Branch** | Back to the nearest **Branch** or **Choice**, so a different path is taken |
| **Global** | The entire attempt, restarted with a different draw |

`Backtrack Scope` and `Max Backtrack Depth` on the **Grammar Growth** strategy bound the whole run. Setting the depth to `0` turns backtracking off, and a failure then behaves as **Skip**.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-backtrack-scopes | SHOWS: How much of a run each backtrack scope discards. | ELEMENTS: One placement tree drawn three times in a row, identical in each: a seed at the base, a fork partway up into two paths, and a failure marked with a cross on a placement near the tip of the right-hand path. In each copy a different set of placements is drawn struck through and dimmed to show what is undone. First, headed Local: only the failing placement itself. Second, headed Branch: the failing placement and everything back to the fork on that path, with the fork itself and the other path untouched. Third, headed Global: every placement in the tree including the other path, with the seed alone remaining. | MUST BE CLEAR: The same single failure discards three wildly different amounts of work. The left-hand path is untouched under Branch and destroyed under Global, and nothing about the failure itself changed.
> One failure, three answers. The cost difference between them is the whole reason the scope is a setting.


## Where backtracking gives up

*Inside work the grammar deferred, a hard failure becomes a warning.*

A grammar does not evaluate everything in the order it is drawn. Structural nodes queue their children and a drain works through them breadth-first, which is what makes growth expand evenly rather than diving down the first path.

Backtracking to **Local** or **Branch** works by unwinding the call stack to a checkpoint: a placement node's retry loop, or a Branch or Choice snapshot. **A subtree reached through the queue has no such checkpoint above it.** Nothing is on the stack to unwind to.

When a hard failure fires there, it cannot be honoured, and it is downgraded to **Skip**: the failure is reported, the placement does not happen, and the run continues.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-backtrack-checkpoints | SHOWS: Why the same constraint is enforceable in one place and downgraded in another. | ELEMENTS: One annotated scene, not panels. A grammar strip drawn in the grammar node style, running downward: a Choice box near the top with two arms, and below the left arm a Module box, and below that a further chain of three boxes. Two kinds of connection are drawn between them and keyed: a direct-call link from the Choice down through the Module, and a queued link from the Module onward to the chain below it, drawn distinctly. A small marker labelled checkpoint sits on the Choice box and on the Module box, and no marker sits on any box in the queued chain. A failure is marked with a cross on a box in the queued chain, and an arrow from it runs upward and stops dead where the queued link begins, annotated as nothing to unwind to. A second failure marked on the Module box has its arrow reaching the Choice checkpoint cleanly. | MUST BE CLEAR: The two failures are identical. What differs is whether a checkpoint sits between the failure and the top, and the queued link is where the chain of checkpoints ends.
> The same failure, two positions. Backtracking climbs to a checkpoint, and a queued subtree has none above it.



> **Warning.**
> **The symptom is a constraint that appears to be ignored**
>
> The run reports it, naming the scope that was requested and the node it fired under, and records it among the run's diagnostics. Read the log before concluding the constraint is wrong.
>
> Two things make it enforceable again. **Backtrack Global** is unaffected, because a global retry needs no checkpoint. And a constraint placed where it is evaluated inside a Choice, a Repeat or a placement node's own loop has a checkpoint above it by construction.


## Global retry

*The whole attempt, discarded and re-rolled.*

A **Backtrack Global** failure abandons everything: placements, frontier, footprints and spawn tallies are all rewound to the state before the grammar ran, and the run starts again with a different random seed. Every seed's draw stream is re-rolled with it, so a retry is a genuinely different result rather than the same one with a patch.

Retries are capped at **three**, which is fixed rather than a setting. After that the run keeps whatever the last attempt produced.

One case escalates into this on its own. A region left unclosed, as [Regions and Rules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/regions-and-rules) explains, has no **End Region** to validate it, so its exit constraints are checked in a sweep at the end of the attempt. By then there is no local or branch context left to unwind to, so a failure there requests a global retry whatever severity it declared.

## Placeholders

*A diagnostic, and the fastest way to see what a grammar meant to build.*

When a module descriptor, defined back in [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar), resolves to nothing, the placement node has no candidates, places nothing, and takes its entire subtree with it. On a grammar of any size that is hard to read backwards from the result.

`Allow Placeholders` on the strategy substitutes a synthetic stand-in for an unresolvable descriptor so structural expansion continues. The output is not usable content, and that is not what it is for: it shows the shape the grammar would have produced, which locates the descriptor that failed to resolve much faster than reasoning about a missing subtree.

Turn it on when a grammar produces less than expected, and off again once the library and the descriptors agree.

title: Branching
description: Three node types shape control flow across a grammar, and their names are the least reliable in the plugin.
outline: Choice picks one, and keeps a fallback
body:
Three node types shape control flow across a grammar, and their names are the least reliable in the plugin. **Branch** does not branch in the sense of picking a path. **Choice** does. **Merge** is a barrier before it is a union.

## Branch runs every arm

*It fans out, and deals the connectors out between the arms.*

A **Branch** evaluates all of its arms, from the same parent, in one step. Nothing is selected and nothing is skipped.

What makes the arms different from each other is the frontier. Branch takes the open connectors its own input gave it and deals them across the arms round-robin, so the first arm gets the first connector, the second arm the second, and so on, wrapping until they are gone. Each arm then works on its own slice and cannot touch its siblings'.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-branch-round-robin | SHOWS: That a Branch runs every arm and splits the available connectors between them rather than choosing one path. | ELEMENTS: Top, a small grammar strip in the grammar node style: one Module box wired into a Branch box, which fans out to three arm boxes labelled A, B and C. Below it, the structure: one placed module with six open sockets, each socket numbered 1 to 6. Lines run from each socket to the arm that received it, colour-coded per arm, showing sockets 1 and 4 going to A, 2 and 5 to B, 3 and 6 to C. Beside each arm, the resulting pieces it placed, in that arm colour. | MUST BE CLEAR: All three arms ran. The sockets were dealt out one at a time in rotation, not split into contiguous thirds, and no arm can reach a socket that went to another arm.
> Every arm runs. The sockets are dealt out in rotation, and an arm only ever works on the ones it was given.


The upshot is that a Branch is how you say "grow three different things from this piece, one per side" rather than "pick one of three things to grow". For the second, use a Choice.

### More arms than connectors

The deal runs dry when a Branch has more arms than it was given connectors. Wire a piece with two spare sockets into a three-arm Branch, and the third arm is dealt nothing.

`Surplus Arm Scope` settles what that arm gets. It is the edge scope question from [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar), which open connectors a node may work with, asked about the arms the deal never reached.

| Value | The surplus arm sees |
|---|---|
| **Nothing** | An exhausted scope. The arm places nothing. The default. |
| **Parent's Scope** | Everything the Branch itself was given, competing for whatever the earlier arms left. Arms run in order and consume as they go, so there is usually nothing left by the time a surplus arm runs, and something left when an earlier arm placed nothing or when a socket accepts more than one piece. |
| **Full Frontier** | Every open connector in the run. The arm can build anywhere in the structure. |

The setting applies only when the Branch's own input was scoped. A Branch reached by a wire carrying the whole frontier has no slice to run out of, so every one of its arms sees the whole frontier however many arms there are.


> **Warning.**
> **An arm dealt nothing**
>
> A **Module** passes **Produced** on an untouched wire, so a Branch below one is scoped to that module's open sockets, and three arms under a piece with two spare sockets leaves the third arm with nothing to build on.
>
> A Module in that position warns once, to the output log and onto the PCG node, and names the exhausted scope rather than blaming its descriptor. Count the sockets before counting the arms. If the arms were never meant to divide one piece's sockets between them, set the wire into the Branch to **Frontier**, which leaves every arm working on everything still open.


## Choice picks one, and keeps a fallback

*A weighted draw that produces an order, not a single answer.*

A **Choice** carries a weight per option and picks between them randomly. What it does with the result is more forgiving than the name suggests: the weighted draw produces an **order**, and Choice works down that order until an option succeeds.

The first option that succeeds wins and the rest are never tried. An option that fails is rolled back before the next is attempted, so nothing it placed and no rule state it touched survives into the next attempt. A Choice therefore does not dead-end because the draw happened to land on an option that could not run.

Weights decide which option is most likely to be attempted first. They do not decide which one runs, because that is settled by which one can.

## The continuation output

*Both nodes have one, and it fires after everything else.*

**Branch** and **Choice** each expose a continuation output alongside their arms. It is excluded from the arm count and from the weighted draw, and it fires last: for a Branch after every arm has finished draining, for a Choice after the option loop ends.

That is where "once all of that is done, carry on" goes. Wiring the follow-up onto an arm instead makes it one of the alternatives, which for a Choice means it runs only when the draw reaches it.

The continuation fires whether or not the arms succeeded. On a Choice, that includes the case where every option failed.

A continuation wire also defaults differently from an arm. Left alone it resolves to **Frontier**, so the follow-up sees everything still open rather than inheriting whichever slice the last arm was working on.

## Merge waits

*The union is the simple half. The waiting is what the name leaves out.*

A **Merge** collects the frontier slices arriving from every path wired into it, and dispatches its own output **once**, after every one of those paths has finished. Until then, nothing downstream of the Merge runs at all.

That barrier is the reason to use one. It is how a grammar expresses "build the east wing and the west wing, then put the roof on once both are standing", which no amount of sequencing can express when the two wings are separate paths of arbitrary length.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-merge-barrier | SHOWS: That a Merge holds its downstream until every incoming path has finished, then fires once. | ELEMENTS: A horizontal time axis running left to right, labelled as run progress rather than seconds. Three lanes stacked vertically, one per incoming path, each drawn as a bar that starts at the left and ends at a different point: the top path finishes early, the middle path later, the bottom path last. A vertical line drops from the end of the LAST bar down to a single Merge box, and one arrow leaves that box to a downstream box. The two paths that finished earlier are drawn with a flat waiting segment extending to the same vertical line. | MUST BE CLEAR: The downstream fires once, at the moment the slowest path finishes, not once per incoming path and not when the first one arrives.
> Downstream fires once, when the last path finishes. The earlier arrivals wait.


Two details worth knowing. The union removes duplicates, so a connector reached by two different paths is contributed once. And the region rules in force are captured from the **first** path to arrive, on the assumption that every path into one Merge came from the same enclosing region. The same first-arrival rule decides which seed point's values apply after the Merge when a grammar reads its numbers from the seed points and the paths came from several seeds.

A wire leaving a Merge carries that union whichever scope it is set to, because the union is both what the Merge was left holding and what it produced. A union whose connectors have all been built on by the time it fires carries nothing onward.

A Merge reconvenes paths that are wired together, and fires once. Connectors that some later, unconnected section should build on instead are a [Stashing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/stashing) job.

## Rule state across a fork

*Every rule declares what happens to its counters when the flow splits.*

Biases and constraints that keep state (pity counters, quotas, running tallies) have to answer a question the moment a Branch or a Choice forks: does each arm get its own copy, or do they all feed one pool.

Every rule carries `Branch State Policy` for exactly this.

| Policy | Arms | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| **Shared** | Contribute to one pool. The default. | "No more than three of these in the whole structure", counted across everything the fork produced |
| **Forked** | Each gets an independent copy | "No more than three of these per wing", counted separately down each arm |

Forked needs the rule's state to be copyable. A rule whose state cannot be cloned falls back to Shared and warns rather than silently keeping a shared counter under a Forked label.

title: Data Bindings
description: A grammar asset is one recipe, and every building it grows follows it with the same numbers.
outline: The row is the one PCGEx uses everywhere
A bound value is checked where it is read, and some are corrected
body:
A grammar asset is one recipe, and every building it grows follows it with the same numbers. Almost every number and switch on a grammar node or rule can instead be read from the seed points, so the same asset grows five storeys from one point and two from the next, with nothing authored twice.

## The row is the one PCGEx uses everywhere

_A constant by default. Set it to Attribute and it reads from the data._

Each bindable field is the input shorthand PCGEx nodes use for their own inputs: a typed value, an `Input` switch between **Constant** and **Attribute**, and an attribute selector that only matters in the second case. Left on **Constant** the field is the value typed on it and nothing about the grammar changes.

Set to **Attribute**, the selector decides which of two things it reads.



| Selector                                                 | Reads                                  | Resolves to                                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| A `@Data` attribute                                      | The data domain of the seed point data | One value per input dataset, applied to everything grown from that input |
| An element attribute or property, `Height` or `$Scale.Z` | The seed point itself                  | One value per seed point, applied to everything grown from that point    |

A selector is one or the other, so a single field has one source. Both are read from the seed points fed to **Valency : Grow Points** or **Valency : Grow Cluster**, the same data the growth node already takes its seeds from, and nothing else is consulted.

### What can be bound

A plain number or a plain switch on a node or a rule can be bound. A choice between named options, a name, or a descriptor cannot.

| On                                                                                                                                     | Bindable                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Repeat**                                                                   | `Repeat Min`, `Repeat Max`                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Optional**                                                               | `Probability`                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Growth**, **Fill** | `Max Growth Depth`, `Max Placements`, `Growth Min`, `Growth Max`, `Fill Max Modules`, `Partial Counts As Success`                                                                              |
| **Seek**, **Route**   | Every distance, tolerance, budget and switch on the node, and the shared corridor settings: `Exclude Own Branch`, `Reach Is Success`, `Min Target Hops`, `Keep Partial`, `Bridge Only Closing` |
| **Join**                                                                       | `Min Depth Delta`, `Max Depth Delta`, `Cross Branch Only`, `Max Bridges`, `Distance Tolerance`                                                                                                 |
| **Filter**                                                                   | `Max Connectors`                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Prune**                                                                     | `Max Subtree Depth`, `Max Retractions`, `Cascade`, `Bonds Count As Progress`, `Settle First`                                                                                                   |
| **Seed**                                                                       | `Weight`                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Every placing node                                                                                                                     | `Multi Spawn Max Per Connector`, `Prioritize Partial Spawns`                                                                                                                                   |
| Every bias                                                                                                                             | `Influence`, `Contrast`                                                                                                                                                                        |
| Every rule                                                                                                                             | Its own numbers: `Cooldown Steps`, `Target Ratio`, `Weight Multiplier`, `Reference Distance`, `Min Count`, `Max Count`, `Max Distance`, and the rest                                           |
| A region, or a node's `Inline Rules`                                                                                                   | `Slot Sharpness`                                                                                                                                                                               |

What stays typed: enums such as `Depth Mode`, `Pair Scope`, `Scope` and `Severity`; a Choice's weights; descriptors and their tag predicates; region names and mute lists; a rule's `Enabled`, `Branch State Policy` and `Active Where`; and the switches that open a group, `Support Multi Spawn`, `Subtree Search` and `Keep In Scope`. A rule's own switches stay typed too, `Match Is Multiplier`, `Normalize Across Pool`, `Per Module` and `Absolute` among them.

## Which seed a value follows

_A per-seed value belongs to a lineage, and the lineage is carried through the whole run._

A `@Data` value needs no tracking: it is the same for the whole input. A per-seed value has to know which seed point each step descends from, and the grammar carries that as a lineage on every evaluation, stamped when a **Seed** node adopts its seed module and copied wherever the evaluation goes.

| The evaluation                                                          | Reads the value of                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Anything below a Seed node, through any chain                           | That seed point                        |
| A **Branch** arm, a **Repeat** body, a parked **Seek** or **Route**     | The seed the arm or body descends from |
| Everything after a **Merge** whose contributions all came from one seed | That seed                              |
| Everything after a **Merge** of several seeds                           | The first path to arrive               |
| A **Merge** whose contributions were all consumed before it fired       | The typed constant                     |

The mixed Merge follows the rule the Merge already uses for region rules, covered in [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching): the first path to arrive decides, and later paths are assumed to agree. A **Join** or a closing corridor keeps the lineage of the side it was grown from.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-binding-lineage | SHOWS: That a per-seed value is decided by which seed point the work descends from, and that after a Merge fed by several seeds the first path to arrive decides. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both panels share the same two structures: a seed point on a ground line tagged Storeys 5 with a tower of five pieces grown above its seed module, and a second seed point tagged Storeys 2 with a tower of two pieces, every tower drawn from a mix of module outlines and every placed piece carrying the number it read. Panel one headed Per seed: a grammar strip of Seed then Growth in the grammar node style, the Growth annotated Growth Max bound to Storeys, and the two towers below reading 5 and 2 respectively. Panel two headed After a Merge of both seeds: the strip gains a Merge and a second Growth, also annotated. The two towers are restated exactly and dimmed as structure the step is not working on, the top of the left tower marked first to arrive and the right marked second, and the pieces the second Growth placed on top of both towers are drawn in ink, every one of them reading 5, including the one on the tower whose seed point says 2. | MUST BE CLEAR: The value is decided by descent from a seed point, never by where the piece sits, so the two towers read different numbers. After the Merge one seed wins, and it is the first path to arrive rather than the larger or the nearer one, which is why a piece placed on the right tower now reads 5.
> Descent decides the value, not position. After a merge of several seeds, the first path to arrive decides.


Two rules read per candidate rather than per evaluation, because what they measure belongs to the candidate: the **Count** constraint's `Max Count` and the **Reach** constraint's `Max Distance` resolve against the seed owning the connector the candidate would grow from. On a **Frontier** wire that mixes sockets from several seeds, each candidate is judged by its own seed's value. A **Seed** node's `Weight` resolves against the seed point being assigned, before any lineage exists.

## When the attribute is missing

_The typed value is used, and the growth node says so._

A binding whose attribute is absent, on the input for a `@Data` selector or on the seed points for an element selector, reads the typed constant instead. It is reported once per binding and per input, on the growth node and in the log like every other run diagnostic in [Debugging](concept:working-with-valency/systems/debugging), naming the field and the attribute:

```
Binding 'Payload<PCGExGrammarNodePayload_Growth>.GrowthMax': attribute 'Storeys' is missing on the seed points; the authored constant is used.
```

A field set to **Attribute** with no selector at all is caught earlier, when the grammar compiles, and reads the constant the same way.


> **Warning.**
> **A bound value is checked where it is read, and some are corrected**
>
> A typed constant is checked when the grammar compiles, and a bad pair such as a `Growth Max` below `Growth Min` is fixed there. A bound value arrives too late for that, so the same corrections are applied each time it is read.
>
> Nothing else is corrected. A negative `Max Placements` or a `Probability` above `1` is read as it comes, so the attribute has to carry a sensible value.


| Bound value                                                                                                                                                      | Is corrected to                    |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| `Growth Max`, `Repeat Max`, `Max Depth Delta`                                                                                                                    | No lower than the matching minimum |
| `Fill Max Modules`, Seek's `Close Distance` and `No Progress Limit`, Route's `Max Expansions`, `Max Path Length`, `Heuristic Weight` and `Pose Epsilon Rotation` | No lower than `1`                  |
| Route's `Mate Tolerance`                                                                                                                                         | Above zero                         |
| Seed `Weight`, `Slot Sharpness`, Seek's `Min Progress`, Route's `Close Distance`, `Pose Epsilon Position` and both drift tolerances                              | No lower than `0`                  |

## What it costs

_Nothing until something is bound, and one read per value after that._

A grammar with every field on **Constant** carries no binding machinery at all. Once a field is bound, a `@Data` value is read once per input before the run starts, and from then on it costs the same as the constant it replaced. A per-seed value is read once per seed point at the start of the run, into a table the evaluation indexes for the rest of it, and **Valency : Grow Points** and **Valency : Grow Cluster** fetch the attributes it needs up front rather than during the run.

The row's `Cleanup Attribute` toggle marks the attribute as consumed, and the growth node's `Cleanup Consumable Attributes` decides whether consumed attributes are deleted from its output. That applies to both sources, so a `@Data` attribute read by a grammar is removed on output the same way a point attribute is.

## Grammars saved before bindings existed

_They load as they were. Save them once._

Every field that is now bindable used to be a plain value, and a grammar saved that way loads with each value as the constant it was and every `Input` on **Constant**. Nothing about the run changes. Save the asset once so the migrated form is what is on disk.

title: Grammar Nodes
description: Every grammar node type in one place, what each one does in a sentence, and which page explains it.
body:
Every node type, for looking one up. Each line says what the node does rather than what its name suggests, because several of them differ.

## Every node

| Node                                                                                      | Does                                                                                                   | Explained in                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Begin Region**          | Opens a span of grammar that a set of biases and constraints applies to                                | [Regions and Rules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/regions-and-rules)           |
| **Branch**                      | Runs every arm, dealing its open connectors out between them                                           | [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching)                           |
| **Choice**                      | Draws a weighted order over its options and takes the first that succeeds                              | [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching)                           |
| **End Region**              | Closes the matching Begin Region and runs its exit constraints                                         | [Regions and Rules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/regions-and-rules)           |
| **Fill**                          | Places until nothing more fits. Built to cap open ends, given a descriptor that names your end pieces. | [Placing Modules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/placing-modules)               |
| **Filter**                      | Narrows which open connectors the nodes below may use, five ways at once. Places nothing.              | [Narrowing the Frontier](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/narrowing-the-frontier) |
| **Graph Input**   | Marks one named entry of a grammar used as a subgraph                                                  | [Subgraphs](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/subgraphs)                           |
| **Graph Output** | Marks one named exit of a grammar used as a subgraph                                                   | [Subgraphs](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/subgraphs)                           |
| **Growth**                      | Places a count drawn between its Min and Max, feeding new connectors back as it goes                   | [Placing Modules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/placing-modules)               |
| **Join**                          | Pairs two open connectors and places a spanning module across the gap                                  | [Joining and Pruning](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/joining-and-pruning)       |
| **Merge**                        | Waits for every incoming path to finish, then fires once with their union                              | [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching)                           |
| **Module**                      | Places exactly one module matching its descriptor                                                      | [Placing Modules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/placing-modules)               |
| **Optional**                  | Rolls a probability, runs its body on a hit, and reports success either way                            | [Sequencing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/sequencing)                         |
| **Prune**                        | Retracts placements that led nowhere and hands their sockets back to the frontier                      | [Joining and Pruning](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/joining-and-pruning)       |
| **Repeat**                      | Runs its body a count drawn between its Min and Max                                                    | [Sequencing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/sequencing)                         |
| **Route**                        | Solves an exact corridor to a target before placing anything, or reports that none exists              | [Targets](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/targets)                               |
| **Seed**                          | The entry point. Adopts a pre-placed seed module and grows its subtree from there.                     | [Placing Modules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/placing-modules)                                                |
| **Seek**                          | Grows a corridor toward a target, steering as it goes, and may never arrive                            | [Targets](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/targets)                               |
| **Sequence**                  | Runs its steps in order, finishing each one's subtree before the next begins                           | [Sequencing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/sequencing)                         |
| **Stash**                        | Banks the connectors reaching it under a name. A sink: nothing flows out of it                          | [Stashing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/stashing)                             |
| **Subgraph**                       | Runs another grammar asset as one unit, in the caller's lineage, with its own frontier and rollback   | [Subgraphs](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/subgraphs)                           |
| **Unstash**                    | Publishes whatever the bank of that name still has open, wherever flow reaches it                      | [Stashing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/stashing)                             |
| **Yield**                        | Captures the frontier for the next iteration of the Repeat it sits in                                  | [Sequencing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/sequencing)                         |

### Where they sit in the palette

_The editor groups them differently from this book, so both orders are here._

| Category      | Holds                                   |
| ------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| **Growth**    | Module, Growth, Fill, Join, Seek, Route |
| **Control**   | Sequence, Branch, Repeat, Merge, Yield, Stash, Unstash |
| **Chance**    | Choice, Optional                        |
| **Filter**    | Filter, Prune                           |
| **Region**    | Begin Region, End Region                |
| **Boundary**  | Graph Input, Graph Output               |
| **Reference** | Subgraph                                |
| **Flow**      | Seed                                    |

### The names worth double-checking

_The ones that describe themselves poorly enough to send someone the wrong way._

| Node                   | Reads as          | Actually                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Branch**             | Picks a path      | Runs all of them. **Choice** is the one that picks.                |
| **Merge**              | Combines flows    | Waits for all of them first. The barrier is the feature.           |
| **Yield**              | Emits something   | Rewires the loop above it, overriding its body scope               |
| **Seek** and **Route** | Synonyms          | Opposites. Seek searches by building; Route searches, then builds. |
| **Prune**              | Deletes dead ends | Retracts against a definition of "dead end" that you author        |
| **Unstash**            | Takes it out      | Reads the bank without emptying it. Several Unstashes can read one |

title: Joining and Pruning
description: Join and Prune: the nodes that work on what a grammar already built, one closing gaps between branches and one taking back what led nowhere.
outline: Both Ends In Scope and Cross Branch Only cancel out
A Prune only ever examines what its wire handed it
Settle First, and why it is off
body:
Every other grammar node extends the structure. **Join** and **Prune** work on what is already there: Join closes a gap between two open connectors, and Prune takes placements back out and returns their sockets to the frontier.

## Join spans two open connectors

_It pairs them up, then places a module across the gap._

A **Join** looks for pairs of open connectors it can bridge, and places a spanning module between each pair it accepts. Both connectors are consumed, and each one can take part in at most one join per evaluation.

Four settings decide which pairs are eligible.

| Setting             | Excludes a pair when                                                                                                         |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Pair Scope`        | An endpoint sits outside the incoming edge scope. Covered below.                                                             |
| `Cross Branch Only` | Both connectors are on the same branch, following any bridge merges already made. On by default.                             |
| `Depth Mode`        | `Same Depth` rejects any depth difference; `Depth Range` rejects differences outside `Min` and `Max`. `Any` rejects nothing. |
| `Max Bridges`       | That many joins have already been placed this evaluation                                                                     |

Eligible pairs are then shuffled, so a Join placed under a cap takes a varied selection rather than whichever pairs the frontier happened to list first.

`Max Bridges`, `Distance Tolerance`, `Cross Branch Only` and the depth range can each be read from the seed points instead of typed. A bound `Max Depth Delta` below `Min Depth Delta` is raised to it.

A Join that places nothing says why, on the node and in the log, naming whichever of these emptied the search.

### Which connectors it may pair

_A join takes two ends, so a scope has two readings._

A Join consumes two connectors at once, so an edge scope reaching it has two readings. `Pair Scope` picks one, and the scopes themselves are in [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar).

| `Pair Scope`           | A pair is eligible when                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Both Ends In Scope** | Both endpoints are in the incoming scope. The default.                                                                                            |
| **One End In Scope**   | One endpoint is in the incoming scope, and the partner is any open connector. This is the setting that joins a scoped set to the wider structure. |
| **Full Frontier**      | Always. Pairs are drawn from every open connector in the run, as though the incoming scope had been discarded.                                    |

An unscoped input leaves the search unconfined whatever this says, there being nothing to confine it to. In every case the scope still governs what the Join passes downstream.

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-join-pair-scope | SHOWS: How Pair Scope changes which pairs a Join may consider, and why the default finds nothing on a single-branch scope. | ELEMENTS: Three panels compared, separated by vertical rules. Every panel shows the same structure: two branches in different colours grown from a shared origin, open sockets along both, and a dashed outline marking the incoming scope which covers four sockets on the left branch only. Panel one headed Both Ends In Scope: candidate pair lines are drawn only between sockets inside the outline, every one of them struck through and annotated as same branch, leaving no eligible pair. Panel two headed One End In Scope: pair lines run from sockets inside the outline out to sockets on the right branch, drawn as eligible, with one selected and a spanning module placed across it. Panel three headed Full Frontier: pair lines run between sockets anywhere including two on the right branch with the outline greyed out to show it was disregarded. | MUST BE CLEAR: The structure and the scope are identical in all three. Panel one produces nothing not because the scope is empty but because every pair inside one branch is rejected by Cross Branch Only.
> Same scope, three readings. A scope covering one branch offers no valid pair to the default, which is what One End In Scope is for.

> **Warning.**
> **Both Ends In Scope and Cross Branch Only cancel out**
>
> `Cross Branch Only` is on by default and rejects any pair whose endpoints share a branch. A scope covering a single branch, which is what a **Filter** from [Narrowing the Frontier](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/narrowing-the-frontier) on one arm gives you, therefore offers no eligible pair at all: every candidate pair inside it is same-branch by construction.
>
> `One End In Scope` is the setting for that shape. The Join anchors on the filtered connectors and reaches out to the rest of the structure for the other end.

### The module it spans with

_Its descriptor narrows the bridge pool, which is the opposite of what a Seek's does._

A Join draws its spanning module from the **Bridge Only** modules in the library. Give the node a descriptor and it draws from that instead, which is how one grammar can use different spanning pieces in different places.

That is worth holding next to [Targets](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/targets), where the same word means something else. Their descriptor names the modules the **corridor** is built from, and closing has a field of its own, `Closing Descriptor`. A Join places only the spanning module, so its one descriptor is the closing pool.

> Modules already at their spawn limit are dropped before selection, so a cap on a bridge piece removes it from the running rather than having it win and be refused.

## Prune takes placements back

_Two descriptors: which placements to examine, and what counts as leading somewhere._

A **Prune** examines the placements that own its incoming connectors and retracts the ones that led nowhere, handing their sockets back to the frontier so something else can use them.

> **Warning.**
> **A Prune only ever examines what its wire handed it**
>
> Prune considers the placements that own its **incoming** connectors. Chained onto a **Growth**, whose wire defaults to **Produced**, that is the handful of modules that Growth just placed, and every dead end elsewhere in the structure is outside its view.
>
> Nothing reports this, because nothing went wrong. The node was asked a narrow question and answered it.
>
> Make it a step of a **Sequence** instead, whose steps see the whole frontier, or set the wire feeding it to **Frontier** by hand. See chaining narrows, a Sequence step resets.

"Led nowhere" is not built in. You define it, with two separate descriptors.

| Descriptor         | Answers                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Consider`         | Which placements are even considered. Leave it empty and everything reachable is a candidate.                                 |
| `Dead End Unless`  | What a candidate's subtree must contain for it to count as leading somewhere. Leave it empty and **any child at all** counts. |

So a Prune with both empty retracts placements with no children whatsoever. A Prune whose `Dead End Unless` names your stairwells retracts anything that failed to reach one, however much else it built.

> Two settings widen or narrow that test. `Subtree Search` looks through the whole subtree rather than direct children only, bounded by `Max Subtree Depth`. And `Bonds Count As Progress` treats a live bridge bond as leading somewhere, which matters because a bond joins two things without adding a child link, so a module that closed a loop looks childless without it.

## Cascade walks the chain back

_Retracting a tip puts its parent in scope._

Retracting a placement re-opens the socket on its parent, which can make the parent a dead end in turn. `Cascade` keeps re-examining until nothing more qualifies, which is what lets one Prune unwind an entire dangling corridor rather than trimming one module off the end of it.

Each pass after the first looks **only at what the previous pass freed**. It does not widen to the live frontier, so a cascade follows the chain it is unwinding instead of spreading into unrelated structure.

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-prune-cascade | SHOWS: How cascade unwinds a whole dangling chain rather than trimming one module. | ELEMENTS: Three panels left to right, one structure. A hub module with two chains grown from it: a short chain ending in a piece marked as satisfying the dead-end descriptor, and a longer chain of four pieces ending in nothing. Panel one, the starting state, with the tip of the long chain marked as the only candidate. Panel two, that tip retracted and drawn as an outline where it was, its parent's socket now drawn open, and the parent now marked as a candidate. Panel three, the whole long chain gone back to the hub, its sockets open, and the short chain untouched throughout because its end piece satisfies the descriptor. | MUST BE CLEAR: One evaluation removed four modules, one at a time, each becoming a candidate only because the one after it was removed. The satisfying chain was never in danger.
> Each retraction re-opens a parent, which makes the parent the next candidate. The chain unwinds one module at a time.

`Max Retractions` caps how much one evaluation may take back. Like `Max Subtree Depth`, `Cascade`, `Bonds Count As Progress` and `Settle First`, it can be read from the seed points instead of typed.

## What Prune refuses to touch

_It will not retract anything the grammar might still be about to build on._

A Prune runs while other parts of the grammar may still have work queued. Retracting a placement that a pending step was about to extend would be destructive, so it checks first and skips any candidate whose subtree something queued could still reach.

There is a stronger version of that check. If **any** queued step has an unbounded scope, meaning it could place on any open connector anywhere, then nothing can be shown to be safe and the Prune retracts nothing at all.

That is the explanation for a Prune that runs and does nothing on a structure visibly full of dead ends. The dead ends are real; the timing is wrong.

Both refusals report, on the node and in the log. The narrower one names how many candidates it skipped for pending work of their own. The unbounded one says that is what happened and names the step responsible, since the candidates it skipped may have had no pending work at all. The remedy is the same either way: place the Prune after a **Sequence** step, or turn on `Settle First`.

> **Note.**
> **Settle First, and why it is off**
>
> `Settle First` drains the pending work before the Prune evaluates, which removes the uncertainty above entirely.
>
> It is off by default because the drain is **global**: one queue for the whole run, shared across every seed under **Parallel** execution. Settling before one Prune settles everything, which reorders work that had no reason to wait.
>
> Turn it on when a Prune needs to see a finished structure and you can afford the ordering change.

## What it hands downstream

_Three answers, and the default is the narrow one._

| `Output Scope`          | Children see                                                                                                          |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Freed Only**          | The sockets this Prune re-opened. The default, and what lets a following placement land exactly on the cleared spots. |
| **Freed And Surviving** | Those, plus the incoming connectors that were not retracted                                                           |
| **Full Frontier**       | Everything open, as though the incoming scope had been discarded                                                      |

Whichever is chosen, the result is an explicit set. A Prune that freed nothing hands its children an empty set rather than falling back to the whole frontier.

title: Narrowing the Frontier
description: Everything a Filter can do is a narrowing, and there are five of them.
outline: When the library and the predicate disagree
An empty result is an empty result
body:
**Filter** places nothing. It takes the open connectors reaching it, removes some, and hands the rest to its children. That is the whole node, and it is how a grammar says "of everything available here, only these are eligible for what comes next".

Everything a Filter can do is a narrowing, and there are five of them. They are independent, they all run, and the word on the node covers all five equally.

## Where it starts from

*The set it narrows is whatever the incoming wire gave it.*

A Filter narrows the connectors delivered by the edge scope [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar) defines. Reached by a wire carrying the whole frontier, it narrows the whole frontier; reached by a **Produced** wire, it narrows the sockets of the piece just placed.

One case is deliberately not widened: a wire that delivered an **exhausted** set, meaning a scope that resolved to nothing rather than a scope that was never applied, stays empty. A Filter never recovers the full frontier from an upstream step that ran out of connectors.

What it hands on is the set that survived, whichever scope the wire below carries. **Inherited** and **Produced** both resolve to the survivors on a wire leaving a Filter, because the survivors are the only thing the node produced.

## The five narrowings

*All of them apply, in this order, and the order changes the result.*

| Narrowing | Keeps a connector when |
|---|---|
| `Connector Type Filter` | Its connector type is in the listed set |
| `Identifier Filter` | Its socket name is in the set, or outside it, per `Must be any of` / `Must not be any of` |
| `Keep In Scope` | The module that **owns** it is inside the chosen placement scope |
| `Module Filter` | A module in `Module Scope`, anchored at that connector, matches the descriptor |
| `Max Connectors` | It survives a random draw down to that many |


> **Note.**
> `Connector Type Filter` and `Identifier Filter` sit on **every** grammar node with a flow input, and narrow what that node reads before it does its own job. A **Module** node can restrict itself to `Corridor` sockets with no Filter in front of it.
>
> What a Filter adds is the other three, and the ability to narrow without placing anything, which is what makes it usable as a gate on whether a subtree runs at all.


The count cap runs last, on purpose. Applying it earlier would trim the set before the meaningful narrowings had a say, and the cap would then take a sample of things that were about to be discarded anyway.

The cap is also a **random** sample, not the first however-many. Every survivor of the four narrowings above is equally likely to be kept, so a Filter capped at two is a way of saying "any two of these", not "the two that happen to come first".

`Max Connectors` can be read from the seed points instead of typed, like any other number on a grammar node.

## Two narrowings that look alike

*They ask about the same placement scope from opposite ends.*

`Keep In Scope` and `Module Filter` both take a placement scope, from separate fields, and they use it for completely different questions.

**Keep In Scope** anchors at the module the grammar is currently building from, works out which placements are in scope from there, and keeps only the connectors owned by those placements. It is a structural test: *is this socket part of the thing I am working on?*

**Module Filter** anchors at each connector's own owning module, works out `Module Scope` from there, and keeps the connector when any module in that scope matches its descriptor. It is a question about identity: *does this socket belong to a neighbourhood that looks like this?* A descriptor can ask by name, by tag, by connector signature, or by all of them at once. It defaults to **Owning module**, which asks only about the piece the socket is on.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-filter-anchors | SHOWS: That the two scope-based narrowings anchor at opposite ends and therefore keep different connectors. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same structure: a placed module marked as the current anchor, a chain of three modules grown from it, and a second unrelated chain of three modules elsewhere, with open sockets throughout and a few modules marked as matching the filter's descriptor. Left panel headed Keep In Scope: an outline encloses the anchor and its own chain, and only the sockets owned by modules inside that outline are highlighted, the second chain entirely dimmed. Right panel headed Module Filter: no outline around the anchor; instead each socket in the whole picture is tested, and the highlighted ones are those whose own surrounding modules match the descriptor, which includes sockets on the second chain and excludes some on the first. | MUST BE CLEAR: The same placement scope setting produces different survivors because the anchor differs. Keep In Scope radiates from the module being built from; the filter is evaluated separately around each candidate socket.
> Same scope setting, opposite anchors. One asks where the socket is, the other asks what is around it.



> **Warning.**
> **Keep In Scope fails closed**
>
> The structural test needs a placement to anchor at. On a flow where nothing has been placed yet there is no anchor, and rather than quietly keeping everything, the Filter drops every connector and warns.
>
> That is the safer of the two wrong answers, and it produces a visible symptom: a Filter that suddenly passes nothing, on a path where nothing has been built. Place something before filtering by structure.


## When the library and the predicate disagree

*Two library-level conditions turn a predicate into something other than what it says.*

Tag predicates are evaluated against the tag space the [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) compiled, and two states of that space change the outcome without changing the predicate.

| Library state | The predicate |
|---|---|
| No module tags at all | Is skipped entirely. Every connector passes, and the node warns. |
| Every tag in a `Require Any` clause is unknown to the library | Can never match, so it drops every connector, and the node warns |

Both are worth recognising by their symptom rather than by reading the predicate, because in both cases the predicate is written correctly and the library is what disagrees. The first looks like a Filter doing nothing; the second looks like a Filter blocking everything.

Both are reported once per run, naming the grammar node, and a Filter the run never reaches is reported too. The disagreement is between the predicate and the library, so it is settled the moment the grammar is paired with a **Bonding Rules** asset.

## An empty result is an empty result

*A Filter that removes everything is not a Filter that did nothing.*

When every connector is removed, the children see zero candidates. They do not fall back to the live frontier, which is what an unset scope would have given them.

This is what makes a Filter usable as a gate on whether a subtree runs at all. Narrow to the connectors that satisfy some condition, and the chain below runs only where that condition held.

title: Placing Modules
description: Three of the twenty-one grammar node types put modules in the world.
outline: A placement node that places nothing takes its subtree with it
Both cases warn, and the warning says which of three things went wrong
Prioritize Partial Spawns needs a bias to have an effect
body:
Three of the twenty-one grammar node types put modules in the world. Everything else exists to decide which of them runs, on what, and under which rules. They differ in one thing only: how many placements one evaluation makes.

## Three ways to place

_One, a drawn count, or as many as fit._

| Node                                                                 | Places                                                         | Stops when                                  |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Module** | Exactly one                                                    | Always, after one attempt                   |
| **Growth** | A count drawn per evaluation from `Growth Min` to `Growth Max` | The count is reached, or nothing more fits  |
| **Fill**     | As many as it can                                              | Nothing more fits, or the safety cap is hit |

All three take a module descriptor from ., all three accept inline rules that apply to every placement they make, and all three default their outgoing wire to **Produced**, so a child sees the sockets of what its parent placed rather than the wider frontier.

### What Fill is for

_Its original job is closing off open ends, and the descriptor is what makes it do that._

Fill was built to cap dead ends. Growth finishes, or the budget runs out, and the structure is left holding open sockets that could have carried more but are better walled off. A Fill whose descriptor matches your end pieces, your caps and your blank walls turns every one of those into a proper termination in a single evaluation.

> Nothing in the node enforces that, which is the flexibility and the trap in one. The descriptor is the only thing making a Fill a capping pass. Point it at the whole library and it is undirected growth that runs until nothing fits, which is a perfectly good way to use it and also exactly what an empty descriptor gets you by accident.

The safety cap below exists for that second case. It is there to stop an unbounded Fill, not to shape a deliberate one.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-placement-nodes | SHOWS: How the same starting point and the same library produce three different amounts of structure under the three placement nodes. | ELEMENTS: Three panels compared, separated by vertical rules. Each shows an identical starting module with three open sockets, drawn as an outline with an inside corner. Panel one headed Module: exactly one new piece attached to one socket, the other two sockets still open. Panel two headed Growth: four new pieces attached across several sockets and one second-generation piece, with a small tally reading 4 of a drawn target of 4. Panel three headed Fill: pieces attached everywhere until no socket in reach remains open, roughly a dozen, with the outermost sockets marked as having nothing compatible left. | MUST BE CLEAR: The three panels differ only in how many placements one evaluation made. The starting structure, the library, and the sockets available are identical in all three.
> One evaluation of each, from the same start. The only difference is how many placements it makes.


## A placement node that places nothing takes its subtree with it

_The most expensive thing to misdiagnose in a grammar._

Children are dispatched from the placement-committed path. A **Module** node that fails to place anything never dispatches its children, so the entire chain hanging off it does not run. From the outside this is indistinguishable from a disconnected wire: no error, no missing asset, and a part of the structure that was never built.

A **Growth** node does the same thing on a different trigger. If it placed fewer than `Growth Min`, the pass counts as a failure and the children are skipped, even though the modules it did place are kept. `Partial Counts As Success` turns that off: a short pass then dispatches its children anyway.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-growth-min-drop | SHOWS: That a Growth node falling short of its minimum keeps its placements but drops its children. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Each shows a small grammar strip at the top, four linked node boxes in the grammar node style: Seed, Growth labelled Min 3, then two further nodes chained after it. Below each strip, the structure produced. Left panel headed Growth Min met: the Growth node and both downstream nodes drawn active, and the structure below shows three grown pieces plus the pieces the downstream chain added. Right panel headed Growth Min not met: the Growth node drawn active, both downstream nodes drawn dimmed and struck, and the structure below shows only two grown pieces and nothing else. | MUST BE CLEAR: The two pieces on the right are kept, not rolled back. What is missing is everything the downstream chain would have added, and nothing in the result says so.
> The short pass keeps what it placed. What it loses is the rest of the chain.


**Fill** behaves differently, and the difference is deliberate. A Fill that placed nothing still dispatches its children unless it is marked `Required`, because running out of room is Fill's normal ending rather than a failure.


> **Tip.**
> **Both cases warn, and the warning says which of three things went wrong**
>
> Neither trap is silent. Each reports once per node and reason, to the Output Log and to the growth node itself, so the message is on the node in the graph rather than only in a log someone has to think to open.
>
> For a Module the message names the reason, then breaks the candidate pool down: how many connectors were in scope, how many modules the descriptor resolved, and for each connector type and polarity present, how many compatible pairs the library offers at all. Those three numbers separate the three ways this goes wrong, which the total on its own cannot:
>
> A Growth node reports the same way, and additionally names which of its exits fired: the run budget, `Max Placements`, `Max Growth Depth`, an exhausted scope, an empty candidate pool, or a constraint that vetoed everything.


| The number that is zero                           | The problem is                                                 |
| ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Connectors in scope                               | The edge scope feeding this node, not the descriptor           |
| Modules resolved                                  | The descriptor. It matches nothing in this library.            |
| Compatible pairs, with both of the above non-zero | Connector types or polarity. The pieces exist and cannot mate. |

## Bounding a loop

_Three independent limits, and whichever fires first wins._

**Growth** and **Fill** both run a placement loop, and both can be bounded three ways that do not interact.

| Setting            | Counts                                                                    | Zero means                        |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `Max Growth Depth` | Hops through the structure from the parent placement, not placements made | Unlimited                         |
| `Max Placements`   | Modules placed by this one evaluation                                     | Unlimited                         |
| `Fill Max Modules` | Fill only. A safety cap against runaway growth, defaulting to `100`.      | Not applicable, it is a plain cap |

`Max Growth Depth` is the one worth being careful with, because it measures something the other two do not. It is anchored at the depth of the parent placement, so a value of `1` means "at most one hop from where this node started", regardless of how many modules that turns out to be. It narrows which connectors are eligible rather than counting what gets placed.

Above them all sits the growth node's own budget. A grammar cannot outspend `Max Total Modules`, and a placement loop that stops early because the run is out of budget reports exactly that.

Every limit here, and `Growth Min` and `Growth Max` with them, can be read from the seed points instead of typed, through the **Attribute** setting on the row, covered in [Data Bindings](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/data-bindings). A bound `Growth Max` below `Growth Min` is raised to it, and a bound `Fill Max Modules` below `1` is raised to `1`.

## Multi-spawn

_Letting one socket host more than one child._

A connector authored with a `Spawn Capacity` above `1` can carry several children, but a grammar will not use that capacity unless the placing node opts in with `Support Multi Spawn`. That is off everywhere except **Growth**, which opts in by default. `Multi Spawn Max Per Connector` then caps it further, or leaves the connector's own capacity to decide.


> **Note.**
> **Prioritize Partial Spawns needs a bias to have an effect**
>
> It raises the priority of a connector that has been used once and has capacity left, so it competes ahead of untouched ones. Nothing in the default draw reads connector priority, so on its own the setting changes nothing.
>
> What reads it is the **Connector Priority** bias. Add one, scoped wherever the multi-spawn is happening, and the boost becomes an ordering.


## Adoption at a Seed
