_The first placement in a run was already made._

Growth places a seed module at each seed point before the grammar runs. The first **Module** evaluated under a **Seed** node therefore adopts that existing placement instead of making a new one, and continues from its sockets.

Adoption is unconditional, which means a seed module that does not satisfy the Seed node's own descriptor is still adopted. That is nearly always an authoring surprise rather than an intent, so it warns once per node and module when it happens.

title: Regions and Rules
description: Regions, and the biases and constraints they carry: where a rule applies, how nesting resolves, and the two-stage draw rules actually steer.
outline: Region state is fresh, inline state persists
body:
A **rule** is a preference or a requirement applied to placement. Fourteen **biases** reshape which module gets drawn, nine **constraints** refuse candidates outright, and a **region** is the span of grammar a set of them applies to.

## Where a rule lives

*On one node, or across a span.*

Rules attach in two places, and the difference is reach.

| Attached to | Applies to |
|---|---|
| A node's own `Inline Rules` | That node alone, and every placement it makes |
| A **Begin Region** | Every node downstream until the matching **End Region** |

Not every node type accepts inline rules. The ones that place things do, which is what makes an inline rule useful on a **Growth** or a **Seek**: the rule applies to every placement inside that node's own loop.

A region is opened by **Begin Region** and closed by **End Region**, matched by identity rather than by position, so an inner region can outlive an outer one. **An unclosed region runs to the end of the grammar**, which is a supported way to author "from here on" and not an error.

> **Note.**
> **Region state is fresh, inline state persists**
>
> Stateful rules (pity counters, quotas, running tallies) behave differently depending on where they are attached.
>
> A region creates new state each time it opens, so re-entering a region starts its counters over. An inline rule's state is kept per node for the whole run, so a node evaluated many times accumulates across all of them.
>
> That is usually what each one is for, and it is worth knowing before moving a rule from one to the other to tidy a graph up.

## Nesting

*Each region declares how it combines with what it inherited, separately for biases and constraints.*

Regions resolve outermost first, and each one decides what happens to the set it inherited.

| `Reconciliation` | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Stack** | Inherited rules stay active alongside the new ones. The default. |
| **Replace** | Every inherited rule of that kind is hidden for the duration of this region |
| **Selective Mute** | Inherited rules of that kind whose **name** is in the mute list are hidden, the rest stay |

Biases and constraints reconcile independently, so a region can replace the inherited biases while continuing to stack constraints. Muting is by rule name, which is why rule names are worth setting on anything a nested region might want to switch off.

## Which placements a rule counts

*The placement scope, and it is not the scope on a wire.*

Rules that ask a question about what has already been placed carry a `Scope`. It selects a slice of the run's placement history relative to the connector being considered.

| Scope | Counts | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Owning module** | Only the module that owns the connector | Constant. The cheapest. |
| **Ancestor chain** | That module and every ancestor up to its seed | Bounded by tree depth |
| **Current region** | Everything placed since the region declaring this rule opened, or everything this run if it has no region | Scans placements since the region opened |
| **Same branch** | Everything on that module's branch, following bridge merges | Scans every placement, resolving each through the branch union |
| **Same seed** | Everything grown from the same seed | Scans every placement |
| **Any placed before** | Everything the grammar placed this run | Scans every placement |

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-placement-scopes | SHOWS: That the scopes are differently shaped slices of the same placement history, which is why their costs differ so much. | ELEMENTS: Four panels compared, separated by vertical rules. Every panel shows the identical placement tree: two seeds at the bottom, each growing a few modules, one seed forking into two branches, and a bridge bond drawn between a module on one branch and a module on the other. In every panel the same single module is marked as the anchor, on the deeper branch of the left seed. Panel one headed Owning module: only the anchor is highlighted. Panel two headed Ancestor chain: the anchor and the unbroken path of parents down to its seed. Panel three headed Same branch: every module on the anchor's branch, and because of the bridge bond this reaches across into the merged branch too. Panel four headed Any placed before: every module in both trees. Everything not in the slice is dimmed rather than struck. | MUST BE CLEAR: One anchor, four different answers, and the shapes are what differ: a point, a path, a merged branch, and everything. Same branch reaching across the bridge is the panel that is easy to get wrong.
> One anchor, four slices of the same history. Current region and Same seed are further cuts of the same axis.

The costs are worth reading, because these run per evaluation. A quota on **Owning module** is free; the same quota on **Any placed before** walks the whole result every time a candidate is considered.

Only rules that answer a question about the placed set show this field. A **Cooldown** measures how long it has been since something was last picked, which is a temporal distance rather than set membership, so it has no scope.

> **Warning.**
> This is not the scope carried on a wire. **Edge scope** selects open connectors and decides where a node may build. **Placement scope**, here, selects placed modules and decides what a rule counts. The editor calls both of them scope.

There is a third axis, and it is a place rather than a set. Every rule carries an `Active Where` precondition that switches it on only where the frontier connector sits inside or outside a named spatial channel, leaving it inert everywhere else. See [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules).

## When a constraint is asked

*Its channels decide, and it can declare several.*

A constraint's `Eval Channels` is a multi-select, and a constraint answers on every channel it carries.

| Channel | Asked |
|---|---|
| **Runtime Filter** | Per candidate during selection. A veto removes that candidate from the pool entirely. |
| **Placement** | Per resolved pose, at the moment of placing. A refusal moves along to the next pose. |
| **Exit Validation** | When the hosting region closes. Where a constraint starts unless its type says otherwise. |

They answer different shapes of question. A runtime filter can say "never this module here"; only exit validation can say "by the time this region ends, at least one of these must exist", because the answer is unknown until the region is done.

Some constraint types support only one channel, and authoring one a type does not implement is caught when the grammar compiles rather than at runtime. The **Spatial** constraint is the one that answers on all three, and [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules) covers what each channel tests and why the three differ.

When every candidate in a pool has been vetoed on the **Runtime Filter** channel, there is nothing to place, and the run backtracks at the severity of the most severe constraint that was active.

## What failure costs

*Five answers, from a warning to stopping the run.*

Each constraint declares a `Severity`, or inherits the region's `Default Severity` when it does not override it.

`Severity` prices a failure on the **Runtime Filter** and **Exit Validation** channels. A **Placement** refusal moves to the next pose with nothing committed and nothing undone, so it never reaches any of the answers below.

| Severity | On failure |
|---|---|
| **Skip** | Warn and carry on. Nothing is undone. |
| **Backtrack Local** | Retry the offending placement with a different candidate |
| **Backtrack Branch** | Undo to the nearest **Branch** or **Choice** and take a different path. The default. |
| **Backtrack Global** | Restart the run with a different draw |
| **Abort** | Stop |

Setting one policy on the region and letting the rules inherit it is the intended shape. Reach for a per-rule override when one requirement is genuinely more serious than its neighbours.

## The draw rules actually steer

*Biases weight modules. The slot is chosen first, and separately.*

Placement is two draws, not one. Given a set of open connectors and the modules that could go on each, a grammar first picks **which connector** to build on, then picks **which module** to put there.

Biases weight the individual candidate pairings. Those weights are then folded down to one number per connector, and that number decides the first draw.

| Setting | Decides |
|---|---|
| `Slot Reduction` | How a connector's weight is derived from its candidates: **Max** takes its best, **Sum** its total, **Mean** its average |
| `Slot Selection` | How the connector is then drawn: **Proportional**, **Sharpened** by `Slot Sharpness`, or **Greedy**, which always takes the best |

The reduction is the choice that decides most results. Under **Max** a connector is as attractive as the single best module it can host, however few it can host. Under **Sum** a connector hosting ten mediocre options outweighs one hosting a single excellent option, because the draw is then equivalent to one flat draw over every pairing.

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-slot-draw | SHOWS: That the reduction, not the module weights, decides which connector gets built on. | ELEMENTS: Three panels compared, separated by vertical rules, sharing one setup drawn across the top of the whole figure: two open connectors labelled A and B on a placed structure, with A listing one candidate module weighted 9 and B listing five candidate modules each weighted 3. Each panel below then shows the same two connectors with one number each, the folded slot weight, and the connector the draw favours marked. Panel one headed Max: A reads 9, B reads 3, A is favoured. Panel two headed Sum: A reads 9, B reads 15, B is favoured. Panel three headed Mean: A reads 9, B reads 3, A is favoured. | MUST BE CLEAR: The module weights are identical in all three panels. Only the fold changed, and it flipped which connector wins between Max and Sum.
> Same candidates, same weights. The fold decides which connector is built on, before any module is chosen.

This is why cranking a bias sometimes changes nothing. If the bias is raising module weights on connectors that were never going to be picked, the first draw settles the outcome before the second one is reached.

Slot settings are declared like rules, and the innermost declaration wins. An inline declaration outranks every region.

`Slot Sharpness`, along with `Influence` and `Contrast` on every bias and the numbers a rule carries of its own, can be read from the seed points instead of typed. A rule bound that way applies a different strength under each seed point, which is how one region can be strict for one building and lenient for the next. A rule's switches, its `Scope`, its severity and its descriptors stay typed.

title: Sequencing
description: Where branching.md decides which paths run, these four decide when.
outline: Sequence finishes each step before the next begins
Sequence steps default to the whole frontier
Repeat draws a count, and can stop early
Yield rewires the loop it sits in
A Yield overrides the Repeat body's edge scope
body:
Where [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching) decides which paths run, these four decide **when**. A **Sequence** puts steps in order, a **Repeat** runs one body several times, an **Optional** rolls for whether its body runs at all, and a **Yield** decides what the next iteration of a Repeat starts from.

## Sequence finishes each step before the next begins

*A barrier between steps, not merely an ordering of them.*

A **Sequence** dispatches its children in order, and each step's entire subtree drains before the next step is dispatched. A step that spawns a Growth, which spawns a Branch, which spawns three more chains does all of that before step two exists.

That is stronger than it sounds. "In order" could mean the steps merely start in order and interleave afterwards. They do not: step two begins against a structure in which everything step one implied is already built and already reflected in the frontier.


> **Note.**
> **Sequence steps default to the whole frontier**
>
> Every other node passes **Inherited** or **Produced** on an untouched wire. A Sequence passes **Frontier**, so each step starts by looking at everything still open rather than at whatever the previous step left in hand.
>
> That is usually what a sequence of build phases wants, and it is the opposite of what a chain of Modules wants. Set the wire explicitly when a step should continue from the step above rather than survey the whole structure.


A step that fails is skipped and the sequence carries on, unless that step is marked `Required`, in which case the whole Sequence fails from there.

## Repeat draws a count, and can stop early

*Between Min and Max, decided per evaluation, and not guaranteed.*

A **Repeat** draws its iteration count uniformly between `Repeat Min` and `Repeat Max` each time it is evaluated, then runs its body that many times, draining fully between iterations exactly as a Sequence does between steps.

Three things end it before the count is reached:

| Ending | Effect |
|---|---|
| The run budget is exhausted | The loop stops where it is, keeping what it built |
| The body fails an iteration | That iteration is rolled back, and the loop stops |
| Nothing left to build on | Reported by the body's own placement nodes, not by Repeat |

A rolled-back iteration leaves nothing behind. Whatever it placed before failing is undone, so a Repeat never leaves a half-built iteration in the result.

The Repeat as a whole counts as successful when it completed at least `Repeat Min` iterations. Below that it fails, with the usual consequence for the chain hanging off it.

Both bounds can be read from the seed points instead of typed, so the number of storeys can be a number on the point that started the building, as [Data Bindings](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/data-bindings) covers. A bound `Repeat Max` below `Repeat Min` is raised to it.

## Optional always succeeds

*The roll decides whether the body runs, never whether the grammar continues.*

An **Optional** rolls against `Probability` and runs its body on a hit. Whatever happens after that, including a body that fails outright, the node reports success and its continuation fires. A skipped roll, an empty body, a successful body and a failed body all leave the grammar running.

A failed body is rolled back first, so an Optional cannot leave partial work behind either.

That makes Optional the safe way to express "sometimes there is a balcony here". It is also why an Optional cannot be used to express a requirement: if the balcony has to exist, the node that places it needs a constraint, not a probability.

`Probability` can be read from the seed points as well, so the odds vary per building rather than per grammar.

## Yield rewires the loop it sits in

*The one node whose presence changes what a wire above it means.*

A **Yield** sits inside a Repeat body and captures the frontier reaching it. At the end of the iteration, the Repeat starts its next iteration from what its Yields captured rather than from where the body happened to finish.

That is how a loop walks: each iteration hands the next one a specific set of sockets to continue from, chosen by where you placed the Yield, rather than the loop drifting wherever the body's last placement left it.

> Without a Yield, a Repeat is a **for** loop: it runs the count it drew, each iteration picking up wherever the body finished. With one it behaves like a **while** loop that has a ceiling. What the captures hand over decides whether the next iteration has anything to work on, so the drawn count becomes an upper bound rather than a target, and a loop whose yields stop producing live sockets ends there.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-yield-feedback | SHOWS: How a Yield decides which sockets the next Repeat iteration starts from. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Each has a small grammar strip at the top in the grammar node style: a Repeat box wrapping a body of three chained boxes. Left panel headed Without a Yield: no Yield in the body, and below it a structure of three iterations where each iteration continues from the tail of the previous one, producing one wandering run. Right panel headed With a Yield: the body strip has a Yield box wired off its middle node, and below it a structure where each iteration continues from the middle piece of the previous iteration instead of its tail, producing a regular branching pattern. In both, the sockets each iteration started from are marked. | MUST BE CLEAR: The body is the same in both. What changed is which sockets carry into the next iteration, and that is decided by where the Yield sits, not by what the body placed last.
> Same body, same count. The Yield decides which sockets the next iteration inherits.


Several Yields in one body compose: their captures are unioned, and a duplicate socket reached twice is contributed once.

A capture belongs to the iteration that made it. Connectors that should outlive the loop, or be built on somewhere the loop has no wire to, go to a named bank instead, which [Stashing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/stashing) covers.


> **Warning.**
> **A Yield overrides the Repeat body's edge scope**
>
> Wiring a Yield anywhere inside a Repeat body changes what the wire **into** that body means. With no Yield, the body wire behaves as authored. With one, the per-iteration input is exclusively what the Yields captured, and the body wire's scope is bypassed.
>
> This is deliberate: yields are the source of truth for what the next iteration works on, and a scope re-applied on iteration entry would undo them. It is worth knowing because the wire still shows whatever it was set to, and it no longer does anything.


Two more details decide how a loop behaves over time. **Captures reset every iteration**, so only the Yields that fired this time around feed the next one; a Yield behind a Choice that lost contributes nothing. And a Yield with no enclosing Repeat does nothing at all, which the grammar reports as a compile diagnostic rather than at runtime.

title: Stashing
description: A grammar often has to come back to connectors it left behind.
outline: An Unstash publishes what is still open
The wire into an Unstash is a trigger
body:
A grammar often has to come back to connectors it left behind. The doorways of every room the first phase placed, the ends of a corridor network, the sockets a branch deliberately did not build on. A wire carries those to the next node. A name carries them anywhere.

## A bank is a name

*Every Stash carrying one name feeds one set of connectors, and that set lasts the run.*

A **Stash** is a sink. Connectors flow in, nothing flows out, and the branch it sits on ends there. What flows in goes into the **bank** its `Stash Name` addresses, as a reference to each connector rather than as a copy of the frontier.

Several Stashes carrying one name feed one bank, from anywhere in the graph, which is how separate phases contribute to the same set. The name is what identifies a bank, so a **Subgraph** inlined twice with a `Stash A` inside it fills one bank rather than two.

What a Stash banks is the wire's decision, the ordinary edge scope question from [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar). A narrowed wire banks that slice. A wire carrying the whole frontier banks everything open at that moment. A wire whose scope is already exhausted banks nothing.

The other sink in the grammar is a **Yield**, and the two are different tools. A Yield hands the frontier to the next iteration of the **Repeat** it sits in, and its captures reset every iteration. A bank belongs to no node, lasts the whole run, and is read by name.

## An Unstash publishes what is still open

*The bank names connectors. The run decides which of them are still there.*

An **Unstash** names a bank and publishes it to everything below it, at the moment flow reaches it. What it publishes is the part of the bank still open: a connector bonded or built on since it was stashed has stopped being a place to build, and it is not offered.

Reading a bank does not empty it. A second Unstash on the same bank publishes whatever is left by then, and an Unstash inside a **Repeat** body sees a smaller set each iteration as the body consumes it.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: stashing-bank-remainder | SHOWS: That an Unstash publishes whatever of a bank is still open, and that reading a bank never empties it. | ELEMENTS: Three stages left to right, separated by thin vertical rules, each with a small grammar strip above it in the grammar node style and a copy of the same structure below it. Stage one headed Stash: the strip is a Module box wired into a Stash box labelled A, and the structure below shows four open sockets, all four marked as banked. Beside that structure, a small list standing for bank A, holding four entries. Stage two headed Building: the strip is a Growth box, the structure has grown a new piece onto two of those four sockets so that pair now reads as bonded rather than open, and the bank list beside it still holds four entries with those two dimmed. Stage three headed Unstash: the strip is an Unstash box labelled A, the bank list is unchanged, and arrows run from its two live entries to the two sockets still open in the structure, which are the only ones highlighted. | MUST BE CLEAR: The bank never shrank between the stages. What changed is how many of its entries still name an open socket, and that is what the Unstash hands downstream. | NOTE: the bank list is a reading aid for the figure, not a panel that exists in the editor.
> The bank is identical in all three. What changes is how much of it is still somewhere to build.


An Unstash with nothing to publish hands its children an empty set, and reports which case it was: nothing has been stashed under that name yet, everything stashed has since been consumed, or the name pairs with no Stash in the graph. A placing node below it then places nothing, and reports that in its own words.


> **Note.**
> Under **Grammar Growth** on Parallel execution the banks are shared across seed points, so an Unstash can publish connectors another seed stashed. Sequential runs each assignment separately and each run starts with empty banks. Merges behave the same way, for the same reason.


## The ordering is yours

*Nothing waits for a bank to fill.*

A **Merge** holds its downstream until every path feeding it has finished. An Unstash holds nothing: it reads the bank as it stands when flow arrives. Reach one before the Stashes that fill it have run, and it publishes a partial bank or an empty one.

A **Sequence** is what settles that. Every step drains completely before the next one begins, so stashing in one step and unstashing in a later step is a guarantee rather than a hope. Anything finer than a step, an arm of a **Branch** against another arm, an arm against a continuation, is not an ordering the grammar promises.

A Stash and an Unstash of the same name inside one **Repeat** body is a rolling accumulator rather than a mistake: each iteration publishes what the previous ones left open and banks whatever it opened in turn. Nothing objects to it, and nothing about a bank is per-iteration.

## The wire into an Unstash is a trigger

*It says when, not what.*

Every other input in a grammar hands a node connectors to work with. An Unstash's input hands it a moment. The frontier arriving there is discarded and the bank replaces it, which is why the editor draws that wire dashed and grey and offers no edge scope on it: there is no scope to set, because nothing of that frontier survives.

To build on the bank and something else together, wire the Unstash and the other path into a **Merge** and continue from the union.


> **Warning.**
> **A disabled Unstash keeps running**
>
> Disabling a node turns it into a pass-through **Filter**, and for most nodes that reads as switching it off. An Unstash disabled this way still passes something on: the frontier that reached its input, which is the one thing it normally throws away. The section below it carries on building, against a different set of connectors than the one it was authored for.


## What the compile tells you

*What a pair can be wrong about, and why none of it stops a run.*

| Reported | Means |
|---|---|
| A Stash has no name | It banks nothing, because nothing can address it. Name it, or remove it. |
| An Unstash matches no Stash | It publishes an empty frontier, and everything under it runs against nothing. |
| A bank is never unstashed | Recorded as information rather than a problem. A phase that banks for a phase you have not built yet is a legitimate thing to have. |

Renaming a Stash carries its Unstashes with it. The pairing records which Stash was picked, not only its name, so the rename reaches every Unstash that named it and the bank keeps its readers.

title: Subgraphs
description: Reusing one grammar inside another: how a subgraph runs as one unit, how its boundaries wire up, what it sees of the frontier, and what Isolate does to the rules around it.
outline: Isolate inside a region compiles a warning
body:
A **Subgraph** node runs another grammar asset as one unit. It is how a staircase, an entrance or a corridor recipe gets authored once and used in several grammars, and how one grammar stays readable past the size where everything fits on one canvas.

## One node, one run

_The body runs when flow reaches the node, in the caller's lineage, and answers as a whole._

The sub-asset's nodes are cloned into the parent when the grammar compiles, so there is one flat graph to execute and a sub-asset is never modified by being used. The Subgraph node itself stays in that graph, and it is what runs the body: when flow reaches one of its input pins, the node enters the body through the matching **Graph Input**, lets everything inside it finish, and only then hands the results out through its output pins.

The body inherits the caller's lineage. The random stream that drives every Choice, Repeat and Optional inside it is the seed point's own stream, so the same seed makes the same decisions whether the recipe is drawn inline or referenced, and two seed points with different seeds diverge inside a subgraph exactly as they do outside one. Regions in force around the node apply inside it (unless the node isolates itself, below), and a Yield inside the body still feeds the Repeat that encloses the node.

Each seed point that reaches the node runs the body on its own. A subgraph reached by twenty seeds runs twenty times, with twenty separate frontiers and twenty separate sets of decisions.

A subgraph that references an asset already being expanded further up the chain is a **cycle**, and compiling reports it and stops rather than expanding forever. Cloning also multiplies: every reference clones the whole sub-asset, so the flattened graph can be far larger than anything you drew, and it is the flattened count that meets the ceiling of 65,535 compiled nodes per grammar. Past it the compile fails with an error naming the count, and the fix it suggests is the real one, less Subgraph nesting or a split grammar.

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-subgraph-scope | SHOWS: That a Subgraph node runs its body as one enclosed unit at run time: flow enters through a named input, the body runs to completion inside its own frontier, and the outputs publish afterwards. | ELEMENTS: A parent grammar strip of node boxes in the grammar node style, with one box labelled Subgraph in the middle carrying two named input pins and one named output pin. Below it, connected by a bracket, the body drawn as an enclosed panel: two Graph Input boxes at its left edge, inner nodes in the middle, one Graph Output box at its right edge. A shaded region inside the panel holds a few connector marks labelled as the connectors handed in plus the ones placed inside; connector marks outside the panel, belonging to the parent, are drawn faded. A small rewind arrow on the panel's frame labelled rolls back if anything inside fails. | MUST BE CLEAR: The body is a unit with its own view of the frontier, not a set of nodes pasted in place. Nothing leaves through the output until the whole body has finished, and a failure inside undoes the whole body.
> The body runs as one enclosed unit. It sees what it was handed and what it places, and its outputs publish only once everything inside has finished.

## Boundaries

_Named ports on the sub-asset, matched to pins on the node that runs it._

A sub-asset declares its edges with **Graph Input** and **Graph Output** nodes. Each carries a **boundary name**, and the Subgraph node in the parent exposes one pin per boundary. Wiring is by name, so renaming a boundary changes which parent pin it answers to.

Graph Input hands whatever arrived on the parent's matching pin to the nodes behind it. Graph Output collects every flow that reaches it while the body runs, and the Subgraph node publishes that collection on the matching output pin once the body is done, to every wire leaving that pin, whatever scope the wire asks for. An output nothing reached publishes nothing, so the nodes behind it stay silent, the same way a Yield nothing reached feeds nothing.

An edge whose pin carries no boundary name binds to the **first** input or output boundary declared in the sub-asset. An edge whose pin names a boundary the sub-asset no longer declares is dropped, and compiling warns with the name. A subgraph that suddenly behaves as though everything is wired to one port, or that has gone quiet on one pin, is worth checking for exactly that after a rename.

Wiring several input pins of the same node runs the body once per arrival, with only that input's boundary handing anything in; compiling warns when it sees it. A recipe that needs every input present before it starts is not expressible yet.

## Failure inside the body

_Anything that fails inside the body undoes the whole body._

Inside a subgraph, a node that fails, whether a required placement that finds nothing or a Sequence whose required step fails, fails the body. Everything the body placed is removed, and the Subgraph node reports the failure to whatever runs it. Under a parent Choice that means the Choice tries its next option, exactly as it would for a failing option drawn inline. With `Required` off on the Subgraph node the body still rolls back, but the node reports success and the flow continues past it with nothing placed.

This is stricter than the same nodes drawn inline, where a failure that surfaces only after the parent has moved on is reported and skipped rather than undone. The subgraph is the unit; it either happens or it does not.

## What the body sees

_The connectors it was handed, and the ones it places._

`Frontier Scope` decides which open connectors a node inside the body may read when it asks for the full frontier, which is what a Sequence step, a Filter with no narrowed wire, or a Growth on a full-frontier wire does.

| Value      | The body                                                                                                          |
| ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Sealed** | Sees the connectors handed to its inputs plus everything it places itself, and nothing else. The default.         |
| **Open**   | Sees the whole live frontier, the parent's open connectors included.                                             |

Sealed is what makes a recipe predictable wherever it is used: a Growth inside it grows from what it was given, never from an open socket three rooms away that happened to be closer. A subgraph nested inside a sealed subgraph sees what its own inputs carried, and once it returns, whatever it placed belongs to the outer body's view too.

## Inherit or Isolate

_Whether the body sees the rules in force around it._

`Rule Scope` decides whether the enclosing region rules reach inside the body.

| Value       | The body                                                                                          |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Inherit** | Sees the parent's enclosing region rules, like any other node in that region. The default.        |
| **Isolate** | Runs under a region of its own that replaces the inherited rules, so nothing from outside applies |

Isolate is what makes a subgraph a genuinely self-contained recipe: whatever biases and constraints the parent has in force, the body behaves the same way everywhere it is used. The isolating region is the node's own; it opens when the body starts and closes when it ends, however many inputs or outputs the sub-asset declares.

> **Warning.**
> **Isolate inside a region compiles a warning**
>
> Placing an **Isolate** subgraph inside a region reads as though the region's rules apply to it. They do not, and that is the whole point of Isolate, so the combination is worth stating out loud rather than letting it look like a rule that failed to take.
>
> Compiling names the subgraph and lists the regions whose rules will be muted inside it. Switch to **Inherit** if you wanted them to apply; leave it if the isolation is deliberate.

## Grammar properties across the boundary

_The sub-asset's overrides survive, and the parent wins a name clash._

A sub-asset declares its own Grammar Properties schema, and its placement nodes' `Property Overrides` were authored against it. Cloning keeps them: the body's nodes arrive with their overrides intact, so a recipe that stamps values on what it places goes on doing so in every parent.

The schemas merge into one registry at compile, the parent's declarations first and then each referenced sub-asset's, deduplicated by name with the first declaration winning. Where the parent and a sub-asset declare the same property name, the parent's type and default are the ones the compiled grammar carries.

## External or embedded

_One of these two is the working path today._

`Subgraph Source` chooses where the referenced grammar lives.

**External** points at a separately saved grammar asset, which is the reusable case and the one to use.

**Embedded** references a grammar instanced inside the parent asset. The data side is complete, but the editor support for authoring one inline is scaffolded rather than finished, so there is currently no comfortable way to build one. Treat it as reserved.

title: Targets
description: Seek and Route: two nodes that build toward somewhere, one by feeling its way and one by solving first, and how a grammar says what to aim at.
outline: A target is a live connector
A target-fed node waits for its contributions
Exclude Own Branch excludes everything on a single-seed run
Corridor modules and closing modules are two pools
A found route can still fail to commit
body:
Most of a grammar builds outward without caring where it ends up. **Seek** and **Route** are the nodes that build _toward_ something: they grow a corridor from where they are to a connector somewhere else in the structure, and try to join onto it.

They read as synonyms and they are opposites. Seek feels its way and may never arrive. Route solves the whole corridor before placing anything, and either finds one or tells you why it could not.

## A target is a live connector

_Nothing is stored, so the set changes underneath you, on purpose._

Targets are resolved against the live frontier every time they are needed. A connector that has since been grown from, or bridged into, stops being a target automatically, with no bookkeeping and nothing to invalidate.

That is what lets a grammar aim at structure it did not build and does not control. The aim points are whatever is genuinely still open at the moment the question is asked.

### Saying what to aim at

_The node has no target selector. You wire one._

Both nodes take target edges on a dedicated **Target** pin, and a wire landing there is a contribution rather than a flow: it adds to the aim set instead of triggering an evaluation.

Narrowing is authored upstream. Route a **Filter** from [Narrowing the Frontier](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/narrowing-the-frontier) into the Target pin and its survivors become the candidates, which is why neither node carries a selector of its own. Anything the Filter can express, the aim set can express.

> **Note.**
> **A target-fed node waits for its contributions**
>
> A Seek or Route with anything wired to its Target pin parks its own evaluation until the dispatch queue reaches a fixed point, so every contribution has landed before it runs. It is the same timing a **Merge** uses, for the same reason, and [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching) covers it.

Two exclusions apply on top of whatever the Filter allowed, and both exist to stop a node aiming at itself.

`Min Target Hops` is a **minimum loop size**. A target closer than that many hops through the placement tree is excluded, because a near ancestor or an immediate child is a degenerate self-target: joining onto it produces a loop of two or three modules rather than the circuit you wanted. A module further back along the same path is a legitimate closure, which is why this is a distance and not a flag.

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-min-target-hops | SHOWS: That the hop count is measured through the placement tree and not through space, so the two can disagree completely. | ELEMENTS: One annotated scene. A structure that has grown in a loose spiral, so that its earliest and latest modules end up physically close together. The connector currently being grown from is marked as the source. Two candidate targets are marked. Target A sits far away across the page but is only two hops from the source through the parent links, and the two links are drawn and counted; it is struck out and annotated as excluded. Target B sits close to the source in space but is nine hops away through the tree, its path traced the long way round the spiral and counted; it is highlighted as eligible. A small key states Min Target Hops is set to three. | MUST BE CLEAR: The excluded target is the far one and the eligible target is the near one. The count runs along the parent links, and physical distance plays no part in the exclusion at all.
> Counted along the parent links, never across the gap. The far target is excluded and the near one is not.

> **Danger.**
> **Exclude Own Branch excludes everything on a single-seed run**
>
> `Exclude Own Branch` is a multi-seed refinement. It drops targets that share a branch with the connector being grown from, following bridge merges.
>
> A run grown from one seed is **one branch**. Turn this on there and every target is excluded, the node never finds anything to aim at, and the symptom is a Seek that reports no live targets on a structure visibly full of open connectors.
>
> Both nodes name this case in their stop message instead of folding it into the hop exclusion, so the log separates it from a `Min Target Hops` set too high.

## Seek grows toward

_A greedy corridor that steers, stalls and gives up._

**Seek** places one module at a time, choosing each next placement by how much closer it gets to the nearest target, with `Facing Influence` deciding how much it also favours connectors already pointing that way. It scores where each candidate module and its attachment would actually land, which is what lets a corridor turn a corner rather than only running straight at the goal.

When it gets within `Close Distance` it tries to join. Two connectors that land coincident bond directly with no module between them; otherwise it reaches for a spanning module.

**Because it is greedy, it can get stuck**, and it is built to notice. `Min Progress` sets how much closer an iteration must get to count as progress, and `No Progress Limit` sets how many fruitless iterations in a row it tolerates before stopping. Without those it would spin against an obstacle until the run's budget ran out.

`Grow From Both Ends` runs a second corridor from the target side back toward the source, alternating which head advances. It is substantially more robust than one greedy head, because two corridors converging can route around an obstacle that would stall either one alone.

> **Warning.**
> **Corridor modules and closing modules are two pools**
>
> A Seek's descriptor names what the corridor is built from, and never what closes the gap. Closing has its own pool and its own setting: `Closing Descriptor`, on both Seek and Route. Left untouched it is the **Bridge Only** modules, the same pool a **Join** draws from in [Joining and Pruning](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/joining-and-pruning).
>
> Fill it in and it **replaces** that pool rather than narrowing it, which is the contract a Join's descriptor already has: a module named there closes whether or not it carries a Bridge Only connector. That is how one Seek closes with an archway and another with a plain corridor piece, from the same library.
>
> An empty closing pool leaves a Seek able to build corridor after corridor and never join. Two connectors landing coincident still bond with no module between them, so this is a narrower failure than it sounds, but any real gap stays open. The node warns once and names which pool came up empty, the library's or the descriptor's, because this is the one failure that looks identical to bad luck.

## Route solves, then commits

_It searches poses before it places anything._

**Route** does not grow. It searches, over virtual placements, for a sequence of modules that gets from here to a target and mates with it. Only once it has one does it place anything.

That makes "there is no corridor" a first-class answer rather than something you infer from a run that wandered off. The search is bounded by `Max Expansions`, and exhausting it is reported as exactly that.

| Setting            | Decides                                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Max Expansions`   | How hard it looks before giving up. Exhausting it is a reported outcome, not a failure state.                                                                 |
| `Max Path Length`  | How long a corridor may be, in modules                                                                                                                        |
| `Heuristic Weight` | `1` finds the shortest corridor. Higher is faster and returns near-minimal ones.                                                                              |
| `Mate Tolerance`   | How exactly a corridor's end must line up with the target to count as an exact mate                                                                           |
| `Close Distance`   | A clamp on top of what the spanning pool can physically bridge. `0` lets the pool decide, and with no Bridge Only modules at all, `0` means exact mates only. |

Every value in this table, and every distance, budget and switch on a Seek, can be read from the seed points instead of typed. A value the search cannot run on is corrected as it is read: Seek raises a bound `Close Distance` or `No Progress Limit` below `1` to `1`, and Route does the same for `Max Expansions`, `Max Path Length`, `Heuristic Weight` and `Pose Epsilon Rotation`, keeping `Mate Tolerance` above zero.

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grammar-seek-vs-route | SHOWS: The difference between feeling a way toward a target and solving the route before placing anything. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both have the same start module on the left, the same target connector on the right, and the same obstacle shape between them. Left panel headed Seek: a corridor of placed modules running from the start toward the target, bending as it goes, with two short dead-end stubs marked as abandoned attempts where it pushed into the obstacle and backed off, and the corridor ending short of the target with a gap marked as never closed. Right panel headed Route: a faint cloud of ghosted candidate poses spread around the obstacle representing the search, and over it one solid committed corridor running cleanly around the obstacle and mating with the target connector. | MUST BE CLEAR: The left corridor is the record of how it searched, because it searched by building. The right one shows searching and building as separate things, and only the found route was ever placed.
> Seek searches by building, so its attempts are in the result. Route searches first and places only what it found.

> **Warning.**
> **A found route can still fail to commit**
>
> The search works on poses. Committing places real modules, and the connector constraint pipeline can move a placement off the pose that was searched. Past `Drift Tolerance Position` or `Drift Tolerance Rotation`, that drift is a failure: Route bans the offending step, re-searches for a different corridor, and abandons the attempt after three tries.
>
> Constraints that introduce variation are the usual cause, which makes this a strange one to diagnose: the search was right, the corridor exists, and the pieces did not land where they were solved to land. The report prints the drift it measured against the tolerance that rejected it, which is what separates a tolerance set too tight from a constraint moving placements further than you meant it to.
>
> Raise the tolerance and the search is unaffected. `Pose Epsilon Position` and `Pose Epsilon Rotation` look like the same numbers and are not: those quantize the **search**, deciding when two poses count as the same one, so coarsening them explores less and loses corridors. The other commit failures are more ordinary: the run's budget running out mid-corridor, a head connector consumed by something else before its step committed, or a constraint vetoing a step.

### Falling short

_Three settings decide what survives, and whether anything downstream runs._

Neither node is required to succeed, and both distinguish arriving from getting close.

| Setting                                                 | Effect                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Reach Is Success`                                      | Getting within close range counts as success even if nothing could span the last gap. The corridor was the deliverable. |
| `Keep Partial Corridor` (Seek) / `Keep Partial` (Route) | The modules placed on a failed attempt stay. Off, the whole attempt is rolled back as if it never ran.                  |
| `Partial Counts As Success`                             | Children dispatch anyway                                                                                                |

Without one of those, a node that failed to join dispatches no children, and the chain below it does not run. Both report the reason once, naming which of their exits fired, how many modules they placed, whether the corridor was kept or rolled back, and whether close range was ever reached.

### Choosing between them

_Ask whether an approximate answer is worth anything._

| Use       | When                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Seek**  | The corridor itself is the point, and a near miss still improves the result. Organic connections, tunnels that should look like they were dug, cases where getting most of the way there is fine. |
| **Route** | The connection has to be exact, or not attempted. Structural links, anything where a corridor that stops short is worse than no corridor, and cases where you need to know that no route exists.  |

Seek is cheaper and produces corridors with character, since its dead ends and detours are visible in the result. Route costs a search and produces the shortest thing that works.

title: Growing
description: Growth keeps a frontier: the set of open connectors it could still expand from.
outline: Weight is spent as well as drawn
body:
**Valency : Grow Points** starts from seed points and builds outward, mating modules connector to connector. Nothing exists before it runs: every position in the result was created by an attachment.

## The loop

*Attach a module, expose its remaining connectors, repeat.*

Growth keeps a **frontier**: the set of open connectors it could still expand from. Each step takes one, finds a module whose connector can mate with it, places that module, and adds whatever connectors the new module brought with it back into the frontier.

Two connectors are consumed by every attachment, the one grown from and the one attached by, so a module with four sockets contributes three new frontier entries rather than four.

Growth ends when the frontier empties, which happens when nothing is left open or nothing will fit, or when a budget stops it first. In practice a budget usually gets there first.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-frontier-loop | SHOWS: How the frontier grows and shrinks as modules are placed. | ELEMENTS: Four steps left to right. Step one, a single seed module with three open connectors, each marked as a frontier entry, count reading 3. Step two, one frontier connector is consumed and a new module attached there, its own consumed connector marked, its two remaining ones added, count reading 4. Step three, another expansion, count reading 5. Step four, an expansion where the new module has only the one connector, count dropping to 4. A small running tally of the frontier count sits under each step. | MUST BE CLEAR: Each attachment removes one entry and adds however many the new module has left over. The count can go up or down, and growth stops when it reaches zero.
> Every attachment spends one open connector and contributes whatever the new module has spare.


## What it needs

| Input | Is |
|---|---|
| **Seed points** | Where growth starts. One structure per seed. |
| [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) | The library to grow from |
| **A growth strategy** | Which frontier connector gets expanded next |

Modules must carry connectors to take part. Growth never reads orbitals.

## Strategies

*Which connector comes off the frontier next, which is the whole silhouette of the result.*

| Strategy | Expands | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| **BFS Growth** | Breadth first | Even radial expansion from each seed |
| **DFS Growth** | Depth first | Long tendrils and corridors |
| **Random Growth** | A random open connector | Organic, unpredictable spread |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-strategy-silhouettes | SHOWS: That the strategy alone decides the shape of the result. | ELEMENTS: Three results side by side, each grown from one seed marked identically, each using the same small set of module shapes, each stopped at the same module count. Left, BFS: a compact roughly circular mass filling outward evenly. Middle, DFS: one or two long snaking runs reaching far from the seed with little width. Right, Random: an irregular blotchy spread, denser in places, with a few short offshoots. Under each, the strategy name only. | MUST BE CLEAR: Same seed, same library, same budget. The three silhouettes are wildly different and nothing but the strategy changed.
> Same seed, same library, same module count. Only the expansion order differs.


This is the cheapest lever in the whole system. Swapping the strategy node changes what you get more than almost any amount of rule tuning, so it is worth trying all three before adjusting anything else.

## Budgets

*Growth expands until something stops it, so something must.*

| Setting | Default | Stops growth when |
|---|---|---|
| **Max Total Modules** | `100` | That many modules have been placed, across everything |
| **Max Depth** | `10` | A branch reaches that many attachments from its seed |
| **Max Weight Per Seed** | `-1`, unlimited | The cumulative weight grown from one seed reaches the budget |
| **Stop On First Failure** | Off | A branch cannot fill one of its sockets, rather than trying the rest |


> **Note.**
> **Weight is spent as well as drawn**
>
> A module's weight decides how often it is picked, and it is also the currency **Max Weight Per Seed** spends. A heavy module is both more likely and more expensive.
>
> That gives you a budget denominated in something meaningful: set a weight budget and expensive pieces naturally appear fewer times than cheap ones, without capping any of them individually.


The two depth-shaped limits do different jobs. **Max Total Modules** bounds the whole run, so with several seeds they compete for one pool. **Max Depth** bounds how far any single branch can reach, which is the one to use when you want breadth without long runs.

## Space, overlap and containment

*Growth checks nothing spatially unless something asks it to.*

Attachment is decided by connectors, and connectors know nothing about volume. Two pieces that mate perfectly can occupy the same space, and growth will place them there quite happily unless told otherwise.

What decides otherwise is **placement conditions**, authored per module. A module carrying none refuses nothing on spatial grounds of its own, which is a deliberate setting rather than an oversight: plenty of modules are decoration that should sit inside other things.

Under a grammar there is a second asker. A rule authored in the grammar can refuse a placement on the same spatial grounds without any module carrying a condition, which [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules) covers.

| Condition | Rejects a placement when |
|---|---|
| **Footprint Overlap** | The candidate's footprint intersects anything already placed |
| **Footprint Overlap (Advanced)** | The same, with per-axis tolerance and tag-based exemptions                                                       |
| **Footprint Penetration** | Overlap exceeds an allowed penetration depth, so touching is fine and burying is not |
| **Spatial Domain** | The candidate falls outside, or inside, a named region you supplied |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-placement-conditions | SHOWS: What each spatial condition does to the same growth run. | ELEMENTS: Three panels, same seed and same library in each. One, no conditions: the structure grows through itself, several modules visibly interpenetrating, marked as accepted. Two, Footprint Overlap: the same growth but the intersecting placements are shown greyed and crossed at the point they were refused, and growth has routed around them into clear space. Three, Spatial Domain: a shaded region outline supplied as input, with growth filling it and stopping cleanly at its boundary, one refused candidate shown crossed just outside the edge. | MUST BE CLEAR: The first panel is not a bug. It is what happens with no conditions authored, and it is sometimes what you want.
> No conditions, overlap rejection, and containment in a supplied region. The same run in all three.


**Spatial Domain** is how growth gets confined to a space. Feed spatial data into the **External Domains** pin, tag it `SpatialChannel:<Name>`, and a condition pointed at that channel keeps growth inside a room, along a wall, or out of a volume you want left clear. See [Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap) for the channels themselves.


> **Warning.**
> **Two opposite symptoms, one setting**
>
> **Pieces growing through each other** means the modules involved carry no overlap condition. Nothing is broken; nothing was ever asked to check.
>
> **Growth stopping far short of its budget** usually means the opposite: conditions are rejecting nearly everything. Footprints authored larger than the pieces they describe are the common cause, since every candidate then collides with its own neighbours.
>
> Both are the same dial, from opposite ends. Check the footprints before adjusting the rules.


## Starting and forbidding with patterns

*Two pattern slots on the strategy, doing opposite things.*

**Seed Patterns** are stamped from the seed points as pre-built groups of modules, so growth begins from an authored arrangement rather than a single piece. Useful when every structure should start with a specific entrance, hub or base.

Every member of a stamp occupies world space like any other placement, and answers the placement conditions like one. The stamp is transactional, so a single refused member abandons the whole arrangement instead of leaving part of it: half a pattern is not a pattern. A stamp landing on a boundary it half-clears therefore reads as no stamp at all.

**Rejection Patterns** forbid arrangements. A placement that would complete one is refused, and growth tries something else. This is how you say "never produce this" without expressing it as a connector rule.

## What comes out

| Output | Is |
|---|---|
| **Vtx and Edges** | A cluster. Everything downstream that takes clusters works on it. |
| **Valency Map** | Required by anything resolving the result |
| **Bridges** | Connections made between separate branches, covered under bridges |

The result being an ordinary cluster is worth noticing: growth produces the same shape of data a solve consumes, which is what makes chaining passes possible at all.

title: Branches and Bridges
description: Growth from a single seed does not produce a single line.
body:
Growth from a single seed does not produce a single line. Every time a placed module leaves more than one connector open, the structure forks, and Valency tracks those forks as **branches**. Bridges are how separate branches get connected back to each other.

## Branches

*Every divergence starts a new line of descent.*

When a newly placed module has several connectors left open, the first one continues the branch it came from and each additional one starts a new branch. So a run from one seed becomes a tree of branches, each identified separately.

That identity exists for one purpose: **a bridge only ever joins connectors on different branches.** Two open connectors on the same branch are already connected to each other, by definition, through the path that produced them. Joining them would add a loop to something that is not actually separate.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-branch-divergence | SHOWS: How a single seed becomes several branches, and which connectors count as separate. | ELEMENTS: A growth tree from one seed. The seed places a module with three open connectors. One path continues in the seed branch colour. The other two start new branches, each drawn in its own colour, and continue outward for several modules keeping that colour. At the far ends, two open connectors from two differently coloured branches sit close together and are marked as a valid bridge candidate. Elsewhere, two open connectors of the same colour sit equally close and are marked as not a candidate. | MUST BE CLEAR: Proximity alone does not make a bridge candidate. The colours decide it, and the same-colour pair is excluded despite being just as close.
> Colour is the branch. Two open connectors are only a bridge candidate if their colours differ.


Connectors marked **Bridge Only** never cause a divergence. They keep their parent's branch, because their whole purpose is to join branches rather than to extend one.

## Natural bridges

*Two open connectors that happen to meet.*

As growth proceeds, an open connector sometimes ends up close to another one on a different branch, facing it, with types and polarity that accept each other. When that happens it is recorded as a bridge and both connectors are consumed, so nothing later grows into either of them.

This costs nothing and is always active. It is what makes growth close loops on its own: two corridors wandering out of the same room and meeting around the back become a connected circuit rather than two dead ends passing near each other.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-natural-bridge | SHOWS: A natural bridge forming, and what it costs the two connectors involved. | ELEMENTS: Three panels of the same growth, left to right. One, two branches in different colours have grown out of a shared origin and curved back toward each other, their leading open connectors still well apart, both drawn as open sockets with their facing arrows. Two, growth has continued and the two connectors now sit coincident and facing each other, highlighted, with a small check mark set showing type accepted, polarity compatible, facing opposed. Three, the same layout with a connection drawn between them, both sockets now filled rather than open, and the whole structure visibly forming a closed circuit rather than two dead ends. No new module appears in any panel. | MUST BE CLEAR: Nothing was placed to make this happen. The two ends grew into each other, and the bridge costs both connectors, so neither remains available for anything else.
> Nothing is placed. Two ends grow into each other, and both sockets are spent closing the loop.



> **Warning.**
> Bridging is an undirected meeting, so it needs **both** connector types to accept each other. A one-way compatibility pair steers growth perfectly well and will never bridge. If two branches refuse to join where they clearly should, check both rows rather than the geometry.


## Active bridging

*Off by default. Goes looking rather than waiting.*

Where natural bridging notices coincidences, active bridging searches for them. Within a configurable radius it gathers open connectors on other branches, scores the candidates, and places a dedicated module to span the gap.

Candidates are scored on three things, each independently weighted:

| Scored on | Prefers |
|---|---|
| **Distance** | Closer pairs |
| **Alignment** | Connectors already facing each other |
| **Branch diversity** | Joining different seeds over joining within one |

The module it places has to be one you authored for the job: a module whose placement policy is **Bridge Only**, which is excluded from ordinary growth and appears only as a span between branches.

A bridge occupies space like any other placement, and is checked like one. Its footprint is tested against everything already placed, and it answers its own placement conditions, which [Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap) covers, plus any grammar rule gating placements where it lands. A **Bridge Only** module authored with a footprint larger than the gaps it is meant to fill produces a run that finds pairs and spans none of them.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-active-bridge | SHOWS: An active bridge being searched for and built across a gap. | ELEMENTS: One scene, annotated. Two branches in different colours end in open connectors separated by a clear gap, too far apart to have met on their own. A faint search radius circle is centred on one of them, and inside it three candidate connectors on other branches are marked, each labelled with its score contributions: distance, alignment, branch diversity. The best-scoring candidate is highlighted. A dedicated bridge module, visibly a distinct piece and labelled Bridge Only, is drawn spanning between that pair and connecting to both. | MUST BE CLEAR: The gap is real and would never have closed by growth alone. A piece was added to span it, chosen from several candidates by score, which is what separates this from a natural bridge.
> The gap would never have closed on its own. A dedicated piece is chosen by score and placed to span it.


## Bridge roles

*Per connector, deciding what it takes part in.*

| Role | Takes part in |
|---|---|
| **Can Bridge** | Both normal growth and bridging. The default. |
| **No Bridge** | Normal growth only, never considered for bridging |
| **Bridge Only** | Bridging only, skipped entirely during normal expansion |

**Bridge Only** on a connector is what lets a module carry sockets that exist purely to be spanned to, without those sockets pulling ordinary growth into them.

## Merging branches

*What a bridge does to the two branches it joined.*

By default, bridging two branches connects them without changing their identities: they stay separate as far as later bridge checks are concerned, so more bridges between them remain possible.

A module can opt into **Merge Branches On Bridge**, which folds the two into one once it spans them. Later checks then treat everything on both sides as a single branch, so no further bridges between them will be considered.

Reach for it when a single connection between two regions is the point, and leave it off when you want a mesh of connections rather than a tree with one link per pair.

## Finding bridges after the fact

*A standalone node, for results that already exist.*

**Valency : Find Bridges** does the same job outside a growth run. It takes points that already carry resolved modules and places bridge modules between those with compatible open connectors, either by blind search or guided by edges that already exist.

That covers the case where the thing you want to connect was not produced by one growth pass: two separately grown structures, a solved layout with gaps, or anything assembled from several sources.

title: Growing From a Cluster
description: It does not care who resolved the input.
outline: The default source reads an attribute a solve never writes
body:
**Valency : Grow Cluster** takes a cluster whose modules are already resolved and grows outward from their open connectors. It is the node where the two connection models meet: solve a structure with orbitals, then grow onto it with connectors.

It does not care who resolved the input. A solve, an earlier growth pass, anything that left resolved modules on a cluster will do.

## It extends the input cluster

_The output is the input cluster with new vtx appended._

Everything that arrived comes out again, in place, with the grown modules added to the same cluster. Nothing is rebuilt and nothing is discarded, so a downstream node sees one structure rather than two that need merging.

Newly grown vtx are flagged, on by default, with an attribute named `Grown`. Everything from the input reads false and everything new reads true, which is what lets you partition the result afterwards, spawn the two halves differently, or run a second pass over only what the first one added.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-cluster-extends | SHOWS: That the input structure survives intact and the result is one cluster, not two. | ELEMENTS: Left, a solved cluster: a compact grid-like arrangement of modules, all drawn solid, with a few open connectors marked on its outer faces. Right, the same arrangement unchanged in the same positions, now with additional modules attached at those open connectors, drawn in a distinct treatment. A small legend maps the two treatments to Grown false and Grown true. | MUST BE CLEAR: The original modules are identical and un-moved between the two sides. The result is a single cluster whose members differ only by a flag.
> The input survives untouched. What is new is flagged, not separated.


## Choosing what to grow from

_An optional vtx filter picks the seeds. Everything else still matters._

Connect a filter to the **Vtx Filters** pin and the vtx that pass become seeds. Connect nothing and every resolved vtx is a seed.

What happens to the rest is the interesting part, and both defaults are on:

| Setting                    | Non-seed modules                                                                      |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Non Seeds As Obstacles** | Register their footprints, so growth will not place through them                      |
| **Non Seeds In Pool**      | Join the growth history, so bridges can reach back to them and a grammar can see them |

Together those mean the parts you did not select still shape the result. They are respected as occupied space and reachable as bridge targets; they do not sprout anything themselves.

### What counts as already used

_The most consequential setting here, and its default suits one input rather than all of them._

Growth only expands genuinely open connectors, so it has to work out which ones the input already spent. There are four ways to decide, and the right one depends on where the cluster came from.

| Source                        | Reads                                                                                                   |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Connector Claims**          | The per-vtx claim mask written by generative growth. A missing attribute means every connector is open. |
| **Edge Connector Attributes** | Per-edge connector data, falling back to orbital inference when absent                                  |
| **Orbital Inference**         | Infers spent connectors from geometry: each edge's world direction against the connector directions on both its endpoints |
| **All Open**                  | Treats every connector as open, so growth may re-enter sockets that are already connected               |

**Orbital Inference** claims conservatively. Where several connectors on one module point the same way, an edge along that direction claims all of them, because leaving one unclaimed would let growth re-enter a socket that is already connected. The node says so in a warning, and it is worth reading as an instruction to supply the real data instead: a cluster carrying claims or per-edge connector attributes never has to guess.


> **Note.**
> **The default source reads an attribute a solve never writes**
>
> **Connector Claims** is the default, and it reads an attribute that _generative growth_ writes. A cluster that came from a solve has no such attribute, and a missing attribute is taken to mean **everything is open**.
>
> So feeding solve output straight in, on defaults, lets growth attach into connectors that are already occupied. The structure grows through its own connections.
>
> For a solved cluster, use **Orbital Inference**: it works out what is spent from the cluster edges themselves, which is exactly the information a solve leaves behind. Keep **Connector Claims** for input that came from a growth pass.


A seed with no free connectors left is quietly demoted to a non-seed, so a fully-connected interior does not need excluding by hand.

## Budgets and limits count differently

_Two things that both sound like caps, and only one ignores the input._

**Max Total Modules** caps the modules this pass **adds**. Whatever arrived does not count against it, so a budget of fifty means fifty new pieces regardless of how large the input was.

**Spawn limits** from the library behave the opposite way by default: every input vtx resolved against the ruleset counts toward its module's limits, seed or not. A module already used ten times in the input has ten fewer uses available.

That combination is usually what you want. The budget bounds the work this node does; the limits bound how much of a given piece exists in total. It is worth being deliberate about the second one when extending a result several times, since each pass inherits the tally of every pass before it.

## What comes out

| Output            | Is                                                             |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Vtx and Edges** | The input cluster, extended, with grown vtx flagged            |
| **Valency Map**   | Including the grown entries. This is the one to chain onward.  |
| **Bridges**       | Any connections made between separate branches during the pass |

Because grown modules add entries to the map, the map this node emits supersedes the one it was given. Feeding a downstream node the input map instead resolves the original modules and loses everything this pass added.

title: Tensor Guidance
description: Growth expands wherever its strategy happens to look next, which is why the strategies produce such different silhouettes from the same library.
outline: A seed whose connectors are all pruned places one module and stops
body:
Growth expands wherever its strategy happens to look next, which is why the strategies produce such different silhouettes from the same library. Tensor guidance gives that choice a direction to prefer: every open connector is scored on how well it points along a sampled field, and the frontier is reordered, or thinned, by that score.

## What alignment measures

_One dot product per connector, taken once, at the moment it enters the frontier._

An open connector has a position and a forward axis, as [Connectors](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/connectors) sets out, and its forward points out into the space the next module will occupy. Guidance samples the field at that connector's own transform and compares the two directions, producing a signed value: `1` for pointing straight downfield, `0` for perpendicular, `-1` for pointing straight back up it.

That value is computed once, when the connector is created, and never revisited. A connector that waits a long time in the frontier keeps the alignment it was born with, whatever has been built around it since.

Where no effector reaches, the sample fails and the connector is scored exactly neutral. It is also never pruned, so growth beyond the field's reach behaves as though guidance were switched off rather than as though the field opposed it.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-tensor-alignment | SHOWS: What alignment measures, and where it is measured. | ELEMENTS: A field drawn as a sparse set of faint direction marks curving gently left to right across the panel. One placed module sits in it, an L outline with an inside corner, carrying four open connectors: one on a long face pointing downfield, one in the notch pointing across, one on the short end pointing back upfield, and one on the far side sitting past the last field mark. Each of the first three shows its own forward arrow beside the field direction sampled at that exact location, with the angle between the pair marked and the resulting value labelled: near 1, near 0, near -1. The fourth carries no angle mark and is labelled no field. | MUST BE CLEAR: The comparison is between one connector forward and the field where that connector sits, not where its module sits. The connector with no field is not scored low, it is scored neutral. | NOTE: A field direction mark is a fifth kind of arrow, which the four link kinds in DIAGRAMS.md do not cover. Settle what it looks like there rather than reusing the flow arrow.
> Measured per connector, at the connector, against the field where it actually sits.


Only the sample's direction is read. Alignment is a dot against a normalized field direction, so nothing about the field's magnitude reaches the score. `Invert`, under `Tensor Sampling Settings`, does change the outcome, because reversing the field swaps which connectors count as aligned.

### Turning it on

_Two switches, and neither does anything alone._

Guidance runs when `Enabled` is set under `Tensor Guidance` **and** tensor factories are connected to the `Tensors` pin. With one but not the other, growth runs exactly as it would with no guidance at all and says nothing about it.

> The pin sits in the _advanced_ list until `Enabled` is set, at which point it joins the normal pins.

If the tensor handler fails to initialise, the node warns and grows unguided rather than failing the run.


> **Note.**
> Where a tensor's behaviour depends on the point doing the sampling, that point is the seed its branch grew from, not the connector being scored. Every connector in a branch resolves against the same one, so varying the seed points varies the field response per structure.


## How each strategy reads it

_The same numbers, three different amounts of effect._

| Strategy          | Reads alignment as                                             | Effect                                                   |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Random Growth** | The weight in a weighted draw over the whole frontier          | Strongest. The score is the weight.                      |
| **DFS Growth**    | Push order, so the stack pops the best-aligned connector first | Strong. Tendrils dive along field lines.                 |
| **BFS Growth**    | The final tiebreak, after depth and connector priority         | Weakest. Separates only connectors already tied on both. |

BFS keeps its layering under guidance: it still finishes one depth ring before starting the next, and alignment only sorts within a ring. For growth that visibly follows a field, DFS and Random are the two that respond.

## Shaping the preference

_Two dials for how hard alignment pushes, and one that changes what it pushes toward._

`Influence` blends between neutral and the full alignment score. `Power` is a falloff exponent applied before that blend, so values above `1` sharpen the preference and leave meaningful weight only on the well-aligned.

Both change the magnitude of the preference, and only **Random Growth** reads magnitudes. DFS and BFS read the ranking, which any positive `Influence` and `Power` leave in the same order. Setting `Influence` to `0` flattens the ranking too, which leaves the gate below as the only thing guidance still does.

`Absolute` works on the ranking itself.
