It scores a connector on how parallel it is to the field in either direction, so pointing back upfield scores as well as pointing down it and perpendicular scores lowest. Because it reorders rather than rescales, it reaches every strategy. Reach for it when the structure should run along a field rather than flow down one.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-tensor-absolute | SHOWS: How Absolute changes which connectors score well. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. The same field of parallel direction marks in both, and the same module outline with an inside corner carrying four open connectors: one pointing downfield, one pointing upfield, two pointing across. Left panel headed Signed: the downfield connector at full strength, the two across middling, the upfield one faintest. Right panel headed Absolute: the downfield and upfield connectors both at full strength, the two across faintest. A short scale strip under each panel maps strength to score. | MUST BE CLEAR: Absolute does not make the preference stronger or weaker, it changes which directions the preference is for. Perpendicular is the worst case on the right and a middling case on the left.
> Signed prefers downfield. Absolute prefers the field axis, either way along it.


## The hard gate

_Prune Against Field removes connectors from the frontier instead of demoting them._

Weighting makes growth against the field unlikely and leaves it possible, which is the right answer when the field is a suggestion. When it is a rule, `Prune Against Field` refuses the connectors outright: anything scoring below `Prune Threshold` never enters the frontier, so nothing is ever grown from it.

The threshold is compared against the raw signed alignment.

| Threshold        | Prunes                                            |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------- |
| `-1`             | Nothing                                           |
| `-0.5` (default) | Connectors pointing appreciably back up the field |
| `0`              | Anything with a backward component at all         |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: grow-tensor-prune-gate | SHOWS: What the gate does to a run that weighting alone would not. | ELEMENTS: Two panels of the same run compared, separated by a vertical rule. Same field of parallel direction marks, same seed, same budget in both. Left panel headed Weighting only: growth has spread in every direction, denser downfield, with two branches doubling back upfield. Right panel headed Prune Against Field: those two upfield branches are absent, the connectors that would have started them drawn struck at the point of refusal, and the same budget has carried growth much further downfield instead. One connector at the far edge, past the last field mark, survives in both panels and is labelled no field. | MUST BE CLEAR: The gate did not make upfield growth rarer, it made it impossible, and the budget went downfield instead. The unsampled connector survives the gate in both panels.
> Weighting makes upfield growth unlikely. The gate makes it impossible, and the budget goes somewhere else.



> **Warning.**
> **The gate ignores Absolute**
>
> `Absolute` decides what scores well. The gate is tested on the signed alignment either way, so with both on, a connector pointing back up the field scores at the very top and is pruned regardless.
>
> For structure that should run along a field in both directions, leave `Prune Against Field` off.



> **Danger.**
> **A seed whose connectors are all pruned places one module and stops**
>
> Seeds go through the same gate as everything else. A seed that lands with every connector pointing across or against the field has its whole frontier taken at once, and that structure is one module.
>
> The symptom is a run that produces far fewer modules than its budget allows, concentrated wherever the seeds happened to be favourably oriented. Rotating the seeds fixes it. So does lowering `Prune Threshold` toward `-1`.



> **Tip.**
> Pruning takes a connector out of the frontier and out of nothing else. A connector left at the default **Can Bridge** role keeps its place in the bridge pool, so a branch arriving from elsewhere can still meet and close on it. Steering growth away from a direction does not make that side of the structure unjoinable.


## With a grammar

_The node caches the numbers, and the grammar reads them through a bias of its own._

A grammar takes over connector selection completely, so the strategy-level weighting never runs. `Influence` and `Power` shape a score a grammar never reads.

What guidance still does is the two things that happen before selection: it samples the field onto every connector entering the frontier, and it applies the gate. The **Tensor Alignment** bias then turns that cached alignment into a candidate weight, using its own `Aligned Weight`, `Misaligned Weight`, `Power` and `Absolute`, scoped to whichever region carries the rule. Several regions can respond to one field differently.

The bias returns a neutral weight whenever guidance is inactive, so a grammar built around it does nothing at all until `Enabled` is set and tensors are connected on the growth node.

title: Output
description: A solve or a growth produces points that know which module they are.
body:
A solve or a growth produces points that **know which module they are**. They do not produce anything that spawns. **Valency : Staging** is the step between the two, and without it a perfectly good result renders as nothing at all.

## What a resolved point carries

*One opaque number, and a pin that makes it mean something.*

Every point a solve or a growth resolves carries a **Valency Entry**: an attribute at `PCGEx/V/Entry/{suffix}`, defaulting to `PCGEx/V/Entry/Main`. The value is a hash, and by itself it identifies nothing.

The **Valency Map** travelling alongside on its own pin is what turns it into a module, and [Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating) covers what else rides along. Every consumer needs both, which is why the map pin is required on all of them.


> **Warning.**
> Staging reads the entry attribute named by its own `Entry Suffix`. If that does not match the suffix the producing node wrote, the attribute is missing and the run stops with an error naming exactly which attribute it looked for. Default to `Main` at both ends unless you have a reason not to.


## What Staging does

*Resolves valency-space into collection-space, and writes the pick.*

**Valency : Staging** takes the entry hash, resolves it through the map to a module, finds the collection entry that module refers to, and writes that choice onto the point.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: output-two-maps | SHOWS: That Staging sits between two different maps, taking one in and emitting the other. | ELEMENTS: A left-to-right flow of three stages. On the left, a points icon labelled resolved points carrying an attribute row reading PCGEx slash V slash Entry slash Main with an opaque hash value, and beneath it a separate pin block labelled Valency Map, both feeding into the middle. In the middle, a node box labelled Valency Staging. On the right, two outputs leaving it: the same points now carrying a second attribute row labelled collection entry pick, and a separate pin block labelled Collection Map. Small captions under each map state what it resolves: the Valency Map resolves a hash to a module, the Collection Map resolves a pick to an asset. | MUST BE CLEAR: These are two different maps travelling on two different pins, one consumed and one produced. The point keeps its entry attribute and gains a second one.
> Two maps, not one. The Valency Map comes in and resolves a hash to a module; the Collection Map goes out and resolves a pick to an asset.


| Pin | Direction | Carries |
|---|---|---|
| Points | In | The resolved result |
| **Valency Map** | In, required | What the entry hashes mean |
| Points | Out | The same points, now carrying a collection entry pick |
| **Map** | Out, required | The Collection Map a spawner needs to turn picks into assets |

Where a module refers to a whole collection rather than one entry, Staging runs that collection's own weighted picker, descending through nested sub-collections until it reaches a real asset. The point's own `$Seed` drives that draw, so the pick is stable for a given point and reshuffles when you change its seed.

## Where PCGEx takes over

*Staging ends the Valency half of the pipeline.*

Points plus a Collection Map is a PCGEx contract, not a Valency one. Everything that actually puts things in the world is the PCGEx **Staging** family: distributing instances, spawning actors, spawning level instances, loading sockets, building spline meshes.

Valency's job finishes at the pick. Which spawner follows, and how it is configured, is covered in the [PCGEx book](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex).

Which spawner reads a point depends on the module's asset type. Mesh, actor and level modules go straight to the matching spawner. A module authored by an [Assembly Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/assembly-cages) stages as a PCG data asset holding the exported arrangement, and needs **[Staging : Load PCGData](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/node-library/staging/staging-load-pcgdata)** first: it unpacks the asset's mesh, actor and level points and merges the maps they carry, and the ordinary spawners take over from there.

## Points a pattern already absorbed

*Off by default, and turning it on spawns things twice.*

Where a match from [Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/patterns) substitutes a single asset for an arrangement, the positions it absorbed stay in the cluster. They are still points, they still carry an entry, and the pattern's own output already represents them.

`Stage Consumed` decides what happens to those. Left off, they are written an explicitly invalid pick and spawn nothing, which is what you want: the pattern's replacement is already standing there. Turn it on and both appear, occupying the same space.

## Fitting and transforms

*Two settings that are off until you ask for them.*

`Scale To Fit` and `Justification` are the standard PCGEx fitting controls, applied here so a staged point's bounds can be reconciled with the asset going into them. Both default to doing nothing.

`Apply Local Transforms` is separate and also off by default. Turn it on to apply the module's own authored transform offset to the point, which matters when a cage authored its content off its own origin.

title: Reading Properties
description: Properties authored on a cage travel through compilation and sit on the module.
outline: One name, two types, and the override quietly loses
body:
Properties authored on a cage travel through compilation and sit on the module. **Valency : Load Properties** is what puts them back onto points, as ordinary attributes anything downstream can read.

It is how authored data reaches the rest of a graph: a material index chosen per piece, a gameplay value, a flag that decides what spawns alongside the module.

## What it needs

*A resolved result, and its map.*

The node reads the entry attribute at `PCGEx/V/Entry/{Entry Suffix}`, defaulting to `Main`, and resolves it through the **Valency Map** from [Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating) to find which module each point holds. Both are required, exactly as they are throughout [Output](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output).

It writes onto the points it was given and changes nothing else, so it can sit anywhere after resolution.

## Three kinds of output

*Properties, names and tags, each independently switched on.*

| Output | Writes |
|---|---|
| **Properties** | The typed property values, one attribute per mapped property, each resolved per point as described below |
| `Module Name` | The module's name, off by default |
| `Module Tags` | The module's gameplay tags, off by default |

All three are off or empty until asked for, so the node does nothing until configured. That is the first thing to check when it appears to be doing nothing.

## Mapping properties

*You name which properties come out and what they are called.*

`Properties Mapping` is a list of configurations, one per property you want written, each naming the property and the attribute to write it to. Nothing comes out that is not listed.

Two things save you filling that list by hand. `Included Schemas` pulls in property schema assets, so a shared set of properties is declared once and reused. And **Import Bonding Rules Property Output Configs** reads the configurations straight off a [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) asset, which is the fastest way to get a mapping that matches the library you are actually using.

## Where a value comes from

*Per point: the placing grammar node, then the module, then the defaults.*

For most results the answer is short: the value the cage authored, with the **Bonding Rules** asset's `Default Properties` standing in where the module never carried the property at all.

A result grown under [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar) adds a tier above both. Placing nodes there can carry property overrides against the grammar's own schema, and growth writes which node placed each point at `PCGEx/V/Grammar/{Entry Suffix}`, alongside the entry. Where that attribute is present, each property resolves per point in order:

| Tier | Wins when |
|---|---|
| The placing grammar node's override | The node carries an enabled override for the property |
| The module's own property | The cage authored it |
| The two defaults | Neither did. `Defaults Precedence` orders them, the rules asset's `Default Properties` against the grammar schema's own default values, with **Rules Defaults First** the default |

The grammar travels in the Valency Map exactly as the rules asset does, so the standing rule, take the map from the node that grew the points, is also what makes the top tier resolvable. On data no grammar produced the attribute is absent and resolution starts at the module, with nothing to configure: `Defaults Precedence` is only ever consulted for grammar-grown points.

A property the grammar declares that no module carries still comes out. Name it in the mapping and its attribute is created, with points the grammar never overrode keeping the schema's default value.


> **Warning.**
> **One name, two types, and the override quietly loses**
>
> A property name that resolves to a different concrete type on a different tier is an authoring conflict, and the mismatched source is skipped rather than converted: those points keep the attribute's default value. The symptom is an override that appears ignored, so when a grammar override is not arriving, check that the grammar schema, the cages and the rules defaults all declare the property as the same type.


## Tags as a string

*One attribute, comma-separated.*

`Module Tags` writes every tag on the module into a single comma-separated string attribute rather than one attribute per tag. That keeps the attribute count fixed whatever the library does, at the cost of needing a string test downstream rather than a boolean one.

`Short Names` emits only the leaf segment of each tag, so `Structure.Corner.Outer` becomes `Outer`. Useful when the hierarchy is for authoring and the leaf is what downstream logic cares about, and worth avoiding when two branches share a leaf name.

## Where it sits

*Anywhere after resolution, and often before staging.*

Load Properties and **Staging** are independent. Staging turns entries into asset picks; this turns entries into data. Running both is normal, in either order, and running only this one is a perfectly good way to use a Valency result as a source of information rather than of geometry.

That is worth knowing because it makes a solve usable without spawning anything: resolve modules onto a cluster, read their properties, and drive something else entirely with the answer.

title: Write Connectors
description: Connector points are positions with a facing and a type, which is exactly the shape of input a second pass wants.
outline: Claimed gives you both sides separately
body:
**Valency : Write Connectors** takes a finished result and emits one point per connector on its resolved modules, each carrying a packed reference back to the connector it came from.

Connector points are positions with a facing and a type, which is exactly the shape of input a second pass wants. That is the node's main use: chaining, so a solve or a growth can be followed by something that builds onto its sockets.

## Which connectors qualify

*Claim state decides, and the default is the chaining one.*

| `Claim Scope` | Emits |
|---|---|
| **Unclaimed** | Only connectors still open. The default. |
| **Claimed** | Only connectors a structural connection consumed |
| **Any** | Every connector |

**Unclaimed** is what chaining wants, since open sockets are where more can be built.


> **Warning.**
> On growth or grammar output where everything bonded, **Unclaimed** emits nothing at all. That is correct rather than broken: a fully closed structure has no open sockets to hand on.
>
> If a chained pass is producing nothing, check whether the upstream run left anything open before looking at this node.


## Claimed gives you both sides separately

*One point per connector, so a bond produces two.*

Each connector gets its own point, so a bonded pair emits two collocated points, each knowing only its own half of the connection.

For one point per connection, carrying both sides and knowing whether the bond was mated or spanning, use [Junctions](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/junctions). That node exists for exactly this question, and reaching for **Claimed** here is usually a sign the other node was wanted.

## What each point carries

Beyond the packed connector reference, three optional attributes describe the point.

| Attribute | Holds |
|---|---|
| `SourceIndex` | The vertex the connector belonged to. On by default. |
| `ConnectorIdentifier` | The socket's authored name. Off by default. |
| `ConnectorType` | The connector's type. Off by default. |

`SourceIndex` is the one that matters for chaining: it is what lets a downstream pass find its way back to the module that owned the socket, rather than treating the points as unrelated positions.

Vertex filters on their own pin narrow which modules contribute connectors at all, which is how a second pass is confined to part of a structure.

## Which node to reach for

| Question | Node |
|---|---|
| A second pass should build onto what a first left open | **Write Connectors**, scope **Unclaimed** |
| Something should be placed at each connection | [Junctions](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/junctions) |
| A cluster needs orbital data before solving | [Write Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/write-orbitals), or [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) if the cluster does not exist yet |

title: Solving
description: Solving never moves, adds or removes a position.
outline: Entries from another rule set are re-solved
body:
**Valency : Solve** takes a cluster you supply and works out which module belongs at each position, so that every connection between them is legal. It is Wave Function Collapse, generalised off the grid.

Solving never moves, adds or removes a position. It answers one question per node: what goes here.

## What it needs

_Three inputs, and only one of them is points._

| Input             | Is                                                                                |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Vtx and Edges** | The cluster to fill, carrying orbital data from [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) or [Write Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/write-orbitals) |
| [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) | The library to pick modules from                                                  |
| **Solver**        | Which strategy to use, as a factory node                                          |

Everything else on the node is optional and exists to steer the result.

## How a solve proceeds

_Commit a module, narrow the neighbours, repeat._

The loop is the classic one: choose a position, pick a module that fits what is already committed around it, then narrow what its neighbours can still be. Which position gets chosen next is exactly what the [Solver Strategies](concept:working-with-valency/generating/solve/solver-strategies) differ on.

The part worth knowing is what happens before a commit. **Forward checking**, on by default, rejects a candidate if committing it would leave an unresolved neighbour with no options at all. The solve looks one step ahead and declines moves that paint it into a corner.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: solve-forward-checking | SHOWS: Why a legal-looking module can still be refused. | ELEMENTS: A small cluster of five positions. One is already committed and drawn solid. A neighbouring position is being decided, with three candidate modules shown beside it. Below each candidate, the resulting candidate list of the position beyond it: the first two leave two or three options, the third leaves an empty list drawn with a cross. The third candidate is marked refused even though its own connection to the committed piece is drawn as valid. | MUST BE CLEAR: The refused candidate fits perfectly where it would sit. It is refused for what it would do to a position one step further out, which is a place the reader has to look to understand the decision.
> The refused module fits where it would go. It is refused for what it leaves the next position with.


Forward checking is what stops most dead ends before they happen, and it is why a solve on a well-authored library usually completes on the first pass.

### When positions stay unsolved

_Some positions end up with nothing that fits, and that is information._

If a pass leaves positions unsolved, the solve does not give up there. It retries, re-seeded, up to a configurable number of extra attempts, and keeps the best result rather than the last one.

When attempts run out, the unsolved positions stay unsolved. That is a genuine answer: the rules could not be satisfied there. Loosening everything until something appears will produce output that no longer means what you intended, so it is worth reading the result first.

| Usual cause                                                   | Looks like                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| A side asserts **Boundary** where the cluster has a neighbour | Positions at edges or interfaces failing |
| No module offers the combination of orbitals a position needs | Scattered failures with no pattern       |
| Spawn limits exhausted before the cluster was filled          | Failures clustered late in the solve     |
| The library genuinely lacks a piece                           | The same position fails on every restart |


> **Note.**
> **Validate Spawn Feasibility**, off by default, checks up front whether minimum-spawn requirements can be met at all and errors if the library is over-constrained. Worth turning on while you are still shaping a ruleset, since it names the problem before the solve rather than after.


## Solving part of a cluster

_Two controls narrow what gets solved, and everything they leave out is respected as it arrived._

The optional **Vtx Filters** pin gates which positions are solved. What makes this useful is what happens to the rest: positions that fail the filter keep the module they arrived with, and that module becomes **fixed context** the solve has to work around.

So a second solve over a partly-solved cluster can re-decide one region while treating everything around it as settled. Re-rolling a room without disturbing the building is a filter, not a separate graph.

### Solve Target

`Solve Target` narrows by what a position already carries, rather than by what a filter says about it.

| Value             | Solves                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **All**           | Every position the filters pass, whatever it arrived carrying. The default.               |
| **Unsolved Only** | Only positions with no module. Anything that arrived with one is kept as fixed context.   |

**Unsolved Only** exists for the pass that finishes what an earlier one started. The usual shape is to solve one part of a cluster first, the roads say, with vtx filters restricting that pass to them, then solve everything else with the same filters inverted. Inverting a filter set is fiddly to maintain and filters cost real time on a large cluster, so the second pass is better expressed as no filters at all and **Unsolved Only**: the node keeps whatever already carries a module and solves the remainder.

Both controls narrow, and neither widens the other. A position is re-solved only if the filters pass it **and** `Solve Target` does not exclude it, so **Unsolved Only** on a filtered pass shrinks that pass further rather than reaching back for positions the filters rejected.

A kept position behaves exactly like a filter-locked one that carries a module. It is fixed context for its neighbours, its entry passes through untouched with any pattern membership intact, its transform is left where it was, and fixed picks skip it.

On input carrying no modules at all there is nothing to keep, and **Unsolved Only** does what **All** does.


> **Warning.**
> **Entries from another rule set are re-solved**
>
> A position counts as solved when it carries a module the node can read under the rules it is solving with. In a merged Valency Map carrying several rule sets, an entry written under a different one resolves to nothing here, so **Unsolved Only** leaves that position eligible and it re-solves.
>
> The solve warns when this happens and names the count, because such a position cannot be returned to its unposed transform before being re-solved.


There is also a choice about what an unsolved position does with an entry it arrived carrying: keep it, or clear it up front so that only a successful solve writes one. Clearing is the honest setting when you want a failed position to read as empty rather than as whatever it used to be. It applies to the positions this pass is solving, so a position kept by `Solve Target` or by a filter is untouched either way.

## Steering the outcome

_Everything below is optional, and each has its own page._

| Lever                 | Does                                                                             |
| --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Fixed picks**       | Pre-assign a module to a position by name, read from an attribute                |
| [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases)            | Reshape the draw per position, data-driven                                       |
| **Affinity maps**     | Bias selection by tag relationships between neighbours                           |
| **Guidance patterns** | Steer selection toward arrangements you want to see, with an adjustable strength |

Weights, spawn limits and placement policies come from the library rather than the node, and apply here without being configured. How all of these combine is covered in [Guiding a Solve](concept:working-with-valency/generating/solve/guiding-a-solve).

title: Guiding a Solve
description: A solve obeys the library.
outline: Forcing a pick can produce something the rules forbid
A partial pre-solve is often the better tool
Guidance and Find Patterns are the same assets doing opposite jobs
Where weights and limits come from
body:
A solve obeys the library. Almost everything on this page changes **which of the legal answers you get**, not what counts as legal, and keeping that distinction straight is what stops steering from turning into debugging. ## Hard and soft _Only one lever here can produce something the rules forbid._ | Lever | Lives on | Effect | | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | Rules, weights, spawn limits, placement policy | The library | Decide what is legal, and the baseline odds | | **Fixed picks** | The node | Pin a specific module to a position. Can be forced past legality. | | [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases), **affinity maps**, **guidance patterns** | The node | Reshape the odds among options that are already legal | The soft levers cannot make an illegal placement legal. If a module is not allowed at a position, no amount of bias will put it there, and a bias that appears to do nothing is usually a bias whose favoured module was never a candidate. > Figure: DIAGRAM | id: solve-guiding-layers | SHOWS: That steering happens inside the set of legal options, never outside it. | ELEMENTS: Three stacked bands, narrowing left to right. Band one, the whole library, twelve module chips. Band two, labelled legal here, four of those chips survive and eight are greyed out, with a label attributing the cut to the rules. Band three, labelled steered, the same four chips at visibly different sizes representing reshaped odds, with one highlighted as chosen. An arrow from a bias node points only at band three. A greyed chip in band two has a dotted arrow from the bias node to it, drawn crossed out. | MUST BE CLEAR: The bias only ever acts on the four survivors. The crossed dotted arrow shows the thing readers assume can happen and cannot: a bias reaching back into what the rules already excluded. > The rules decide the shortlist. Steering only ever reshapes the odds within it. ## Fixed picks _Name the module you want at a position, read from an attribute._ Off by default. Turned on, it reads a per-point attribute holding a **module name**, and pre-assigns that module before solving. An empty value means no fixed pick for that position, so a sparse attribute pins a few positions and leaves the rest to the solve. A name is a group rather than a unique key, so several modules can answer to one. Which one you get is a choice: | Selection mode | Picks | | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | | **Weighted Random** | Among the matching modules, by weight. Deterministic. The default. | | **First Match** | The first matching module. Deterministic. | | **Best Fit** | The one whose orbital configuration best matches the position | **Best Fit** is the interesting one for pinning a role rather than a piece: name the group `Doorway` and let the solve choose the doorway variant that actually suits the position it landed on. There is also a filter pin controlling which positions are eligible for fixed picking at all, so eligibility and the name attribute are separate decisions. > **Warning.** > **Forcing a pick can produce something the rules forbid** > > When a pinned module does not fit the position's orbital configuration, the default is to **skip** it: the pick is ignored, the solve decides normally, and it warns you. > > The alternative is to **force** it, which places the module regardless of fit. That is the one lever on this page that can put an illegal module into a result, and everything downstream will treat it as legitimate. Use it deliberately, and expect neighbours around it to fail if they had counted on a connection that is no longer there. > **Note.** > **A partial pre-solve is often the better tool** > > Fixed picks pin a module by name, which means plumbing a name attribute and living with whatever that name resolves to. There is another route to the same control: **solve part of the cluster first**, with vtx filters restricting that pass to the positions you care about, then solve the rest in a second pass. Positions decided by the first pass arrive as fixed context and the second solve works around them. > > The second pass needs no filters of its own. Set its `Solve Target` to **Unsolved Only** and it keeps everything the first pass decided, which is covered on the Solving page. > > That is usually easier to manage and more flexible. The pinned modules were chosen by a solve, so they are legal by construction rather than by your promise, and the first pass can carry its own strategy, biases and guidance. The cost is verbosity: more nodes and more wiring for something fixed picks express in a single attribute. > > Reach for fixed picks when the choice genuinely comes from data you already have on the points. Reach for a pre-solve when what you actually mean is "these positions should be decided differently from the rest". ## Biases _Reshape the odds per position, data-driven._ Biases arrive as factory nodes on the **Biases** pin, and each carries its own filter deciding which positions it applies to. Two exist: | Node | Biases by | | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Valency : Bias** | Tag-matched modules, weighted by a constant or a per-point attribute | | **Valency : Bias (Channel)** | A per-point attribute matched against a Channel Map's per-module values | The first is the general one: pick modules by tag, push their weight up or down, optionally varying that per point so the same bias behaves differently across the cluster. The second reads a value per position and looks it up per module, which suits gradients and any continuous quantity, like biasing toward heavier pieces where a density attribute is high. Because each bias carries a filter, several can coexist and apply in different regions without contradicting each other. How they compose is covered under Systems. ## Affinity maps _Bias by what the neighbours are._
> Figure: The Affinity Map asset icon > Affinity Map > Figure: The Channel Map asset icon > Channel Map
An **Affinity Map** asset biases selection based on tag relationships, so a module can prefer or avoid sitting next to particular kinds of thing. Where an ordinary bias asks "what should go here", affinity asks "what is already next to here". Several can be supplied at once, and they are set on the node rather than the solver, so they apply whichever strategy you use. ## Guidance patterns _Steer the solve toward arrangements you want to see._ Supply pattern assets and the solve biases module selection toward completing those arrangements as it goes. A **Strength** setting controls how much: `0` is off, `1` weighs a pattern about as heavily as module weight does, and it goes up to `10` for cases where the arrangement matters more than ordinary variety. > **Note.** > **Guidance and Find Patterns are the same assets doing opposite jobs** > > **Guidance patterns** act **during** the solve, nudging it toward producing an arrangement. > > **Valency : Find Patterns** acts **after**, recognising arrangements that already exist and doing something to them. > > The same pattern asset can serve both. Steering toward a T-junction while solving, then finding every T-junction afterwards to swap in a purpose-built mesh, is one asset used twice. ## Where weights and limits come from Module weights, spawn limits and placement policies come from the library and apply to every solve without appearing on the node. If a module never shows up, check its weight and its limits before adding a bias to compensate: a bias fighting a spawn cap loses.

title: Solver Strategies
description: A solve needs a solver, supplied as a factory node.
outline: Why the order matters at all
body:
A solve needs a solver, supplied as a factory node. All four fill the same cluster from the same library and obey the same rules. What differs is **the order they decide positions in**, and what they do when that order runs into trouble.

## Why the order matters at all

_Every commit narrows what is still possible around it, so early choices are expensive._

Solving is greedy. Once a module is committed at a position, its neighbours lose every candidate that will not sit beside it, and their neighbours lose options in turn. A choice made early where there was lots of freedom can leave a position across the cluster with nothing that fits.

Which is why the default strategy deliberately decides the **hardest** positions first.

## The four

| Strategy                | Decides next by                        | Reach for it when                                             |
| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Entropy Solver**      | Fewest remaining candidates            | Always, unless you have a reason not to. This is the default. |
| **Priority Solver**     | An attribute you supply, highest first | The structure has an order you already know                   |
| **Constraint Solver**   | Urgency of unmet minimum spawns        | The library has minimums that must be hit                     |
| **Backtracking Solver** | Fewest candidates, but undoes commits  | A tight library where the others leave holes                  |


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: solve-entropy-order | SHOWS: Why deciding the most constrained position first is the safe default. | ELEMENTS: A partially solved cluster. Several committed positions drawn solid. Four undecided positions, each labelled with how many candidates it has left: 7, 5, 2 and 6. The one showing 2 is circled as the next to be decided. To the side, a small inset showing the alternative: the 7 is decided first, and the 2 subsequently drops to 0, drawn with a cross. | MUST BE CLEAR: Both positions were legal to decide. Deciding the roomy one first is what destroyed the tight one, and the count on each open position is the whole basis of the choice.
> Least freedom first. The position with two options left is the one that can still be lost.


### Entropy

_Fewest candidates first. The default, and the right answer most of the time._

The classic WFC heuristic: always decide the position with the least freedom remaining, because it is the one most likely to run out. Positions with many options can afford to wait, since they will still have options later.

Start here. The other three exist for specific situations, and if you cannot name which situation you are in, this is the one you want.

### Priority

_You supply the order, as an attribute._

Reads a per-point attribute and decides positions from the highest value down, or the lowest first if you invert it. Use it when the structure has an order you already understand and want respected: solve a spine before the details that hang off it, or work floors from the ground up.

The trade is that you have given up the entropy heuristic, so a priority order that ignores where the constraints actually are can strand positions the default would have saved.

### Constraint

_Aims to hit minimum spawn counts, and pushes hard for them._

Where the library asks for a module at least so many times, this strategy tracks how far behind each one is and boosts the urgent ones aggressively. Its urgency multiplier defaults to a much stronger figure than the ordinary minimum-spawn boost, which is the point of it: the best odds available of hitting minimums that can be hit at all.

Reach for it when a result is expected to contain specific things, rather than merely being valid.

### Backtracking

_Undoes commits to escape dead ends._

Uses the same fewest-candidates ordering, but when it reaches a position with nothing that fits, it takes commits back and tries different ones rather than accepting the hole. It gives up after a configurable number of placement attempts and falls back to fillers.

This is the one to reach for when a library is genuinely tight and the other strategies leave unsolved positions that you know are solvable. It costs time, so it is worth confirming the problem is dead ends rather than a missing piece first.


> **Note.**
> **Minimum spawn boosts are shared**
>
> Most strategies carry a weight multiplier applied to modules that still owe minimum spawns, so a module behind on its quota competes better without being forced. The Constraint solver replaces this with its own, far more aggressive urgency scheme.
>
> They shift the odds rather than guaranteeing anything, which is exactly what you want for a preference and not enough on its own for a requirement.


## Choosing one

| If                                                                       | Use              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------- |
| You are starting out, or nothing below applies                           | **Entropy**      |
| Some positions must be decided before others, and you know which         | **Priority**     |
| The result must contain certain modules, not merely be valid             | **Constraint**   |
| The library is tight and you are getting holes you believe are avoidable | [Backtracking](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/backtracking) |

Swapping strategies is a one-node change, so trying another is cheap. If two produce equally good results, keep the faster one.

title: Utility Nodes
description: Solving, growing and staging are stages: every pipeline has them, in that order.
outline: Where they sit in a pipeline
body:
Solving, growing and staging are stages: every pipeline has them, in that order. These four are not stages. Each does one self-contained job on the cluster rather than on modules, and a pipeline reaches for one when it has that particular job.

They are grouped here because of what they operate on, not because they share machinery. They do not.

## What each one is for

| Node                           | Does                                                                                                                       | When                                                                  |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Valency : Write Orbitals**   | Writes the orbital data a solve reads onto an existing cluster                                                             | Before any solve, on any cluster Lattice did not build                |
| **Valency : Lattice**          | Quantizes shapes, surfaces and volumes onto an orbital lattice, producing the cluster **and** its orbital data in one step | Before a solve, instead of authoring a cluster by hand                |
| **Valency : Planar Partition** | Decomposes a cluster into floors and regions, annotating vertices so later stages can act per floor or per region          | Before resolution, when parts of a structure need different treatment |
| **Valency : Write Junctions**  | Emits one point per bonded connector pair, and optionally inserts them into the cluster                                    | After growth, when connections need to exist as positions             |


> **Warning.**
> **Write Orbitals is a prerequisite**
>
> The other three are conveniences you reach for when they help. [Write Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/write-orbitals) is not: a solve reads orbital data off the cluster, and a cluster nobody wrote it to carries none.
>
> [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) is the only escape, because it writes the same data while building the cluster. Every pipeline that solves a cluster from anywhere else needs Write Orbitals first.


## Where they sit in a pipeline

_Three before resolution, one after._

**Write Orbitals**, **Lattice** and [Planar Partition](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/planar-partition) all run on the way in, preparing or annotating the cluster a solve will fill. The first two are alternatives rather than a sequence: use Lattice when the cluster does not exist yet, Write Orbitals when it does.

**Write Junctions** runs on the way out, on points that already carry resolved modules, so it needs the **Valency Map** alongside them like everything else that reads a result. See [Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating).

**Valency : Find Patterns** is deliberately not here. It is the only entry point to the whole pattern subsystem, which reaches from cage authoring through to what a result becomes, so it sits alongside solving and growing rather than among the one-job nodes.

title: Junctions
description: Growth records connections as cluster edges.
body:
Growth records connections as cluster edges. **Valency : Write Junctions** turns each of those into a **point**: one per bonded connector pair, sitting where the pair meets, carrying what met there.

The reason to want them is that the joint is where a lot of content lives. Doors go in doorways, seams go where two walls meet, transitions go where a corridor becomes a room. Those are all connections rather than modules, and until this node runs there is nothing there to place anything on.

## Mated and spanning bonds

_Two shapes of connection, and they produce different numbers of points._

Most bonds are **mated**: two connectors occupy the same place, so the joint is one location and the node emits one point at it.

A bridge is not. Its two connectors are apart, with the gap spanned by a module or by nothing, so there is no single meeting point. Those emit **one point per connector end**.

`Mated Distance Tolerance` is the threshold between the two, defaulting to a tenth of a unit. Anything closer is treated as mated.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: junctions-mated-vs-spanning | SHOWS: That a mated bond emits one junction point and a spanning bond emits two, one at each end of the gap. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Left panel headed Mated: two modules drawn as outlines with inside corners, meeting flush, their two connectors coincident at one location in FFA627, and a single junction point drawn on top of that location as a filled marker with an orientation arrow. A readout beside it reads one point, Span Length 0. Right panel headed Spanning: two modules apart with a bridge module between them, their two connectors sitting at opposite ends of the gap, and TWO junction points drawn, one at each connector, each with its own orientation arrow. A dimension line runs between the two points labelled Span Length. Both panels label the Start and End sides on the same axis so the pairing is readable. | MUST BE CLEAR: The count is the reading. One meeting place gives one point; a gap has no single meeting place, so each end gets its own. The Span Length dimension exists only on the right. | NOTE: Modules get inside corners. Connectors are FFA627 since no type distinction is being drawn, and the figure spends no green.
> A mated bond has one place where the pair meets. A spanning one has none, so each end gets a point of its own.


With `Write Span` on, every junction says which it is: a `Spanning` flag, and a `SpanLength` holding the connector-to-connector distance, which is `0` on a mated junction.

## Which end is which

_A pair has two sides, and several attributes are written per side._

Attributes come in `_Start` and `_End` pairs, so the node needs to know which connector is which. `Primary Side` decides.

| Mode               | Start is                                                                                                                 |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Edge Direction** | The edge's start endpoint. On growth output that is the parent, since growth authors edges parent to child. The default. |
| **Polarity**       | The `Plug` side of the pair                                                                                              |

**Polarity** only has an answer when exactly one side is a plug. A `Universal`/`Universal`, `Plug`/`Plug` or `Port`/`Universal` pair has no plug side to pick, and those fall back to the authored endpoint order.

The same choice orients the junction point itself, so it also decides which way anything spawned there faces.

## What a junction carries

| Attribute                            | Holds                                        |
| ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------- |
| `ConnectorType_Start` / `_End`       | The two connector type names                 |
| `TypePair`                           | Both types as one lexically sorted `A+B` key |
| `VtxIndex_Start` / `_End`            | The endpoint vertices this joint came from   |
| `ConnectorIdentifier_Start` / `_End` | The two socket names. Off by default.        |
| `Spanning`, `SpanLength`             | Whether this is a bridge, and how wide       |

`TypePair` is the one worth knowing about. Matching on `_Start` and `_End` means handling both permutations of every pair, because which type landed on which side depends on the direction growth happened to travel. The sorted key removes that: one value per type meeting, whichever way round it occurred.

This is also where connector `Identifier` earns its keep. It takes no part in matching during generation, but on the way out it is the name that says which specific socket this joint came from.

## Splitting the cluster

_The second output mode, which changes the cluster rather than describing it._

By default clusters pass through untouched and junctions exist only on their own pin.

`Output Mode` set to **Split Cluster** rebuilds the cluster with the junction vertices inserted into it. Each bonded edge `A-B` becomes `A-J-B`, and a spanning bridge becomes `A-J1-J2-B` since it has two ends.

That gives a cluster whose topology contains the joints, which is what you want when a second pass should treat connections as positions in their own right.


> **Warning.**
> Junction vertices carry **no Valency Entry**. They are joints, not modules, and nothing downstream will resolve them to an asset.
>
> With `Flag Junction Vtx` on, they are marked `IsJunction`, which is what lets a later stage tell them apart from the module vertices they were inserted between.


## Narrowing which joints are written

_An optional vertex filter, and both ends have to pass._

Connect vertex filters and only the bonds whose **both** endpoints pass produce junctions. That is deliberately strict: a joint half of which was filtered out is not a joint you asked for.

It is the tool for "doors only between rooms" or "seams only on the ground floor", where the condition is a property of the modules rather than of the connection.

## Driven by the map

The bonding rules, orbital set and connector set all come from the **Valency Map** travelling with the cluster, described in [Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating), so there is nothing to pick on the node.

title: Lattice
description: A solve needs a cluster whose edges already carry orbital directions.
outline: One cluster, or one per group
Two different suffixes, and only one of them defaults to Main
body:
A solve needs a cluster whose edges already carry orbital directions. Building that by hand means producing the points, connecting them along the right axes, and running **Valency : Write Orbitals** over the result.

**Valency : Lattice** does all of it from shapes you draw. Give it splines, polygons or volumes and an **Orbital Set**, and it returns a cluster snapped to that set's axes with the orbital data already written. It is the shortest path from "I have a floor plan" to "I have something to solve".

## What it takes in

_Three pins, all optional, at least one carrying data._

There is no main points input. Everything arrives on the node's own pins, and each is treated differently.

| Pin          | Takes                                       | Becomes                                                        |
| ------------ | ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Shapes**   | Points, splines or polygons, open or closed | A linear spine. The outline is quantized, not its interior.    |
| **Surfaces** | Closed shapes                               | A filled interior. An open shape here degrades to its outline. |
| **Volumes**  | Points, volumes or primitives               | 3D occupancy, unioned with the other two                       |

Points on the **Volumes** pin each contribute their own oriented box, which makes a scattered point cloud a usable occupancy source. Primitive components need cooked, registered collision before they report overlaps at all.

`Capture Radius` is the brush, read per shape from `@Data.Radius`. On **Shapes** it dilates the spine, with `0` giving a one-node-wide line. On **Surfaces** it grows the fill, and negative values erode it, to the point where a small enough shape disappears entirely.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: lattice-pins-and-radius | SHOWS: That the same drawn outline produces completely different clusters depending on which pin it arrives on, and what Capture Radius does on each. | ELEMENTS: Two rows over a shared input drawn once at the left: a single closed curve, a rounded rectangle with a notch. Row one headed Shapes: three quantized results left to right at Capture Radius 0, then a larger radius. At 0 the outline alone is painted, one node wide, interior empty. At the larger radius the painted band thickens outward and inward from the outline, interior still empty. Row two headed Surfaces: the same curve at Capture Radius 0, then a positive radius, then a negative one. At 0 the whole interior is filled. Positive grows the filled region past the outline. Negative erodes it inward, and a small satellite shape drawn alongside disappears entirely at that value, marked as gone. Every result is drawn as vtx dots on the lattice with edges between them along the orbital axes, and the underlying lattice is drawn faintly behind all of them so the quantization is visible. A third small panel at the far right headed Volumes shows a scattered point cloud on the Volumes pin becoming a solid block of occupancy. | MUST BE CLEAR: One input, three pins, three unrelated answers: an outline, a fill, and an occupancy block. Capture Radius thickens on Shapes and grows or shrinks the fill on Surfaces, and it can erode a small shape out of existence. | NOTE: No perspective. The lattice is flat and drawn from directly above.
> The pin decides what the shape means. The radius decides how much of it survives quantization.


## The lattice itself

_An orbital set supplies the axes. Cell size supplies the scale._

The **Orbital Set** decides which directions the lattice runs along, so a hex set produces a hex lattice and a 3D set a volumetric one, with nothing else changing. Leave the field null and the node takes the set from a [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) asset instead, which is the usual setup since you already have one.

`Cell Size` is the base spacing. Each orbital steps by `Cell Size` multiplied by its own normalized length, so a set mixing long and short axes keeps their proportions.

The frame those axes sit in has its own controls. `Lattice Rotation` turns the whole lattice and `Origin` offsets it. `Base Mode` decides where the frame sits along the directions the lattice does **not** span, which is what matters when a flat lattice is fed shapes at varying heights: `Average` is the default, `Min` and `Max` pin it to the extremes, and `Flat` ignores the inputs entirely and uses `Origin` exactly. A lattice spanning all three axes has nothing unspanned, so the setting does nothing there.


> **Warning.**
> `Spline Fidelity` is a **tolerance**, so lower means finer. Keep it well below `Cell Size`: at coarser values the polyline chords cut inside the arcs of a curved spline, and nodes that should have been painted are never visited.


## One cluster, or one per group

_Matching partitions every pin at once._

By default the node merges everything into a single cluster on one frame. That is the common case and needs no configuration.

Turn matching on and the inputs of **all three pins** are partitioned into exclusive groups, each of which paints and emits its own cluster. Anything unmatched becomes a cluster of its own.

Holes respect that boundary. A shape flagged `@Data.IsHole` on the **Surfaces** pin subtracts from its own group's output and no other, so two buildings can each carry their own courtyards without either carving the other.


> **Note.**
> A hole carves within its own extents rather than projecting through the result. A flat hole laid over a thick **Volumes** fill removes its own lattice layer, not a prism through the whole depth.


Grouped output shares one frame only if you ask for it. `Shared Frame` infers a single base from every input so the group lattices stay co-registered; left off, each group gets a base snug to its own contents.

## What comes out

| Output                | Is                                                                             |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Vtx** and **Edges** | A cluster, already carrying the orbital mask and per-edge orbital data         |
| **Valency Map**       | Emitted here, so the substrate this node just wrote is discoverable downstream |

Because the map comes out of the node itself, a Lattice feeds **Valency : Solve** directly with no orbital-writing step between them.

The attributes land under `PCGEx/V/Mask/{Suffix}` and `PCGEx/V/Orbital/{Suffix}`. Left at `None`, `Suffix` resolves to the **orbital set's own identifier**, which is what lets a consumer find the substrate without being told where it is. **Valency : Write Orbitals** does the same, for the same reason.


> **Note.**
> **Two different suffixes, and only one of them defaults to Main**
>
> The one here names an orbital **substrate**, and defaults to the set that defines it.
>
> `Entry Suffix`, on **Valency : Staging**, **Valency : Load Properties** and the growth nodes, names a **resolution** instead: which set of resolved-module attributes to read at `PCGEx/V/Entry/{suffix}`. That one defaults to `Main`.
>
> They are different axes with similar names. Setting one because a page mentioned the other is the mistake to avoid.


## When to reach for it

_Whenever the shape is easier to draw than the cluster._

Lattice suits any layout that starts as geometry: a floor plan as closed polygons, a road network as splines, a building mass as volumes. It suits iteration for the same reason, since editing a spline and re-running beats re-authoring a cluster.

It is the wrong tool when the cluster is itself the authored artefact, a hand-built graph whose topology carries meaning the geometry does not. Then the cluster comes from wherever you built it and **Valency : Write Orbitals** supplies the orbital data.

title: Planar Partition
description: A cluster is one undifferentiated set of positions.
body:
A cluster is one undifferentiated set of positions. **Valency : Planar Partition** finds structure in it: which floor each vertex sits on, and which connected region of that floor it belongs to.

Nothing is placed and nothing is moved. The node annotates vertices so that everything downstream, spawn limits, biases and filters alike, can ask "which floor is this" and act on the answer.

## It runs before resolution

_What it writes is meant to be read while modules are being chosen._

The point of knowing the floor is to use it: a ground floor drawing from different modules than the ones above it, a stairwell capped per floor rather than per structure, a bias that prefers windows on the outermost region.

All of that happens during a solve or a growth, so the partition has to exist before them. Run it on the cluster on the way in, not on the result on the way out.

## Finding the floors

_A plane, then everything that lies in it._

Floors need an up direction, and the node derives one rather than assuming world up.

| `Plane Source`   | Normal comes from                                    |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| **Auto**         | The plane containing the most orbitals. The default. |
| **From Orbital** | A named orbital's direction                          |
| **Custom**       | An explicit vector                                   |

**Auto** can be genuinely undecided: a cube-symmetric orbital set has three equally good planes, and `Up Hint` breaks the tie by picking the one best aligned with it.

For the other two the **sign is respected exactly as authored**, which is a lever rather than a nuisance. Naming a downward orbital puts floor `0` at the top and numbers downward.

With a plane chosen, an orbital counts as lying in it when it sits within `Planarity Tolerance Degrees` of perpendicular to the normal.


> **Warning.**
> `Planarity Tolerance Degrees` defaults to one degree, and loose values are the failure to watch for. An orbital that genuinely steps between levels but is admitted as in-plane merges two real floors into one, and the result reads as though floor detection is broken rather than as though the tolerance is wrong.


## Numbering across disconnected parts

_Two structures that never touch still have to agree what floor two means._

Floor `0` sits at the extreme opposite the plane normal, and empty levels are skipped rather than numbered. That is straightforward while the cluster is one connected thing.

When it is not, `Floor Reconcile` decides.

| Mode            | Numbering                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Measured**    | One shared numbering, using a layer height measured from the cluster itself. The default, and what you want when two towers should agree about floor three. |
| **Independent** | Each disconnected part numbers from its own extreme, so separate structures get overlapping floor numbers                                                   |

`Layer Quantization Tolerance` supports the measured mode: an orbital whose step strays too far from a whole multiple of the smallest one is dropped from floor propagation rather than distorting the measurement.

## Regions

_Within one floor, what is connected to what._

A **region** is a set of vertices on the same floor reachable from each other through in-plane orbitals. Two wings joined only by a bridge on the floor above are two regions, and the same building on the floor below may be one.

That is what makes regions worth having: they are the unit that answers "is this the same space", which a floor number alone cannot.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: planar-partition-floors-and-regions | SHOWS: That a floor number and a region are different questions about the same vertex, and that the region count can change from floor to floor on one unchanged structure. | ELEMENTS: One structure drawn twice, side by side, identical in both: a building of two wings that are joined across their full width on the lower floor and joined only by a single narrow link on the upper floor. Cluster vtx are drawn as position squares with edges between them, in-plane edges drawn plainly and the vertical edges between floors drawn distinctly so the two levels read apart without perspective. Left copy headed Floors: every vertex tinted by floor, two tints, with the floor numbers 0 and 1 labelled once each at the edge. Right copy headed Regions: the same vertices tinted by region instead, and the counts differ between the levels: floor 0 is ONE region across both wings, floor 1 is TWO regions because the narrow link is not an in-plane connection between them. A small readout beside each floor states its region count. | MUST BE CLEAR: The structure does not change between the two copies. Floor 0 answers one region and floor 1 answers two, from the same building, which is the thing a floor number alone cannot tell you. | NOTE: Flat, no receding axis. Separate the two levels by drawing them as two stacked plans joined by the vertical edges, never as a 3D box.
> Same building, two questions. The lower floor is one space and the upper floor is two, and only the region answers that.


## What it writes

| Attribute      | Holds                                                         |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `FloorIndex`   | The floor this vertex sits on                                 |
| `RegionIndex`  | The region's ordinal within that floor                        |
| `RegionHash`   | Floor and region packed into one key, never `0`               |
| `RegionsAbove` | How many distinct regions on the floor above link to this one |
| `RegionsBelow` | The same, downward                                            |

`RegionHash` is the one to reach for when a limit or a match needs to be per region: it is a single value that is unique across the whole cluster, so it can be fed straight to **Partitioned Limits** on a bonding node or to **Valency : Find Patterns**.

The two adjacency counts are mirrored onto every vertex by default so they can be filtered on directly. `Regions Above` of `0` on a floor that is not the top means a region nothing above it connects to, which is how a dead-end wing or an isolated roof section is found.

## The Regions output

_One point per region, on its own pin._

`Output Regions`, on by default, also emits a point for each region, oriented to that region's own spread and bounded to enclose its members. That gives a coarse representation of the structure, one point per space rather than per position, which is useful for scattering, for labelling, or for driving anything that should act once per region.

`Min Region Extent` keeps those points usable. A region of one vertex spreads along no axis and a region of two spreads along a single line, so without a floor their boxes would be degenerate.

## Driven by the map

_The Valency Map already knows._

There is no orbital set to pick and no bonding rules to supply. The map travelling with the cluster records which orbital set produced the substrate, its layer and its size, and this node reads the orbital substrate and nothing else.

title: Write Orbitals
description: A solve does not work out for itself which direction each connection runs in.
body:
A solve does not work out for itself which direction each connection runs in. It reads that from the cluster, per edge, and a cluster that has never been told carries nothing for it to read.

**Valency : Write Orbitals** is what tells it. On any cluster you built yourself, this is the step between having a shape and having something Valency can solve.

## Where it sits

_Before the solve, and after nothing in particular._

The node takes a cluster and writes connection data onto it. It places no modules, needs no library, and cares about nothing except geometry and an **Orbital Set**.

There is one case where it is unnecessary. [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) builds a cluster and writes the same data in one step, so a pipeline that starts from shapes rather than from an authored cluster never needs this node. Every other pipeline does.

## How an orbital is assigned

_Two sources, and only one of them works on an arbitrary cluster._

| `Assignment Mode` | Assigns from                                                              |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Direction**     | The edge's world direction, matched against the orbital set. The default. |
| **Connector**     | The packed per-edge connector references that generative growth writes    |

**Direction** is geometric. It measures where each edge points and finds the orbital closest to it within the set's tolerance, which works on any cluster from any source.

**Connector** reads an attribute instead, so it only works on input a growth pass produced. Its use is giving a grown structure orbital data consistent with the connectors that actually built it, rather than with wherever its edges happen to point. On a cluster with no such attribute it has nothing to read.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: write-orbitals-assignment-mode | SHOWS: That the two modes can assign different orbitals to the same edge, because one measures the edge and the other reads what built it. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule, showing the identical grown structure: three modules drawn as outlines with inside corners, joined by two edges, with the connector that made each bond drawn on both its ends in FFA627 and clearly NOT parallel to the edge between the two module origins. A small orbital rosette of six directions sits beside the structure as a key, each direction named. Left panel headed Direction: a dashed measurement line is drawn along each edge from origin to origin, an angle mark shows it being matched to the nearest rosette direction, and each edge is labelled with the orbital that wins. Right panel headed Connector: no measurement line at all; instead a leader runs from each edge to the connector pair that formed it, and each edge is labelled with the orbital that connector's own facing implies. One of the two edges carries a DIFFERENT orbital name between the panels, and that edge is marked in both. | MUST BE CLEAR: The structure, the edges and the connectors are identical on both sides. One mode measures where the edge points and the other reads what actually bonded, and the marked edge is where those two answers disagree. | NOTE: The disagreement needs the connectors to sit off-centre on their faces, which is also what DIAGRAMS.md asks of a connector figure.
> Same structure, same edges. Direction measures where an edge points; Connector reads what bonded, and the two can disagree.



> **Warning.**
> `Warn On No Match` reports edges whose direction matched no orbital within tolerance, and it is worth leaving on while a set is being built.
>
> An unmatched edge is not an error at this stage and nothing stops. It surfaces later, as a position that will not solve for no visible reason, which is a much harder thing to trace back here.


## What it writes

The per-vertex orbital mask lands at `PCGEx/V/Mask/{Suffix}` and the per-edge orbital at `PCGEx/V/Orbital/{Suffix}`.


> **Note.**
> Left at `None`, `Suffix` resolves to the **source set's own identifier**: the orbital set's in Direction mode, the connector set's layer name in Connector mode. That is deliberate, and it is how a consumer locates the substrate without being told where it is.
>
> **Valency : Lattice** resolves its suffix the same way, which is what makes the two interchangeable from the perspective of whatever reads them.


The node also emits a **Valency Map**, so a cluster prepared here arrives at a solve already carrying what it needs.

## Getting the tolerance right

_The orbital set decides what counts as pointing along a direction._

Matching an edge to an orbital is an angular test, and the tolerance belongs to the orbital set, as [Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/orbitals) sets out, rather than to this node. A set with tight tolerance on a cluster whose edges are slightly off-axis produces unmatched edges; a set with loose tolerance on a dense set of directions produces edges matched to the wrong one.

Both symptoms show up here first, which is why the warning is the fastest diagnostic available for an orbital set that has not been tuned to the clusters it is used on.

title: Systems
description: Authoring is level work.
body:
Authoring is level work. Generating is graph work. These pages are neither: each covers a subsystem that both halves reach into, so putting it under either one would leave the other half pointing at a page that seemed to belong somewhere else. Nothing here is a step you perform. They are the things the steps are made of. ## What each one owns
PageOwns
[Debugging](concept:working-with-valency/systems/debugging)Where Valency reports a problem, and what the common quiet failures look like
[Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases)Every way to reshape which module gets drawn, and how several compose
[Facts and Gates](concept:working-with-valency/systems/facts-and-gates)The queryable statements about orbitals and connectors, and what reads them
[Spawn Limits](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spawn-limits)Capping how often a module appears, and why the minimum is not the mirror of the maximum
[Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap)The placement conditions that refuse a candidate on spatial grounds
[Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules)Asking where a placement is, as a grammar rule or as a precondition on one
[Filters](concept:working-with-valency/systems/filters)The point filters that test Valency data
## Where to start _Only one of these is worth reading before you need it._ [Debugging](concept:working-with-valency/systems/debugging) is the exception, because it is mostly a table of symptoms and the page you want open the first time a result is smaller than expected. Reading it early means recognising a failure instead of investigating one. The rest are reference. Reach for them when a page in Authoring or Generating sends you here, which it will: each of these subsystems is named from several places and explained in exactly one.

title: Biases
description: Every way to reshape which module gets picked, how the two families differ, and how several biases compose into one number.
outline: A bias that reshapes weights on positions nobody picks changes nothing
body:
A **bias** reshapes a draw. It makes some modules more likely and others less, and it never makes anything impossible: that is a constraint's job.

There are two families, and they live in different places. Which one you reach for is decided by which half of the plugin you are in, not by what you want to express.

## Two families

*One steers a solve from the graph. One steers a grammar from inside it.*

| | Where it lives | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| **Bias nodes** | PCG graph, feeding a solve on its own pin | Positions in a cluster, chosen by a node filter |
| **Grammar biases** | Inside a **Structural Grammar**, on a region or a node | Placements a grammar makes, scoped by where the rule sits |

They do not overlap and neither substitutes for the other. A grammar bias cannot reach a solve, and a bias node cannot see the grammar's structure.

## Bias nodes

*Two of them, both answering "where" and "what" separately.*

**Valency : Bias** boosts or suppresses modules matching a tag predicate, by a weight that is either a constant or read per vertex from an attribute. **Valency : Bias (Channel)** does the same thing indirectly: it matches a per-vertex attribute against a **Channel Map**'s per-module values.

Both take a **node filter** on their own pin. That is the "where": leave it empty and the bias applies at every position, connect filters and it applies only where they pass. The predicate or channel is the "what".

That split is what makes them useful. "Prefer tall modules" is a weight; "prefer tall modules near the edge" is the same weight with a filter, and neither half needs to know about the other.

Because the weight can come from an attribute, a bias node can vary continuously across a cluster. Anything that produced a per-vertex number, a noise field, a distance, a [Planar Partition](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/planar-partition) floor index, can drive it.

## Channel maps

*Matching a value rather than a tag.*

A **Channel Map** asset gives modules typed values under named channels: numbers, vectors, colors or names, assigned by tag predicate. **Valency : Bias (Channel)** then reads a per-vertex attribute and prefers modules whose channel value matches it.

That is how a colour painted onto a cluster picks matching modules, or how a numeric gradient selects along a scale, without authoring a separate bias per value.

Each channel carries its own `Match Weight` and `Miss Weight`, defaulting to `2.0` and `0.5`, and individual entries can override them. `No Match Weight` covers modules the channel says nothing about at all, which is a different case from a value that failed to match.

## Affinity maps

*How strongly modules want each other.*

An **Affinity Map** is a list of module pairs with a weight, expressing attraction above `1` and repulsion below it. Entries are symmetric by default, so stating that two things like each other does not need saying twice, and the flag can be cleared where the relation genuinely runs one way.

Affinity is consumed by growth and by the grammar's **Affinity** bias rather than by a bias node, because it is a statement about what a module is placed *next to*, which only means something once there is a neighbour to be next to.

## Grammar biases

*Fourteen of them, all folding into one number.*

Inside a grammar, biases attach to a **Begin Region** or inline on a single node, and the [Regions and Rules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/regions-and-rules) decide where they apply.

| Bias | Prefers by |
|---|---|
| **Tag Weight** | Module tags |
| **Affinity** | An affinity map, against what is already placed |
| **Attribute Driven** | Growth depth, for one tagged family, across a band. Despite the name it reads no attribute. |
| **Connector Type Preference** | The type of connector being grown from |
| **Connector Identifier** | The socket's name |
| **Connector Priority** | The connector's authored priority |
| **Depth Preference** | How deep the placement is |
| **Distance Preference** | How far it is from something |
| **Target Proximity** | Nearness to a live target |
| **Tensor Alignment** | Alignment with a sampled field |
| **Spatial** | Which side of an external [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules) the connector sits on |
| **Quota** | How many of a kind have been placed |
| **Cooldown** | How long since this was last picked |
