| **Pity Counter** | How long since this was last picked, from the other direction |

Several are stateful, and what happens to that state when control flow forks is the `Branch State Policy` covered under [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching).

## How several biases combine

*Multiplicatively, each softened by its own influence.*

Every active bias produces one weight per candidate, where `1` means it does not care, above `1` pushes the candidate up and below `1` pushes it down. Those are then multiplied together.

Multiplication is why biases stack the way they do. Two biases that both mildly prefer a candidate reinforce each other, and one that strongly dislikes it drags the product down whatever the others said.

Each bias has two dials before its contribution reaches that product.

| Setting | Does |
|---|---|
| `Influence` | Lerps this bias toward neutral. `1` is its full opinion, `0` makes it inert. |
| `Contrast` | Sharpens this bias alone. Its weights are normalised and raised to this power, so a preference can be made more decisive without touching authored module weight or any other bias. |

> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: biases-multiplicative-fold | SHOWS: How several biases fold into one weight per candidate, and what Contrast does to one of them without touching the others. | ELEMENTS: A grid. Five candidate modules as columns, drawn as distinct outlines across the top so they read as a library rather than one shape repeated. Three bias rows below them, each labelled, each showing its own weight per candidate as a horizontal bar with the value set in mono. A neutral line at 1 runs across every row so above and below are readable at a glance. Under the three rows, a product row showing the folded result per candidate, its bars visibly the product rather than the sum: the candidate that one row pushed well below 1 comes out low even though the other two rows liked it, and that column is marked. To the right, a fourth narrow panel headed Contrast raised showing the SAME three rows with only the middle row redrawn, its bars spread further from the neutral line while keeping their order, and the product row recomputed so a different candidate now wins. | MUST BE CLEAR: The fold is a product, so one row below 1 drags a candidate down whatever the others said. Contrast changes the spread of one row only and leaves the other two and the authored module weights untouched. | NOTE: Not a chart with axes. Bars against a neutral line, mono for the values, no green.
> One row below neutral is enough to sink a candidate the other two liked. Contrast spreads one row without touching the rest.

`Contrast` is the one worth reaching for when a bias is pointing the right way and not strongly enough. Raising the weights themselves competes with every other bias; raising the contrast makes this one more decisive about its own ranking and leaves the rest alone.

Both dials, and every number a grammar bias carries of its own, can be read from the seed points instead of typed. A grammar bias bound that way varies per seed rather than per vertex, which is the nearest a grammar comes to what a bias node does with an attribute.

> **Warning.**
> **A bias that reshapes weights on positions nobody picks changes nothing**
>
> In a grammar, placement is two draws: the connector first, then the module. Biases weight the pairings, which are folded to one number per connector before the first draw.
>
> So a bias that raises weights on candidates hosted by connectors the first draw was never going to reach has no visible effect, however hard it is cranked. That fold is `Slot Reduction`, and it is covered under [Regions and Rules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/regions-and-rules).

## Bias or constraint

*Ask whether the answer is ever acceptable.*

A bias says "prefer". A constraint says "no". Reaching for a bias with a weight of `0` to express a rule works until something else outweighs it, or until every candidate is suppressed and the draw picks one anyway.

If a placement must never happen, use a constraint and let it fail loudly. Keep biases for the shape of a result rather than its legality.

title: Debugging
description: Where Valency tells you what went wrong, what the common failures look like from the outside, and which page fixes each one.
outline: What the common failures look like
body:
Most Valency failures are quiet. Nothing errors, nothing is missing, and the result is smaller or emptier than it should be. That is by design in almost every case: a node was asked a narrow question and answered it.

The work is therefore reading, not guessing. There are three places Valency talks, and one of them is on by default and easy to miss.

## Diagnostics land on the node

*The growth and grammar nodes report their own failures, in the graph.*

Growth, and every grammar node inside it, accumulates a diagnostic whenever it does less than it looks like it should: a placement node that placed nothing, a loop that fell short of its minimum, a corridor that never joined, a Prune that skipped candidates. At the end of the run those are reported as warnings on the node itself and in the log at the same time.

They are worth reading closely, because they are specific. A **Module** that placed nothing names how many connectors were in scope, how many modules its descriptor resolved, and how many compatible pairings the library offers, which separates three unrelated causes that look identical from the outside.

> **Warning.**
> Only the first **12** diagnostics are reported, followed by a line saying how many were dropped. A run that produced dozens of distinct failures shows you a sample, so fix what is reported and run again rather than assuming the list is complete.

Each distinct problem reports once per node, not once per occurrence, so a node failing five hundred times contributes one line.

## The Output Log

*Everything the nodes report, plus the detail they leave out.*

The plugin logs under a set of ordinary Unreal log categories, so the console controls them. `LogValency` carries the general channel, and the grammar subsystems have their own: compilation, execution, the dispatch drain, and one per constraint family.

```bash
log LogPCGExGrammarExec Verbose
```

Those default to showing warnings and errors, which is usually enough. Raise one to `Verbose` when a specific subsystem is the suspect and the node-level diagnostic has not narrowed it far enough.

## Valency's own categories

*Nine of them, at `Warning` until you raise one, and the console is where you raise it.*

Separately from the Unreal categories, Valency has its own set covering the parts of the plugin that are not PCG nodes at all: `Building`, `Compilation`, `Solver`, `Staging`, `EditorMode`, `Cages`, `Mirror`, `Rebuild` and `Growth`.

All nine sit at `Warning`, so warnings and errors arrive without asking, and `Info` and `Verbose` are what the console commands are for. Errors are never gated at all, and reach you even from a category set to `Off`.

Four console commands drive them.

```bash
PCGEx.Valency.Log.EnableAll
```

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `PCGEx.Valency.Log.SetVerbosity <Category> <Verbosity>` | Sets one category, or `All`. Verbosity is `Off`, `Error`, `Warning`, `Info` or `Verbose`. |
| `PCGEx.Valency.Log.ShowVerbosity` | Prints every category's current setting |
| `PCGEx.Valency.Log.EnableAll` | Everything to `Verbose` |
| `PCGEx.Valency.Log.DisableAll` | Everything to `Off` |

`EnableAll` is the first move on a problem you cannot place, and `SetVerbosity All Warning` puts things back afterwards. `DisableAll` goes past the default and silences the warnings you started with. Turning on one category is for when you already know which part of the plugin is involved.

Which category owns a message is not always where you would look for it. Connection detection reports under `Cages` rather than `Building`, so the habitual pairing of `Building` and `Compilation` shows none of it.

## What the common failures look like

*Symptom first, because that is the order you meet them in.*

| What you see | Usually means | Where |
|---|---|---|
| A chain of grammar nodes stops producing partway | A **Module** or short **Growth** placed nothing and dropped its subtree | [Placing Modules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/placing-modules) |
| A node late in a chain acts on far less than expected | `Produced` compounding: each link narrows to what the one before it made | [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar) |
| A **Branch** arm builds nothing while its siblings do | The deal ran out of connectors before that arm, and `Surplus Arm Scope` gives a surplus arm nothing by default | [Branching](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/branching) |
| A **Join** runs and joins nothing | `Pair Scope` wants both ends in scope, and `Cross Branch Only` rejects every pair a single-branch scope can offer | [Joining and Pruning](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/joining-and-pruning) |
| A **Prune** runs and retracts nothing | Its wire handed it a keyhole, or something queued elsewhere is unbounded | [Joining and Pruning](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/joining-and-pruning) |
| A **Seek** builds corridors and never joins | The closing pool is empty, which is separate from the corridor descriptor | [Targets](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/targets) |
| A **Seek** or **Route** finds no target at all | `Exclude Own Branch` on a single-seed run excludes everything | [Targets](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/targets) |
| A **Filter** passes nothing, on a path where nothing was built | `Keep In Scope` has no anchor and fails closed | [Narrowing the Frontier](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/narrowing-the-frontier) |
| A **Filter** passes everything despite a predicate | The library compiled no module tags, so the predicate is skipped | [Narrowing the Frontier](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/narrowing-the-frontier) |
| A constraint appears to be ignored entirely | It fired inside queued work, where Local and Branch backtracking downgrade to Skip | [Backtracking](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/backtracking) |
| A grammar node's property override never arrives | The same property name carries a different type on another tier, and a mismatched source is skipped in favour of the default | [Reading Properties](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/reading-properties) |
| A grammar value set to **Attribute** behaves as if it were the typed constant | The attribute is missing on that input or on the seed points, and the run warned once per binding on the growth node | [Data Bindings](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/data-bindings) |
| A per-seed value is the wrong seed's after a **Merge** | Several seeds merged, and everything after the Merge reads the first path to arrive | [Data Bindings](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/data-bindings) |
| Growth stops far short of its budget | Placement conditions are rejecting nearly everything, usually oversized footprints | [Growing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow) |
| Pieces grow through each other | No placement condition asked for an overlap check | [Growing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow) |
| Growth spills outside a region it should be confined to | The **Spatial Domain** channel name does not match what the input is tagged with, and an unsupplied domain passes | [Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap) |
| A piece meant to bed slightly into a wall is refused outright | A **Polygon** footprint marker has no depth test, so Penetration falls back to plain overlap | [Footprints](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/footprints) |
| A rule meant to apply inside one channel applies everywhere | Its `Active Where` names a channel nothing was baked into, and an unsupplied channel passes, so the precondition passes too | [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules) |
| A rule with an `Active Where` does nothing where it should work | The connector it was evaluated at sits on the other side of the channel, and a rule sitting out reports nothing | [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules) |
| A growth report blames a rule by name rather than a condition | A **Placement** channel veto attributes to the rule's `Rule Name`, so the refusal came from the grammar and not from the module | [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules) |
| Growth re-enters connectors that are already connected | The open-connector source is reading an attribute the producer never wrote | [Growing From a Cluster](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow/from-a-cluster) |
| A result resolves but nothing spawns | No **Valency : Staging**, or its entry suffix does not match the producer's | [Output](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output) |
| Things spawn twice in the same place | `Stage Consumed` is on, and a pattern already represents those points | [Output](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output) |
| Modules you never authored, or results that differ between sessions | A stale contribution in a level cache with no live source | [Module Cages](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-cages) |

## Narrowing it down

*Three questions, in this order.*

**Did the descriptor resolve to anything?** Most silent grammar failures are a descriptor matching no module, and the node's own diagnostic answers this directly. `Allow Placeholders` on the strategy makes the answer visible in the result rather than in a log, by substituting a stand-in so the shape of the run survives.

**What did the wire hand it?** A node acts on the connectors its incoming edge scope delivered, and every default differs by the node the wire leaves. This accounts for most cases where a node behaves correctly on something other than what you meant.

**Is the library the one disagreeing?** Tag predicates, connector compatibility and spawn limits are library-side, and a correctly written grammar meets all three. When a node reports plenty of connectors and plenty of resolved modules but no compatible pairings, the grammar is fine and the pieces cannot mate.

## Seeing it in the level

*The editor mode draws what compiled, not what you authored.*

Connection and connector problems are usually faster to see than to read about. The **Valency editor mode** draws orbital connections, connector shapes and their polarity, footprints, mirror links and volume extents directly in the viewport, which is where a mis-authored connector or an unintended detection shows up immediately.

That surface is covered under [Authoring](concept:working-with-valency/authoring).

title: Facts and Gates
description: A fact is a question Valency can answer about a position or a module, as a set of bits.
outline: The seam between the two models
body:
A **fact** is a question Valency can answer about a position or a module, as a set of bits. Which orbitals here have a neighbour. Which of this module's sockets are still open. Which sides it requires to face nothing.

Nothing consumes a fact by itself. Facts exist so that **gates**, **constraints** and **filters** can ask them, and the same small vocabulary serves all three.

## Two vocabularies

*Orbital facts and connector facts are separate, and never mix.*

| Orbital fact | Answers |
|---|---|
| **Occupancy** | Which orbitals have a neighbour |
| **Vacant** | Which have none. The complement, bounded to orbitals that exist. |
| **Module : Orbital** | Which orbitals the resolved module requires a connection on |
| **Module : Boundary** | Which it requires to have no neighbour |
| **Module : Wildcard** | Which it requires to have some neighbour |
| **Module : Accept Any** | Which it accepts any neighbour on |

| Connector fact | Answers |
|---|---|
| **Claimed** | Which connector instances a structural connection consumed |
| **Unclaimed** | Which are still open. The complement, bounded to the instances the module has. |

The split runs deeper than the names. **Occupancy** and **Vacant** describe **the position**: they are read from the orbital substrate, so they are answerable before anything is solved and need no Valency Map. The four `Module :` facts describe **the module resolved there**, so they need a solved entry and a map to interpret it.

That difference decides what can be asked at a given moment, and it is behind most confusion about why one fact works where another does not.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: facts-two-vocabularies | SHOWS: That the substrate facts and the module facts describe different things about the same position, and can disagree about the same orbital. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the identical situation drawn at the top: one module at a position with six orbitals around it, three of them linked to a neighbouring module and three with nothing there. Left panel headed Read from the position: two rings below the situation, one labelled Occupancy with the three linked orbitals lit, one labelled Vacant with the other three lit. Right panel headed Read from the module: two rings, one labelled Module Boundary with only ONE orbital lit and it is one of the three that were vacant, one labelled Module Wildcard with one orbital lit that is currently linked. The two orbitals that are vacant but not boundary are marked in both panels so the eye can follow them across. | MUST BE CLEAR: Two orbitals are lit in Vacant and dark in Boundary. Vacant means nothing is there; Boundary means the module requires nothing to be there, and most empty orbitals are empty because nothing asked either way. | NOTE: Bead marks per DIAGRAMS.md, so Boundary carries its bar and Wildcard its plus.
> The same six orbitals, asked two different questions. Vacant and Boundary disagree, and that gap is the usual case rather than the exception.



> **Note.**
> **Vacant is wider than Boundary.** Vacant means nothing is there. Boundary means the module *requires* nothing to be there. An orbital is often vacant because nothing constrained it either way, which a boundary never is.


## Asking a fact

*A fact, a selection, and how to compare them.*

Every fact test has the same three parts, whatever is doing the asking.

The **fact** supplies a set of bits. The **selection** names which orbitals or connectors take part: by name, by index, by connector type, or all of them. Names and indices resolve when the rules compile, and anything selecting nothing warns rather than passing silently.

`Test Mode` then decides how the two are compared.

| Mode | Asks |
|---|---|
| **Bitwise** | Whether the fact's bits and the selection overlap in the required way |
| **Count** | How many of the selected bits the fact covers, against a threshold |

**Count** is what expresses "at least two neighbours" or "no more than one open socket", which a bitwise comparison cannot say.

## Unanswerable tests

*Every fact test declares what to do when the data is absent.*

A substrate fact asked where there is no substrate has no answer. That is not an error case: it is the normal condition during growth, which produces positions rather than reading them from an existing cluster.

`Fallback` says what happens.

| Fallback | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Throw Error** | Fail the consuming element loudly |
| **Pass** | Treat the check as passed |
| **Fail** | Treat the check as failed |

Choosing between **Pass** and **Fail** is choosing whether the rule is permissive or strict where it cannot be evaluated, and both are legitimate. **Throw Error** is for when the absence means the graph is wired wrongly and you would rather find out.

## Connector gates

*A fact test that decides whether a socket exists at all.*

A connector on a module can carry **Orbital Gates** and **Claim Gates**. Each is a fact test, all of them must pass, and an empty list leaves the connector unconditional.

What separates a gate from a filter is what it decides. A gate does not narrow a choice, it decides whether the connector is **there**: one that fails its test is absent, so nothing grows from it and nothing can bridge to it.

That is how a module carries a socket which only exists in some situations. A doorway that appears only where the wall behind it is occupied; an attachment point that exists only on a piece nothing has been built onto yet.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: facts-gate-existence | SHOWS: That a failing gate removes the connector rather than refusing what wants to attach to it. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. The same module in both, an outline with an inside corner, carrying three connectors: two plain and one marked as gated. Left panel headed Gate passes: the gated connector drawn as a normal socket, with a second module attached through it, and a bridge line arriving at it from a branch off to the side. Right panel headed Gate fails: the gated connector drawn only as a ghost at 25 percent scale where it would have been, no module attached, and the same bridge line from the side stopping short with nothing to arrive at. The two ungated connectors are identical in both panels. | MUST BE CLEAR: On the right the socket is ABSENT, not refused. There is nothing to grow from and nothing to bridge to, which is why the ghost is drawn rather than a struck-through socket. | NOTE: Use the implied-not-placed form from DIAGRAMS.md for the ghost, never the refused form, since refused would say the opposite.
> A gate that fails does not turn a socket down. There is no socket, so nothing grows from it and nothing can reach it.


**Claim Gates** ask about the module's *own* other connectors, which is how one socket is made mutually exclusive with a sibling: gate it on that sibling being unclaimed, and only one of the two is ever used.


> **Warning.**
> An `All` selection on a Claim Gate includes the gated connector itself. There is no implicit self-exclusion, so a connector gated on "all of my connectors are unclaimed" is testing itself among them.


## Where else facts are read

*The same vocabulary, three more places.*

**Grammar constraints.** **Orbital Facts** and **Claim Facts** are two of the nine grammar constraints in [Regions and Rules](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/regions-and-rules), vetoing placement candidates by a fact of the parent or of the candidate module.

**Point filters.** The Valency filter family tests the same facts on points, which is how a fact reaches anything downstream that takes filters.

**Growth.** Connector gates are evaluated as growth works out which sockets a placed module actually exposes, which is where the substrate fallback matters most.

## The seam between the two models

*This is where orbitals reach into connector growth.*

Connector gates are the main place the two [Connection Models](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/connection-models) inform each other. A connector-grown module can be gated on an orbital fact, so growth is constrained by directional information it never places with.

The line holds in one direction only. Orbitals never place a connector-grown module, but they can decide which of its sockets exist. Module facts are compiled and always answerable; substrate facts need a real orbital substrate, which in practice means growing from a solved cluster.

title: Filters
description: Four point filters test things only Valency knows: what module a point resolved to, which of its orbitals have neighbours, which of its connectors are still open.
outline: When there is nothing to test
body:
Four point filters test things only Valency knows: what module a point resolved to, which of its orbitals have neighbours, which of its connectors are still open.

They are ordinary PCGEx point filters, so anything that takes a filter takes these. What makes them their own family is that each has to find a **Valency Map**, the pin [Generating](concept:working-with-valency/generating) describes, before it can answer anything, and where it looks is the first setting on all four.

## The four

| Filter | Tests |
|---|---|
| **✱ Filter : Has Module** | Whether the point carries a placed module at all |
| **✱ Filter : Module Tag** | The resolved module against a gameplay-tag predicate |
| **✱ Filter : Orbitals** | An orbital fact: occupancy, vacancy, boundaries, wildcards |
| **✱ Filter : Connectors** | A connector fact: which instances are claimed or still open |

The last two are the [Facts and Gates](concept:working-with-valency/systems/facts-and-gates) exposed as filters, sharing its vocabulary exactly. Anything a gate or a grammar constraint can ask, a filter can ask of a point.

## Finding the map

*Two answers, and the right one depends on what the filter is plugged into.*

Every one of these filters needs to resolve an entry hash to a module, which takes a map. `Map Source` says where to get it.

| Source | Reads the map |
|---|---|
| **Host Context** | From the node evaluating the filter. The default. |
| **Pin** | From a dedicated pin on the filter node itself |

**Host Context** works when the consuming node is a Valency node that already took a map, which covers most uses: vertex filters on a growth node, seed filters, pattern gating.

**Pin** is for everywhere else. Feeding one of these filters to an ordinary PCGEx node, which has no map of its own, needs the map supplied directly.


> **Warning.**
> A filter set to **Host Context** on a node that consumes no map has nothing to resolve against. Reach for **Pin** whenever the filter is not sitting inside a Valency node.


Suffixes follow the same idea. `Inherit Suffix`, and its orbital and claim equivalents, take the layer names from the host rather than restating them, which keeps a filter working when the host is retargeted. Turning inheritance off exposes the name so it can be set by hand.

## Testing orbitals

*A fact, a selection, and what to compare it against.*

**✱ Filter : Orbitals** takes an orbital fact and a selection of orbitals to test it over, exactly as a gate does. The selection has one more option here than elsewhere.

| Selection | Means |
|---|---|
| **All** | Every orbital the set defines |
| **Named** | Orbitals picked by name |
| **Indices** | Orbitals picked by raw index |
| **Attribute** | A per-point orbital bitmask read from an attribute |
| **Fact** | Another orbital fact |

**Attribute** is what makes the filter data-driven: the set of orbitals being asked about can vary per point, computed by anything upstream.

**Fact** is the interesting one. It compares one fact against another rather than against a fixed selection, so "which of this module's boundaries are actually occupied" becomes a single test. That is a question about the *disagreement* between two facts, and it has no equivalent in a fixed list.

## Testing connectors

**✱ Filter : Connectors** works the same way over connector facts, selecting by identifier, by connector type, by raw index, or all of them.

Because connector claims are written by growth, this is mostly a filter for results: finding the pieces that still have somewhere to build, or the ones that are fully consumed.

## When there is nothing to test

*Three separate ways a point can have no answer, each with its own fallback.*

A filter can be handed a point that carries no module, or one whose entry does not resolve, or one a pattern consumed. Those are different situations and the tag filter distinguishes all three.

| Fallback | Covers |
|---|---|
| `No Module Fallback` | The point carries no entry at all |
| `Unresolved Fallback` | It carries one that resolves to nothing |
| `Consumed Fallback` | A pattern absorbed it |

All three default to **Fail**, which keeps unanswerable points out of a positive selection. Set one to **Pass** when the absence is what you are selecting for.

**✱ Filter : Has Module** exists for the simplest of those questions. `Require Resolvable` decides whether merely carrying an entry is enough or whether it must resolve, and `Consumed Counts` decides whether a pattern-absorbed point still counts as carrying its module. Inverting it is how you select the positions a solve could not fill.

## What they are for

*Mostly, telling one part of a result from another.*

These filters are how a second pass is aimed. Growth seeded only from the modules tagged as entrances, a pattern search confined to positions with an open connector, a bias applied only where an orbital faces nothing.

They are also the fastest way to see what a result contains, since a filter that selects nothing is itself an answer about the data.

title: Footprints and Overlap
description: Attachment is decided by connectors, and connectors know nothing about volume.
body:
Attachment is decided by connectors, and connectors know nothing about volume. Two pieces that mate perfectly can occupy the same space, and growth will put them there unless something checks.

**Placement conditions** are what check. Each is authored on a module, each answers yes or no about one candidate placement, and **every condition in a stack must pass** for the placement to happen.

That is the module tier, and it is this page's subject. A grammar can also refuse on spatial grounds, through a rule authored in the grammar rather than on any module, which is [Spatial Rules](concept:working-with-valency/systems/spatial-rules). The two share the channels below and nothing else.

## The four conditions

| Condition                        | Refuses when                                                                        |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Footprint Overlap**            | The candidate's footprint intersects anything already placed                        |
| **Footprint Overlap (Advanced)** | The same, with per-axis tolerance and tag-based exemptions                          |
| **Footprint Penetration**        | Overlap is deeper than an allowed threshold, so touching is fine and burying is not |
| **Spatial Domain**               | The candidate falls outside, or inside, a region you supplied                       |

The first three read the footprint the module carries, authored under [Footprints](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/footprints). The fourth reads geometry fed in from the graph, and needs no footprint at all.

An empty stack means the module itself refuses nothing on spatial grounds, leaving a grammar rule as the only thing that could. That is intentional, and it is a **project default** rather than a fixed rule: `Default Placement Conditions` under **Project Settings** decides what a newly created cage starts with. See [Module Settings](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/cages/module-settings).

## Ignoring the parent

_Every overlap condition skips it by default, and has to._

A module attaches to its parent, so their footprints frequently touch: that is what mating means. `Skip Parent Bounds` is on by default across all three footprint conditions, and turning it off is how you get growth that refuses to place anything at all.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: overlap-skip-parent | SHOWS: Why an overlap condition that includes the parent makes attachment structurally impossible. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same parent module with an open connector, and the same child module offered onto it, their two connector frames mated so the pieces meet flush at the joint. The two footprints are drawn in both panels and visibly share the contact face at the joint, with that shared face highlighted. Left panel headed Skip Parent Bounds on: the shared face marked as excluded from the test, and the child drawn accepted. Right panel headed Skip Parent Bounds off: the same shared face marked as an intersection, and the child drawn refused, dimmed and struck, with a short note that every other candidate meets the same face the same way. | MUST BE CLEAR: The contact at the joint is not a mistake, it is what mating produces. Counting it as an overlap refuses every candidate, not merely this one.
> Mating makes the footprints meet. Counting that contact as an overlap refuses every candidate there is.


Reach for it only when a module genuinely must not overlap the thing it attaches to, and expect to loosen the footprints to match.

## Overlap, with exceptions

_The Advanced variant is the same test with two escape hatches._

`Extent Offset` shrinks or grows the candidate's extents for the purposes of the test only, per axis, without changing the authored footprint. Negative values are the more useful direction: they buy tolerance for pieces that meet flush and would otherwise register as intersecting.

`Skip Predicate` exempts whole classes of module by tag. Decoration that should be allowed to sit inside structure, or a floor that everything stands on, is expressed once as a predicate rather than by removing the condition from everything else.

Both offsets are applied uniformly across the whole footprint. Per-marker tolerance has to be authored into the markers themselves.

## Penetration

_Overlap as a matter of degree._

**Footprint Penetration** allows intersection while its depth stays under `Max Penetration`, defaulting to five units, and rejects on the first violation.

That is the condition for pieces meant to embed slightly: trim that sinks into a wall, rocks that bed into terrain, anything where zero tolerance is wrong but burying is worse. It measures actual penetration depth rather than testing a shrunken shape, so a piece that grazes deeply along one face is caught where an extent offset would have let it through.

Depth is measured against boxes, so what the footprint is made of decides whether this condition can do its job at all. A **Polygon** spline marker has no depth test and falls back to rejecting any overlap against it, however generous `Max Penetration` is.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: overlap-penetration-vs-offset | SHOWS: That shrinking the test shape and measuring the depth of an intersection give different answers on the same geometry. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same two cases side by side within the panel: case A, a module bedded shallowly into a wall along its whole face; case B, a module cutting deeply into the wall but only along a narrow strip at one corner. Left panel headed Extent Offset: the candidate drawn with a visibly shrunken dashed test rectangle inside its real footprint; case A passes and case B also passes, because the narrow deep strip falls outside the shrunken shape, and B is marked accepted with a note that it should not have been. Right panel headed Penetration: the real footprints drawn unshrunken with the intersection region filled and a depth measure drawn across it in each case; case A is under the threshold and accepted, case B is over it and drawn refused, dimmed and struck. | MUST BE CLEAR: Case B is the same geometry in both panels and gets opposite answers. Shrinking the shape asks whether a smaller version still collides; penetration asks how deep the real collision goes.
> Same geometry, opposite verdicts. One asks whether a smaller shape still collides, the other asks how deep the real collision is.


## Spatial domains

_Confining growth to a shape supplied from the graph._

**Spatial Domain** is the condition that keeps growth inside a room, along a wall, or out of a volume that should stay clear. It reads geometry from the growth node's **External Domains** pin rather than from any module.

Geometry arrives on that pin in named **spatial channels**. Tag an input `SpatialChannel:<Name>` and it feeds the channel called `<Name>`; an input carrying no such tag is still baked, landing on the fallback channel rather than being dropped. Channel names are registered per project under `Project Settings > Plugins > PCGEx | Spatial Domains`, where `Default` always sits first, and a condition picks its `Channel Key` from that list.

Point a condition at a channel and choose which side counts.

| Mode                | Placement is valid     |
| ------------------- | ---------------------- |
| **Must Be Inside**  | Only inside the domain |
| **Must Be Outside** | Only outside it        |

`Margin` softens the boundary in either direction, letting a piece hang slightly over an edge or requiring it to keep clear by a set distance.

Splines bake to extruded prisms and points bake to oriented boxes, so the shape a domain takes is whatever is convenient to author.


> **Warning.**
> **A domain nobody supplied passes**
>
> A **Spatial Domain** condition whose `Channel Key` no upstream node fed lets every candidate through, rather than failing or erroring. That is deliberate, so a graph missing its domain input still runs, and it means a typo in the channel name reads as a condition that was never there.
>
> The symptom is growth spilling outside a region it should have been confined to, with the condition sitting on the module looking correct. Check the channel name against what the **External Domains** input is tagged with.


## Obstacles

_Space that is not part of the result and still blocks it._

Growth also refuses placements that would land on registered footprints belonging to nothing it placed. **Valency : Grow Cluster** can register the footprints of non-seed resolved modules as obstacles, so a growth pass extends an existing structure without growing through the parts it was not asked to touch.

That is how a second pass respects a first one without the two sharing a run.

## Reading the two symptoms

_The same subsystem produces opposite complaints._

| Symptom                                 | Cause                                                                                                    |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Pieces growing through each other       | The modules involved carry no condition. Nothing was asked to check.                                     |
| Growth stopping far short of its budget | Conditions rejecting nearly everything, usually footprints authored larger than the pieces they describe |

The second is the more confusing, because the run reports a budget it did not spend and nothing looks wrong in the level. Check the footprints against the geometry before adjusting rules: a box that swallows the empty part of an L-shaped piece makes every neighbour a collision.

`Skip Parent Bounds` turned off is the other reliable way to produce it, since a module that must not touch its own parent has nowhere legal to attach.

title: Node Index
description: Valency adds nineteen nodes and eight asset types.
outline: Grammar nodes live in the grammar asset
body:
Valency adds **nineteen nodes** and **eight asset types**. This page is the lookup table: what each one is, and where in this book it is explained.

## Reading the list

*Two conventions worth knowing before you search the picker.*

Nodes named **`Valency : Something`** process points. Nodes prefixed **`✱`** are parameter nodes: they build a factory that plugs into another node's pin rather than doing anything on their own. Valency puts the star on its filters and its probe.

Anything that consumes a resolved result also takes a **Valency Map** pin alongside the points. That contract, and why both are needed, is covered under [Output](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output).

## Resolving modules

*The nodes that decide what goes where.*

| Node | Does |
|---|---|
| [Solving](concept:working-with-valency/generating/solve) | Assigns modules to the vertices of an existing cluster, WFC-style, from orbital compatibility |
| [Growing](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow) | Grows a structure outward from seed points, attaching modules at connectors |
| [Growing From a Cluster](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow/from-a-cluster) | Grows from the open connectors of a cluster that is already resolved |
| [Branches and Bridges](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grow/branches-and-bridges) | Places bridge modules between resolved points with compatible open connectors |
| [Finding Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/generating/finding-patterns) | Detects authored arrangements in a result and swaps, substitutes or annotates them |

## Preparing a cluster

*Getting orbital data onto the thing a solve is about to read.*

| Node | Does |
|---|---|
| [Write Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/write-orbitals) | Computes and writes the orbital masks and indices a solve reads |
| [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) | Quantizes shapes, surfaces and volumes onto an orbital lattice, producing the cluster and its orbital data together |
| [Planar Partition](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/planar-partition) | Decomposes a cluster into floors and, within each floor, connected regions |
| **✱ Probe : Orbital** | Connects points along orbital directions, for PCGEx cluster generation. Described below. |

## Reading a result

*Turning resolved points into something downstream can use.*

| Node | Does |
|---|---|
| [Output](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output) | Resolves each point's module to a collection entry, so a PCGEx spawner can place it |
| [Reading Properties](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/reading-properties) | Writes module properties, names and tags onto points as attributes |
| [Write Connectors](concept:working-with-valency/generating/output/write-connectors) | Emits module connectors as points, for chained solving or for placing things at sockets |
| [Junctions](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/junctions) | Emits one point per bonded connector pair, read from cluster edges |

## Steering a run

*Parameter nodes that shape what the five resolvers choose.*

| Node | Does |
|---|---|
| [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases) | Boosts or suppresses modules matching a tag predicate, by a constant or a per-vertex attribute |
| [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases) | Matches a per-vertex attribute against a Channel Map's per-module values |
| [Filters](concept:working-with-valency/systems/filters) | Whether a point carries a placed module at all |
| [Filters](concept:working-with-valency/systems/filters) | The resolved module against a gameplay-tag predicate |
| [Filters](concept:working-with-valency/systems/filters) | An orbital fact: occupancy, vacancy, boundaries, wildcards |
| [Filters](concept:working-with-valency/systems/filters) | A connector fact: which instances are claimed and which are still open |

## Probe : Orbital

*The one node with no page of its own.*

**✱ Probe : Orbital** belongs to PCGEx's probing family rather than to any Valency stage. It feeds a cluster-generation node, and it builds edges by orbital direction, in the sense of [Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/orbitals): for each point, it keeps the single best candidate along each of the orbital set's directions, subject to that set's own alignment threshold.

`Favor` decides what "best" means when several candidates qualify, either the closest one or the best aligned. Closest is the default.


> **Note.**
> A constant `Search Radius` is multiplied by the orbital set's longest normalised length, so an orbital reaching two steps out is still found. An **attribute-driven** radius is used as given, and the node warns when the set contains an orbital longer than one step.


This is the tool for turning a loose point cloud into a cluster whose edges already run along orbital directions. Where the positions are regular enough to describe as a grid, [Lattice](concept:working-with-valency/generating/utility-nodes/lattice) is the shorter route, and it writes the orbital data as well.

## Assets

*Created from the content browser, all prefixed `[PCGEx] Valency`.*

| Asset | Is |
|---|---|
| [Bonding Rules](concept:working-with-valency/concepts/bonding-rules) | The module library, and the only asset a PCG graph consumes directly |
| [Authoring Orbitals](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/authoring-orbitals) | The named directions a ruleset speaks, and the symmetries they imply |
| [Authoring Connectors](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/authoring-connectors) | Connector types, their compatibility, and their default constraints |
| [Authoring Patterns](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/authoring-patterns) | An arrangement that can be recognised in a result |
| [Grammar](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar) | A recipe with control flow, driving what growth builds and in what order |
| [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases) | Typed per-module values under named channels, read by the Channel bias |
| [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases) | Pairwise module preferences, read as a bias during solving and growth |
| [Connector Constraints](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/connector-constraints) | A reusable fragment of connector constraint pipeline |


> **Note.**
> **Grammar nodes live in the grammar asset**
>
> Searching the PCG picker for Growth, Branch or Prune finds nothing. Those belong to a **Structural Grammar** asset's own graph, and a grammar reaches a run as a reference on a growth node.
>
> The twenty-one of them are listed under [Grammar Nodes](concept:working-with-valency/generating/grammar/grammar-nodes), and the biases and constraints authored inside a grammar are likewise outside the PCG picker.

title: Spatial Rules
description: A grammar can ask whether a placement sits inside or outside a named piece of geometry fed in from the graph.
outline: A channel nothing was baked into passes
A connector is a point, a module is a pose
Severity is read on two channels of the three
body:
A grammar can ask whether a placement sits inside or outside a named piece of geometry fed in from the graph. It is one question, and three rules ask it: one refuses on the answer, one reweights on it, and one uses it to decide whether some other rule applies at all.

## One question, three rules

_A constraint, a bias, and a precondition that any rule can carry._

| Rule                        | Does with the answer                          |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| The **Spatial** constraint  | Refuses the placement                         |
| The **Spatial** bias        | Prefers candidates on one side of the channel |
| `Active Where`, on any rule | Decides whether that rule participates        |

All three carry the same control, one row reading as a sentence: a side, a **spatial channel**, and a probe size.

`Side` is **Inside**, **Outside**, or **Disabled**, and **Disabled** is the off switch. Every rule in a grammar carries an `Active Where`, so that field starts **Disabled** and the row collapses to it. The two **Spatial** rules start on **Inside** against the `Default` channel, because authoring one of those is itself the spatial question. `Probe Extent` sizes the box used for the point test, and a larger one tolerates a connector sitting slightly outside the channel it should be in.


> Figure: STILL | id: spatial-rules-check-row | SHOWS: That the whole spatial test is one row reading as a sentence, and that switching the side off collapses the rest of it. | FRAME: The details panel of a grammar rule in the Structural Grammar editor, default layout, one rule selected and nothing else expanded. Two states of the same row, shot separately and shown one above the other: the row set to Inside with a channel picked and the probe field visible, then the same row set to Disabled with the channel picker and the probe field gone. | CALLOUTS: The side dropdown first, the channel picker second, the unlabelled probe field third. | SOURCE: A sample grammar carrying a Spatial constraint plus one other rule with Active Where authored, on a project whose spatial channel registry has more than the Default entry. | NOTE: The probe field carries no label by design and is identified only by its tooltip, so the callout has to point at it rather than name it.
> Side, channel, probe. Switching the side off is what retires the test, and the row says so by collapsing.


A **Spatial** grammar constraint is a different thing from a connector constraint, which shapes where a connector's candidate transforms may land, and from the **Spatial Domain** placement condition, which is authored on a module and travels with it. A grammar rule is authored in the grammar and applies wherever the grammar puts it. For the connector-side rules, see [Connector Constraints](concept:working-with-valency/authoring/connector-constraints).

## Naming a channel

_Channels arrive on the External Domains pin, and a rule addresses one by name._

A **spatial channel** is a named bag of geometry supplied from the graph. Tag an input `SpatialChannel:<Name>` and it feeds the channel called `<Name>`. An input carrying no such tag still gets baked, landing on the fallback channel rather than being dropped.

Channel names are registered per project, under `Project Settings > Plugins > PCGEx | Spatial Domains`, where `Default` always sits first. A rule picks its channel from that list.

The same channels feed the **Spatial Domain** placement condition, and [Footprints and Overlap](concept:working-with-valency/systems/footprints-and-overlap) covers that side of the story: which shapes splines and points bake into, and how a condition authored on a module reads them.


> **Warning.**
> **A channel nothing was baked into passes**
>
> A rule naming a channel that nothing was baked into passes, rather than failing or erroring. That is deliberate: a graph missing its spatial input still runs, and an unconnected **External Domains** pin never empties a frontier.
>
> It also means a typo in a channel name reads as a rule that was never authored. On a **Spatial** constraint that surfaces as growth going somewhere it should have been kept out of. On `Active Where` it reads the other way round: the precondition passes, so the rule it guards applies **everywhere** instead of only inside the channel it names.


## A connector is a point, a module is a pose

_Two subjects, and only one of them exists while candidates are still being weighed._

A grammar asks two different spatial questions, and only one of them can be asked early.

A frontier connector is a **position**. It exists the moment the connector is open, before anything has been chosen to go on it, and it is tested by probing a small box at its world transform. That makes it the cheap question, and the one available while candidates are still being narrowed.

A candidate's footprint is a **pose**. It exists only once a module and a transform have both been resolved, inside the placement attempt itself, and it is tested against the real footprint the module carries. That makes it the exact question, and the late one.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: spatial-rules-point-vs-pose | SHOWS: That the early test and the late test have different subjects, because only the connector exists while candidates are still being weighed. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical hair rule in rule colour. Both share one setup: a placed module drawn as an outline with an inside corner, one open connector on it in FFA627, and a spatial channel drawn as a region-dashed rectangle in 9595E8 whose edge runs between the connector and the space beyond it. Panel one headed Runtime Filter, with a second line reading the connector as a point. It marks the connector with a small solid probe box centred on it at the authored probe size, and leaves the space where a module would go completely EMPTY. Three candidate module outlines sit in a list beside that panel, drawn as list items rather than placed, bracketed together and labelled as sharing one verdict. Panel two headed Placement, with a second line reading the module as a pose. It resolves one of those three candidates onto the connector at a real transform, drawing its footprint as an oriented rectangle in E8BC59 that crosses the channel edge, dimmed and struck with a diagonal cross in FF897C. Two further transforms of the SAME module are drawn at 25 percent scale and half stroke weight as implied poses, one of them marked as the pose tried next. | MUST BE CLEAR: Panel one contains no module at all, and one verdict covers every candidate on that connector. Panel two contains exactly one module at one transform, and refusing it moves along to another transform of the same module rather than removing the module. | NOTE: The channel borrows 9595E8 and the region dash because the palette carries no external-extent colour and E8BC59 is already the footprint. No Context Volume appears here, so the two cannot be read for each other. The figure spends no green.
> The same rule, two subjects. The connector exists before anything is chosen for it, and the footprint exists only once something is.


## When the constraint is asked

_Three channels, and one of them has nothing to backtrack._

`Eval Channels` is a multi-select rather than a choice: a constraint answers on every channel it declares.

| Channel             | Asked                                       | About                                           |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| **Runtime Filter**  | Per candidate, during selection             | The frontier connector, as a point              |
| **Placement**       | Per resolved pose, at the moment of placing | The footprint of the candidate module           |
| **Exit Validation** | When the hosting region closes              | The footprint of every module the region placed |

The **Spatial** constraint answers on all three, and ships authored for **Runtime Filter** and **Placement**. Every other constraint type starts on **Exit Validation** alone. Each type declares which channels it implements, and authoring one it does not is caught when the grammar compiles rather than at runtime.

Only exit validation can say "by the time this region ends, at least one of these must exist", because the answer is unknown until the region is done. A runtime filter answers per candidate, so it can say "never this module here" and nothing about the region as a whole.

When every candidate in a pool has been vetoed on the **Runtime Filter** channel, there is nothing left to place, and the run backtracks at the severity of the most severe constraint that was active.


> **Warning.**
> **Severity is read on two channels of the three**
>
> A **Placement** refusal means try the next pose. One candidate fans out to several transforms through the connector constraint pipeline, and each is offered separately, so a refusal moves to the next transform, then to the next module. Nothing was committed, so nothing is undone, and there is no failure for `Severity` to price.
>
> The consequence is worth authoring around: on that channel, "this module is forbidden here" is beyond what the rule can express, because the run works through the remaining poses before it gives up on the module. A veto that has to reach backtracking belongs on **Runtime Filter**, where an emptied pool escalates, or on **Exit Validation**, which fails the region outright.


## Inside means touches

_The test is an overlap, so a piece hanging out of a channel still counts as in it._

**Inside** asks whether the subject intersects the channel, which is weaker than asking whether it sits wholly within one. A module hanging halfway out of a room still reads as inside it. The same test drives **Outside**, so a connector a hair inside a keep-out volume counts as intersecting it and fails.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: spatial-rules-inside-is-touching | SHOWS: That Inside is satisfied by contact rather than containment, and that the extents the test uses are what changes the answer. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical hair rule in rule colour. Both draw one spatial channel as a region-dashed rectangle in 9595E8. Panel one headed Inside: four copies of the same module outline with an inside corner, placed against that one channel and drawn from the shared piece library so they read as one kit. The first sits wholly within the channel, the second straddles the edge with one arm hanging outside, the third meets the channel with a single corner only, and the fourth sits clear of it entirely. The first three are drawn solid and marked accepted with a short tick; the fourth is dimmed to 0.35 and struck with a diagonal cross in FF897C. Panel two headed Footprint Extent Offset: the corner-touching module alone, at exactly the position it held in panel one, its real footprint drawn as an oriented rectangle in E8BC59 with a shrunken test rectangle inside it in the region dash, the inset marked once with a short offset tick between the two edges. The shrunken rectangle clears the channel, and the module is drawn dimmed and struck. | MUST BE CLEAR: In panel one the straddling copy and the corner-touching copy get the same verdict as the wholly contained one, and only the copy making no contact at all is refused. In panel two nothing has moved and the geometry is identical to its panel one twin, so the only thing that changed is the extents the test used, and that is what flipped the verdict. | NOTE: The channel borrows 9595E8 and the region dash for the reason given on spatial-rules-point-vs-pose. Every module comes out of the one piece library, per the rule against drawing a run from a single shape. The figure spends no green.
> Contact is enough. Only the copy touching nothing is refused, and the extents the test uses are the lever.


Where the difference matters, there are two levers: tighten the channel geometry, or shrink the extents the test uses. `Footprint Extent Offset` does the second, is signed, and takes negative values, which is the useful direction. It is read on the **Placement** and **Exit Validation** channels, the two that test a footprint.

## Making a rule conditional

_Active Where decides whether a rule applies, and decides nothing else._

`Active Where` is authored on every grammar rule, beside `Rule Name` and `Scope`. **Reach**, **Forbid Pair**, **Quota** and the rest can each be made to apply only where the frontier connector sits on a given side of a channel.

While its test fails, the rule does not participate: a constraint vetoes nothing, and a bias contributes exactly neutral, which in the multiplicative fold of [Biases](concept:working-with-valency/systems/biases) is `1`. A rule whose precondition failed and a rule that was never authored produce the same result.

That is the whole distinction between a precondition and a spatial rule. A **Spatial** bias with a low `Miss Weight` pushes candidates down on the wrong side of a channel. A precondition on the same channel pushes nothing anywhere; it steps out.

The precondition is read on connector-anchored channels only, which is why the control appears on some rules and not others. Biases always score a connector, so they always carry it. A constraint carries it while it answers on **Runtime Filter**, and turning that channel off retires the control with it: **Placement** holds a resolved pose, which is a better anchor than the connector, and **Exit Validation** has neither a candidate nor a connector to test.


> **Warning.**
> **An inert rule reports nothing**
>
> A rule sitting out is indistinguishable, in the result and in the diagnostics, from a rule that was never authored. There is no warning, because stepping out is what the precondition is for.
>
> So a rule that appears to do nothing where you expected it to work is worth checking from the precondition inwards: the connector it was evaluated at may be on the other side of the channel, or the channel may be one nothing was baked into. [Debugging](concept:working-with-valency/systems/debugging) carries both symptoms.


## Which one a problem wants

_Ask whether the wrong side is ever acceptable, then how exact the answer has to be._

| When                                                                   | Reach for                                      |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
| The wrong side is never acceptable                                     | The **Spatial** constraint                     |
| The wrong side is a last resort rather than a refusal                  | The **Spatial** bias, with a low `Miss Weight` |
| Some other rule should apply in one place and stay out of it elsewhere | `Active Where` on that rule                    |

The two **Spatial** rules answer the same question and differ in what a wrong answer costs. A constraint removes the candidate; a bias leaves it in the draw and makes it unlikely, so a `Miss Weight` of zero is a soft veto at full `Influence` and anything above zero still lets the candidate through when it is the only one left.

The channel choice is a cost decision too. Put the cheap connector cull on **Runtime Filter**, and reserve **Placement** for cases where footprint accuracy is what decides the answer. A connector test is answered once per frontier slot and shared by every candidate on it; a pose test is paid again for every transform of every candidate offered there.

Name the rules. `Selective Mute` targets a rule by name, and a **Placement** refusal is reported by name in the growth diagnostic, so an unnamed rule refusing placements reports an unnamed refusal.

title: Spawn Limits
description: Weight decides how likely a module is.
outline: What a relative cap measures against under growth
body:
Weight decides how *likely* a module is. A **spawn limit** decides how *many* there may be, which weight alone can never guarantee: a piece weighted low still appears twenty times in a large enough result, and one weighted high may never appear at all.

Limits are authored per module and applied during resolution. Only one half of a limit is a hard rule, though, and the difference between the two halves is the first thing to know about them.

## Min and max

*Two halves that sound symmetrical and are enforced completely differently.*

| Setting | Means |
|---|---|
| `Min` | This many **should** be placed. `0` is no minimum. Always an absolute count. |
| `Max` | No more than this many. `-1` is unlimited. |

`Max` is a hard rule. A module at its cap is removed from the candidate pool before selection, so it cannot win a draw that would then have to be refused. Nothing placed ever exceeds a maximum.

`Min` is not the mirror of that, and reading it as one is the mistake this page exists to prevent.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: limits-max-vs-min | SHOWS: That a maximum removes a module from the draw while a minimum only makes it heavier, so the favoured module can still lose. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same candidate pool at one position, drawn as five module chips in a row, each sized by its weight, above a draw arrow pointing down into the pool. Left panel headed At maximum: one chip is lifted clear of the row and set aside behind a line, greyed, labelled removed before the draw, and the draw arrow can only reach the remaining four. Right panel headed Owing a minimum: all five chips are still in the row, one of them drawn at double size with a times two marker on it, and the draw arrow is drawn as several faint alternative arrows landing on different chips including the small ones. | MUST BE CLEAR: Left, the capped module cannot be drawn at all. Right, the owing module is merely likelier and one of the other four can still win, which is why a minimum can be missed.
> A maximum takes a module out of the draw. A minimum leaves it in and makes it heavier, so it can still lose.



> **Danger.**
> **A minimum is a preference**
>
> There is no mechanism that forces a minimum to be met. What a minimum does is **multiply the weight** of modules that have not reached theirs yet, making them likelier to win draws they were already eligible for.
>
> If the structure has no position a module fits, or the draw goes elsewhere, the minimum is quietly missed. The solve reports `Minimum spawn constraints were not satisfied` and returns the result anyway.
>
> For anything that genuinely must exist, place it deliberately: a fixed pick, a grammar that places it, or a **Count** constraint that fails loudly. A minimum expresses "lean towards this", and no amount of raising it changes that.


Two more things follow from it being a weight boost.

**The boost is a solver setting, not a per-module one.** `Minimum Spawn Weight Boost` lives on the solver and defaults to `2`, so every under-served module is pushed by the same factor. A module with a minimum of ten is not pushed harder than one with a minimum of one.

**Restarts barely weigh it.** When a solve retries and picks its best attempt, an unmet minimum scores one point of badness against a thousand for a single unsolvable position. An attempt that solved everything and missed every minimum still beats one that missed a single position.

## Growth ignores minimums entirely

*Only a solve consults them.*

Growth and grammar enforce maximums, through the same tracker and with the same hard exclusion from the candidate pool. They never read the minimum side at all.

That follows from what growth is. A minimum is a statement about a finished population, and growth has no bounded population to be finished: it stops when a budget runs out, and there is no point at which anything could check whether a minimum was reached and do something about it.

Authoring a minimum on a module used only by growth is therefore inert. It is not an error and nothing warns, so it is worth knowing before relying on one.

## A cap as a proportion

*`Relative Max` measures against a population instead of counting.*

Turn on `Relative Max` and the cap becomes `Max Rel`, a ratio between `0` and `1`, rounded up. "At most a fifth of this" scales with the result instead of needing a different number for every size of input.

The population it is measured against is `Workspace`.

| Workspace | Denominator |
|---|---|
| **In Scope** | States this solve may fill, plus pre-resolved states already consuming budget. Excludes boundary states and filter-locked ones. The default. |
| **All States** | Every non-boundary state, including filter-locked ones |

The difference matters when part of a cluster is locked by filters for a partial re-solve. **In Scope** measures the proportion against what this pass can actually change, which is usually what "a fifth of them" means when you say it.


> **Note.**
> **What a relative cap measures against under growth**
>
> A solve knows how many positions exist before it starts. Growth does not: it produces positions as it goes, so there is no denominator.
>
> Under growth and grammar both workspace modes resolve against the growth budget's `Max Total Modules` instead. A relative cap still works, and it is measured against how much the run is allowed to build rather than against how much exists.


A relative cap resolving below `Min` clamps up to `Min`, so the cap never sits under the floor the author asked for. That pair arises on its own from a small denominator, and it raises the ceiling rather than guaranteeing the floor is reached.

## Sharing one budget

*Several modules counted together instead of separately.*

Per-module limits answer "how many of this piece". Sometimes the question is "how many of these pieces", across a set that should be scarce collectively while any one of them is free to be the one that appears.

That is `Spawn Limits Source` on a collection entry or reference.

| Source | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Inherit** | Use the cage's own module settings. The default. |
| **Override** | Replace the per-module limits with the ones authored here |
| **Shared Budget** | Per-module limits still inherit; the limits here become **one budget covering every module this entry materializes** |

**Shared Budget** is the one worth understanding. Ten variants of a rare statue can each keep their own weights and their own individual caps, while the whole family is collectively capped at three. Without it, capping the family means capping each variant at a number that only works if the draw happens to spread evenly.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: limits-shared-budget | SHOWS: That a shared budget caps a family collectively while leaving each member its own weight and its own cap. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same four statue variants as chips, each with its own weight shown and its own counter beneath reading a cap of 2. Left panel headed Per module only: four independent counters, and a result above showing eight statues placed, two of each, all within their caps and far more than intended. Right panel headed Shared Budget: the same four chips with the same individual caps, plus one bracket drawn around all four feeding a single counter reading 3, and a result above showing three statues of mixed variants. A short note under the right panel states the individual caps still apply inside the shared one. | MUST BE CLEAR: The individual caps are identical in both panels. What the bracket adds is one count over the whole family, and it is the family count that decides when the group stops.
> Same per-variant caps in both. The bracket adds one count over the family, which is what makes a group scarce.


## Partitioned limits

*The same caps, applied per region instead of per result.*

A cap of three across a whole city is a different rule from three per building, and by default limits are the first kind.

`Enable Partitioned Limits` changes that. Point `Partition Attribute` at an int32 or int64 vertex attribute and the limits are enforced **per distinct value** of it, so each partition gets its own allowance. Vertices where the attribute is missing share one bucket between them.


> Figure: DIAGRAM | id: limits-partitioned | SHOWS: That the same authored cap means a different total once it is enforced per partition. | ELEMENTS: Two panels compared, separated by a vertical rule. Both show the same layout from above: three separate buildings, each drawn as a cluster of positions and tinted its own colour. A small card at the top of each panel states the same authored cap, at most 3 stairwells. Left panel headed Unpartitioned: three stairwell markers total across the whole layout, all of them landing in the first two buildings and the third having none. Right panel headed Partitioned by region: three stairwell markers inside each building, nine in total, each building tinted as its own partition. | MUST BE CLEAR: The authored number is 3 in both panels. Partitioning changed the total from three to nine, and it also stopped one building being left with none.
> The same authored cap. Enforced per partition it becomes three per building rather than three in total.


That attribute is usually not hand-authored. **Valency : Planar Partition** writes `RegionHash` for exactly this, which is a single value unique across the cluster, so partitioning by it gives per-region limits with nothing to wire up.

## What enforces them

*One tracker, consulted before every placement.*

Limits are not checked afterwards and corrected. A module already at its maximum is removed from the candidate pool before selection, so it never wins a draw it would have to be refused.

The same tracker holds the minimum side, keeping a list of modules still short of theirs, and it resolves relative caps against whichever workspace applies once the population is known.


> **Warning.**
> **One count per module family**
>
> Where a module has been registered in several rotations, whether through orbital variants or through folding, those share one family and one count. Placing any of them consumes the same allowance.
>
> That is what makes a cap mean what it says. Counting rotations separately would let a cap of one place four pieces that look identical.


## Limits or weight

*Ask whether the number matters or the ratio does.*

Reach for **weight** when the answer is "roughly this often", and for a **limit** when it is "no more than". For "at least" and "exactly one", neither is enough on its own: a maximum caps the top and a minimum only leans on the bottom, so the floor has to come from a fixed pick, a grammar, or a constraint that fails.

The two are not alternatives and most libraries use both: weight to shape the mix, limits on the handful of pieces where a count is part of the design. A library that expresses everything through limits produces the same result every time and has given up the variety it was built for.

title: Attribute Overrides
description: Most of what the node does is decided by one setting applied to a whole cluster.
outline: Switching a value to an attribute
Authoring the masks without knowing the bits
body:
Most of what the node does is decided by one setting applied to a whole cluster. Almost all of those settings will read from an attribute instead, which is how one cluster produces intersections of different sizes and roads of different profiles.

## Switching a value to an attribute

*Three mechanisms, and which one you get depends on the value.*

A **checkbox beside the value** replaces it with an attribute name. `Radius (Attr)`, `Polygon Routing (Attr)`, `Polygon Point Type (Attr)`, `Road Point Type (Attr)`, `Lane Profile (Attr)` and `Merge Group` all work this way: tick the toggle and the field beside it becomes the name to read.

A **mode dropdown** does it for the two bitmask values. `Intersection Tags Mode` and `Connection Restriction Mode` both start at **None** and reveal an attribute name once set to **Raw Bitmask** or **Value Map**.

An **`Input` dropdown** does it for the shorthand values: `Primary Turn Radius`, `Secondary Turn Radius`, `Primary Roll`, `Secondary Roll` and the tangent `Length`. Each carries its own **Constant** or **Attribute** choice, and the attribute name only matters in the second.

## What can be driven

*The whole set, with the dataset each is read from.*

| Setting | Reads from | Type | Default name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Radius (Attr)` | Vtx | `double` | `PolygonRadius` |
| `Polygon Routing (Attr)` | Vtx | `int32`, `0` Bezier, `1` Arcs | `PolygonRoutingType` |
| `Polygon Point Type (Attr)` | Vtx | `int32`, `0` to `3` | `PolygonPointType` |
| `Road Point Type (Attr)` | Vtx | `int32`, `0` to `3` | `RoadPointType` |
| Intersection tags | Vtx | `int32` | `IntersectionTags` |
| `Length`, tangent, Manual mode only | Vtx | `double` | `TangentLength` |
| `Merge Group` | Vtx | `int32` | `MergeGroup` |
| `Lane Profile (Attr)` | Edges | `FName` | `LaneProfile` |
| `Primary` and `Secondary Turn Radius` | Edges | `float` | `InnerTurnRadius` |
| `Primary` and `Secondary Roll` | Edges | `float` | `Roll` |
| Connection restrictions | Edges | `int32` | `ConnectionRestrictions` |

Both shape point type values are indices into ZoneGraph's own list, in its order: `0` Sharp, `1` Bezier, `2` Auto Bezier, `3` Lane Profile. Values outside the range are clamped rather than rejected.

Which dataset a value reads from follows the decomposition rather than convenience, and [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons) covers why. The short version: a polygon is one Vtx, a road is many edges, and a branching Vtx has nowhere to put four different lane profiles.


> **Note.**
> A value read from edges is resolved to one value per road before anything is built. The lane profile and the flip decision are majority votes across the road's edges; turn radius, roll and connection restrictions are read from the road's first and last edge. Painting a value on one edge in the middle of a long road changes nothing.


## Bitmask attributes

*Two values are flag sets, and both offer a raw and an indirect way to supply them.*

Intersection tags and connection restrictions are bitmasks rather than numbers, which makes them awkward to author upstream. Each takes the same two-way choice.

**Raw Bitmask** reads the `int32` and uses it as the mask directly. Correct when whatever produced the attribute already knows the bit layout.

**Value Map** reads the `int32` as a key into a table you fill in on the node, and uses the mask that key returns. Correct when your upstream data carries category ids (`0`, `1`, `2`) and the mapping from category to flags belongs to the node. A key with no entry yields no flags.

Intersection tags then union with the node's `Additional Intersection Tags`, in both modes, so the node-level tags always apply and the attribute adds to them.


> **Tip.**
> **Authoring the masks without knowing the bits**
>
> The plugin registers two PCGEx property types for this: **ZG Intersection Tags** and **ZG Connection Restrictions**. Both give you the engine's own editing widget, the tag picker and the restriction checkboxes, inside PCGEx's property system, and both write out as the `int32` this node reads. Point one at `IntersectionTags` or `ConnectionRestrictions` upstream and Raw Bitmask works with no bit arithmetic anywhere.


## When an attribute is missing

*Every case logs an error. What follows the error differs, and two of them are severe.*

| Missing attribute | What the node does |
|---|---|
| `Radius (Attr)`, `Polygon Routing (Attr)`, `Polygon Point Type (Attr)`, `Road Point Type (Attr)` | Falls back to the constant beside it |
| Intersection tags | Only `Additional Intersection Tags` is applied |
| Connection restrictions | No restrictions are applied |
| `Lane Profile (Attr)` | Every road uses the node's `Lane Profile` |
| Turn radius or roll, in Attribute mode | Falls back to `100` and `0`, **not** to the `Constant` field beside the dropdown |
| Tangent `Length`, in Attribute mode | The cluster fails to process |
| `Merge Group` | **Merging is disabled for the whole cluster** |

The last two are worth watching for. A missing merge group disables merging rather than ignoring the group restriction, because ignoring it would fuse polygons you had opted out; the result is a graph where nothing merges and the reason is one attribute name. A missing tangent attribute takes the cluster with it.

The turn radius and roll fallback catches people out for a different reason: the value used is the property's own default, so raising `Constant` to `250` and then switching to **Attribute** with a name that does not resolve gives you `100`, not `250`.

## Related

* [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons)
