* [Connection Properties](concept:working-with-zonegraph/connection-properties)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Connection Properties
description: A connection point carries more than a position.
outline: Different values at a road's two ends
Which end counts as primary follows the road's direction
body:
A connection point carries more than a position. Three of its values come from the road arriving there, and one more belongs to the intersection itself. All four are what ZoneGraph uses to decide how lanes actually route across the junction.

## What a road hands over

*Three values, read from the road's first and last edge.*

| Property | What it does |
|---|---|
| `Primary` / `Secondary Turn Radius` | The inner radius arcs follow through the connection. **Only consulted while `Polygon Routing Type` is Arcs**; a Bezier polygon ignores it entirely. |
| `Primary` / `Secondary Roll` | Banking, in degrees, applied to the connection point. ZoneGraph leaves roll alone when it recomputes point rotations, so what you set here survives. |
| Connection restrictions | A bitmask limiting which lanes may connect through the point: no left turn, no right turn, one lane per destination, merge lanes to one destination lane. |

All three sit in the Polygon Settings block, under `INNER TURN RADIUS`, `ROLL` and `CONNECTION RESTRICTIONS`. Turn radius and roll are shorthand inputs, so each carries its own **Constant** or **Attribute** choice; see [Attribute Overrides](concept:working-with-zonegraph/attribute-overrides) for how that switch works and what a missing attribute costs.

## Different values at a road's two ends

*The `Separate Secondary` toggles, and which end is which.*

By default a road hands the same value to both of the intersections it touches, taken from its first edge. Ticking `Separate Inner Turn Radius Secondary` or `Separate Roll Secondary` gives the far end its own value, read from the road's last edge, so a road can taper its turn radius or its banking from one junction to the next.


> **Warning.**
> **Which end counts as primary follows the road's direction**
>
> Primary is the road's logical start and secondary its logical end, and the road's direction is decided network-wide before any of this is read. Change the orientation mode and the two ends swap, so a road that tapered one way tapers the other. See [Road Orientation](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-orientation).


Connection restrictions have no separate-secondary toggle. They are read from the first and last edge unconditionally, so each end already carries its own value.

## Intersection tags

*A tag mask on the polygon itself, rather than on any one connection.*

`Additional Intersection Tags` applies to every polygon in the cluster, and `Intersection Tags Mode` adds a per-Vtx attribute on top of it. The two combine rather than compete: whatever the attribute supplies is unioned with the node-level mask, so the node-level tags always apply.

Tags travel through a merge. A fused polygon carries the union of the tags of every polygon that went into it, which is worth knowing before you tag intersections you also intend to merge. See [Polygon Merging](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-merging).

Both intersection tags and connection restrictions are bitmasks, and both take the same **Raw Bitmask** or **Value Map** choice for how an attribute supplies them. That choice, and the two property types that let you author the masks without touching a bit, are on [Attribute Overrides](concept:working-with-zonegraph/attribute-overrides).

## Related

* [Attribute Overrides](concept:working-with-zonegraph/attribute-overrides)
* [Polygon Merging](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-merging)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Convex Fit Radius
description: The other per-road modes size each connection from its own road's profile and ignore everything else at the junction.
body:
The other per-road modes size each connection from its own road's profile and ignore everything else at the junction. That holds until two roads meet at a sharp angle, where their lane strips overlap well before either reaches the boundary and the intersection geometry tangles.

**Convex Fit** sizes each connection from its neighbors instead. It is one of the `Auto Radius Mode` values, so the `Auto Radius Policy` applies to it exactly as it does to the others.

## What it fits to

*Each connection is pushed out until the roads beside it have cleared its centerline.*

For one road, the node walks every other road at the polygon and asks where that neighbor's lane strip would cross this road's centerline. The largest of those distances becomes the radius:

```
radius = the largest of, over every other road at the polygon,
         that road's profile half-width / |sin(angle between the two roads)|
```

Two things fall straight out of that sine. The sharper the angle between two roads, the smaller the sine and the further out both connections have to sit. And **a road's own width never enters its own radius**: what pushes a connection out is the roads next to it, never the road itself. A lone wide road at a junction of narrow ones stays close to the center while pushing everything else away.


> Figure: Two roads leaving a polygon center at an acute angle, each drawn with its lane-width strip. The neighbor's strip edge is extended until it crosses the subject road's centerline, and the distance from the center to that crossing is the fitted radius. The subject road's own strip is marked, and takes no part in it.
> The neighbor's strip edge decides where this road's connection lands. Its own width does not.


## When nothing constrains a road

*Two roads running straight through a polygon constrain each other not at all, and the fallback covers it.*

A pair of roads within a whisker of collinear is skipped rather than measured, because the sine approaches zero and the distance approaches infinity. If every other road at a polygon is skipped that way, the road has no constraint left and `Fallback` supplies one.

The case is more common than the wording suggests, and it has a name elsewhere in this book: a polygon forced onto a straight run by **Break Conditions** has exactly two roads, pointing opposite ways. Neither constrains the other, so both take the fallback. See [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons).

| Fallback | Value |
|---|---|
| **Smallest Profile** | The smallest profile half-width across every road at that polygon. A minimal non-zero size. |
| **Largest Profile** | The largest. A roomier polygon, which reads better where profiles change across the junction. |

The fallback is a radius like any other, computed before `Auto Radius Policy` runs, so **Use as Min** will still raise it toward your manual radius and **Additive** will still add to it.

## The clamp

*`Clamp` caps every fitted radius at a multiple of the largest half-profile at that polygon.*

As two roads approach parallel their fitted radius runs toward infinity, and the pair that is skipped entirely at near-zero sine is the only pair that escapes it. `Clamp` bounds the result: no radius at a polygon exceeds `Clamp` times the largest profile half-width found there. It defaults to `4.0` and will not go below `1.0`.

Two properties of that cap are worth holding on to. It applies to **every** road's radius at the polygon, not only to the ones that ran away. And its reference is the largest half-profile *at that polygon*, so the cap scales with the junction rather than being an absolute distance: adding one wide road raises the ceiling for every arm there.

`Clamp` and `Fallback` share the **Convex Fit** row under `GEOMETRY` in the Polygon Settings block, side by side, and the row appears only while `Auto Radius Mode` is **Convex Fit**.

## Related

* [Polygon Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-radius)
* [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Multiple Lane Profiles
description: One Lane Profile on the node gives every road in the cluster the same cross-section.
outline: Flipping a profile without turning the road
body:
One `Lane Profile` on the node gives every road in the cluster the same cross-section. Painting an attribute on your edges instead lets one cluster carry a highway, a residential street and an alley, and lets them meet at the same intersection without any manual matching.

## Painting a profile onto edges

*An `FName` per edge, resolved to one profile per road by majority vote.*

Tick `Override Lane Profile` under `LANE PROFILE` in the Road Settings block and name the attribute to read. Each road then counts the profile names across all of its own edges and takes the most common one. A road of five edges where three carry `Highway` is a highway.

The name has to match a profile registered under `Project Settings > Zone Graph`. A name that resolves to nothing falls back to the node's own `Lane Profile` setting, which is a value you can see and change, rather than to anything of ZoneGraph's.

Each polygon connection point then takes the profile of the road arriving there, so an intersection where a four-lane road meets a two-lane one carries both cross-sections on its own boundary and routes between them.


> **Warning.**
> **Profiles live on edges**
>
> A junction Vtx is shared by every road meeting it, so there is nowhere on it to write four different profiles. Edges belong to exactly one road, which is what makes a per-road value possible at all. Painting a profile name onto junction vertices produces nothing.


Profiles resolve before any polygon is sized, which is what lets `Auto Radius Mode` read lane widths off them. See [Polygon Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-radius).

## Flipping a profile without turning the road

*A majority vote of the **Flip Conditions** filter reverses which way the profile reads.*

A road's direction and its profile's direction are two axes, not one. Reversing the road turns the whole thing around; reversing the profile mirrors the cross-section while the road keeps running the way it did. A one-way pair, where two parallel roads carry mirrored profiles, needs the second and not the first.

Turning on `Enable Flip Filters` promotes the **Flip Conditions** pin, which takes edge filters. Each road counts how many of its edges pass and flips its profile when a strict majority do, so two edges need both to pass and three need two.

The flip reaches the geometry in two places at once: the road component carries it, and each polygon connection point carries its opposite. That disagreement is what makes the two sides of a connection mate.


> **Note.**
> Which way a road **runs** is decided network-wide by a different mechanism, and nothing on this page changes it. See [Road Orientation](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-orientation).


## Related

* [Road Orientation](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-orientation)
* [Attribute Overrides](concept:working-with-zonegraph/attribute-overrides)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Overview
description: The default decomposition needs nothing configured, and it is the last thing in this section that does.
body:
The default decomposition needs nothing configured, and it is the last thing in this section that does. Everything below is a decision the node makes on your behalf and will hand back if you ask for it.


> **Note.**
> Every mechanic here is a setting on one node, and **Cluster to Zone Graph** is the property-level reference for all of them. These pages teach the model; that page enumerates.


## The model

_Which parts of a cluster become roads, which become polygons, and how to move that line._

The node counts the connections at each Vtx and decides from the count. Everything else in this section assumes that rule.


See [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons).


## Sizing an intersection

_How far each connection sits from its center, and when two intersections should be one._


See [Polygon Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-radius).



See [Convex Fit Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/convex-fit-radius).



See [Polygon Merging](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-merging).


## Shaping a road

_Where it stops, which way it runs, which lanes it carries, and how it curves._


See [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints).



See [Road Orientation](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-orientation).



See [Multiple Lane Profiles](concept:working-with-zonegraph/multiple-lane-profiles).



See [Tangent Control](concept:working-with-zonegraph/tangent-control).


## What a connection carries

_The properties a road hands to each intersection it touches._


See [Connection Properties](concept:working-with-zonegraph/connection-properties).


## Data in, geometry out

_Reading the settings from point attributes, and getting the result back as PCG paths._


See [Attribute Overrides](concept:working-with-zonegraph/attribute-overrides).



See [Path Outputs](concept:working-with-zonegraph/path-outputs).

title: Path Outputs
description: The Zone Graph itself lands on the target actor as components, out of reach of the rest of your graph.
outline: Only while `Polygon Point Type` is Lane Profile
body:
The Zone Graph itself lands on the target actor as components, out of reach of the rest of your graph. Two optional pins hand the same geometry back as ordinary PCG paths, so the shapes the node produced can drive whatever comes next.

Both are under `Settings > Output`. Each pin sits on the node as an Advanced pin until its toggle is on, and is deactivated rather than empty while it is off.

## Road Paths

*One open path per road, carrying the compiled spline's tangents.*

Each road that survives is emitted as a path whose points sit at the road's final shape points, with two `FVector` attributes per point: `ArriveTangent` and `LeaveTangent`, named by `Arrive Name` and `Leave Name` if the defaults collide with something upstream.

The geometry is read back off the compiled component, after trimming, after the tangent pass and after ZoneGraph has had its say. So a road path matches the road that was actually built, including tangents this node did not choose. Feed one to a Create Spline node and you get a spline that follows the Zone Graph road closely.

Roads that were dropped emit no path, which includes roads a merge contracted. See [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints).

## Polygon Paths

*One closed path per intersection, two points per connection.*

Each polygon is emitted as a closed path. Every connection contributes a pair of points, right then left, offset from the connection point along its own facing, which traces the intersection's boundary rather than its center.

The offset is the connection's cached lane half-width, which makes each pair span the full width of the road arriving there.


> **Warning.**
> **Only while `Polygon Point Type` is Lane Profile**
>
> The half-width the offset uses is a field ZoneGraph fills in for lane-profile points and reuses for something else on every other point type. Set `Polygon Point Type` to `Sharp`, `Bezier` or `Auto Bezier` and the same field holds a bezier tangent length or zero, so the pairs collapse toward the connection centers and the path stops describing a boundary.
>
> `Polygon Point Type` defaults to **Lane Profile**, so this bites when you change it, not out of the box.


The paths are flagged closed, so downstream nodes treating them as loops get a loop. They make a reasonable safe-zone region around an intersection: feed them to an inclusion filter such as [Filter : Inclusion (Path/Splines)](https://pcgex.gitbook.io/pcgex/node-library/filters/point-filters/spatial/filter-inclusion-path-splines) to keep props and clutter off the junction.

## Related

* [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons)
* [Tangent Control](concept:working-with-zonegraph/tangent-control)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Polygon Merging
description: Two intersections joined by a short stub of road that you would rather see as one intersection: a divided road that briefly splits and rejoins, or a pair of junctions that landed too close together.
outline: What a seam has to pass
What a fused intersection is made of
body:
Two intersections joined by a short stub of road that you would rather see as one intersection: a divided road that briefly splits and rejoins, or a pair of junctions that landed too close together. Merging fuses them and dissolves the road between.

`Enable Merge` turns on a post-process that runs after every road and polygon has been built. It looks for **seams**, roads that join two polygons, and contracts the ones that qualify. Merges are transitive, so a run of qualifying seams collapses into a single polygon.

## What a seam has to pass

*Three gates, in order, and all three have to agree.*

**The filter.** Enabling merge promotes a **Merge Conditions** pin, which takes Vtx filters. Both polygons at the ends of a seam have to pass it. With nothing wired the filter is not a restriction at all and every polygon is eligible, which means the guards below are doing all the work.

**The group, if you use one.** `Use Merge Groups` reads an `int32` per Vtx and requires the two ends to relate. `0` on either end opts that intersection out entirely. `Match` sets how two non-zero ids must relate: equal, different, within `Tolerance`, or beyond it. The four comparisons are all symmetric, because a seam is an unordered pair of nodes and a `<` would depend on internal ordering.

**The geometric guards.** Four of them, each independently switchable, combined by `Guard Combine` as **All (AND)** or **Any (OR)**.

| Guard | Passes when | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `Max Face Gap` | The signed gap between the two facing connection points is at or below the threshold. Positive leaves road between them, `0` means touching, negative demands overlap. | **On**, at `0` |
| `Max Seam Angle` | The two arms are near-collinear: their misalignment in degrees is at or below the threshold, `0` being perfectly inline. | Off, at `30` |
| `Guard Single Edge` | The seam is a single cluster edge, with no pass-through vertices along it. | Off |
| `Max Arms` | Both intersections have at most this many **other** connections, the seam itself excluded. Stops you dissolving a busy junction. | Off, at `4` |

With every guard switched off, the filter and the group decide alone.


> **Warning.**
> **Why nothing merged**
>
> `Max Face Gap` is on out of the box at `0`, which requires the two intersections to be already touching or overlapping. On a network where the junctions are a road's length apart, that is every seam rejected and no warning about it, because rejecting a seam is the normal outcome rather than an error.
>
> Raise `Max Face Gap` to the length of stub you consider a mistake, and it will start contracting.



> Figure: Two polygons joined by one road, drawn three times at different separations. The gap is measured between the two facing connection points rather than between the polygon centers: positive while a span of road remains between them, zero when they coincide, and negative once the two polygons overlap and the points have crossed past each other.
> The gap is measured face to face, so it goes negative once the two intersections overlap.


## What a fused intersection is made of

*The surviving arms, exactly where they already were.*

Merging gathers every connection point of every member that was not itself a seam, re-sorts them by bearing around their shared centroid, and emits one polygon carrying them. **No geometry is recomputed.** No radius is resolved again and no road is re-trimmed, so a fused intersection is the ring the original arms already described rather than a fresh circle drawn around the group.

Its other properties come from one **primary member**: the polygon that contributed the most surviving arms, ties going to the lowest Vtx index. Routing type, shape point type, common lane profile and radius are all that member's. Intersection tags are the exception and are unioned across every member.

## When it declines to merge

*Three fail-safes, each preferring to do nothing over doing something wrong.*

A group that would be left with fewer than two arms is abandoned. Its members stay separate, the seams between them are restored as ordinary roads, and a warning is logged. That is the one case where the log tells you.

`Use Merge Groups` with a missing group attribute disables merging for the whole cluster rather than proceeding without the restriction, since ignoring it would fuse the intersections you had opted out.

A **Merge Conditions** filter that fails to initialize disables merging and leaves the rest of the node alone, so a broken filter costs you the merge pass and not your Zone Graph.


> **Note.**
> A road that was already degenerate is still allowed to be a seam. A road between two polygons only degenerates when those polygons overlap, which is the exact case merging exists to collapse, and fusing also clears the connection points it would otherwise leave dangling. See [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints).


Two more conditions rule a seam out before any gate runs. A cluster with fewer than two polygons has nothing to fuse. And a road whose two ends attach to the same polygon, which is what a self-connecting loop is, can never be a seam.

## Related

* [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons)
* [Connection Properties](concept:working-with-zonegraph/connection-properties)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Polygon Radius
description: A polygon is a ring of connection points around a Vtx, and the radius is what puts them there.
outline: Combining auto with a manual radius
**Use as Min** takes the larger value
body:
A polygon is a ring of connection points around a Vtx, and the radius is what puts them there. One number covers every intersection in the cluster, which is fine until a four-lane arterial and a footpath meet at the same one.

## Where a connection point sits

*Center, outward along the road, radius.*

Each road arriving at a polygon gets one connection point. It sits at the polygon's Vtx position, pushed out along the direction of the road's own edge at that Vtx, by that connection's radius. `Polygon Radius` supplies the distance, and `Radius (Attr)` overrides it per Vtx from a `double` attribute so different intersections can be different sizes. Both live under `GEOMETRY` in the Polygon Settings block.

The same distance does a second job: it is the boundary road endpoints are clipped against. Growing a polygon eats road, and past a point it deletes roads outright. That half of the story is on [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints).


> Figure: A three-road junction. One connection point is highlighted, sitting where the direction of the road leaving the center meets the radius measured along it. The polygon boundary is drawn as a dashed ring through all three connection points.
> The direction is the road's. The distance is the radius. The connection point is where they meet.


## Sizing from the roads instead

*`Auto Radius Mode` derives the distance from lane profiles rather than from a number you picked.*

Every road resolves its lane profile before any polygon is sized, so by the time the radius is computed the node knows each road's total profile width and its widest single lane. `Auto Radius Mode` turns those measurements into a distance. A wide road produces a wide footprint without anyone maintaining a per-junction number.

Five modes are live, and they split into two families that behave differently enough to choose between first.

| Mode | Family | Distance |
|---|---|---|
| **Widest Lane** | Per-road | That road's own widest single lane width |
| **Half Profile** | Per-road | Half that road's own total lane-profile width |
| **Convex Fit** | Per-road | Fitted so the connection clears its neighbors' lane strips |
| **Max Widest Lane** | Aggregate | The largest widest-lane across every road at this polygon |
| **Max Half Profile** | Aggregate | The largest half-profile across every road at this polygon |

**Widest Lane** and **Half Profile** are different numbers, and the gap between them grows with lane count. A six-lane profile of equal lanes has a widest lane one sixth of its total width and a half profile three times that.

## Per-road and aggregate

*A per-road mode gives every connection its own distance, so the polygon stops being a circle.*

The two families answer different questions. A per-road mode asks how far out *this* road needs to be, and gives each connection its own answer, so an arterial arm sits far from the center while the alley next to it sits close. An aggregate mode computes one value across every road at the polygon and applies it to all of them, keeping the ring circular.

Both aggregate modes take the maximum, so the widest road at the junction sets the size and every other arm is pushed out to match it.


> Figure: One four-road junction whose roads carry different profile widths, sized twice. Under Half Profile each connection sits at its own half-width and the ring is irregular. Under Max Half Profile every connection sits at the widest road's half-width, so the narrow arms move outward and the widest one does not move at all.
> Same profiles, same junction. The aggregate mode pushes the narrow arms out to meet the widest one.


## Combining auto with a manual radius

*`Auto Radius Policy` decides what happens to the number you already set.*

The auto value does not have to replace the manual one. `Auto Radius Policy` appears as soon as a mode is chosen and picks the arithmetic. The manual side of that arithmetic is whatever `Radius (Attr)` resolved for this Vtx, falling back to `Polygon Radius`, so a per-Vtx radius keeps working under every policy.

| Policy | Result | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|
| **Replace** | `auto` | You want profile-driven sizing and nothing else |
| **Use as Min** | `max(manual, auto)` | You want a size floor that wide roads are allowed to exceed |
| **Use as Max** | `min(manual, auto)` | You want to cap how large an intersection can grow |
| **Additive** | `auto + manual` | You want profile sizing plus a fixed margin at every junction |


> **Warning.**
> ****Use as Min** takes the larger value**
>
> Read the two middle names as the role the auto value plays in the result, not as an operation performed on it. **Use as Min** makes the auto value a floor under the radius, so the result is the larger of the two, and it is never a cap on the auto value. **Use as Max** makes it a ceiling, so the result is the smaller.
>
> The consequence worth holding on to: under **Use as Min**, a wide road grows its connection past your manual radius, and under **Use as Max** it cannot.



> **Note.**
> The policy used to be baked into the mode: two older values combined a source with a minimum in one setting. Both are hidden now, and a graph saved with either is migrated on load to the matching mode plus **Use as Min**, so a graph that changes mode under you on first open has done the right thing.


## Related

* [Convex Fit Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/convex-fit-radius)
* [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints)
* [Multiple Lane Profiles](concept:working-with-zonegraph/multiple-lane-profiles)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Road Endpoints
description: A road built straight from cluster points ends on the Vtx its polygon sits on, which puts its last stretch inside the intersection.
body:
A road built straight from cluster points ends on the Vtx its polygon sits on, which puts its last stretch inside the intersection. Both ways of resolving that land the road's final point in the same place; what differs is whether the points behind it survive.

## Where a road stops

*On its polygon's connection point, whether trimming is on or off.*

Every polygon hands each road arriving at it a connection point, and that point is where the road is meant to end. With `Trim Road Endpoints` on, the node finds where the road reaches that distance, drops the points behind it, and inserts a fresh shape point exactly on the connection. With it off, the road's terminal point is moved out onto the same connection and nothing else changes.

So the choice is about the interior, not the end. Turning trimming off keeps every original point, including any that sit inside the polygon, which is what tangles routing at a busy junction. Turning it on removes them and costs you road length.

Both settings live under `ENDPOINTS` in the Road Settings block.


> **Note.**
> Neither runs at a leaf. A road ending in open air has no polygon and no boundary to meet, so its endpoint is left exactly where the cluster put it.


## Trimming

*Clip at the connection distance, then insert a point there.*

The node walks the road's shape points from the end being trimmed, measuring each one along that connection's own outward direction. The first point to reach the connection distance is the crossing: everything from there back to the road's tip is removed, and one new shape point is inserted at the connection.

Two details change what you predict. The measurement is a projection along the arm, so what a road is clipped against is square to that arm at the connection distance rather than the polygon's outline; a road curving hard away from a junction can keep points that are closer to the center than the radius. And the distance is that connection's own radius, so under a per-road auto mode the two ends of one road are cut at different distances.


> Figure: One road running into a polygon, shown twice at the same coordinates. Untrimmed, three of its shape points sit inside the boundary and its tip is on the polygon center. Trimmed, those three are dimmed and struck, one new crossing point sits exactly on the connection, and every surviving point is where it already was.
> Nothing that survives the trim moves. The road gains one point and loses the rest of its tip.


The scan runs from each end toward the middle, so it takes the crossing nearest the end it is trimming. A road that dips back inside the boundary somewhere along its length keeps everything beyond that dip.

**How a loop that returns to its own polygon is trimmed**


A closed chain that leaves a branching Vtx and comes back to it attaches both road ends to that one polygon, and the two ends are handled differently.

The start point already sits on the polygon center, so snapping it out to the boundary is the same operation as trimming the first segment. The far end is an ordinary chain node rather than the center, so overwriting it would skip that node and any near it whenever the loop is larger than the polygon. Instead the node appends a new crossing point on the implicit closing edge, leaving the last chain node in place.

The tangent pass treats such a loop as an open spline, because from ZoneGraph's side it now is one: both its ends terminate on polygon arms.



## The trim buffer

*Drop what survives too close to the point trimming inserted.*

Trimming stops at the first crossing, so a road point sitting slightly beyond it survives and ends up near-coincident with the inserted point. Two points that close make bezier control lengths overshoot, and the road bulges where it leaves the intersection.

`Endpoint Trim Buffer` removes them. After the crossing point is inserted, any road point within this distance **of the crossing point** is dropped, one after another, until the next one is far enough away or only two shape points remain. It defaults to `0`, which does nothing. Small values are the useful range: enough to swallow a coincident point, short enough to leave the road its shape.

The measurement is a straight line to that single inserted point, not a distance to the polygon boundary. For a road approaching off-axis those differ, and the buffer removes less than a distance-to-boundary reading would.


> Figure: A trimmed road endpoint with the crossing point inserted on the polygon connection. A dashed circle of the buffer distance is centered on that crossing point, not on the polygon center. The road point inside it is dimmed and struck; the first point beyond it is kept, and removal stops there.
> The buffer is measured from the inserted point, so it clears coincidence rather than clearing the intersection.



> **Note.**
> The bulge the buffer prevents is a tangent problem, and the tangent settings carry a second fix for it that works on the spacing rather than on the points. See [Tangent Control](concept:working-with-zonegraph/tangent-control).


## Roads that get dropped

*A road that never leaves its polygon carries no navigation, so it is discarded.*

One condition accounts for almost every disappearing road: at one of its ends, the road never gets past the connection distance. The node finds no crossing to insert, and the whole span lies inside the intersection, so the road is dropped without emitting a component.

The second is a guard rather than a behavior. ZoneGraph cannot build a shape from fewer than two points, so a road left below that is dropped too. Trimming and the buffer both stop at two, which is why the buffer can never be what deletes a road: a road cut to its floor comes out as a straight line between its two polygon arms, and that is a road ZoneGraph builds.

If roads are vanishing where you expected them, the polygon at one end has grown past them. Lower `Polygon Radius`, or lower whatever the auto radius resolved to there, or space the vertices further apart. Merging is the other reason a road stops being emitted, and that one is deliberate.

## Related

* [Polygon Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-radius)
* [Tangent Control](concept:working-with-zonegraph/tangent-control)
* [Polygon Merging](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-merging)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Road Orientation
description: A lane profile is directional.
body:
A lane profile is directional. A profile describing a left lane and a right lane reads one way from one end of a road and the mirror of that from the other, so a road that runs the wrong way carries its lanes the wrong way. Orientation is decided **network-wide**, before any geometry is built.

## Traffic Flow

*The default. Direction is anchored at the network's dead ends and propagates inward from there.*

Every road with exactly one leaf end is oriented so the leaf is its start, pointing in toward the junction. Those junctions then become the seeds: each road leaving one takes its direction from it, and each junction that reaches sets the direction of the roads leaving *it*, until the connected network is consistent.

The result is what you want almost everywhere. Traffic reads as flowing out of the dead ends and through the network, lanes align at every junction they meet, and no road needs configuring individually.


> Figure: A branching network of two junctions and four leaves. Every road with a leaf end is drawn heavier and carries a direction chevron pointing away from its leaf and into the junction. The road between the two junctions is labeled as inheriting its direction rather than choosing one.
> Three leaves anchor the network. Every interior road takes its direction from the junction that reached it first.


A road with a leaf at both ends is left as it is: an isolated two-ended segment has nothing to be consistent with.


> **Note.**
> **Rings beyond every leaf**
>
> A ring that no leaf can reach has no anchor, so one road in it is seeded and the rest of that loop is made consistent from there. The seed is chosen by comparing the road's straight start-to-end chord against `Orientation Direction`, and reversed if the two oppose. With `Orientation Direction` at zero the seed falls back to a stable comparison of the two endpoints, which is arbitrary but repeatable.
>
> The visible effect is a winding choice: the vector decides which way round the loop runs.



> **Warning.**
> **Traffic Flow (Legacy)** in the dropdown is a deprecated alias. It resolves to the same leaf-inward propagation as **Traffic Flow**, with no separate depth-first behavior behind it any more. It exists so older saved graphs keep loading. Leave new graphs on **Traffic Flow**.


## Global Direction

*Every road is turned to agree with one world-space vector.*

Each road compares its own direction against `Orientation Direction` and reverses if the two oppose. Useful for grid-like networks where traffic should read as running consistently one way across the whole map.

The comparison uses the **straight chord between the road's two endpoints**, not the path it actually takes. A road that curves right round and comes back near where it started has a chord that says little about its shape, so it can end up oriented against the way it visibly runs.

## Sort Direction

*Hands the decision to the edge-direction system.*

The only mode that consults `Direction Settings`, and the only one where the sorting rules under it do anything. Choosing **Endpoints Sort** as the direction method also surfaces the **Direction Sorting** input pin, which is where the rules are plugged in.

This is the manual option: full control, and more to configure than the other three.

## Invert Orientation

*Flips every road once the mode has finished.*

Applied on top of **Traffic Flow**, **Traffic Flow (Legacy)** and **Global Direction**. **Sort Direction** never sees it, which is why the setting hides in that mode: reverse the sorting rules there instead.


> **Note.**
> Orientation decides which way a road runs. Which way its **lane profile** reads along it is a separate axis with its own control, and reversing one does not reverse the other. See [Multiple Lane Profiles](concept:working-with-zonegraph/multiple-lane-profiles).


## Related

* [Multiple Lane Profiles](concept:working-with-zonegraph/multiple-lane-profiles)
* [Roads and Polygons](concept:working-with-zonegraph/roads-and-polygons)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Roads and Polygons
description: The node never asks you where the intersections go.
outline: Two shapes, and the cluster decides both
A forced polygon eats road on both sides
One breakpoint on a ring changes nothing
Which values come from Vtx, and which from edges
body:
The node never asks you where the intersections go. It counts connections, and the count decides. Knowing that rule is the difference between fighting the decomposition and steering it.

## Two shapes, and the cluster decides both

*Every component the node emits is either a road or a polygon.*

A **road** is a `UZoneShapeComponent` of spline type, built from a run of cluster edges. A **polygon** is a `UZoneShapeComponent` of polygon type, sitting on exactly one Vtx. There is no third kind.

A road is not an edge. One road usually spans many edges, and the per-road values it resolves are votes taken across all of them. A polygon is not a point either: it is a ring of connection points around a Vtx, one for each road arriving there.

## What a Vtx becomes

*Count its connections.*

| Connections | Called | Becomes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Leaf | Nothing. It is where a road stops. |
| 2 | Binary | Nothing. It is absorbed into the road passing through it. |
| 3 or more | Branching | A polygon. |

Roads are built between those decisions. The node walks the cluster into **chains**: a chain starts at a leaf or a branching Vtx, runs through every binary Vtx it meets, and stops at the next leaf or branching Vtx. One chain becomes one road, and the binary Vtx along it become that road's interior shape points.

So a Vtx either carries a polygon or becomes a point on a road, and never both.


> Figure: The same eight-vertex cluster shown twice. On the left it is connectivity: four leaves, two binary vertices and two branching vertices with their edges. On the right the two branching vertices carry polygon shapes, the runs between them are roads, the binary vertices sit dimmed as interior points on a road, and each leaf is a road end with no shape of its own.
> Two branching Vtx, two polygons. Everything between them is one road.


## Forcing a polygon

*A filter on **Break Conditions** promotes a binary Vtx to a chain end.*

Wire any PCGEx filter that tests a Vtx into the **Break Conditions** pin. Every Vtx that passes becomes a chain end, so the chain running through it splits in two and the Vtx gets a polygon. The usual approach is to flag the vertices you want upstream with a boolean or numeric attribute, then compare against it here.

The pin is optional. With nothing wired, no Vtx is flagged and the connection count decides alone.

Forcing a break buys three things a continuous road has no equivalent of. Lanes cross the new polygon by its `Polygon Routing Type` rather than following one spline, so the turn is routed rather than curved. Each of the two new connection points carries its own `Inner Turn Radius`, `Roll` and connection restrictions. And because each of the two shorter roads now takes its own majority vote, a break is where a lane profile can change along what used to be one road.


> Figure: One road through a gentle bend, shown twice at the same coordinates. Unflagged, the bend vertex is an ordinary interior shape point on a single road. Flagged, it carries a polygon with two connection points, the roads either side stop at the polygon boundary, and the span between them is struck as lost.
> Same geometry, same Vtx position. Flagging it costs the road the span the new polygon now covers.



> **Warning.**
> **A forced polygon eats road on both sides**
>
> The new polygon trims the two roads either side of it back to its boundary, exactly as any other polygon does. On a densely sampled chain with the default `Polygon Radius` of 100, the stub between two nearby breakpoints can end up entirely inside them and be dropped. Lower the radius, or space the flagged vertices further apart.



> **Note.**
> Flagging a leaf or a branching Vtx changes nothing. A leaf is already where a road stops and never carries a polygon; a branching Vtx already has one.


## Closed loops

*A ring that never reaches a branching Vtx has no junction, so it gets no polygon.*

Two shapes come out of a closed chain, and which one you get depends on what the chain closes onto.

A **roaming loop** is a ring whose chain ends are both binary. It is emitted as a single road that closes on itself, with no polygon anywhere on it. A ring of points fed straight into the node is this case.

A **self-connecting loop** is a chain that leaves a branching Vtx and returns to it. Both ends of the one road attach to that single polygon, which then carries two connection points for the same road.


> **Warning.**
> **One breakpoint on a ring changes nothing**
>
> Flagging a single Vtx on a ring does not split it. The chain walk tests the flag on each Vtx it steps into and never on the one it started from, so a ring seeded at its only flagged Vtx walks the whole way round and closes anyway, staying a roaming loop with no polygon.
>
> Two flagged vertices do split it: walking from the first, the second is reached as an ordinary step, the chain ends there, and both become polygons. **A ring needs at least two breakpoints before any polygon appears on it.**


## Which values come from Vtx, and which from edges

*A polygon is one Vtx; a road is many edges. Each reads from the one it is made of.*

The split in the details panel follows the decomposition rather than convenience. A polygon sits on a single Vtx, so everything about the polygon itself reads from Vtx: its radius, its routing type, its shape point type, its intersection tags.

A road spans many edges and, more to the point, a branching Vtx is shared by every road meeting it. There is nowhere on that Vtx to write four different lane profiles. So everything belonging to a road reads from edges: the lane profile, the flip decision, and the inner turn radius, roll and connection restrictions the road hands to each polygon it touches.

Road shape point type and manual tangent length are the exceptions, and for the same reason inverted: they describe individual points along a road, and those points are Vtx.

Values read per-edge are resolved to one value per road before anything is built, either by a majority vote across the road's edges or by reading its first and last edge. For the full list of what can be driven from an attribute, with the source and type of each, see [Attribute Overrides](concept:working-with-zonegraph/attribute-overrides).

## Related

* [Polygon Radius](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-radius)
* [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints)
* [Polygon Merging](concept:working-with-zonegraph/polygon-merging)
* **Cluster to Zone Graph**

title: Tangent Control
description: A road's shape between its points is a bezier, and the tangent length at each point is what decides how tightly it turns.
outline: Why the settings are usually hidden
body:
A road's shape between its points is a bezier, and the tangent length at each point is what decides how tightly it turns. `Tangent Length Mode` chooses where that number comes from.

## The four modes

*One picks nothing, one reads a value, two compute from the neighbors.*

| Mode | Tangent length |
|---|---|
| **Default** | Left alone. ZoneGraph works it out. |
| **Manual** | The `Length` value, constant or read from a per-Vtx attribute. |
| **Auto** | The mean of the distances to the two neighboring points, divided by three. |
| **Catmull-Rom** | The straight distance from the previous point to the next, divided by six. |

`Scale` multiplies whatever the mode produced, in every mode except **Default**.

**Auto** and **Catmull-Rom** do a second thing the table cannot show: they overwrite each point's rotation with the smoothed direction from its previous neighbor to its next, which is what makes a road read as one continuous curve rather than a chain of segments. They also run **after** endpoint trimming, over the road's final positions, so the point trimming inserted at each polygon boundary is included in the calculation rather than bolted on afterwards.

A closed loop wraps its tangents around only when it attaches to no polygon at all. A loop that terminates on polygon arms is an open spline from ZoneGraph's side, and wrapping it would compute a tangent straight across the intersection.

## Why the settings are usually hidden

*ZoneGraph re-derives tangents on every point type except Bezier, so on those the settings would do nothing.*

`Tangent Length Mode` and everything under it appear only when `Road Point Type` is `Bezier`, or when the road point type is being driven by an attribute and could therefore be `Bezier` on some points.

The reason is downstream of this node. When ZoneGraph updates a shape it recomputes rotation and tangent length for every `AutoBezier` and `Sharp` point, discarding whatever was written there. `Bezier` points are the ones it leaves alone, which makes them the only points a tangent setting can actually reach. The default `Road Point Type` is `AutoBezier`, so out of the box the tangents belong to ZoneGraph and these settings stay out of the way.


> **Note.**
> The visibility rule is about the settings, not about the work. A mode set while the settings were visible keeps running if you later change the point type back; its result is overwritten again on the point types that hide it.


## Clamp to Short Neighbor

*Caps a computed length at a third of the shorter of the two neighboring gaps.*

Trimming inserts a point exactly on each polygon boundary, and that point often sits close to its inward neighbor while the next point along the road is far away. **Auto** and **Catmull-Rom** both average across that asymmetry, which produces a tangent longer than the short side can carry, and the curve bulges out of the intersection.

`Clamp Tangent to Short Neighbor` caps each computed length at a third of the shorter neighboring gap, the standard no-overshoot bezier rule. It is available on **Auto** and **Catmull-Rom** only, and it is off by default so existing graphs keep the averaged behavior they were tuned against.

Turn it on when trimmed endpoints balloon. The other lever on the same problem works on the points rather than on the lengths: see [Road Endpoints](concept:working-with-zonegraph/road-endpoints).


> **Note.**
> **Manual** mode handles the inserted crossing point differently: it interpolates a length between the two road points the crossing sits between, rather than taking either one whole.
